The analytical gradient framework is transferable to sensor placement problems across multiple disciplines, and the three-method toolchain offers a graduated accuracy–efficiency trade-off for practical deployment optimization.
bce115d3eb6158a9: Foreshock activity is a key consideration in traffic-light protocol (TLP) to mitigate seismic risk from injection-induced earthquakes (IIEs). However, the seismogenic processes of IIE foreshocks remain poorly understood. Using an enhanced western Canada catalog (2014–2024), we analyzed 77 IIE sequences to statistically delineate foreshock patterns before local magnitude ( M L ) ≥ 3 mainshocks. We found that 92% are preceded by foreshocks and that foreshock productivity and spatiotemporal patterns reflect the interplay among fluid injection, the seismogenic index, and the fault stress state. Sequence-specific analyses elucidate three nucleation models: fluid-driven preslip with weakened source asperity, fluid-driven preslip with intact source asperity, and fluid-driven cascade, highlighting the central role of fluids in enabling aseismic slip and interevent stress transfer before mainshock rupture. These results imply that IIE monitoring strategies should be spatially conditioned according to foreshock productivity.
5dd8985fc03bde9c: Geodynamic activity in the western Ohře (Eger) Rift area, Bohemian Massif, comprises seismic swarms, CO2 emanations, and Cenozoic volcanic activity, with relationships between individual phenomena remaining debated and largely unknown. Above that, seismic studies and petrological observations of mantle xenoliths in the area suggest a possibility of (sub)recent magma underplating and ponding at crust/mantle boundary. In this contribution, we integrate new and existing lithospheric thermal models with phase equilibria calculations and CO2 solubility models. By this approach, we determine the release dynamics of CO2 from crystallizing magmatic underplate, to shed light on a possible connection between CO2 emanations and underplating in the area. We show that CO2 flow rates estimated in the western Ohře Rift (order of 100 t/day) may be related to the underplate body, providing it is being actively filled with a new magma (ca. 0.001 km3/year), or the underplate is relatively recently emplaced (ca. <1 My). Long-term activity of CO2 degassing, as evidenced by local travertine occurrences, may thus be of magmatic origin providing it is episodic, in response to fluctuating magma generation or emplacement rates.
d349e85ffd7f6785: Campi Flegrei caldera has experienced increasing rates of uplift over the past 20 years, paired with increased seismicity rates and magnitudes since 2005, becoming even more pronounced after 2018. While magma transport from depth is often invoked to explain deformation patterns, other studies highlight shallow fluid accumulation as the primary driver of deformation. Disentangling these processes is challenging, as no modelling framework currently reproduces both processes while considering geophysical, geochemical and petrological constraints on geometry and material properties. Here, we compare thermo-mechanical and thermo-poro-viscoelastic models to assess the relative contributions of deep magma migration and shallow reservoir pressurization. We first integrate seismic imaging, geodesy, and rock physics constraints into a three-dimensional thermo-mechanical model with viscoelasto-plastic rheologies. The model includes magma influx from 8 km depth feeding a reservoir whose top reaches 4.25 km, together with a weak tuff layer and hydrothermal system. We then model a thermo-poro-viscoelastic inclusion representing a shallow gas-rich reservoir with its top at 2 km depth. Comparison with InSAR and GNSS observations shows that magma migration reproduces the first-order deformation pattern but not its full amplitude and temporal evolution when independent constraints are considered. Gas accumulation and hydrothermal pressurization can instead recover the spatiotemporal deformation history, with some spatial discrepancies after the onset of seismic unrest. This approach provides insights into how much of the deformation history we can reproduce using competitive interpretations, the full interdisciplinary information available, and advanced modelling frameworks. Plain Language Summary Scientists at Campi Flegrei have conflicting opinions about whether deep magma or shallow gas and fluids are producing the ongoing ground deformation, started in the 2000s, and seismicity, which has been steadily rising since 2015. Advances in modelling allow testing these interpretations under a common modelling framework, including all evidence and data the volcano continuously produces. While the effect of magma progressively rising to surface can model part of the ground deformation, shallow gas and fluids are necessary to reproduce the 25-years deformation-history at the caldera, at least until the recent, more intense seismic unrest. These models show that coupling these two mechanisms is key to understanding the volcano, and likely necessary to forecast the next eruption.
aa19466c069ee309: Approximately 90% of global shallow great earthquakes (M≥7) are concentrated along the Circum-Pacific subduction zones and continental collision belts, while ancient cratons exhibit remarkably sparse strong earthquake records. This study proposes a thermal-mechanical coupling framework, based on the spatial correlation between radioactive element distribution, terrestrial heat flow, and seismic activity, to explain the pronounced heterogeneity in the global distribution of great earthquakes. We find a significant negative correlation between crustal heat flow and the density of M≥7 earthquakes (Pearson r = -0.68, p
7407e0a1998b61d4: The coseismic temperature along faults is critical for evaluating earthquake energy budgets and thermally activated dynamic weakening mechanisms. However, coseismic temperatures cannot be measured directly during natural earthquakes and remain difficult to constrain in laboratory experiments, mainly because of technical limitations. Here, we develop a method that integrates infrared thermal imaging with numerical heat-conduction modeling to infer fault-surface temperatures during laboratory earthquakes. The approach explicitly accounts for the finite spatial resolution of the thermocamera, the geometry of the experimental setup, the distribution of heat sources, and the real-to-nominal contact area ratio (Ac/A). We apply this framework to a high-velocity rotary shear experiment on limestone exhibiting pronounced velocity weakening. By fitting time-dependent temperature fields extracted from thermal imagery, we constrain the distribution and magnitude of frictional heat sources along the slipping surface. For realistic real-to-nominal contact area ratios (0.2 We conclude that flash-heating-induced weakening mechanisms were absent in our experiment and that other processes, such as thermal softening or powder lubrication, must have caused the observed weakening. More broadly, our study provides constraints on earthquake energy budgets and the role of thermal processes during seismic slip.
7fb959a7f9b0bdb3: The asthenosphere is a key layer between lithospheric plates and the deep mantle. Traditional models treat it as a passive viscous "conveyor belt" driven by overriding-plate drag. We propose a two-interface driving model based on an equivalent friction framework (μ∝v/H) and an interface-selection principle that selects optimal frictional interfaces. We apply these tools to asthenospheric kinematics. Our analysis predicts a continuous velocity profile: an upper drag layer (~30 km, velocity decreasing from v_L to zero), and a return-flow zone (~150 km) rising from zero to a broad peak of 0.6–0.8v_L before decaying to zero. At the LAB we obtain μ≈0.0067 (effective creep-layer thickness ~366 m); at the mantle-transition-zone top, μ≈0.3‰–0.8‰. Average return-flow velocity reaches ~0.5v_L, consistent with force-balance constraints and rheological inversions. Two key advances are reported. First, depth-dependent shear stress from vertical velocity gradients drives dislocation creep and olivine-lattice rotation, generating predictable 3‑D a‑axis tilting testable by SKS splitting, establishing a macroscopic-to-crystal causal link for LPO fabric. Second, shear-creep thickness is controlled by melt fraction via solid grain size: melt fraction → grain size → deformation thickness → friction. In the fully molten limit this reduces to fluid friction; in the solid limit it yields Byerlee-type friction, unifying fluid, partial-melt, and solid friction within one continuum. The asthenosphere thus behaves as an active layered domain: velocity structure follows interface selection, and return flow is governed by mass conservation.
ef4e61b484d2a59a: The plate tectonic paradigm, while successful in explaining first-order surface features, has accumulated 31 systemic observational contradictions—ranging from deep continental roots and the mechanical feasibility of large-scale plate motion to the episodic nature of orogenesis, complex magnetic anomaly patterns, and the antipodal distribution of continents—that increasingly demand ad‑hoc auxiliary assumptions to maintain internal consistency. This study presents a fundamentally reimagined geodynamic framework in which these contradictions are resolved through a cyclical pulsating Earth model driven by coupled thermoelectric, electrochemical, and thermodynamic feedback mechanisms operating within the Large Low Shear Velocity Provinces (LLSVPs) and their embedded Ultra‑Low Velocity Zones (ULSVPs) at the base of the lower mantle. The proposed physical engine operates as follows: thermal gradients between the iron‑rich LLSVPs and the surrounding silicate mantle generate thermoelectric voltages via the Seebeck effect (S ≈ 0.1–0.5 mV/K), which are augmented by electrochemical potentials arising from perovskite‑to‑post‑perovskite phase transitions and iron redox reactions (Fe2+ ⇌ Fe3+ + e-). These driving voltages produce electric currents that are amplified through three positive feedback loops: (1) Peltier heating at the LLSVP‑mantle boundary, (2) adiabatic compression under volumetric confinement, and (3) Arrhenius‑type increases in electrical conductivity (small polaron hopping, ionic conduction, and partial melt conduction). The resulting self‑sustaining heating and cooling cycles drive periodic radial expansion and contraction of the planet, generating extensional tectonics (seafloor spreading, continental rifting) during heating phases and compressional tectonics (subduction, orogenesis) during cooling phases. Quantitative validation demonstrates that the LLSVP‑ULSVP‑outer core system generates a total magnetic flux of 1.916 × 1025 flux lines—falling precisely at the algorithmic midpoint of the scientifically expected range (4.8 × 1024 to 4.8 × 1025 flux lines)—without requiring parameter tuning beyond established mineral‑physics constraints. Furthermore, the model yields a total radial expansion of 324.4 km over 20 million years; after deducting 11.4% for mechanical work (lithospheric uplift, faulting, deformation resistance and in exhausting the cooling wave in mantle from the previous stage), the net new crustal area corresponds to 287.3 km, exactly matching the observed oceanic crust production documented by Müller et al. (2008). The derived heating cycle duration of 45,000 years (natural range: 37,000–56,000 years) and peak surface velocities of approximately 19 mm/yr provide explicit, testable predictions for geodetic, paleomagnetic, and cosmogenic isotope records, including the interpretation of the Laschamp (~41 ka) and Mono Lake (~33–34 ka) geomagnetic excursions as LLSVP phase‑transition markers. This pulsating framework resolves all 31 tectonic problems cataloged by Pratt (2000) within a unified mechanical and thermodynamic ontology, eliminating the need for ad‑hoc secondary hypotheses. It provides a coherent explanation for the coexistence of extensional and compressional structures within the same tectonic provinces, the episodic nature of mountain building, the presence of continental fragments within ocean basins, the complex geometry of accretionary wedges, and the antipodal distribution of continents. By grounding the driving mechanism in experimentally verified thermoelectric and electrochemical properties of lower mantle minerals—the Seebeck and Peltier effects, redox chemistry, and solid‑state defect physics—the model advances a falsifiable, quantitatively robust alternative to conventional plate tectonics, inviting rigorous testing through continued space‑geodetic monitoring, high‑resolution seismic tomography, and spectral analysis of paleoclimatic and paleomagnetic archives. The Earth, it appears, breathes through cycles of thermal‑electrical pulsation; the tectonic features we observe are the surface expressions of this deep, rhythmic respiration.
ff9bc3ab5033de79: Anti-similar earthquakes, those with nearly identical but flipped waveforms, remain an uncommon observation. We document three locations where these events occur at intermediate depth. The first of these is Colombia, including the well-established source of anti-similar events in the Bucaramanga Nest, and new reports in other intermediate depth seismicity clusters in the Wadati-Benioff zones of Colombia. The second is the Alaska subduction zone, and the third is the Vrancea seismic nest in Romania. These new observations, combined with reports from Japan and Chile, provide mounting evidence that anti-similar earthquake sequences might be a common or characteristic process of intermediate-depth seismicity. Either conjugate faulting promoted by eclogitization induced stresses or sub-parallel faulting can explain their occurrence at these depths. Careful examination of seismicity in other productive intermediate depth seismicity zones might reveal an even more widespread geography for anti-similar earthquakes and place tighter constraints on their underlying mechanism.
ab82ba88276977f2: Large natural earthquakes are typically mediated by frictional pulse-like rupture, which features a finite slipping zone. Recently, a comprehensive two-dimensional theory of frictional slip pulses has been developed. It predicts that pulses are categorically unstable rupture modes, whose evolution is intrinsically slow. Unsteady pulses satisfy an equation of motion expressed in terms of discrete observables, which is inherently related to their steady-state counterparts. The theory also predicts a transition from decaying to slowly growing pulses. Here, we perform extensive lab earthquake experiments to test the theory. The experiments confirm the theoretical predictions for pulse-like lab earthquakes over a range of prestress levels, rupture nucleation conditions and small-scale fault roughness amplitudes. Specifically, the predicted time-dependent dynamics are tested in a plane defined by the evolving pulse size and peak slip rate, along with measurements of the dimensionless growth rate of pulses, demonstrating their intrinsically slow unsteady nature. The predicted transition between decaying and growing pulses is also experimentally demonstrated. These results constitute major progress in understanding a dominant earthquake rupture mode.
70c356a488907987: Three-dimensional probabilistic inversion of time-domain airborne electromagnetic (AEM) data is limited by the cost of the forward solve. Even though one simulation takes only tens of seconds, a Bayesian inversion of a survey of millions of soundings requires of order $10^{10}$ forward evaluations. To address this, we develop a continually learning neural-operator surrogate of the three-dimensional AEM forward operator that replaces the solver inside the Bayesian inversion. We start from the point of view that regardless of what geological prior is specified, Maxwell's laws remain invariant. Secondly, we avoid the limitation of learning on a single prior by continual learning on consecutive priors, which means our surrogate becomes richer as it is applied in future case studies, either by the authors, or by the scientific community. We use a validity check built on ensemble disagreement to divert cases with measurements outside the training range to the solver. Driven by the surrogate, the identical Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler reproduces the full-solver posterior, and its credible intervals cover the truth within 2.6 percentage points. Applied to the 2013 Capricorn TEMPEST survey in Western Australia, the surrogate inverts over two million soundings in seconds, a computation infeasible for the solver. Testing the geological prior against the entire survey costs minutes. The framework delivers uncertainty-quantified conductivity imaging at survey scale, which we believe is essential to perform near real-time mineral-systems targeting with geophysics.
017fa1b1275538ae: We propose GeoFormer, a Geometry-Aware Transformer architecture specifically designed for prestack seismic data. Unlike Vision Transformer, whose tokens are extracted from 2D patches and primarily encode visual patterns, GeoFormer is designed for prestack seismic data by explicitly incorporating acquisition geometry. Each seismic trace is represented by a 5D unit consisting of the waveform and four source-receiver coordinates, from which two geometric attributes are derived: offset and relative elevation, where relative elevation is the receiver elevation minus the source elevation. GeoFormer therefore performs trace-level tokenization, where each token combines the waveform with these geometric attributes. To exploit these geometric attributes, GeoFormer introduces three geometry injection mechanisms operating at different levels of the Transformer pipeline. At the token level, GeomMLP replaces the classification token with a per-trace geometric representation derived from offset and elevation. At the normalization level, GeomAdaLN replaces uniform layer normalization with geometry-conditioned feature modulation. At the attention level, GeomAttnBias injects a parameter-free physical prior that geometrically proximate traces should attend more to each other. We validate GeoFormer on first-arrival picking, a representative seismic processing task that relies heavily on acquisition geometry. Experiments on four field datasets demonstrate that GeoFormer outperforms Vision Transformer and two task-specific baselines. Crucially, GeoFormer maintains robust picking accuracy under strong noise because its trace-level tokens encode geometric attributes that provide a physical prior independent of waveform quality. Ablation studies confirm that GeomMLP, GeomAdaLN, and GeomAttnBias each contribute to GeoFormer's picking accuracy.
8a0703cf0ea999ca: We develop a nonergodic ground-motion model (GMM) for southern California by training a graph neural network (GNN) on approximately 400,000 simulated earthquakes from CyberShake. Our analysis focuses on long-period responses at rupture distances of 200 km or less. Each rupture is modeled as a graph, with nodes representing CyberShake sites connected to their closest neighbors. The resulting nonergodic, or region-specific, GMM includes site conditions, source properties, and path properties, as well as absolute source and site locations (via latitude and longitude), relative source-to-site distances, and intersite distances. The GNN model predictions are residuals relative to an ergodic GMM. Using the graph structure, the GNN learns spatially correlated residual patterns, such as source-to-site and local site interactions. Consequently, the GNN captures site-specific and spatially varying features, such as basin amplification and azimuthal variations of ground motion with respect to the fault, features that are often missed by traditional ergodic GMMs. In addition, the GNN model maintains magnitude scaling and period-dependent trends that are consistent with empirical relations across sources in southern California. We select the 2019 Mw 7.1 Ridgecrest earthquake as a case study to evaluate the performance of the GNN. By leveraging the spatial and physical characteristics of CyberShake simulations, the GNN achieves lower mean residuals than ergodic GMMs at T = 5.0 s and shows comparable performance at other periods. GNN-based nonergodic GMMs offer a promising framework for ground-motion modeling and hazard analysis.
32adcbeb5bb5ee33: Identifying diagnostic signatures of coseismic slip in the geological record is essential for constraining fault rheology and earthquake dynamics, yet unambiguous geological markers of past seismic ruptures are still scarce. Among seismic slip indicators, solidified frictional melt is widely regarded as the most reliable; however, its restrictive formation conditions and poor preservation limit the geological record of seismic rupture. Here, we investigated fluidized fault gouge injections into host cataclasites preserved in the clay-rich fault zones of the Altyn Tagh fault (northern Tibetan Plateau) and Carboneras fault (southeast Spain), two structurally distinct strike-slip systems showing similar injection geometries and microstructures. The injections display elongate tips with pinch-out terminations and internal undulated foliation surfaces with irregular, lobate geometries, indicating flow within relatively more viscous, quartz-rich host cataclasites. The injected material embeds clasts derived from the host rock, and fractal dimensions of the clast size distribution exceeding 3 are consistent with extreme comminution comparable to that documented in faults accommodating coseismic slip. We interpret gouge fluidization and injection as resulting from transient fluid overpressure, a process that may play a key role in dynamic fault weakening. Therefore, such injections may represent reliable geological indicators of past earthquakes and provide constraints on rupture dynamics in structurally and rheologically complex fault zones.
ae0809e43d9c3508: We present an analytical framework for ionospheric ion velocity and density perturbations driven by acoustic-gravity waves generated by seismic sources. Neutral motions are computed using a horizontally layered model, and ion responses are obtained from the linearized frequency-domain momentum and continuity equations, including neutral-ion collisions and geomagnetic effects. Simulations show that ion motion undergoes an altitude-dependent transition from a collision-dominated regime to a magnetically controlled regime, producing strong anisotropy. We further show that total electron content (TEC) disturbances are strongly controlled by the geometry between the Line-of-Sight and the wavefront. A case study of the 2025 Kamchatka earthquake demonstrates that the modeled TEC perturbations reproduce key observational features, including Rayleigh-wave and gravity-wave arrivals. These results provide new insights into seismic-ionospheric coupling and support analytical modeling of coseismic TEC responses.
4924fdd6443cd0a5: Waveform inversion seeks to estimate the wave speed of a heterogeneous, inaccessible medium, from time-resolved measurements of the waves at user controlled sensors. We consider this inverse problem for acoustic waves and an active array of source/receiver sensors that emit probing signals and measure the generated pressure waves. The forward map, from the wave speed to the measurements, is nonlinear and oscillatory. The oscillations cause cycle skipping, the main impediment to using the standard, nonlinear least-squares data fitting formulation, known as full waveform inversion (FWI). A recently introduced alternative waveform inversion approach computes from the measurements an algebraic surrogate of the wave operator, a reduced order model (ROM) matrix, which is then used to estimate the wave speed. The mapping from the measurements to the ROM is nonlinear, but well understood. It is computed efficiently, in a non-iterative manner. The nonlinear mapping from the ROM to the wave speed is less understood, and its approximation involves time-consuming optimization. Our goal in this paper is to use a neural network to map the ROM matrix to a nearby one, that has a simpler and explicit dependence on the wave speed. This simplifies and reduces the computational cost of the ROM-based waveform inversion. We introduce the methodology, called ROMNet, and test it with numerical simulations, using two training data sets: The first set consists of random media with variations of the wave speed modeled by a superposition of Gaussians with random amplitudes and standard deviations. The second is the publicly available GeoFWI dataset introduced for benchmarking FWI using deep learning. We compare the performance of ROMNet with the direct ROM-based inversion and with two representative deep learning approaches to FWI: ``Fourier-DeepONet" and ``InversionNet".
5a7de53fbbb278ad: Physics-based probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA), in which 3D numerical simulations replace traditional ground-motion models, has been under development for several decades. The development of high-performance computing capabilities and techniques has enabled significant advancements, such as the inclusion of complex near-fault source and path effects, which allow the extrapolation of ground motion to that of rare events at close distances; however, a gap remains between research and practice. This article compares and contrasts traditional PSHA with current physics-based PSHA and shows that method aleatory variability, which is apparent aleatory variability due to simplifications in the simulation method, is missing from current physics-based PSHA calculations. We highlight the need for proper separation and quantification of apparent aleatory variability and epistemic uncertainty, as well as validation of the distribution of the simulated ground motions for a given scenario. We discuss how the standard deviation of the misfits from simulation validations often includes both method aleatory variability and parametric epistemic uncertainty in the median, which is from scientific uncertainty in simulation inputs that are not part of the traditional hazard calculation as part of the source model. The limitations of the simulation method are often difficult to estimate directly from the validation because it is challenging to separate its effects from those of incorrect inputs. We provide an overview of simulation simplifications that lead to method aleatory variability, methods of incorporating method aleatory variability, and a list of recommendations for advancing physics-based PSHA from research to practice.
da0ff485ec997b8b: The International Federation of Digital Seismograph Networks has established the fdsnws-station application programming interface (API) standard for read-only access to seismic station metadata, provided primarily in an extensible markup language (XML) format called StationXML. Here, we present an extension of the standard API that introduces controlled operations for interacting with the underlying metadata repository. The proposed interface is designed to support direct handling of StationXML documents within distributed service-oriented infrastructures. We implemented the extended API using a framework that provides a native XML database management system and an embedded application platform. This approach offers a design advantage because the schema-less database allows ingestion of metadata from heterogeneous sources while preserving the XML structure. The software implementation, exist-fdsn-station, is containerized and can be integrated as a reusable component within larger infrastructures. Performance tests show that the system scales predictably with the size of the returned data and can support large aggregated metadata collections. The software is currently used in operational environments at the Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia (INGV) data center, including the public fdsnws-station endpoint.
60f513a741f1dddf: Receiver function data from 50 closely spaced seismic stations of the Kachchh array network, along with data from 17 nearby permanent stations, were analyzed to determine the 3D crustal structure of the seismic source zone in the Kachchh rift basin, Gujarat. The stations were located within the seismically active source zone of the catastrophic Mw 7.7 Bhuj earthquake (2001) and its surrounding tectonic features, including the Wagad uplift (WU), Samakhiali basin (SB), and Kachchh mainland uplift (KMU). We performed velocity–depth inversions for all sites using a Bayesian inversion technique, which provides estimates of crustal thickness, individual crustal layer thicknesses, corresponding S-wave velocities, and VP/VS ratio. To image the seismogenic layer, we generated common conversion point stacked sections both along and across the study area. Our results reveal a relatively thick crust (∼42 to 45 km) beneath the highly active SB, which is uplifted by ∼5 km toward the north (WU) and south (KMU). We infer the process of underplating for the thick crust beneath this area. In and around the seismically active SB, we identified a sedimentary layer 1.5–2.5 km thick, consistent with previous results from gravity, resistivity, and seismic studies indicating 1–3 km sedimentary thickness. This sedimentary layer is overlying a prominent high-velocity zone around 4.0 km in thickness, which appears consistently throughout the study region and is interpreted as a gneiss–granitic basement. A notable feature of the crustal structure is the presence of an undulating intracrustal low-velocity zone (LVZ) with a thickness of 5–8 km, occurring at depths between ∼18 and 26 km. Despite the existence of this LVZ, seismicity is distributed from the mid-crust to the lower crust, suggesting complex seismotectonic interactions and possible fluid or compositional heterogeneities within the crust beneath the SB and its associated seismicity.
9fd92e3d974fb889: The Kiskatinaw Seismic Monitoring and Mitigation Area (KSMMA) in northeastern British Columbia, Canada, has experienced increasing induced seismicity from hydraulic fracturing and fluid injection, prompting regulatory measures requiring the suspension of industrial operations for earthquakes of local magnitude (ML) 3.0 or greater. Accurate magnitude estimation is therefore critical, yet a widely used regional ML scale may misestimate shallow, near-source events typical of KSMMA. To address this limitation, we developed a KSMMA-calibrated ML scale using continuous seismic records during 2020 from 15 stations of the Earth-System Observing Network–Réseau d’Observation du Système terrestrE (EON-ROSE) dense array and eight stations of the Geological Survey of Canada (GSC)–British Columbia Oil and Gas Commission (BCOGC; now BC Energy Regulator, BCER) Induced Seismicity Study network. Event information from an existing catalog was used to supplement the dataset, but waveforms were reprocessed and Wood–Anderson amplitudes were remeasured uniformly. Earthquakes were detected using the phase-picking, association, location, and matched-filter (PALM) algorithm, which combines the ratio of short-term to long-term average, kurtosis, association, and matched-filter methods. Hypocenters were located with both absolute (HYPOINVERSE-2000) and relative (hypoDD) methods. The ML was developed following Richter’s definition, with distance corrections referenced to 17 km. Station corrections and attenuation coefficients were derived through generalized linear inversion. Amplitudes were measured on vertical-component Wood–Anderson simulated seismograms using a 1 Hz high-pass filter. The final dataset consisted of 4043 earthquakes, with ML values ranging from −0.53 to 3.04. Compared with previously used scales, the new calibration systematically yielded magnitudes approximately 0.3 units lower on average. Application of a KSMMA-specific ML scale, together with station corrections, yielded more consistent network-wide ML estimates and reduced scatter in event–station magnitude residuals. This regionally tailored ML scale improves characterization of induced seismicity in the KSMMA and supports more reliable seismic hazard assessment and risk management.
bf82e0b0044552c2: Summary The statistics of earthquake populations are governed by stress changes and event interactions at various scales which promote non-linear event cascades and seismicity clustering. Earthquake clustering in space and time is observed in both tectonic and volcanically dominated regions; however, notable differences exist for instance during eruptive sequences. Here, we characterize seismicity statistics in California and Hawaii and quantify differences in background rates and clustering. We compare three statistical approaches, i.e, i) Reasenberg declustering, ii) Gamma distribution fit, and iii) Nearest Neighbor Clustering which are applied to seismicity in Hawaii, southern California, and ETAS catalogs with known clustering characteristics. Tests with ETAS-catalogs suggest that background rate variations are more consistently resolvable using the Nearest Neighbor and Gamma distribution algorithm without requiring parameter adjustments to the specific study area. The Nearest Neighbor method tends to overestimate background rates, whereas the Gamma distribution algorithm shows systematic underestimation, suggesting that an ensemble model can improve the performance over any single method. Uncertainties in background rate estimates based on small magnitude events (e.g., M≥2.5) are high, in particular for the Reasenberg method, which overpredicts true rates by up to a factor of 4, and extrapolations to larger magnitudes need to be treated cautiously. Our analysis shows that the combination of the three approaches generates new insights into the processes that govern seismicity clustering. The analysis of southern California seismicity produces consistent results between the different methods, and the distribution of background seismicity rates is indistinguishable from Poissonian rates at magnitudes above 3.5. Conversely, the seismicity in Hawaii exhibits notable non-Poissonian background rate changes. Results from the Nearest Neighbor clustering analysis suggest notable differences between tectonic and volcano seismicity, including background rate changes and more pronounced spatiotemporal clustering around active volcanoes. Hawaiian seismicity is characterized by more localized spatial-temporal clustering, in particular during the 2018 eruption. This difference may be a result of magmatic, hydrothermal and eruptive processes, which make volcanic areas susceptible to stress perturbations and earthquake triggering at small scales.
0e0965ee5a9fdc5b: Magma generation and transport governs planetary evolution. Although oxygen is the most abundant anion in Earth’s silicate interior, its role in magma is conventionally ignored, with magma oxygen contents assumed to be simply fixed by cation stoichiometry. Here we show, using high-pressure and high-temperature experiments supported by molecular dynamics simulations, that silicate magma can incorporate substantially more oxygen than permitted by traditional valence-state constraints. Excess oxygen acts as a previously unrecognized volatile component, increasing in concentration from near zero at 1 atmosphere to >∼5 wt.% above 5 GPa, more than five times the maximum oxygen increase attainable in Earth’s solid mantle through iron redox changes. As oxygen-rich magmas ascend and decompress, their capacity to retain excess oxygen decreases, driving the release of O2. This behaviour provides a direct mechanism with the potential to link mantle melting to oxidation of Earth’s shallow interior and atmosphere, and identifies magma as a dynamic reservoir in planetary oxygen cycles.
a16c7d411d7a3016: Regional tectonic loading on a connected fault system can often be treated, to first order, as a slowly varying background process. Here we test the feasibility of representing several distinct earthquakes on the same fault system as ordered source units of one complex composite event. The method compresses inter-event origin-time separations but does not time-warp the waveform samples within each event. For the proportional mapping, C1, C2, C34 and C5 are placed at 0, 6.94, 355.7 and 419 s, superposed and inverted on a common 600 × 200 km plane discretised into 30 × 10 subfaults of 20 × 20 km. Under the proportional temporal mapping, the direct C12345 composite inversion is compared with the time-shifted sum of the separately inverted C1, C2, C34 and C5 source models, yielding a source-time-function correlation of 0.865. A 19-case sensitivity suite gives a median spatial correlation of 0.710, a median source-time-function correlation of 0.965 and a median centroid shift of 7.49 km, indicating that local patch geometry is less stable than the first-order spatial and temporal organisation. A constrained convolutional image model, trained on the 0–700 s slip-image sequence and combined with adjacent-front, depth and increment caps, is then used to examine slip-increase and rupture-growth tendency over 700–1000 s. The resulting zones show partial retrospective proximity to later M ≥ 5.0 earthquakes. The present results support the feasibility of a unified time-compressed multi-event representation.
522f11557fdd6c9c: Axial Seamount, a hotspot volcano on the Juan de Fuca Ridge, has been monitored through three eruptions with vertical geodesy documenting cycles of inflation and deflation. However, vertical motions alone cannot fully discriminate between distributed volumetric inflation and fault-accommodated uplift. We present three years of horizontal acoustic ranging observations (2022-2025) across Axial caldera from seafloor transponders defining 1.8-, 1.6-, and 3.3-km baselines spanning the western and eastern sides of the caldera and its full width. We observe 30 cm of extension across the caldera that is asymmetric with 24 cm of extension on the eastern baseline. Modeling of horizontal and vertical geodetic observation demonstrates that the observed deformation is primarily from volumetric inflation rather than fault motion. The data is consistent with a deeper pressure source coincident with a stacked sill complex under the southern caldera and a smaller shallow source under the northeastern caldera where eruptions originate.
c274d2755bdb4217: We present coseismic deformation observations of the 10 August 2026 Mw 7.4 Chocó, Colombia earthquake from two independent L-band and C-band SAR missions: NASA-ISRO's newly operational NISAR and ESA's Sentinel-1. A NISAR ascending interferogram (24-day baseline) was initially degraded by an orbit-ephemeris mismatch between a Forecast Orbit Ephemeris (FOE) Urgent-Response product and a Medium-precision Orbit Ephemeris (MOE) reference scene, reducing mean coherence to 0.060; reprocessing with a MOE-orbit product recovered a usable, though still spatially limited, coseismic signal (mean coherence 0.145, largest phase-connected component covering ~11% of the scene). Sentinel-1 ascending and descending interferograms, processed via ASF's HyP3 on-demand service with 6-day baselines, achieved substantially higher coherence (mean 0.36-0.37, ~50% coverage) and physically plausible line-of-sight displacements of several centimeters. Decomposing the ascending and descending measurements into east-west and vertical components reveals up to ~9 cm of eastward motion and ~11 cm of uplift concentrated on the eastern side of the Cauca-Romeral fault system, spatially consistent with USGS's oblique reverse-left-lateral focal mechanism. A separate attempt to extend NISAR coverage southward, toward a secondary displacement signal near Tuluá, failed an overlap-consistency check against the validated result (mean offset -33 cm, correlation -0.09 to -0.54 depending on correction) and is reported here as a negative result and methodological caution rather than a geophysical finding. We cross-reference our results against an independent Copernicus EMSR916 Pléiades-derived building-damage grading product for Pereira (182 graded buildings) and discuss implications for rapid multi-sensor InSAR response to future events.
eb38ee07e167db38: We invert horizontal 𝑺-wave Fourier acceleration spectra between 0.5 and 25 Hz from 7,452 earthquakes in the 2010 𝑴𝐰 8.8 Maule aftershock sequence to estimate source, path, and site terms in south-central Chile using a nonparametric generalized inversion technique. The dataset contains 101,566 event-station records from 2,257 crustal and 5,195 slab-related earthquakes recorded by 114 stations during the first 10 months after the mainshock. To account for propagation heterogeneity, we perform separate inversions for spatially coherent event clusters within both seismotectonic regimes, assign cluster-specific shear-wave velocity from a 3D velocity model, and use 100 randomized clustering iterations to evaluate the variance of the recovered terms. We find that relative site responses remain stable between inversion strategies. At some stations, relative amplification approaches a factor of 10 at 2–3 Hz. Effective attenuation varies markedly across the rupture area, with 𝑸𝟎 values of approximately 30–160 and frequency exponents of 0.4–1.5. Crustal clusters generally have lower 𝑸𝟎 and stronger frequency dependence than slab-related clusters. We fit the recovered source spectra with an 𝝎𝟐 model. Stress-drop distributions overlap between crustal and slab-related earthquakes, with median values of 0.95 and 0.78 MPa, respectively. Source scaling is close to self-similar above approximately 𝑴𝐰 3.5, where the weak dependence of stress drop on seismic moment becomes nearly flat. A slab-related seismicity band between 42.5 and 52.5 km depth contains systematically higher stress-drop values, with a median value of 1.75 MPa. These results show that resolving spatially variable propagation is necessary for interpreting source variability. The resulting empirical model provides a basis for regional ground-motion characterization and for tracking postseismic fault evolution across the Maule rupture zone.
5c982fb44fe589e6: The critical bottleneck in earthquake early warning is no longer the precision of data acquisition. Modern high-sensitivity seismic sensors can already detect ground displacements at the nanometer scale. The real challenge is to distinguish pre-seismic precursor signals from the massive background of ambient noise. This paper proposes a signal-identification model based on two independent criteria using P-waves and S-waves. The first criterion is the arrival-time difference between P- and S-waves. This determines the distance from the source to the receiver. The second criterion is the energy-attenuation ratio between P- and S-waves. Because P-waves and S-waves attenuate at different rates as they propagate through rock, this ratio provides a physical signature that distinguishes seismic waves from non-seismic sources such as explosions, heavy traffic, and industrial machinery. Only when both criteria are satisfied does the system confirm that the incoming signal originates from an earthquake precursor. This model directly addresses three persistent obstacles in earthquake early warning. First, it enables the extraction of micro-fracture signals from ambient noise, potentially extending the warning window from the conventional tens of seconds before the main shock to hours or even days in advance. Second, the dual-criteria verification substantially reduces the false-alarm rate. Third, the system shifts from a passive waiting mode—listening for the main shock P-wave—to an active monitoring mode that continuously searches for precursor patterns.
fe04ece6c53ea1b5: We present a variational--adjoint interpretation of quantum mechanics in which the interaction between forward and adjoint wavefunctions defines a general sensitivity kernel of the system. This Fréchet interaction density quantifies how perturbations in the wavefunction (or system parameters) influence a chosen observable. The familiar Born probability density appears as a special case when the adjoint wavefunction is chosen as the complex conjugate of the forward wavefunction, for which the interaction density becomes real and non-negative. Within this framework, probability is a particular positive-definite form of sensitivity described by the Fréchet interaction density. In general, the variational--adjoint interpretation also produces Fréchet sensitivity kernels associated with other quantum observables, including momentum, energy, and spin. This suggests that the Born probability density belongs to a broader class of Fréchet sensitivity kernels associated with quantum observables. The proposed interpretation also provides a connection with time-symmetric interpretations of quantum mechanics and possible future applications in quantum control and quantum metrology.
040d5a79354a7a77: Coseismic permanent ground displacement is essential for understanding earthquake rupture mechanisms and assessing seismic hazards. However, traditional geodetic methods are often limited by sparse spatiotemporal coverage and high costs. Strong-motion records offer a valuable supplement but are frequently contaminated by baseline offsets. Existing baseline correction methods largely rely on visual inspection and empirical image-based judgments, lacking a clear physical foundation and sufficient robustness. As a result, they are ill-suited for the automated processing of large-scale strong-motion datasets, and the valuable displacement information contained in these records remains underutilized. This study breaks away from conventional approaches by reformulating baseline correction as an inverse problem in robot trajectory planning and proposing a fully automated correction framework based on jerk constraints. The method achieves fully automated processing and effectively handles challenging scenarios such as velocity pulses, complex waveform distortions, and nonideal instrument states. Its strong cross-event adaptability is validated using records from the Chi-Chi, Wenchuan, and Kahramanmaraş earthquakes. By providing a physical interpretation of baseline offsets, this work eliminates the dependence on empirical, image-based adjustments and offers a novel, physically grounded approach for strong-motion signal processing.
847e6e42f6344475: We present three-dimensional (3D) spectral-element simulations of seismic wave propagation in the Swiss Rhône Valley to quantify how realistic Alpine topography affects ground motion across frequency bands. The simulations incorporate a digital elevation model–based free surface topography representation, a 3D crustal velocity model, and geotechnically constrained near-surface layers. The simulations are performed for three local earthquakes (Mw 3.2–4.5) recorded in two different configurations: topographic and flat-surface with basin geometry preserved. Topo/flat spectral ratios reveal a systematic component asymmetry in the topographic response. At mountain sites sampled by a spatially uniform synthetic grid, horizontal motion is deamplified across the dominant low-to-intermediate frequency bands (median 0.80–0.97× at 0.05–0.50 Hz), whereas vertical motion is consistently amplified (1.16–2.32×). The real seismic network with preferential sites confirms the strong vertical amplification, whereas the horizontal regime yields weak deamplification (0.65–1.00×). Basin sites exhibit mixed horizontal response and strong vertical amplification, consistent with coupled topographic scattering and basin-wave interactions as well as excitation of the Rhône basin’s fundamental frequencies. The observed asymmetry is consistent with topography-induced mode conversion and constructive interference associated with Alpine ridge geometry. These results demonstrate that realistic surface topography can fundamentally redistribute seismic energy between motion components and that sparse observational networks may incompletely capture this behavior. Physics-based simulations with realistic relief and spatially unbiased receiver sampling therefore provide a complementary framework for seismic hazard assessment in mountainous terrain.
dd663cb1c53a995b: At volcanoes reawakening after prolonged quiescence, local seismicity commonly increases before eruption. The earthquakes occur as crust extends over a zone of pressurising fluid several kilometres underground. The deformation causes existing faults to slip and new fractures to open. An eruption is most likely when the fractures grow large enough to rupture the crust. Fracture growth coincides with a net decrease in the elastic energy stored in the crust. Here we present a method for following changes in stored energy through a balance between the energy supplied by the pressure source and lost by seismicity. We test the method against unrest sequences at two large calderas, Sierra Negra and Campi Flegrei. The results provide a practical procedure for identifying the onset of fracture growth and, hence, for recognising an increased potential for crustal rupture.
f8902221d0a6222e: Slab tearing and associated asthenospheric upwelling can profoundly affect arc magmatism by heating subducting slabs, yet continuous temporal magmatic records for such slab thermal perturbations remain elusive. Here, we document a magmatic shift in Stromboli volcano, eastern Aeolian arc, where potassium-rich rocks emerged since ~ 13,000 years ago and show isotopic and elemental evidence for high-temperature sediment melting. In contrast, rocks with ages > 13,000 years across the arc record incorporation of bulk sediment without experiencing obvious melting, consistent with a cold subduction setting. These results evidence a transition from cold-slab to hot-slab, linked to a mantle upwelling induced by slab tearing occurred in the early Pleistocene. This tectono-magmatic coupling accounts for the southeastward progression of potassium-rich volcanism across the Italian Peninsula, which coincides with tomographically and topographically inferred slab-tearing propagation. Our results demonstrate rapid (<1-2 million years) magmatic response to sub-slab mantle upwelling and offer critical insights into the drivers of recent volcanism in southeastern Italy, including Mount Vesuvius.
01764b611ba29967: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) is an emerging seismic measurement technique that enables meter-scale sampling of strain along fiber-optic cables. Its applications in seismology have expanded rapidly, including studies of moment tensor estimation in controlled environments such as reservoir monitoring within boreholes. However, its performance in less controlled settings, such as volcanic unrest, remains poorly investigated. Here, we assess the feasibility of moment tensor inversion using DAS measurements during volcanic unrest on the Reykjanes Peninsula, Iceland. The inversion is based on simulated DAS measurements derived from simulated velocity waveforms generated by the MTUQ software. Previously calculated reference moment tensors were used as the basis for the forward modeling and to estimate amplitude coupling factors along the fiber optic cable. Moment tensor inversion is then performed using a Simulated Annealing (SA) approach. The resulting moment tensors exhibit poor waveform fits and complex mechanisms that are inconsistent with the expected tectonic setting of the region. The results indicate that DAS-derived moment tensor inversions do not reliably recover the true moment tensor compared to conventional seismic methods within highly heterogeneous environments. These findings suggest that the heterogeneity of the subsurface and its affects on the DAS measurements should be investigated and accounted for, to increase the reliability of solely DAS-derived moment tensor inversions within volcanic environments.
2ee0a54628e6a840: Global plate motion velocities vary significantly—from ~8.5 cm/a for the Nazca Plate to ~2 cm/a for the Antarctic Plate—a disparity that traditional "slab pull" models have difficulty explaining quantitatively. This paper establishes a unified quantitative model for plate velocities based on the force balance between horizontal thrust—generated by the solid-fluid pressure contrast at the lithosphere-asthenosphere boundary (LAB)—and basal/side frictional resistance, which is proportional to velocity. The model incorporates four core parameters: thrust magnitude (determined by arc magma source depth or maximum plate thickness), force transmission loss (related to plate length and dip angle), trench friction (related to dip angle), and plate-type resistance coefficients (oceanic, mixed, and continental). Systematic calculations for 11 major plates show that the model predicts velocities with an average deviation of <5% for oceanic plates, ~22% for mixed plates, and deviations for complex continental plates attributable to local thrust cancellation or remote force transmission. The central conclusion is that plate velocity is inversely proportional to total resistance, which itself is proportional to velocity—i.e., R ∝ *v*—constituting the physical basis for plate motion stability. The primary driver is the distributed horizontal thrust, with slab pull playing a secondary role (<3% contribution). The model predictions are consistent with the LAB structure-velocity positive correlation observed by Yang et al. (2026), indicating that LAB slope (the rate of lithospheric thickness change from mid-ocean ridge to trench) is an effective geometric indicator of thrust—steeper slopes correspond to greater thrust density per unit area.
38f7df2f05a73b72: Slidequake (cluster_pub.pkl), deformation and environmental data (inp_data_pub.pkl) used in Slumgullion slidequake analysis from Sep 13th 2023 to Oct 8th 2023.
57372919a8972cc2: Slidequake (cluster_pub.pkl), deformation and environmental data (inp_data_pub.pkl) used in Slumgullion slidequake analysis from Sep 13th 2023 to Oct 8th 2023.
a5a1af4097374865: The Bandt-Pompe permutation entropy framework, alongside the complexity-entropy causality plane, has become a standard tool for characterizing the dynamical properties of time series. However, observational noise distorts ordinal pattern probability distributions in ways that can systematically misplace time series within the causality plane, compromising dynamical classification. This effect is particularly relevant for geophysical signals, which are typically poorly and irregularly sampled, and have a low signal-to-noise level. In this work, we characterize the distortions on ordinal pattern statistics using the formalism of majorization. We provide theoretical results and propose corrective strategies that restore discriminability under realistic measurement conditions. To achieve this, we introduce methodology that allows the characterization of noisy dynamical series and further allows the quantification of observational noise without the need of a fitting procedure. Finally, we illustrate our methodology by analyzing paleomagnetic records to determine if the geological evolution of the Earth dipole is better described by a stochastic or chaotic system.
df559c3c7182dc39: This paper presents a scalable Bayesian framework for the inference of modern-day sea-level change and surface mass redistribution. To motivate this approach, we first review and quantify the performance of some standard methods for the analysis of satellite gravity and ocean altimetry observations. We find that these methods substantially underestimate uncertainties and are subject to systematic biases, deficiencies that stem from their incomplete treatment of sea-level physics and from uncertainty estimates based solely on the propagation of observational noise. To address these limitations, our approach combines three advances. First, we use recent developments in adjoint sea-level theory to embed the full physics into the forward and inverse modelling. Second, we formulate the Bayesian inverse problem in an infinite-dimensional setting, thereby avoiding discretisation artefacts and the underestimation of uncertainties inherent in truncated model spaces. Finally, our computational methods render such inversions tractable at full observational resolution while supporting joint model spaces and multiple data types. By employing a matrix-free approach with iterative solvers and randomised low-rank decompositions -- implemented in the linked open-source libraries pygeoinf and pyslfp -- basic calculations are possible on a single laptop, with the most intensive tasks parallelising trivially across available cores. We demonstrate the methodology through a series of synthetic experiments, culminating in a joint inversion of satellite gravity and ocean altimetry data that decomposes regionally averaged sea-level change into steric and manometric components with quantified uncertainties, including the degeneracies that remain.
c2db2d0049122f94: Quantifying the interactions between neighboring projects will be essential as carbon storage operations expand in scale. However, many existing basin-scale studies are deterministic or rely on hypothetical scenarios. In addition, simulations that do not fully account for neighboring projects may suffice for initial permitting. In this study, we develop a unified basin-scale model for the Broom Creek Formation in North Dakota. The model includes a total of five (existing and planned) projects, involving 18~injection wells with a maximum potential injection rate of 30~MTPA. The unified model, constructed by integrating publicly available geological and project data, contains $44\times10^6$ cells and requires over two days to run. To enable faster simulations, we present a multilevel treatment that combines four-level nested local grid refinement, constructed through the solution of a constraint-satisfaction problem, with optimized power averaging for permeability in coarse regions. After demonstrating the accuracy of the coarse model, we use it to assess uncertainty in key quantities of interest (QoIs), including total CO$_2$ injected and plume area after 50~years, across a wide range of geological realizations and model parameters. In addition, we develop a deep learning surrogate model, which is used in global sensitivity analyses to identify dominant contributors to QoI variance. Comparisons between the unified model and standalone project simulations are presented to quantify inter-project interference. This can be substantial in some cases, e.g., for one project, the median total CO$_2$ injected decreases from 271~MT (standalone) to 192~MT (unified model).
4a8baeb4cb3ed184: Ultraslow spreading ridges are a vital part of mid-ocean ridge systems, consisting of both magmatic and amagmatic spreading segments. Hydrothermal vents play a key role in the transfer of matter and heat from the lithosphere to the hydrosphere and biosphere. However, research on the relationship between magmatism, faulting, and hydrothermal circulation beneath vent fields on ultraslow spreading ridges is still limited. Here, we investigate Jøtul vent field, situated on a magmatic segment of Knipovich Ridge. We provide continuous passive seismic data recorded by a network of up to 15 broadband ocean bottom seismometers covering up to 50 km along-axis and the time from July 2023 to August 2024. We present our correction for nonlinear clock drift using ambient noise cross-correlation and sensor orientation from Rayleigh wave polarization analysis. Probabilistic power spectral density plots show a clear double-frequency microseismic noise peak. Noise bands at periods of 0.2-0.4 s are likely related to sediment layers and ocean currents. Vibrations of the radio beacon antenna produce noise at periods of 0.16 s. Despite this ambient seismic noise, transient signals of teleseismic, regional, and local earthquakes, and air-gun signals are clearly visible in the dataset enabling studies of seismicity and seismic structure.
60f8ddc3e002569d: Data-driven methods for earthquake and tsunami early warning rely on large ensembles of rupture scenarios and their resulting waveforms, but generating such datasets with repeated high-fidelity seismic and tsunami simulations is prohibitively expensive. We exploit the linear time-invariant structure of both dynamics to precompute elastic Green's functions and acoustic-gravity adjoint responses, reducing the source-to-waveform map to two consecutive convolution operators. We evaluate these convolutions with a distributed, FFT-accelerated GPU pipeline that partitions the large seafloor grid across GPUs and directly generates the final observation waveforms. We demonstrate the scalability of this pipeline for the Cascadia Subduction Zone with 963 subfaults, 2,416,530 seafloor grid points, 64 observation locations, and 256 timesteps, requiring 9.45 TiB of aggregate GPU memory. On 64 GB200 GPUs within one NVL72 domain, the pipeline generates waveforms in 24 ms per rupture once the response operators are resident, enabling large rupture ensembles to be evaluated within minutes.
225255647d343f1f: Video recordings can reveal how rapidly fault displacement develops at the Earth's surface, but camera motion and recording artifacts can obscure the ground signal. We analyze a secondary copy of security-camera footage that captured surface displacement during the 28 July 2026 Kumamoto earthquake; the native recording was unavailable and could not be recovered. Two independent image-tracking methods were used. Optical flow follows identifiable image features, whereas normalized cross-correlation (NCC) template matching follows fixed image patches by their similarity. Both measured target-region motion relative to spatially separated reference regions while correcting motion shared by the recording. Image displacement was calibrated to the magnitude of the field-measured offset vector: 1.05 m right-lateral and 0.90 m east-side-up, or 1.383 m in total. We characterize the principal rise by the time required for displacement to progress from 20% to 80% of the selected final level. Across prespecified endpoint choices, optical flow gives 0.866-0.901 s and NCC gives 0.910-0.928 s. These durations correspond to average rates of 0.920-0.958 and 0.895-0.912 m/s, respectively. Checks using independently published tracking windows reproduce the displacement scale, although exact timing is more sensitive in spatially restricted tests. The record also shows an early apparent peak and decline followed by renewed apparent horizontal displacement. Because that later motion may represent either continued ground displacement or the geometry of the secondary recording, neither the permanent endpoint nor physical overshoot can be determined. The most robust conclusion is that the central part of the surface displacement developed in approximately 0.9 s at an average rate near 0.9 m/s.
1c706fee534f3827: Even for tension-dominated fracture propagation, porous materials may deform plastically adjacent to the propagating fracture. As is common for porous materials, existing phase-field models typically employ a non-associative flow rule for plasticity, and a Helmholtz free energy based on strain and fluid pressure. This work revisits the hydromechanically coupled formulation of the phase-field model for fracture in poro-elastoplastic media by analyzing the strength surface and fracture driving force. Our analyses show that these common choices of flow rule and free energy will lead to a discontinuous strength surface across the tension-compression transition. A non-associative flow rule introduces a jump at the strength surface, while treating fluid pressure-rather than fluid content-as the independent variable in the Helmholtz free energy omits a coupling term from the phase-field driving force, also breaking continuity. Incorporating an associative Drucker-Prager flow rule and this omitted coupling term ensures a continuous strength surface and the accurate fracture driving force. The proposed model exhibits improved accuracy in hydromechanical responses when compared against the analytical solution of the Kristianovich-Geertsma-de Klerk hydraulic fracturing benchmark. Numerical simulations of hydraulic fracturing and biaxial compression in poro-elastoplastic media show that the model can reproduce both shear-dominated fractures induced by mechanical disturbance and tension-dominated fractures driven by fluid injection in saturated porous media.
1326430d384a5871: Large earthquakes commonly rupture across multiple fault segments and exhibit complex spatiotemporal evolution. The Multiple Centroid Moment Tensor (Multi-CMT) representation models the source as a sequence of independent subevents without prescribing fault geometry or rupture speed. Multi-CMT inversion is, however, nonlinear and ill-posed, and existing approaches either identify subevents sequentially at the cost of ordering biases or treat them jointly through Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling that requires more than 105 forward simulations to resolve only a few subevents. Here we present EKI-MultiCMT, a Multi-CMT inversion framework based on Ensemble Kalman Inversion (EKI), a derivative-free, ensemble-based optimization method that updates all subevent parameters collectively through iterations analogous to Gauss-Newton optimization. We incorporate physical priors through the Tikhonov-regularized formulation and augmented observations, comprising a kernel-density estimate of plausible subevent locations from aftershock catalogs together with cross-correlation similarity and lag-time measurements that constrain waveform shape and timing. A Randomize-then-optimize strategy then yields an ensemble of solutions consistent with the observations, characterizing the solution variability. The framework reduces the number of forward simulations by two to three orders of magnitude relative to MCMC sampling of comparable Multi-CMT problems. We validate EKI-MultiCMT on synthetic cases and apply it to three real earthquakes, including the 2016 M w 7.8 Kaikoura earthquake and 2024 M w 7.5 Noto Peninsula earthquake. The number of subevents is determined by the data using the Bayesian Information Criterion, and the resolved six-subevent model of the Noto Peninsula earthquake reproduces the first-order multi-segment, bilateral, multi-episode rupture identified by independent inversions of the same event. Our results suggest that routine Multi-CMT inversion of complex events is possible and that EKI-MultiCMT provides a flexible framework for incorporating additional geophysical observations and priors within a single iterative inversion.
330403cc5fe71b72: Earthquakes occur on a timescale of seconds and are experienced by humans as sudden, devastating disasters. However, the tectonic systems that determine where they occur are shaped over millions of years. To understand the present-day seismicity, earthquake cycle, and splay faulting in particular, various dynamic deformation mechanisms need to be considered across all timescales. However, numerical models have not been able to achieve this. We present a 2D seismo-thermo-mechanical model with adaptive time-stepping and invariant rate- and state-dependent friction (STM-RSF), which for the first time simulates sequences of fully dynamic ruptures in a self-consistently evolved subduction zone described by a visco-elasto-plastic rheology. Faults form and evolve spontaneously according to heterogeneous, temperature-dependent material parameters and the local stress field during both the initial 3.5 million years of subduction and the subsequent seismic phase. Sequences of large earthquakes are nearly periodic, despite the potential for deviating rupture paths in the subduction channel. Splay faults in the outer wedge need to be sufficiently weak to be activated during a megathrust earthquake, since they cannot accumulate stress over time because velocity-strengthening afterslip relaxes their stresses. Dynamic triggering of a splay fault transfers slip from the megathrust, which alters the long-term deformation compared to a purely geodynamic model. We observe that reflected seismic waves change the slip distribution in a similar manner as has been found using a dynamic rupture model. Our model thus successfully combines aspects of established geodynamic models and dynamic rupture models, providing a missing link between the long-term and the short-term.
fc75928f13c5d33d: Constraining seismogenic fault structures is critical in the densely populated area such as the Seoul metropolitan area of the Korean Peninsula, where historical records document damaging earthquakes. Recent increase in clustered seismicity has highlighted the need for improved characterization of subsurface fault systems, motivating the deployment of dense seismic arrays that enable high-resolution imaging of the crust and upper mantle. In this study, we perform a joint inversion of S-wave travel times and Rayleigh-wave phase and group velocities recorded by the dense seismic arrays to resolve low-velocity anomalies associated with major faults down to 40 km depth. Our results reveal a shallow low-velocity anomaly along the Pocheon Fault and a deeper anomaly along the Wangsukcheon Fault extending into the upper mantle, including previously unrecognized fault extensions. An earthquake swarm in northern Seoul appears to be associated with the southwestward extension of the Pocheon Fault. We also image, for the first time, the Gyeonggang Fault dipping at ~ 60° to the northwest. These findings provide new constraints on subsurface fault geometry and highlight the importance of high-resolution seismic imaging for assessing seismic hazards in intraplate urban setting.
1939b20fbecb7962: Because faults have a finite seismogenic depth, the largest earthquakes grow by developing horizontally-elongated ruptures. This can also be the case for induced seismicity: for instance, on faults intersecting a gas field, ruptures may be confined to depths within or in the vicinity of the reservoir layer. Thus, the development of physics-based approaches for the hazard assessment of natural and induced seismicity should account for elongated ruptures. Existing theory successfully predicts the propagation and arrest of elongated ruptures with fixed width and with uniform fault properties along depth, but these assumptions are too restrictive. Here, we extend the theory to ruptures with unpinned rupture width, with fault stress and strength heterogeneities along both depth and strike, and with non-linear slip-weakening such as arising from thermal pressurisation of fault zone fluids. We validate these theoretical developments through dynamic rupture simulations. With the extended theory, we propose a computationally efficient two-step procedure to predict earthquake rupture sizes, in which rupture widths are first determined by two-dimensional fracture mechanics theory applied on each vertical section, then rupture lengths are constrained by the theoretical equation of motion of elongated ruptures. We compile and calculate averaged parameters from seismologically-inferred slip models of global earthquakes, and identify scaling relations for the fracture energy and the energy release rate. We propose to use this method as an efficient tool for physics-based seismic hazard assessment, applicable to both natural and induced earthquakes. Plain Language Summary Most large earthquakes have rupture lengths that exceed their widths, a geometry referred to as elongated ruptures. Existing theory successfully predicts the propagation and arrest of elongated ruptures with fixed width and with uniform fault properties along depth, but these assumptions are too restrictive. This work extends the theory to elongated ruptures with unpinned rupture widths, non-linear continued slip-weakening, and along-dip stress and strength heterogeneities. We numerically validate the extended theoretical model. Based on the extended theory, we propose a computationally efficient two-step procedure to predict earthquake rupture sizes, in which rupture widths are first –2– determined by two-dimensional fracture mechanics theory applied on each vertical section, then rupture lengths are constrained by the theoretical equation of motion of elongated ruptures. This method can serve as an efficient tool for physics-based seismic hazard assessment, applicable to both natural and induced earthquakes.
ca5dfb5199ef1d45: The Mesozoic breakup of northernmost Pangea led to the formation of the Canada Basin, via the rifting of Arctic Alaska and parts of Siberia from the north-west Canadian margin. Previous work on the region has highlighted two different opening styles, rotational and translational, which are both still debated within the current literature. Furthermore, there has been limited research into the mechanism for such rift initiation. Given that earlier plate tectonic processes can influence continental breakup, the pre-rift architecture of Arctic Pangea may offer insight into rift initiation. Here, we hypothesize that inherited structures from the Paleozoic assemblage of Arctic Pangea and late Proterozoic large igneous provinces may play a fundamental role in subsequent rifting and the opening of the Canada Basin. For the first time, we test this hypothesis using 3D numerical models under two extensional regimes (e.g., rotation and translation), applying four inherited structure scenarios from the pre-breakup conditions of Arctic Pangea. In the context of the latest geological and geophysics interpretations, we find our best fit model to be that of a translational opening in the presence of a relict transform fault (e.g., the Canadian Arctic transform system), though these models do not fully discount rotational kinematics. Our 3D numerical models of continental rifting add to the discussion on Canada Basin opening, emphasizing the importance of geological history and highlighting the fundamental role of relict deformational structures on the tectonic evolution of a region.
a01cd4dd4f13a24e: This study presents a detailed geotechnical characterization of an industrial development site in Ain Sokhna, Egypt, a strategic location within the new industrial zone of the Suez Canal, using integrated P-wave (V p ) and S-wave (V s ) tomography. The seismic velocity models reveal three subsurface layers, starting from unconsolidated wadi sediments at the surface to compacted sandstone bedrock at depth. Compressional wave V p values ranging from 400 m/s in the near surface to 3500 m/s in the deepest layer, while shear wave V s values rise from as low as 130 m/s to approximately 1896 m/s, reflecting a marked enhancement in material stiffness with depth. From these velocity profiles and estimated densities, the dynamic elastic moduli were derived. The shear modulus (G) increases from about 0.069 up to 7.91 GPa, and Young’s modulus (E) from 0.043 to 14.2 GPa, attended by a rise in bulk modulus (K) from the order of 0.01 to 10 GPa with depth. These high moduli values in the bedrock layer indicate a highly stiff, well-consolidated ground. Geotechnical parameters including stress ratio, material index, concentration index, standard penetration resistance (N-value), ultimate bearing capacity, and settlement were also calculated to measure soil and rock competence. The results indicate an increase in bearing capacity and decreasing settlement in deeper layers, consistent with the transition from loose soil to strong bedrock. Notably, the time-averaged V s to 30 m depth (Vs₃₀) is consistently high across the site (800–1100 m/s), leading to a NEHRP Site Classification of B (rock/very stiff soil). This integrated geophysical-geotechnical approach provides a comprehensive assessment of subsurface conditions, yielding critical parameters for seismic hazard evaluation and safe foundation design in the Ain Sokhna region on the coastal side of the Gulf of Suez (GOS).
6114749ec7fafb33: Seismic stratigraphic interpretation of shelf-edge clinothems is essential for revealing tectonic evolution, paleoclimate change, depositional dynamic conditions and hydrocarbon generation and accumulation during basin filling. However, traditional interpretation methods remain labour-intensive, time-consuming and highly subjective. Although AI-based method offer a potential solution for automating this task, its development has been limited by the scarcity of comprehensive and representative benchmark data sets for shelf-edge clinothems. This limitation primarily arises from limited field data availability, the scarcity of reliable geological labels and the structural complexity and strong variability of clinothem-dominated systems. To address this gap, we develop a hybrid benchmark data set through two complementary strategies of field data curation and geological and geophysical forward modelling, ultimately generating 3000 unlabelled field and 4000 labelled synthetic seismic data, respectively. We further evaluate several representative baseline deep learning models on these data sets, and the accurate results demonstrate that the curated data set provides an effective and representative basis for model training, quantitative assessment and practical application. Finally, we have publicly released this hybrid benchmark data set (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20769762) to facilitate the development, validation and assessment of deep learning methods for automated seismic stratigraphic interpretation.
a962ea29e94ba787: Acoustic wave propagation under pressure is inherently nonlinear and often exhibits hysteresis in elastic properties. Understanding this behaviour is important in rock physics and exploration seismology because pressure-dependent elastic responses contain information on evolving rock microstructure. We present a petrophysical model that describes the relationship between acoustic P- and S-wave velocities and effective rock pressure during both loading and unloading phases. Instead of prescribing a single microscopic mechanism, the model introduces an effective extensive state variable that represents the cumulative effect of pressure-induced microstructural evolution. Depending on the dominant physical process, this variable may be associated with compliant pore and microcrack volume, grain-contact evolution, or other pressure-sensitive structural descriptors. The model distinguishes between open and closed microstructural states and describes their stress-dependent evolution through different sensitivities during loading and unloading, thereby reproducing irreversible velocity–pressure behaviour within a unified framework. Model parameters are estimated from laboratory-measured acoustic velocities using linearized joint inversion. The inversion further enables the reconstruction of an acoustically weighted effective descriptor that characterizes the pressure-dependent contribution of compliant microstructural evolution to the observed velocity response. In parallel, we apply the Preisach theory of hysteresis to pressure-dependent acoustic velocities. In this framework, compliant microstructural features are represented by effective hysteretic units (hysteron) characterized by distributed closing and opening pressures. The resulting Preisach model reproduces the measured hysteresis with high accuracy and enables a model-dependent reconstruction of the Preisach density function, which provides an effective, non-unique representation of hysteretic switching contributions across closing and opening pressures.
