01320ff8f8012d28: Earthquake forecasting remains a difficult scientific problem because seismic rupture is controlled by complex interactions among tectonic loading, fault friction, crustal deformation, hydrological forcing, and heterogeneous geological structures. Bangladesh and the adjacent Indo-Burman region are particularly important for developing probabilistic forecasting methods because the region contains active plate-boundary deformation and densely populated urban areas. This study presents a reproducible multi-parameter ensemble framework that combines seismicity, geodetic deformation, and hydrological observations using Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting (GB), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models. Model outputs are integrated using a Bayesian-inspired weighting strategy to generate probabilistic earthquake-risk scores rather than deterministic predictions. The framework uses spatially gridded and temporally aligned observations and evaluates model performance using precision, recall, F1-score, and root-mean-square error (RMSE). Preliminary event-based evaluations supplied for April–August 2026 indicate that the ensemble produced higher precision and recall than the simple Gutenberg–Richter reference formulation in the reported case studies, with a reported RMSE reduction of approximately 18% for one evaluation period. These results are treated as preliminary because the 2026 observation window is short and independent prospective validation remains necessary. The results suggest that multi-source machine learning can provide a useful framework for probabilistic seismic-risk characterization in Bangladesh and the Indo-Burman region. The study does not claim deterministic earthquake prediction, nor does it establish that individual geophysical anomalies uniquely precede earthquakes. Instead, it demonstrates a computational framework for combining heterogeneous observations while explicitly representing uncertainty. Future work should use frozen real-time datasets, prospective testing, calibration, uncertainty quantification, and independent replication before operational forecasting is considered.
6ddfd61b4c0aa916: Keywords: Interseismic deformation; 2D fault modelling; slip rate; earthquake potential; Himalayan tectonics; GPS; InSAR Abstract We present an integrated geodetic and remote-sensing investigation of present-day crustal deformation and fault kinematics in the Nainital region of northwestern India. The analysis combines four years of GPS observations (2013–2017), three years of ALOS PALSAR persistent-scatterer interferometry, GPS-derived strain-rate estimation, and two-dimensional kinematic fault modelling. Twenty-two GPS stations were analysed in the ITRF2014 reference frame, while 11 ascending L-band ALOS PALSAR scenes were processed using a persistent-scatterer approach. The results reveal deformation partitioning across the NNW–SSE-striking Garampani–Kathgodam Fault (G-KF). GPS horizontal velocities range from approximately 31 to 52 mm/yr, while relative vertical velocities reach about 12.8 mm/yr in the ITRF2014 solution and up to approximately 21 mm/yr relative to a local reference station. The PSInSAR results show spatial LOS-velocity gradients of approximately 10–20 mm/yr across major structures. GPS strain analysis indicates dilatational strain rates of approximately 0.2–0.6 microstrain/yr and maximum shear strain of about 1.6 microstrain/yr, with predominantly compressional deformation and local extension near the G-KF. Two-dimensional modelling yields fault slip rates of approximately 1.6–4.8 mm/yr and locking depths of about 2.0–7.2 km for the principal faults. Under the adopted elastic fault model and parameterisation, the MBT and G-KF exhibit the largest model-derived seismic-moment accumulation rates, corresponding approximately to Mw 6 and Mw 5 equivalent earthquake scales, respectively. These values represent model-based hazard indicators rather than deterministic earthquake predictions. The integrated results demonstrate that GPS, InSAR and fault modelling provide mutually informative constraints on contemporary Himalayan deformation and support improved seismic-risk assessment in the Nainital area. 1. Introduction The Himalayan mountain belt formed through the continuing collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates and remains one of the world's most active continental deformation systems [1], [2]. Convergence is accommodated by shortening, underthrusting, distributed crustal deformation and lateral motion along a network of thrust and strike-slip structures [3], [6], [7]. Present-day deformation is expressed through active seismicity, uplift and subsidence, geomorphic instability and measurable geodetic strain [4], [5].
15cc03ddfc8ab691: Repeating earthquakes provide key observational constraints on aseismic slip and fault-zone structure. Here, we identify and characterize a specific subtype, repeated burst (rb) sequences, defined by short, dense clusters of several events that recur after substantially longer quiescent intervals and persist over many years and recurrence cycles. In North Chile, we detect 19 rb-families and analyze three in extensive detail using high-precision relative relocation, waveformsimilarity subclustering, and empirical moment-to-slip scaling. We find that rb-sequences are not compatible with single-asperity repeaters. Instead, they reflect multi-asperity systems where closely spaced patches repeatedly fail in rapid, burst-type succession. Building on prior modeling of interacting asperities, we propose that rb-sequences occur where several velocity-weakening patches are embedded within a creeping, velocity-strengthening fault-zone. Mechanical coupling via postseismic creep and elevated stressing rates enables failure of one patch to promote rapid failure of its neighbors, producing recurrent, strongly synchronized bursts. These observations provide natural examples of earthquake synchronization on small spatial and temporal scales and suggest that analogous behavior may be present, but under-recognized, in other repeating-earthquake datasets. Overall, this work aims to highlight the existence of these event groups and to motivate their potential for improving fault-property inference and for advancing studies of earthquake synchronization.
642fe48104134d2a: The tectonic setting of the Irazú-Turrialba volcanic complex in central Costa Rica is characterised by a diverse tectonic interplay, including oblique subduction of the Cocos Plate beneath the Caribbean Plate and a diffuse region of deformation known as the Central Costa Rica Deformed Belt. The western (inferred) limits of this deformation region consist of the northwest propagation of a tectonic forearc sliver along the strike of the Central America Volcanic Arc. The eastern limit is attributed to the northeast escape of the overriding Panama Microplate. We exploit the recordings of a dedicated seismic network composed of 42 stations, operating from April 2018 to March 2019, to investigate this complex deformation associated with volcanic systems. Our local network improved the magnitude of completeness and allowed us to invert focal mechanisms that revealed the kinematics of tectonic and magmatic structures. We detected and located 967 local earthquakes, and constrained a new, local 1D velocity model for the investigated volcanic region. The relocated seismicity and associated focal mechanisms constrained for major earthquakes point out local crustal deformation, obliquely-orientated from the major regional tectonic blocks. We propose a conceptual geological model suggesting that deformation occurring at each volcano is subject to distinct tectonic regimes. In particular, we suggest that Irazú is sensitive to motion accumulated from the forearc sliver, while Turrialba is affected by the regional subduction.
a03904267bda7365: Irregular Mare Patches (IMPs) represent one of the most enigmatic volcanic features on the Moon, as their unusually young apparent ages are difficult to reconcile with the thermal evolution of the lunar interior. Here, we investigate IMP clusters in the Gruithuisen region on the Moon using integrated geomorphological and compositional analyses. Our results show that these IMPs systematically form clustered depressions with sharp rims, commonly exhibiting a recurring sharp rim–moat–depression structure across multiple spatial scales. This morphological regularity implies that their formation is governed by common physical controls rather than stochastic processes. Compositional variations further reveal systematic offsets between depression centers, surrounding smooth units, and regional basalts, consistent with the exposure of subsurface stratigraphy associated with shallow structural modification. To evaluate this interpretation, we identified a class of small irregular collapse structures within the basaltic lava plateau of the Jingpohu volcanic field in northeastern China that exhibit strong morphological similarities to the Gruithuisen IMPs. Our investigation of the terrestrial analog suggests that similar morphologies can develop from instability of the solidified lava crust driven by subsurface mass evacuation within basaltic plateaus. Collectively, these observations indicate that at least some small-scale Gruithuisen IMPs may preserve the final geomorphic expression of shallow collapse and structural reorganization within post-emplacement mare units rather than primary eruptive activity alone. This interpretation can account for both the morphological consistency and compositional heterogeneity of small IMPs, and provides new constraints on the late-stage evolution and surface modification of lunar mare volcanic units.
f8414bb0b7fae5e5: Accurate source localization is critical for monitoring volcanic tremors, microseismic events and earthquakes. Compared to other source localization algorithms, waveform-based interferometric imaging exhibits superior robustness. It proves particularly effective when confronting weak signal phase signatures, noise interference and inaccurate velocity models. Despite shared methodological commonalities, high-resolution imaging and localization of volcanic tremors prove notably more challenging than other passive seismic tasks. This difficulty primarily arises from sparse monitoring networks, complex wavefield interactions with the subsurface and the indistinct phase signatures inherent in tremor signals. Consequently, waveform-based interferometric imaging tends to suffer from more severe blurring effects (i.e. poorer spatial resolution) when applied to volcanic tremor localization and compared against other application fields. To address these resolution limitations, we propose a maximum likelihood estimation-based iterative peeling interferometric imaging method. This approach synergizes the inherent noise robustness of interferometry with a rigorous iterative framework designed to deblur the source image. By constructing data-driven empirical wavelets and employing an adaptive whitening filter dynamically updated via the Sherman–Morrison formula, the method sequentially strips source responses from the residual wavefield. This adaptive procedure directly counters the energy smearing caused by sparse arrays, effectively suppressing sidelobe interference to achieve a highly focused source resolution. Synthetic tests based on the Katla scenario demonstrate that the proposed method yields significantly higher spatial resolution than existing techniques. Furthermore, it exhibits robust performance even under adverse array geometries, concurrent multisource interference and velocity model inaccuracies. Field application to the 2011 Katla data further validates this by recovering source locations consistent with known ice cauldrons.
5d1eef03018546e9: While well-log data provide direct measurements of subsurface properties essential for building lithofacies models, their sparse distribution and limited availability in exploration areas introduce significant uncertainty. This study presents an approach that integrates seismic data, rock physics, machine learning and geostatistics to construct a regional-scale 3-D lithofacies model in the Jeju Basin, located offshore the southern Korean Peninsula. The proposed workflow comprises three integrated steps: performing simultaneous pre-stack inversion on processed seismic data to derive rock properties, training neural networks for lithofacies prediction and expanding the 2-D predictions into a 3-D lithofacies model using sequential indicator simulation. The prediction networks reproduced the interpretation-derived lithofacies labels with reasonable accuracy for the primary sedimentary classes, as demonstrated by quantitative evaluation metrics. The resulting 3-D lithofacies model captured key geological features indicated by 2-D seismic data, including faults and sedimentary structures, exhibiting improved spatial continuity and detail compared to conventional well-log-only geostatistical simulation. Comparison with a borehole outside the training volume demonstrated reasonable agreement between the predicted and well-log-derived lithofacies. This observation preliminarily implies the workflow’s applicability to field data beyond the 3-D seismic coverage, though this assessment is based on a single well location. This integrated approach offers a cost-effective solution for lithofacies characterization in frontier exploration sites where regional 3-D seismic surveys are economically unfeasible and well control is limited.
920f5cffd7801940: The central United States has experienced a surge in induced seismicity linked to wastewater injection, with Oklahoma as a key study area. While the broader effects of large-scale injection are well documented, the relationship between local injection activities and short-term seismicity fluctuations is less understood. Using deep learning and dense seismic monitoring, we developed an enhanced earthquake catalogue and identified four persistent, low-magnitude (${{M}_\mathrm{ L}} = \ - 0.69\ \rm to\ 2.83)$ seismic clusters within an active saltwater-disposal region. These clusters, several located near mapped faults, exhibit near-daily activity and provide case studies for examining local injection–seismicity dynamics. We find that injection histories for wells within approximately 8–10 km of the clusters generally exhibit stronger temporal correspondence with seismicity than those aggregated over larger spatial scales. Analysis of individual wells further identifies injection histories exhibiting comparatively strong short-term temporal correspondence with observed seismicity, independent of average injection rate or well distance. These relationships are interpreted as statistical associations within a pre-existing regional stress and pore-pressure state rather than evidence of direct hydraulic causality. Compared with higher-moment induced-seismicity cases, the detected clusters exhibit comparable patterns of cumulative seismic moment growth but at predominantly lower magnitudes. These low-moment sequences demonstrate how deep learning-augmented, high-resolution earthquake catalogues can reveal short-term variations in seismic response that are poorly resolved by conventional regional catalogues. Our results suggest that temporal similarity metrics may complement established injection rate and distance criteria by identifying individual wells for further evaluation in induced-seismicity monitoring and mitigation strategies.
636d836a2e46f73c: In August 2024, Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) stations observed changes in the displacement pattern of the Santorini Volcanic Complex, accompanied by microseismic activity, showing a potential sign of unrest. Here, we analyse and discuss surface deformation patterns related to the Santorini caldera unrest, spanning from summer 2024 to January 2025. Synthetic Aperture Radar interferometry was performed exploiting the persistent scatterer interferometry technique. We used both satellite geometries of the Sentinel-1 mission, producing line-of-sight deformation maps and displacement decomposition in vertical and horizontal components. The observed displacements were combined with measurements from seven GNSS stations across the Santorini Volcanic Complex. The results highlight horizontal movements and uplift up to 70 mm yr−1 with a radial inflation pattern centred around the Kameni Islands, reminiscent of the 2011-2012 inflation episode. The geophysical model for the 2024-2025 period suggests a positive volume rate change at 3.15 km depth. Compared to the 2011-2012 unrest, the volume rate change is smaller; potentially a mix of magma and gas may be causing pressure along Kameni’s volcanotectonic line, this time with a shallower source than the previous unrest. We address this particular period as the ‘first phase’ of the 2024-2025 unrest, since subsequent GNSS observations reveal a shift in the deformation, indicating the initialization of a different displacement pattern.
cb5548591987c6c6: Earthquake early warning requires reliable uncertainty estimates from short initial waveforms. We evaluate split conformal prediction (CP) and conformalized quantile regression (CQR) for single-station peak ground acceleration using event-partitioned K-NET records. Each 3 s waveform is normalized by component while retaining amplitude scales measured before normalization. The convolutional neural network (CNN)–Transformer that retains amplitude information is more accurate and yields narrower intervals than the waveform-only ablation. At the nominal 90 per cent level, CQR attains 90.03 per cent coverage; raw quantile regression and split CP are also near nominal, whereas heteroscedastic deep ensemble and MC-dropout baselines are more conservative and wider. Event-cluster bootstrap and repeated event-level resplits support marginal-coverage stability, although performance degrades for rare large earthquakes. Upper-bound screening trades increased recall for more false alarms, so the intervals are an uncertainty-quantification and screening layer rather than a standalone alert system. Under exact exchangeability, conformal prediction supplies finite-sample marginal coverage; record-level exchangeability is not established for this event-clustered sample and event-conditional reliability is not guaranteed.
9c645bbce679ad3a: Studies indicate that the Cascadia Subduction Zone is capable of producing great earthquakes, and, like many other subduction zones, it exhibits along-strike differences in rupture history and plate coupling. Paleoseismic data, locking models, and microseismicity point to a change in seismic behavior around 44.5°N, offshore central Oregon. In this study, we use controlled-source seismic data from four shoreline-crossing experiments to invert for the P-wave velocity structure and Moho interface between 43.6°N and 45.2°N and to investigate changes in seismic structure within the forearc. The model reveals changes in the backstop geometry and an interpreted mafic dike embedded within an accreted terrane. WNW trending low velocity anomalies along the Alvin Canyon Fault suggest the fault cuts through both the accretionary wedge and subducting oceanic plate. At the top of the subducting slab, nine circular high-velocity anomalies are present that we interpret to be seamounts at various stages of subduction. The final Moho interface shows significant changes in depth related to the density of accreted terranes within the overriding plate. We propose that the subducted topography is partially responsible for large slides and scars at the deformation front and that subducting seamounts may have uplifted broad regions along the margin. Evidence for ongoing deformation is provided by seismicity clustered near two of the proposed seamounts. Finally, we suggest that this rough plate interface may lead to lower coupling and/or have acted as a rupture barrier in past megathrust earthquakes.
397567a6e095f348: The Moon's ancient magnetic field provides critical insights into lunar thermal and magnetic evolution, yet the lifetime of the interior dynamo remains debated. Returned samples yield complex and contradictory paleomagnetic records, while orbital data reveal crustal magnetic anomalies of uncertain origin from either a core dynamo or transient impact-generated fields. Here, we jointly invert gravity and magnetic observations in the region around the Dewar swirl, a high-albedo feature associated with the Dewar magnetic anomaly. We identify a shallow, magnetized, high-density body consistent with buried mare basalt. Our estimates require a paleointensity exceeding 11 microtesla, suggesting an active lunar dynamo about 4.2 billion years ago, as constrained by the superposed basin ejecta. The results also show that swirl formation requires horizontal magnetization and iron oxide enrichment. These findings link a magnetic anomaly to its geologic origin and magnetizing field, providing constraints on the lunar magnetic and volcanic history.
07f34cb215baf160: Seismic hazard and structural analyses require broadband ground-motion time histories, yet the high-frequency band (above 1~Hz) is the hardest to obtain: physics-based simulations are too costly at these frequencies, and stochastic methods lose the deterministic phase, directivity, and long-period coherence that control structural demand. We present HighFEM-2, a latent denoising-diffusion waveform model trained with rectified flow matching on a multi-modal diffusion transformer. It synthesizes three-component acceleration up to 50~Hz, conditioned on a low-frequency waveform below the source corner frequency and on magnitude, hypocenter and station location, and $V_{S30}$. The low-frequency waveform supplies the deterministic source, path, and directivity, so the network learns only the regional high-frequency scattering. Conditioning each station on its own waveform lets HighFEM-2 generate records for all stations of an earthquake that share its source and low-frequency path terms. Trained on 195{,}138 Italian INSTANCE records ($M_w$ 1.4--6.5, within 200~km), HighFEM-2 produces realistic waveforms: it reproduces observed peak amplitudes with small bias ($0.042 \pm 0.088$ log units for PGA, $0.057 \pm 0.090$ for PGV) and matches observed envelopes, Fourier spectra, and integrated velocity and displacement. The conditioning waveform can come from a simulation or a filtered record, and ensembles of realizations sample the high-frequency variability given that input. HighFEM-2 thus provides fast, regionally calibrated broadband time histories for hazard and risk assessment, including near-fault scenarios where recordings are scarce.
d3f02ba9104bfd0e: The Eigenray method solves two-point boundary-value ray-tracing problems in heterogeneous anisotropic elastic media using a variational formulation based on the eikonal equation. Here, we extend the method to finite frequencies using the trajectory-mechanics formulation in which finite-frequency effects are represented by a frequency-dependent potential that couples phase and amplitude. We show that finite-frequency propagation can be described within the same variational framework through an equivalent effective medium, preserving the structure of the original method while introducing corrections to trajectories, phase, amplitudes, geometric spreading, wavefront curvature, and caustic behavior. The resulting Eigenwave formulation requires only local modifications of the ray velocity and its derivatives and reduces to classical ray theory in the high-frequency limit. Numerical examples involving multipathing and cusp caustics demonstrate accurate modeling of finite-frequency propagation effects. While ray-based amplitudes become unreliable near caustics, a phase-space (Maslov) treatment successfully reproduces finite-difference wavefield solutions. These results establish Eigenwave theory as a unified framework connecting ray theory and finite-frequency wave propagation in heterogeneous anisotropic media.
56494e8fd94089be: The North Altyn ophiolitic belt was formed by the subduction–closure of the Altyn segment of the Proto–Tethys Ocean and recorded the accretion of Tarim to northern Gondwana, but the timing of initial subduction and detailed tectonic transition processes remain poorly constrained. This study reports the oldest Phanerozoic magmatic record of 537 Ma juvenile I–type granodiorite for the Altyn belt, which was formed under high oxygen fugacity (−14.51 ≤ log f O 2 ≤ −10.96) and water–rich (6.92–9.50 wt%) arc condition. The southward subduction of the North Altyn Ocean thus initiated a priori to about 537 Ma. Coupled I– and S–type granitoids dated at ca. 505–478 Ma, which were generated in subduction ‐ related but relatively reduced and reworked conditions, have also been observed. Moreover, a review of zircon Hf isotopes, crustal thickness, geobarometry and oxygen fugacity of magmas across the belt also argues for the advancing and retreating subduction of the North Altyn Ocean at ca. 537–500 Ma and ca. 500–470 Ma, respectively. The slab rollback event at 500–470 Ma triggered upwelling of reduced low oxygen fugacity mantle materials and also led to crustal thinning, which overlapped well with regional extensional magmatic activities. In addition, renewed increases in these proxies suggest resumed advancing subduction until ocean closure at ca. 450–440 Ma. Thus, magmatic records across the belt suggest a prolonged 100 Ma subduction cycle from initial, advancing and retreating subduction to final closure for the North Altyn Ocean.
ac61364c4ce40847: Understanding mantle flow beneath old oceanic plates is essential for linking present-day plate motions with long-term lithospheric evolution, yet direct constraints remain sparse due to limited offshore observations. Here, we investigate upper-mantle seismic anisotropy beneath the Pacific Triangle, one of the oldest preserved fragments of oceanic lithosphere, using shear-wave splitting measurements from the Oldest-1 broadband ocean-bottom seismometer array. We obtained 128 high-quality measurements using teleseismic XKS and direct S phases as well as ScS phases to characterize upper-mantle anisotropy. Fast polarization directions (FPDs) show pronounced regional variability, with predominantly northwest–southeast to north-northwest–south-southeast orientations in the northwest and east-northeast–west-southwest orientations in the southeast, with a mean delay time of ∼1.5 s, higher than the global average of 1.0 s. These FPD variations cannot be explained solely by absolute plate motion (APM) or paleospreading directions, and instead show systematic spatial correspondence with P-wave velocity anomalies imaged at depths of ∼95 to 305 km. In the northern and western parts of the study region, FPDs exhibit more northward orientations relative to APM predictions. In the central-to-eastern region, FPDs exhibit systematic azimuthal variations around a high-velocity lithospheric domain, suggesting coupling between mantle deformation and a mechanically strong lithosphere. In addition, null measurements are observed near the Magellan Seamount Trail and the paleotriple junction, spatially coincident with low P-wave velocity anomalies. Together, these observations document laterally variable and depth-dependent anisotropy beneath the Pacific Triangle and provide new offshore constraints on upper-mantle deformation beneath the oldest Pacific seafloor.
c68e9ccb8089a3bf: Industrial activities in active foreland fold-and-thrust belts complicate conventional seismic hazard assessment, yet how tectonic deformation and industrial perturbations affect fault stability remains poorly understood. The Hutubi underground gas storage facility, situated within the Hutubi anticline at the deformation front of northern Tian Shan, has experienced a marked increase in seismicity since the start of gas injection and extraction. Here, we integrate seismic-reflection interpretation, growth strata analysis, geomorphic surface survey and optically stimulated luminescence dating, and area-depth-strain analysis to reconstruct the structure and growth history of the Hutubi anticline and quantify its late Quaternary shortening rate. The Hutubi anticline is a detachment fold growing above an 8–9 km-deep detachment. The shortening and uplift rates of the anticline have undergone a marked acceleration, rising from long-term averages of ∼0.06 and ∼0.03 mm yr−1 for the Pliocene–0.4 Ma period to ∼1.1 and ∼1.3 mm yr−1 since ∼0.4 Ma, respectively. This acceleration, consistent with other foreland structures, reflects ongoing basinward propagation of the Tian Shan deformation front in the late Quaternary. Within this tectonic setting, we further modelled the Coulomb stress evolution on secondary faults within the anticline driven by tectonic deformation. Our results indicate that tectonic deformation drives secondary faults to the seismic triggering threshold over a decade, and governs where ruptures nucleate and how they propagate, consistent with relocated earthquake observations in previous studies. Given sustained late Quaternary activity and pronounced injection-extraction perturbations, the potential for moderate-to-strong earthquakes (∼Mw 5.3–7.0) on these faults cannot be ignored in the future. Thus, in active tectonic regions, seismic hazard assessments must incorporate deformation rates to accurately evaluate tectonic deformation and industrial perturbation effects on fault stability.
9d47977d0a208d66: Passing trains act as correlated sources in both space and time, generating powerful waves that illuminate the near-surface below critical infrastructure. We propose an automated workflow for surface wave imaging below railway tracks that uses passing trains as the seismic source, in a context where train signals are far from an ideal isotropic source distribution. We exploit a dense 2-D seismic array situated a few meters from the tracks for 3-D imaging. To accommodate the complex moving source, we retain only correlations that form a limited angle with the moving train. This extends existing methods for a single line of receivers, either parallel or perpendicular to the tracks. We split the data into two cases, where the train is either far from or close to the acquisition setup. When the train is far from the array, sensor pairs mainly parallel to the tracks are important, while sensor pairs perpendicular to the tracks are decisive otherwise. In each case, the signals are time-windowed before computing the cross-correlations. Local dispersion panels are obtained through a Matched Field Processing algorithm. The dispersion curves are computed for various subsets of the array and referred to as patches. Extracting the dispersion curve of the surface wave below many patches results in a 3-D model of the Rayleigh wave phase velocity of the near-surface. Analysing correlations for trains both near and far from the array yields broad-band Rayleigh wave dispersion curves with high-frequency content (above 70 Hz), which is uncommon in passive methods. The velocity model is robust for wavelengths as short as 3 m and sensitive to soils at around 1 m depth, allowing to image what may be a thicker ballast layer formed by previous track settlement issues.
a3466bf45966d38e: Intraplate volcanism in Northeast Asia, located in a distant back‐arc setting, challenges conventional models of mantle convection and volatile cycling. Using receiver function data from over 300 broadband stations, we image the mantle transition zone (MTZ) beneath the Changbaishan/Paektu volcano. Our results show a modest 410‐km depression consistent with melt accumulation caused by slab dehydration and/or a hydrous MTZ, and a depressed 660‐km discontinuity linked to slab stagnation. Notably, lateral variations in the morphology of negative phases above the 410‐km discontinuity may reflect localized variations in upwelling rate and are associated with lateral heterogeneity of the underlying slab and localized uplift of the 660‐km discontinuity, suggesting focused upwelling through a potential slab lens/gap. These observations suggest that MTZ dehydration primarily drives regional intraplate magmatism, with potential lower‐mantle return flow locally enhancing this process, highlighting the critical role of the MTZ in controlling volatile transfer in deep subduction systems.
eff697af70af622f: Despite being one of the most recent major orogenic events, the timing of the Arabia‐Eurasia collision is still debated. Much of the discrepancy arises due to uncertainties over the amount of continental subduction of the Arabian passive margin and the timing of a hard collision of cratonic Arabian lithosphere with Eurasia. Subducted continental lithosphere and underthrusted cratons can be imaged using high resolution seismic tomography, which can be used to improve understanding of the tectonic history of the region. In this study, we perform a full waveform inversion of seismic wave velocity beneath the Turkish‐Iranian plateau, using regional earthquakes, which provide good horizontal and vertical resolution in the upper 500 km of the mantle. We use a normalized cross‐correlation misfit function, which fits both the phase and relative amplitude of multi‐path arrivals, allowing us to extract additional information from complex triplicated waves that provide relatively good coverage of the upper mantle. Our results reveal that 250 km thick Arabian lithosphere extends horizontally beneath Eurasia. When reconstructed back in time, these results indicate that continental underthrusting and collision initiated at ∼22 Ma, which is consistent with accelerated deformation observed at this time in the geological record.
969009db4c66a571: Low‐frequency earthquakes (LFEs) provide key constraints on slow earthquake processes but remain difficult to detect because of their low signal‐to‐noise ratios (SNR) and emergent onsets, particularly in offshore environments where seismic networks are sparse. In this study, we develop a deep learning framework for LFE detection trained on a curated multi‐region data set spanning six tectonic environments. To address uncertainties in arrival timing and improve robustness to noisy waveforms, we employ probabilistic Gaussian labels and incorporate multi‐station waveform inputs within a modified U‐Net architecture. The model demonstrates stable training convergence and consistent detection performance on an independent held out test set containing previously unused events from multiple regions. We apply the trained model to continuous ocean‐bottom seismometer (OBS) data in the Guerrero seismic gap in Mexico. After target‐domain threshold calibration, the workflow recovered 21 events from an existing catalog and identified 25 additional offshore LFE candidates. These detections show temporal clustering and a spatial distribution that differed partly from that of the existing catalog. Our results suggest that deep learning may complement matched‐filter detection in regions where template libraries or offshore observations are limited.
384c95d569934232: The six-month-long Geldingadalir eruption in 2021 was characterised by different episodes of effusion, which changed several times during the eruption. On 2 July 2021, the eruptive crater drained for the first time, followed by several tephra-rich plumes. Several seismic and acoustic signals were also recorded, likely caused by inner crater collapses. These collapses may also have generated the tephra-rich plumes. This collection provides marker files containing the start and end times of the observed tephra-rich plumes and collapses. Additionally, we include a table showing the durations and widths of the collapses. We have provided event files for the eight largest seismic and acoustic events. This collection also contains 2 hours of video footage of early 2 July between 03:00 to 05:00, which is a merged video from two different webcams. The video was provided by mbl.is,a news portal in Iceland. Another video shows a few hours of the erupting volcano alongside a spectrogram of the seismic data.
4ddc4e3586e9e3e7: Accurate earthquake hypocentre determination is essential for a wide range of applications in seismology. Traditionally, researchers estimate hypocentres by inverting seismic body-wave arrival times. The accuracy of such hypocentres depends on the geographical distribution of stations, the accuracy of seismic traveltime models and the precision of the arrival time picks. Past research has sought to validate location accuracy with a set of well-constrained ground-truth locations. We instead use surface deformation determined via Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR), and develop an independent ground-truth set of 42 shallow, Mw 5.5–6.5 (USGS) events using an automated inversion scheme for InSAR-based source parameter estimation. Using this new independent ground-truth data set, we investigate the relative effects of 3-D velocity models, station distribution and pick error on seismic event location. We demonstrate that InSAR source inversions derived via an automated Bayesian processing pipeline can serve as independent ground-truth for validating seismic event locations, with fully represented model error. This data set can be used to test the accuracy of hypocentral locations derived using traveltime corrections from a 3-D velocity model and show that, for our limited data set, there is no improvement on average towards the InSAR-derived ground-truth location. We also show that InSAR-derived locations can be used to test pick accuracy, showing a great improvement towards the InSAR planes with manual picking and proper error handling. Through these demonstrative studies we show the usefulness of the new InSAR catalogue for use in studies requiring a ground-truth location.
192d1826a3a46c6d: This study evaluates the performance of Synthetic Template Matching for seismic event detection in the West Bohemia region (Czechia), comparing it with two established methods: the automated detector-locator PEPiN and Artificial Neural Network. Synthetic Templates are generated using a 1D velocity model and span a grid of five fundamental focal mechanisms (FMs), independent of any prior waveform or FM knowledge. The resulting catalog includes origin time, similarity, magnitude, location, number of detecting templates, and interpreted focal mechanism. In WEBNET data, Synthetic Template Matching with cross-correlation thresholds of 0.4 detected 264 events with completeness magnitude MC=0.1. All the detected seismicity is real and local, its FMs (interpreted within the seismic network) align dominantly with a strike-slip events. Although the method does not outperform PEPiN or Artificial Neural Network in MC, it reliably estimates focal mechanisms and epicentral locations.
83eba65696fc546a: On October 19, 2020, the Mw7.6 Sand Point earthquake occurred near the Shumagin Islands in Alaska. Moment tensor solutions suggest oblique strike-slip faulting, but the earthquake was accompanied by an uncharacteristically large tsunami. Prior models explain this with co-seismic megathrust slip release, or shallow very slow thrust slip in the overriding plate. Here, we analyze the most complete land-based data set available for this earthquake including teleseismic and high-rate GNSS waveforms, static GNSS and InSAR deformation, and relocated aftershock distributions. We test two models: a single strike-slip fault model, and a two-fault model consisting of strike-slip and thrust segments. While both satisfy the observations, neither model reproduces the tsunami well. To locate the tsunami source, we performed a systematic test of thrust-slip models. This suggests that delayed, very long period concentrated aseismic slip on the shallow megathrust caused the tsunami without generating measurable surface displacements. This occurred minutes after the mainshock, at a location with mainshock-induced Coulomb stress increase, suggesting a triggered tsunami earthquake. The partitioning of strike-slip and triggered megathrust slip offers opportunities to better understand tsunami earthquakes, and—if prevalent for megathrust earthquakes—might impact earthquake and tsunami hazards.
6a3f23b893246f25: Mantle‐like helium signatures ( R c / R a up to 2.99) in hot spring gases from tectonic intersection zones in the capital region of China have repeatedly been interpreted as evidence for ongoing mantle‐fluid input. Here, we integrate gas geochemistry, heat‐flow data, geophysical observations, radiogenic 4 He ingrowth calculations, and structural geology to reassess this anomaly. Air‐corrected R c / R a values reach 2.04–2.99 in the intersection zones, well above those of the adjacent tectonic units, whereas their CO 2 is isotopically light ( = −17.1‰ to −10.0‰), is uncorrelated with helium concentrations, and lacks characteristics of active magmatic degassing. The region has relatively low heat flow and reservoir temperatures; although a localized reduced‐velocity zone occurs at ∼50–60 km depth beneath the intersection zones, it cannot be uniquely attributed to present‐day thermal or magmatic activity and is compatible with lithospheric modification inherited from Mesozoic craton destruction. Radiogenic 4 He ingrowth calculations show that relatively U‐ and Th‐poor mafic compositions can retain mantle‐like R c / R a values comparable to observations over representative Early Cretaceous timescales. We therefore propose that mantle‐derived helium introduced during Mesozoic magmatism was subsequently remobilized by Cenozoic tectonic degassing: uplift and denudation lowered pressure and promoted transfer of helium dissolved in ancient pore water into a gas phase, whereas composite strike‐slip‐extensional deformation ruptured helium‐bearing microreservoirs, enhanced permeability, and focused upward migration into the hydrothermal system. These results indicate that mantle‐like helium anomalies in tectonically active nonvolcanic regions may reflect tectonic degassing of ancient crustal reservoirs without requiring substantial present‐day mantle recharge, although a minor low‐flux mantle contribution cannot be excluded.
1284140cb81e9657: Structures crossing active faults are subjected to permanent ground deformation that can impose severe demands on infrastructure. Although probabilistic fault displacement hazard analysis (PFDHA) has advanced considerably, existing principal fault displacement models use aggregate displacement, implicitly assuming that overlapping rupture strands contribute simultaneously to site demand. This assumption is suitable for regional hazard characterization but does not represent finite structural dimensions, where only a subset of ruptures may intersect a structure. This study presents a probabilistic framework that reformulates aggregate principal displacement into a rupture-level representation for infrastructure-specific hazard assessment. Using the Fault Displacement Hazard Initiative (FDHI) database of 75 surface-rupturing earthquakes, principal rupture strands are reconstructed from mapped rupture geometries and displacement observations using event- and segment-based coordinate systems. The framework models three quantities: (1) the number of overlapping principal ruptures, (2) partitioning of aggregate displacement among individual rupture strands while preserving the aggregate displacement budget, and (3) the spatial distribution of rupture strands relative to the primary fault trace. These components are integrated into a generalized PFDHA formulation accounting for earthquake magnitude, style of faulting, rupture curvature, structural footprint, and fault-trace location uncertainty. Benchmark fault-crossing applications demonstrate the framework's ability to estimate the probability that individual rupture strands intersect a structure and the associated displacement demand. The framework provides a physically consistent extension of aggregate-based models and a basis for infrastructure-specific PFDHA that explicitly accounts for rupture geometry and finite crossing dimensions.
7a4b62e48f8dbdf4: Ground roll suppression remains a challenge in land seismic data processing, particularly when strong surface wave energy exhibits significant overlap with effective reflection events in the low frequency band. Conventional approaches, such as frequency-wavenumber (F-K) filtering, Radon transform-based methods, and other spatial filtering techniques, often fail to achieve satisfactory results under such conditions due to limited resolution and poor amplitude preservation. To address this problem, a time-frequency domain ground roll suppression method that integrates the synchrosqueezed wavelet transform (SSWT) with local adaptive subtraction filtering is proposed. First, seismic traces are transformed from the time-space domain into the time-frequency domain using SSWT, which provides a highly concentrated time-frequency representation. Based on the distinct distribution characteristics of ground roll noise and effective reflection signals in the time-frequency domain, a ground roll model is extracted. Subsequently, a local adaptive subtraction filter is applied to adjust the amplitude and phase of the extracted ground roll model, and the corrected model is subtracted from the original seismic data to obtain the final suppressed result. Applications to both synthetic and field seismic data demonstrate that the proposed method effectively attenuates ground roll energy while maximally preserving the amplitude and waveform characteristics of reflection signals. Compared with conventional time-frequency-based ground roll suppression approaches, the proposed method exhibits superior amplitude fidelity and improved noise attenuation performance.
10df138eb6e50f78: Small‐scale subsurface geological discontinuities, such as caves and fractures, can provide storage space for oil and gas. High‐resolution imaging of these small‐scale geological discontinuities is important for the development of oil and gas reservoirs. These small‐scale subsurface discontinuous geological features are manifested as diffracted waves. Diffraction imaging can clearly delineate the spatial distribution of small‐scale structures. However, high‐energy reflections always mask diffractions. An essential prerequisite for diffraction imaging is the removal of strong reflection interference from seismic data. We propose a prestack diffraction separation method based on a Schrödinger equation–based adaptive transform. To extract diffractions from shot gathers, we first apply a normal moveout (NMO) operator to enhance the kinematic differences between diffracted and reflected waves. Subsequently, we apply an adaptive transformation method constructed within a quantum mechanical framework based on the Schrödinger equation. Unlike fixed‐basis transforms, this method employs data‐adaptive wave functions to characterize seismic data, enabling a more effective capture of the amplitude and frequency characteristics of both diffracted and reflected waves in NMO‐corrected shot gathers. Different wave functions, such as those representing the diffracted and reflected components, correspond to distinct components in the data. We reconstructed the reflections using the wave functions corresponding to the reflected components. Through the subtraction of reconstructed reflections from the shot gathers, the diffraction patterns were isolated. The proposed diffraction separation workflow based on the Schrödinger equation–based adaptive transform can effectively extract weak diffractions from seismic data, laying the foundation for subsequent high‐resolution diffraction imaging. Synthetic data tests validated that the method can effectively detect 5‐m karst caves and faults with the same throw. Nankai dataset applications show the capability of the separation workflow to successfully extract fracture‐related diffractions under complex geological conditions, thereby facilitating the detailed characterization of geological features such as fractures.
12f4b190bf59808b: Accurate estimation of anisotropic parameters in vertically transversely isotropic media is essential for reliable velocity modelling and seismic imaging in modern seismic exploration. However, long‐offset seismic data often exhibit pronounced nonhyperbolic moveout, which leads to strong coupling between background velocity and anisotropic parameters and reduces the stability of conventional estimation approaches. To address this issue, we implemented a user‐guided sequential parameter‐estimation workflow within the framework of the classical two‐step parameter‐decoupling strategy. Specifically, a high‐accuracy traveltime operator designed for long‐offset data is employed in place of conventional low‐order or fourth‐order nonhyperbolic moveout approximations and is integrated with a semi‐automatic moveout‐flattening and parameter‐selection procedure. Once the target reflection event, zero‐offset time, offset windows, vertical P‐wave velocity and candidate parameter ranges are specified, an objective‐function‐based grid search is used to select the optimal moveout parameters from the corrected reflection events. The resulting estimates of and are subsequently used to recover the Thomsen anisotropic parameters and . Numerical experiments on undulating layered models and applications to marine field reflection data demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively improves the reliability of anisotropic parameter estimation. The results indicate that the method provides an efficient and robust framework for estimating the anisotropic parameters of vertically transversely isotropic media and can offer reliable initial models for velocity model building and anisotropic seismic imaging under complex geological conditions.
a752281ca54969fa: The timing of the first water ocean formation on Earth is critical for understanding the onset of habitability, but the duration of this process remains poorly constrained. Using a heat-budget model for the early atmosphere-ocean system, this study quantifies the transition from the final solidification of the magma ocean to the establishment of a stable hydrosphere. The results demonstrate that once the mantle transitioned to solid-state convection, a thick primordial steam atmosphere can radiatively cool and condense into a global water ocean within 10,000 years. Sensitivity tests indicate that this rapid condensation timescale is robust across reasonably oxidized volatile scenarios, even when accounting for cloud feedback and alternative mantle rheological trajectories. This finding suggests that a stable hydrosphere emerged almost contemporaneously with the solidification of Earth’s earliest crust, and provides a physical framework for the existence of liquid water by ∼4.4 Ga on the Earth and other terrestrial planets.
b97f9536f0a08de2: The performance of linear and nonlinear vibration absorbers is usually quantified by the percentage of energy transfer and dissipation by the absorber damping content. However, in the case of continuous energy input into the structure like seismic ground motion, the amount of energy transferred into the structure depends on the type of the absorber. The current study introduces a detailed approach for energy analysis based on proposing an alternative mathematical model of the structure which considers absolute coordinates, ground displacement, and ground velocity rather than relative coordinates and ground acceleration. This approach gives a clear insight into the energy content of the structure. Furthermore, the study also investigates the effect of vibration absorbers on the actual energy induced into the structure by ground acceleration and on its stiffness characteristics. Accordingly, the effect of applying a linear tuned mass damper (TMD) or a nonlinear energy sink (NES) on the structural energy content is analyzed. Three historic ground acceleration inputs are employed with a considered 9-story structure to ensure reliable energy analysis. The application of the considered three ground acceleration inputs with structure-TMD and structure-NES system allows more energy transfer from seismic ground energy into the structure. The TMD allows more energy transfer from Kobe earthquake ground acceleration than the NES. However, the NES outperforms the TMD by this action with both El Centro and Northridge earthquake ground accelerations. Consequently, energy-based analysis can be considered as useful supplementary approach for further assessment on how vibration absorbers perform in structures subjected to ground acceleration.
0a98f90fa94848b8: The M w 7.7 Myanmar earthquake on 28 March 2025 ruptured ∼480 km of the Sagaing Fault. Its fault slip distribution remains poorly constrained by three‐dimensional surface displacement data due to sparse GNSS‐coverage near the fault. Satellite‐based synthetic aperture radars capture meters of right‐lateral displacements but isolating vertical crustal movements from these measurements is challenging. We present a new way to map vertical displacements distributed along the fault using ionospheric total electron contents (TEC) variability measured by GNSS stations located >300 km away from the epicenter along the India‐Myanmar border. We identified three distinct peaks in the TEC time‐series. The arrival times and amplitudes of these peaks are used to determine the positions and relative strengths of three acoustic wave sources. These results are compared with slip distribution inferred from seismological observations. The study demonstrates the capability of this innovative‐approach to constrain coseismic uplifts indirectly using ionospheric data at remote GNSS stations.
4a6847c888dcacc2: We investigate the role of the elasticity and density of the forearc mantle wedge corner on the stress distribution in the forearc region of subduction zones, using numerical quasi‐2D lithospheric deformation models for the Cascadia, Nankai, NE Japan, and Costa Rica subduction zones. We incorporate the forearc mantle wedge corner as an elastic domain within the overriding lithosphere with physical properties that reflect reported degrees of serpentinization. In the models, we also incorporate reported values of effective friction coefficient ( μ ) and the downdip extent of frictional coupling (DoC) for the four subduction systems. Our models predict horizontal deviatoric tension in the wedge and the overriding crust in Cascadia and Nankai due to the buoyancy and elasticity of the wedge corner and relatively low DoC and μ . In NE Japan and Costa Rica, the plate coupling force dominates over the effect of the mantle wedge corner, resulting in horizontal deviatoric compression.
b19674f72858f5ff: The nature of mantle sections exhumed at magma‐poor rifted margins remains poorly constrained, largely because direct sampling of mantle in modern passive margins is exceptionally rare. The Iberia–Newfoundland system is unique in providing drilled mantle rocks on both conjugate margins, offering an unprecedented glimpse into mantle heterogeneity across an entire rift system. Here we present new in situ major and trace element data from highly serpentinized peridotites recovered at ODP Hole 1277A (Newfoundland margin). The samples display mylonitic textures and are strongly depleted in clinopyroxene (≤2 vol.%). Despite pervasive serpentinization, relict mantle minerals retain evidence of high melt extraction degrees, as indicated by Al 2 O 3 ‐poor orthopyroxene (2.36–3.19 wt.%) and orthopyroxene trace element systematics. Geochemical modeling of orthopyroxene REE compositions indicates ≥14% melt extraction initiated in the garnet stability field, likely predating the Jurassic rifting. Following depletion, the mantle was locally overprinted by melt‐rock interaction, as highlighted by high and variable spinel Cr#, REE disequilibrium in coexisting pyroxenes, and clinopyroxene with atypical V‐shaped REE profiles (La N /Sm N = 4.3). During Jurassic rifting, the Newfoundland margin mantle section was reactivated and deformed within lithospheric‐scale shear zones, leading to mylonitization and exhumation. The refractory nature of the mantle likely promoted limited melt extraction and retention of these transient melts within the lithosphere, now preserved as spinel‐pyroxene symplectites. Subsequent cooling enabled hydration at ∼500–600°C and ultimately pervasive serpentinization. These results highlight that the pre‐rift evolution of the lithospheric mantle exerts a primary control on the evolution of magma‐poor rifted margins.
1b85d590d6239170: We model olivine crystal preferred orientation (CPO) and shear wave splitting (SWS) in the mantle wedge, using the results of a 3‐D numerical thermomechanical model for the NE Japan subduction zone. The model predicts a quasi‐2‐D trench‐normal (E‐W) mantle wedge flow pattern beneath Tohoku, given the trench‐normal subduction, but a more complex flow pattern beneath Hokkaido due to oblique subduction. The calculations of CPO in the mantle wedge indicate a predominantly E‐W fast axis beneath Tohoku, aligned with the mantle flow, but beneath Hokkaido the fast axis orientation changes laterally and with depth (ranging from approximately N‐S to E‐W) and is generally less aligned with the flow, especially near the base of the mantle wedge. The model calculations for vertical wave propagation yield location‐averaged fast directions consistent with observationally constrained station‐averaged fast directions: E‐W in Tohoku and N‐S in Hokkaido. However, the model significantly overestimates delay times in both study areas. Furthermore, model‐predicted fast directions from individual event‐station pairs cannot explain the variability in the observationally constrained fast directions for the same pairs even when the incidence angle and backazimuth are incorporated into the calculation instead of assuming vertical wave propagation. These discrepancies may reflect the impacts of simplifications in the model calculations and other factors, such as the anisotropy outside of the mantle wedge and data uncertainties.
cd0b5ae80f793dfd: Why splay faults in continental transform fault systems rupture preferentially during strike-slip earthquakes remains an open question. Deciphering the underlying mechanism could enhance the understanding of earthquake physics and seismic hazards. Here, we investigate the 2023 Mw 7.8 Kahramanmaraş earthquake using a simplified 3D elastic–plastic finite-element model to test how fault geometry influences nucleation. Our results show that depth-dependent curvature of the Nurdağı fault (NF; i.e., listric geometry with decreasing dip at depth) leads to nonlinear redistribution of stresses within the East Anatolian fault zone system. This geometry lowers the instability threshold of the splay fault and promotes earlier nucleation compared with planar configurations. When boundary conditions are calibrated to reproduce the average ∼6 m coseismic slip of the 2023 event, the listric case yields slip distributions and hanging-wall subsidence patterns that are more consistent with seismic and geodetic observations than planar models. These findings do not establish that the NF is definitively listric, but they demonstrate that if it has such curvature, nucleation is preferentially promoted on the splay fault, providing a plausible mechanical explanation for the observed rupture initiation.
4479f55222a3a30f: The aquifer system of the northern Mississippi Embayment (NME) supports the water needs of agriculture, industry, and an increasing population in a large region in the central United States. Groundwater usage in Kentucky’s part of the NME, the Jackson Purchase Region (JPR), is experiencing increasing demand, motivating improved monitoring of this currently sparsely monitored resource. Seismic interferometry has successfully monitored groundwater change in areas where long-term recordings of ambient seismic noise are available. However, the JPR, which hosts multiple aquifers from the surface to depths greater than 500 m, is insufficiently instrumented for such monitoring. Thus, we are conducting an approximately four-year interferometric investigation of the JPR using a deployment of 35 densely arranged (∼10 km spacing) seismometers. The array was installed in the winter of 2025–2026, and data collection is ongoing. Here, we present an overview of the project, including the hydrogeological targets, ongoing groundwater and meteorological monitoring in the JPR, and the CLIMBS seismic array. We also present results of our evaluations of cost-effective instruments, as well as initial cross-correlation functions (CCFs) and short-term (two months) velocity-change (dv/v) estimations determined from those CCFs. Our preliminary CCFs demonstrate stable seasonal variations in the coda waves. The preliminary dv/v suggest groundwater level influences seismic velocity variation in the JPR’s unconfined aquifer. In contrast, the relationship between dv/v and groundwater elevation in the confined aquifers is unclear. These observations suggest complex dv/v responses in the project area, and we anticipate identifying the main influencers of dv/v with longer-term array observations. We identified challenges in our initial analyses yet anticipate addressing them and yielding the first high-resolution, regional-scale assessment of groundwater fluctuations within the JPR.
d64bd22e32aec822: The b value of the Gutenberg–Richter law is a fundamental parameter characterizing seismicity, and its temporal variation is often interpreted as reflecting changes in subsurface stress conditions. Sequential estimation of the b value is important for monitoring earthquake and volcanic activity, yet the conventional moving-window-based maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) approach involves an inherent trade-off between temporal stability and adaptability, controlled by a single parameter, the window length. Here, we propose a neural-network-based framework for sequential estimation of time-dependent b values. Because the true b value is never known for real earthquake catalogs, we train the model using synthetic catalogs generated by epidemic-type aftershock sequence simulations, in which realistic temporal clustering is reproduced while the true b value is explicitly prescribed. Our model, based on bidirectional long short-term memory, directly maps a sequence of earthquake magnitudes to the corresponding sequence of b values. The model is trained on piecewise-linear b value variations with instantaneous jumps. For this primary test setting, the proposed model achieves lower root-mean-square errors compared with the moving-window-based MLE. Additional tests with constant and sinusoidally varying b values demonstrate that the model suppresses spurious short-timescale fluctuations while reconstructing reasonably well beyond the training setting. Application to the 2011 Tohoku earthquake sequence confirms a gradual premainshock decrease in b value, consistent with earlier studies, while providing smoother sequential estimates. Although the bidirectional architecture yields retrospective estimates, the framework can be applied in a quasi-real-time manner by updating the analysis as the catalog grows. Comparison with causal estimators further reveals a trade-off between lag and leakage around abrupt changes. The main advantage of the proposed method is a better balance between temporal stability and adaptability without manually specifying a window length.
615cb759c666b824: Full waveform inversion (FWI) has significant potential to reconstruct the subsurface structure at high resolution, but it is a nonlinear and ill-posed problem. Traditional physics-based FWI methods that employ gradient-based optimization algorithms to minimize the discrepancy between observed and synthetic data face several challenges. The aforementioned methods are susceptible to becoming trapped in local minima as a result of cycle-skipping problems and require substantial computational resources, particularly with the increasing size and required resolution of seismic data sets. Nowadays many deep-learning methods are proposed to solve the above challenges. FWI using a generative adversiral network (FWIGAN), a recently proposed unsupervised seismic velocity inversion method based on the Wasserstein generative adversarial network with gradient penalty, has demonstrated certain success in overcoming these challenges. However, FWIGAN enforces the Lipschitz constraint on the critic through a gradient penalty evaluated at dynamically sampled interpolation points between the observed and synthetic data. This strategy introduces additional computational and hyperparameter tuning costs. Motivated by these limitations, we introduce the spectral normalization into the FWIGAN framework, directly constraining the spectral norm of each network layer to control the Lipschitz behaviour of the critic. It can enhance the stability of network training. The proposed method mitigates the dependence on having large labelled data and the pre-training of the network. The new scheme is applied to the Marmousi and Sigsbee models to verify its robust performance. The experimental results clearly indicate that our method outperforms common methods in terms of inversion accuracy.
74efe3fd42c2def5: Deepwater basins have become major targets for commercial oil and gas exploration. However, as exploration advances into ultradeepwater basins, technical challenges become increasingly severe, as exemplified by the Liwan Sag in the northern South China Sea (SCS). The rugged seafloor terrain and great water depth degrade seismic imaging quality and increase uncertainties in drilling and geologic interpretation. Conventional towed-streamer reflection seismic data provide dense reflection information, but are limited by relatively narrow observation angles and limited offset coverage. By contrast, ocean-bottom seismometer (OBS) data provide first-arrival traveltimes at larger offsets, thereby complementing the limited offset coverage of streamer data. In this study, joint OBS and towed-streamer observations from the Liwan Sag were collated and preprocessed to obtain seismic data with an improved signal-to-noise ratio for velocity model building over the full depth range. An integrated workflow with three stages was established: seawater velocity model building, subseafloor background velocity model building, and subseafloor velocity refining. The resulting velocity models were evaluated using traveltime fitting, migration image quality, and common image gather (CIG) flattening, and were then used for imaging in the depth domain and geologic interpretation of the survey line. This case study provided a practical workflow that integrated seismic data preprocessing, full-depth velocity model building, and stratigraphic imaging for ultradeepwater seismic exploration.
0bb3ff97f4ff7018: Pumice clasts from submarine eruptions contain abundant isolated vesicles that are completely encased in glass. As erupted clasts cool, gas inside isolated vesicles contracts, leading to low pressures inside those vesicles. Despite low pressures, isolated vesicles can be preserved in submarine pumice deposits to water depths of approximately 1–2 km because the compressive strength of glass exceeds the stresses created by the pressure difference between the inside of gas‐filled vesicles and the ambient pressure. If pumice rafts require abundant isolated vesicles, vents at greater depths are unlikely to form pumice rafts. Fracturing the glass enclosing isolated vesicles during shearing or slope failure would release low pressure vapor, lowering pore pressure and increasing effective stress in the sediment. Pumice‐rich deposits may thus strengthen during shear, making them more gravitationally and seismically stable than other submarine sediments.
c57f4bfe41ee3eed: The Mariana Trough is an active back‐arc basin formed by subduction of the Pacific Plate beneath the Philippine Sea Plate and provides an ideal setting for investigating the evolution of back‐arc basins. In this study, we compile bathymetric, magnetic, and gravity data to reconstruct the formation history of the entire basin. Based on bathymetry and backscatter intensity, the spreading axis is divided into 18 second‐order segments. Thirteen oceanic core complex–like structures are also identified both near axis and in off‐axis regions using topography and gravity anomaly data. Magnetic anomaly data indicate that seafloor spreading initiated at approximately 6.3 Ma in the central part of the basin near 17°30′N. During the initial stage (6.3–4 Ma), the oceanic crust was anomalously thick (∼8 km), likely reflecting enhanced melt production associated with slab‐derived fluids when the spreading axis was located close to the arc. Abyssal hill patterns and magnetic anomalies suggest that spreading was oriented NE–SW during this stage and began to change toward a trench‐normal direction between 4 and 3 Ma in each region. After 3 Ma, the basin evolved into its present crescent‐shaped geometry, with full spreading rates ranging from 25 to 45 km/Myr, which are higher in the southern region than in the north. Half‐spreading rates are generally higher on the western side of the spreading axis than on the eastern side, indicating persistent asymmetric spreading. Estimates of the Euler pole for the Mariana Plate suggest arc‐parallel extension, implying non‐rigid plate behavior during back‐arc basin opening.
cd1d52ae028e03e7: Accurate determination of rate-and-state friction parameters from experiments is crucial for physics-based modelling of the earthquake source. In this study, we develop a Bayesian inversion framework based on a spring-slider model of the experiment to infer rate-and-state frictional properties from stable velocity-step experiments of a fine-grained quartz gouge that is close to instability. The inversion framework infers frictional parameters with superior precision to conventional methods based on nonlinear least squares. We identify that logarithmic sampling of the characteristic slip $D_{\rm RS}$ is an essential step for accurate inversion. Testing the same gouge material under the same effective normal stress but different pore pressure additionally shows that the presence of pressurized pore fluids changes the inferred rate-and-state properties of the gouge material by increasing rate-and-state parameters a, b and $D_{\rm RS}$. The Bayesian inversion framework provides a valuable tool for inferring accurately rate-and-state parameters of realistic gouge materials close to instability, with a small and quantifiable range of uncertainty in cases where the steady-state behaviour quantified by $a-b$ can be constrained independently. We also find that the steady-state friction properties evolve over the course of the experiment, adding additional uncertainty to the rate-and-state parameter estimates but not altering the conclusion about significant differences between the rate-and-state parameters in the presence of fluids.
785dfb48b7e25299: Evaluating earthquake forecasts is a crucial step in understanding and improving the capabilities of forecasting models. The use of specific metrics to assess the consistency between forecasts and data on one particular aspect of the process is important to understand which aspects of seismicity a model is failing to describe, and, consequently, highlight where new versions of the model should improve. This can be done effectively only by metrics unaffected by inconsistencies in other aspects of the process. The Collaboratory for the Study of Earthquake Predictability (CSEP), which organizes earthquake forecasting experiments around the globe, has developed different tests targeting different aspects of the process, such as the number N-test or the magnitude M-test, assessing (in)consistency between the observed and forecasted number and magnitude distributions of events, respectively. We find that the results of the recently proposed M-test for catalogue-based forecasts (composed of a collection of synthetic catalogues from the model) depend on the N-test, that is, the two tests do not isolate the desired aspects appropriately, rendering uninformative forecast results. Here, we address this problem using simulated data and provide a solution based on resampling of simulated catalogues. We implement this new M-test with resampling in the pyCSEP software toolkit, conduct two analyses using actual earthquake forecasts for Europe (1990–2015) and Switzerland (1933–1962, 1962–1992, 1993–2022) that provide inconsistent earthquake counts compared to observations, and analyse how the test results change using this proposed test. Lastly, we investigate alternative metrics, namely an unnormalized M-test, two Chi-square formulations, the Hellinger distance, the Brier score and a novel Multinomial Log-Likelihood (MLL) score, and compare them based on the ability to find (in)consistency between data and forecast in various synthetic scenarios. We find that there are scenarios in which the alternative metrics outperform the resampled M-test. In particular, the MLL test outperforms the M-test in all the scenarios considered. We also study how the ability of finding inconsistency changes with the number of observations, and the cut-off magnitude, comparing one of the chi-square metrics, the MLL and the M-test against classical statistical methods such as the Kolmogorov–Smirnoff test, the Wilcoxon test and the Anderson–Darling (AD) test. The MLL and the AD test are the ones providing the highest probability of finding inconsistencies for all combinations of number of observations and cut-off magnitude. This study shows how realistic synthetic examples can be used to compare the ability of different metrics in finding inconsistencies between data and forecasts, and shows that the MLL is the metric providing the best trade-off between interpretability and probability of finding inconsistencies and, therefore, should be used.
f35d8f30dad62565: Plagioclase is the most abundant mineral group of the crust and will therefore either control or strongly influence crustal rheology. Yet, we still know little about crystal plasticity in plagioclase as brittle deformation dominates under most laboratory conditions. To overcome past challenges in quantifying crystal plastic deformation in plagioclase, we used micropillar compression to quantify the strength of specific slip systems as well as the stresses necessary for mechanical twinning in anorthite. Pillars with diameters of around 1 micrometre were milled from three differently oriented cuts of the same anorthite single crystals using focused-ion beam. Uniaxial deformation of 36 pillars in total was then conducted inside a scanning-electron microscope under either 25, 300, or 800 degrees Celsius. Most pillars were deformed with a constant displacement rate that corresponds to a strain rate of around 0.001 1/s on the pillars. We find that the critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) for mechanical (pericline) twinning lies at around 300 MPa and is, as expected from previous studies on other materials, insensitive to changes in temperature or strain rate. Pillar deformation in crystals oriented to activate slip exhibit a strong decrease in yield stress with increasing temperature. Among the deformation mechanisms active during pillar deformation, twinning is the easiest under the applied conditions, followed by slip on (011)[100] regardless of temperature. Slip on (011)[0-11] or (0-11)[011] is consistently the hardest mechanism to activate in our anorthite pillars.
a1bf37652a79c8f9: Implicit modeling and Relative Geologic Time are geological modeling techniques that enable more efficient, faster, less biased and more reproducible modeling results. For optimal operation, these techniques require many well-constrained input data. In the framework of the Horizon Europe GO-Forward and MOOI WarmingUP GOO projects and to accelerate Implicit modeling, Machine Learning (ML) methods have been tested and implemented in a toolkit for the interpretation of (onshore) seismic data from the shallow to deep range (+- 300 - 3500 m). The goal is to rapidly characterise this depth domain by efficient interpretation of horizons and faults in seismic data. The first step is to improve the signal by applying AI techniques like self-supervised and semi-supervised contrastive learning CNN's for noise reduction and interpolation. Next, horizons and faults are interpreted with minimal use of human-generated training data by using (semi-) self-supervised methods. The resulting developed toolkit supports the application of the implemented algorithms in an efficient workflow. As a first demonstration, the top of the Dutch Maassluis Formation has been interpreted in the Leeuwarden and Waalwijk 3D seismic cubes. Overall, this study demonstrates that AI-assisted interpretation workflows have reached a level of maturity that allows their integration into applied geological modeling and decision-making.
48aa9a0bb9fed9d4: In marine seismic acquisition, seismic interference (SI) occurs when energy from nearby external seismic source(s) is captured. It typically appears as coherent noise with linear or non-linear movement and varying amplitudes across different sail lines. SI is commonly observed and poses a challenge for seismic data processing. We present a case history of a previously proposed deep neural network (DNN)-based workflow applied for SI attenuation across a marine seismic block in the Camie Field of Angola. This field survey covers over 345 km2 and is marked by the challenge of multiple SI types. The employed DNN-based workflow performs SI attenuation in the common shot domain based on a supervised learning framework: a small subset of the SI-contaminated data was first processed by a conventional geophysical algorithm to obtain an estimate of the SI noise, which was then manually blended with the SI-free common shot gathers from the same survey to generate the training pairs. To ensure signal fidelity, several techniques were applied to improve the DNN's performance. A key highlight of this case history is its scale: this represents a real-world, large-scale processing project and we present a comprehensive comparison of the DNN-based workflow with the conventional geophysical algorithm across the entire survey block, focusing on both processing quality and processing time. The results demonstrate the outstanding performance of the employed DNN-based workflow, which achieved higher SI removal accuracy, with less signal leakage and more complete SI removal. The promising results of this application also open up possibilities for integrating deep learning into other seismic denoising tasks. In addition, we discuss the limitations of this case history, aiming to provide insights for future research and applications in the field.
8b75b5edc85d0e7d: A complete characterization of earthquake induced ground motions require three translational and three rotational components, together with the six components of the strain tensor. Despite the importance of rotational ground motions, their characteristics are not yet completely recognized. Limited observational database and challenges of simulating them in realistic geological media has primarily constrained the research in this domain.
