fc32e9a69ac32ce9: This study reconstructs the Pennsylvanian–late Permian to Early Triassic tectono-stratigraphic evolution of the Loppa High, a long-lived structural high on the southwestern Barents Shelf. We integrate 2D and 3D seismic surveys and key wells across ~35,000 km 2 to map eight regionally correlatable horizons (H1–H8) tied to the Billefjorden, Gipsdalen, Bjarmeland, Tempelfjorden and Sassendalen groups. Two-way travel-time structure maps, time–stratigraphic thickness maps and detailed fault interpretation (>150 faults) reveal three discrete late Palaeozoic extensional fault systems and a multi-phase tectonic evolution of the Loppa High. An ENE–WSW-striking Carboniferous fault system (C) parallels the Asterias Fault Complex and is linked to regionally widespread late Mississippian–middle Pennsylvanian rifting and development of the northern Loppa High as an early Carboniferous basement high. A Pennsylvanian–early Permian NNE–SSW fault system (P), antithetic to the Bjørnøyrenna Fault Complex, segments the northwestern Loppa High into the Neiden, Børselv and Kråketind sub-highs and controls distribution of Ørn Formation carbonates and Fafner evaporites. The C and P fault systems, along with Pennsylvanian regional transgression, exerted important controls on the depositional architecture. The late Permian–Early Triassic N–S-striking fault system (T) is spatially associated with the West Selis Boundary Fault and records rift reorganization associated with tilting, uplift and erosion of the West Selis Boundary Fault footwall and the final drowning of the Polhem Sub-platform. The results demonstrate that the evolution of the Loppa High is tightly coupled to regional fault trends across the northwestern Barents Shelf and Spitsbergen and reflects structural inheritance relevant to the later opening of the Norwegian–Greenland Sea.
7d05395982dbc75b: The Moon's ancient magnetic field provides critical insights into lunar thermal and magnetic evolution, yet the lifetime of the interior dynamo remains debated. Returned samples yield complex and contradictory paleomagnetic records, while orbital data reveal crustal magnetic anomalies of uncertain origin from either a core dynamo or transient impact-generated fields. Here, we jointly invert gravity and magnetic observations in the region around the Dewar swirl, a high-albedo feature associated with the Dewar magnetic anomaly. We identify a shallow, magnetized, high-density body consistent with buried mare basalt. Our estimates require a paleointensity exceeding 11 microtesla, suggesting an active lunar dynamo about 4.2 billion years ago, as constrained by the superposed basin ejecta. The results also show that swirl formation requires horizontal magnetization and iron oxide enrichment. These findings link a magnetic anomaly to its geologic origin and magnetizing field, providing constraints on the lunar magnetic and volcanic history.
07cfb7f57eb5d216: Broadband seismometers are widely used in global observation networks deployed for geophysics research. Recently, the calibration of their sensitivity has become an important factor for ensuring observation accuracy. One of the limiting factors of calibration uncertainty is the temperature dependence of the sensitivity because seismometers operate in a wide range of temperatures. However, systems that accurately measure the temperature coefficient of sensitivity in seismometers have not been established. Herein, we develop such a system using a triaxial vibration exciter combined with a thermostatic chamber. Using this system, we calibrated several broadband seismometers (Trillium Compact 120s, Trillium Horizon 360, and CMG-3T-360) at various temperatures, ranging from −15°C to + 45°C. The power supply and digitizer were kept at room temperature (23°C) so that only the sensor itself was investigated. We found that the temperature coefficient of the midband sensitivity was (0.11 ± 0.01) %/°C, which can be attributed to the internal magnet of the seismometers. The variation of the phase delay corresponded to a change of less than 2 ms in output time delay. In addition, we found that the relative frequency response below 1 Hz was stable against temperature variations. These values are useful for evaluating the measurement accuracy of seismometer observation networks.
990bb374d3a9cf57: Earthquake forecasting along active faults is important for reducing future seismic losses, especially in active zones such as Yunnan Province. However, the major earthquake recurrence patterns of faults in Yunnan remain understudied, and the time-dependent probabilities are still unclear. Here, we collected paleoseismic data on 20 fault segments in Yunnan, fit these data using four types of renewal processes, and calculated the probability of at least one major earthquake occurring on each segment over the next 30 yr. Approximately half of the fault segments show evidence of quasi-periodic recurrence, as indicated by the 95% credible intervals of their shape parameters being inconsistent with the random recurrence boundary. The Weibull renewal process is more likely to best reproduce recurrence times, followed by the lognormal renewal process. Five (≥4%) fault segments have relatively high earthquake occurrence probabilities. We also estimated the distribution of next-event times and found that fault segments with higher earthquake probabilities generally tend to have earlier expected times for the next earthquake. In this study, we conducted long-timescale recurrence analysis under restrictive assumptions, without taking into account multisegment rupture, stress interaction, and magnitude-specific modeling. Therefore, further research is required in these aspects in follow-up research.
518432797f34d9c8: Offshore seismic swarms north of Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands remain poorly characterized due to limited azimuthal coverage from the inland Puerto Rico Seismic Network (network code PR). Here, we integrate data from six U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) ocean-bottom seismometers (ZZ network, mid-2015 to mid-2016) with the PR network using a novel multimodel ensemble approach for machine learning (ML) phase picking, named pick aggregator. ML pickers have automated rapid seismic phase detection, but their performance degrades when applied to data that differ significantly from training datasets. Onshore–offshore experiments with sparse station coverage, complex instrumentation, and lower signal-to-noise ratios provide a challenge. The pick aggregator performs multidomain parallel computations on the SeisBench platform to catalog seismic phases across eight ML model combinations pretrained on ocean and land data. We then aggregate seismic picks identified by at least two models and associate them using a Gaussian Mixture Model Associator. The 1-yr ensemble ML catalog includes 10,948 events, composed of 55,704 P wave and 33,899 S wave picks, with mean probabilities of 0.65 and 0.64, respectively. The ZZ network substantially improves offshore azimuthal coverage and provides thousands of near-source seismic phases (25% of the P wave and 28% of the S wave picks). The relocated-ML catalog with >5.3 M added differential times includes 8025 events (115.8% increase compared with the relocated USGS catalog using the same stations). The relocated-ML catalog reveals an intense seismic swarm in the north-northwest direction southeast of the Main ridge at 20–40 km depth that aligns with the fast shear-wave polarization of previous studies, suggesting an incipient slab tear near 65.1° W. Seismicity depth variations along the strike indicate a steeper western segment with a wider depth range and a retreating eastern segment, supporting a differential rollback mechanism. Our multimodel ensemble approach mitigates inconsistencies among ML pickers pretrained on different datasets, enabling superior performance and robust phase detection in diverse tectonic environments with varying signal characteristics.
61f60396978025fe: Straight faults are considered prone to large supershear ruptures and seismic gaps to likely host future earthquakes. Both predictions may have been fulfilled in the magnitude ( M ) 7.7 Mandalay earthquake of 28 March 2025 on the Sagaing Fault. Exceptional video footage of the fault rupture, high-rate Global Navigation Satellite System, and seismological and remote sensing data reveal a supershear slip pulse that formed early and ruptured a well-identified seismic gap but propagated well beyond it, resulting in an exceptional rupture length of 510 kilometers. By contrast, the slip pulse observed in the video footage has subshear characteristics. These observations can be reconciled by a preferred conceptual interpretation invoking depth-dependent weakening properties, stress heterogeneity, and possible dynamic triggering. These properties allow for energetic ruptures that stay confined to the depth range locked in the interseismic period but are not confined to seismic gaps along strike.
eb60ee76bf1841e9: Deep recycling of surficial carbonates into the mantle may play a critical role in shaping Earth’s long-term habitability, yet its contribution to the deep mantle carbon budget remains uncertain. Magnesium isotopes provide a promising tracer for addressing this issue, because of the uniquely light isotopic signatures of sedimentary carbonates. Here, we present high-precision magnesium isotopic compositions (δ 26 Mg) for 152 globally distributed plume-related lavas sampling diverse mantle end-members. We find that δ 26 Mg values below the bulk silicate Earth range are commonly associated with increasingly pronounced radiogenic isotopic signatures indicative of recycled crustal components. These features are best explained by the incorporation of isotopically light magnesium derived from subducted carbonate-bearing crustal materials into their mantle sources. On the basis of these observations, the lower mantle is estimated to contain up to ∼130 or ∼230–parts per million recycled carbon, potentially constituting a substantial portion of its total carbon budget.
165dfcd5753b7bf0: Chemical heterogeneities in Earth’s deep mantle may record either preserved primordial reservoirs or later core-mantle exchange, but distinguishing between these origins remains challenging. Hydrogen isotopes offer a sensitive tracer, yet whether magma ocean crystallization could generate a deuterium-depleted deep reservoir has not been quantitatively evaluated. Here, we use machine learning–accelerated path-integral simulations to determine equilibrium hydrogen isotope fractionation between silicate melt and bridgmanite, ringwoodite, and wadsleyite under magma ocean conditions. Incorporating these fractionation factors into a magma ocean crystallization model shows that mineral-melt fractionation is intrinsically weak, producing an essentially homogeneous D/H distribution in the primitive mantle. Magma ocean crystallization therefore cannot generate the extremely low δD values observed in some ocean island basalts. Combined with exceptionally high 3 He/ 4 He ratios, these signatures more plausibly reflect selective transfer of primordial volatiles from Earth’s core, implying sustained volatile exchange across the core-mantle boundary.
d10817b05b2cd24f: Understanding P- and S-wave travel-time behaviour is important for characterizing seismic-wave propagation and identifying station-dependent variability within regional seismic networks. This study investigates P- and S-wave travel-time characteristics and station-dependent residuals using local earthquakes recorded by the Ghana Digital Seismic Network (GHDSN). The analysis reexamines the published GHDSN earthquake bulletin and waveform dataset for 2012–2014, comprising 73 detected earthquakes recorded by six broadband stations. Event selection was based on phase coverage, yielding nine earthquakes with paired P- and S-wave arrivals at at least five stations and 47 station-level P+S observations. Hypocentral distances were calculated from earthquake coordinates and focal depths, and first-order linear regressions were used to characterize P- and S-wave travel times. The resulting effective velocities were 6.51 km s⁻¹ for P waves (R² = 0.985) and 3.88 km s⁻¹ for S waves (R² = 0.985). Station median residuals ranged from −0.40 to +1.17 s for P waves and −1.39 to +1.27 s for S waves. Within-event permutation tests yielded p = 0.0080 for P waves and p = 0.0110 for S waves, indicating statistically significant station-associated variability in the selected observations. However, the small ΔR² values indicate that the magnitude of this station-associated contribution is limited. The results provide an empirical characterization of local seismic-wave propagation across the investigated GHDSN stations in southern Ghana and identify station-dependent variability that warrants further investigation using larger datasets, improved earthquake locations, and joint velocity–location–station analyses.
cdeb7182df238248: The mechanical behaviour of the Earth is widely assumed to change with increasing timescale as rocks progressively relax imposed stresses [1]. On short timescales, elasticity dominates and its release drives earthquakes [2]; at intermediate timescales, viscoelastic relaxation facilitates processes such as glacial rebound [3]; whereas over geological timescales viscous deformation dominates, allowing the mantle to flow [4]. Energetically, this progression implies that mechanically stored potential energy becomes increasingly irrelevant to long-term geological processes such as metamorphism. Here we challenge this assumption using time-resolved deformation experiments that isolate changes in stored energy during metamorphic reaction. We show that increasing stored energy causes reaction to occur sooner and faster, increases nucleation density and reduces product grain size. Comparison with experiments from crustal and mantle materials shows that this influence persists across different reactions and deformation regimes. These results demonstrate that stored energy can exert a first-order control on geological transformation despite its comparatively small contribution to the total energy budget. Because stress and stored energy are heterogeneous across materials and scales, our results place stored energy alongside water as a driver of metamorphic change and provide experimental support for a view of the Earth in which changes in Helmholtz energy influence the emergence of material instabilities [5-8].
36f824e49fde9f7d: Shallow-water ocean forcing provides strong broadband passive Scholte-wave illumination along a seabed distributed acoustic sensing cable on the Texas Gulf Coast. We exploit this illumination through direct processing of the uncorrelated wavefield, long-duration frequency–wavenumber stacking, and a multi-aperture strategy that preserves high-frequency spatial localization while resolving low-frequency modes. Constant-wavenumber slices enable spatially consistent multimode tracking across successive array centers. The resulting dispersion spans approximately 0.3–4.5 Hz and supports 400 1D inversions along a 51 km cable segment. These profiles form a pseudo-2D shear-wave velocity model extending from the near seafloor to approximately 2 km depth. Broad shallow low-velocity intervals are consistent with softer incised-valley fill within stiffer Pleistocene deposits. The results demonstrate that existing seabed fiber infrastructure, when coupled with strong shallow-water passive illumination, can deliver broadband regional shear-wave imaging, whereas higher-frequency active sources remain necessary to resolve the uppermost several meters.
2c5486b1cf5cd48f: Accurate three-dimensional (3-D) seismic velocity modelling through seismic traveltime tomography using both active- and passive-source data provides critical underpinning models for seismicity monitoring and hazard assessment. Because traveltime tomography is an inherently ill-posed inverse problem, uncertainty quantification (UQ) of the estimated models using Bayesian methods is also important for reliable downstream interpretations and analyses. However, Bayesian inference for 3-D tomography based on conventional grid-based representations faces the ‘curse of dimensionality’ and severe computational bottlenecks. Consequently, rigorous Bayesian UQ for margin-wide 3-D traveltime tomography has remained largely unexplored, despite its importance for reliable interpretation of large-scale velocity models. In this study, we propose a meshless 3-D Bayesian traveltime tomography method that combines physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) with a neural representation of the velocity structure, enabling tractable and data-efficient Bayesian inference through function-space Particle-based Variational Inference (fParVI). To efficiently integrate passive-source data into the Bayesian estimation of the velocity structure, we introduce an analytical marginalization strategy that treats uncertain parameters related to the origin time and location as nuisance parameters, with passive-source relocation carried out in post-processing. We validated the capability of our approach for 3-D problems through synthetic experiments. These experiments demonstrate its robustness against biased prior source locations compared to standard methods that suffer from overfitting. Furthermore, we applied the method to a real-world data set off the Kii Peninsula, Nankai Trough, using over 380 000 traveltime picks from marine active-source surveys and natural earthquakes. Our probabilistic 3-D ensemble successfully resolves key geological features, such as the Kumano Pluton, and provides data-consistent uncertainty maps that offer new quantitative insights into the reliability of previously debated deep low-velocity zones. The posterior mean hypocenters shifted mainly in the vertical direction by 10–15 km, consistent with the deterministic relocation results of a previous study. Finally, the continuous neural representation drastically reduces storage requirements for the entire ensemble velocity model, highlighting the scalability and data efficiency of the proposed framework for Bayesian seismic traveltime tomography.
aa9feb531092680d: A rigid connection between the optical fiber and the rock allows to properly measure ‘rock strain’ with distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). We demonstrate this by running four interrogator units (IU) on a testbed with single-fiber patch cables being cemented into a groove in the concrete floor of Black Forest Observatory (BFO). The recorded signals are compared with the recordings of a calibrated Invar wire strainmeter array that has been continuously in operation for the last decades at a distance of about $350 \,\mathrm{m}$ to the testbed. In this way, we compare the ‘fiber strain’ against ‘rock strain’ at frequencies below 0.2 Hz. We investigate this on the background of a previous study with DAS cables unreeled on the floor and loaded down by sand and sandbags, where we found a significant loss of strain amplitude between rock and fiber. Waveform similarity for strong earthquake signals is high with typical values of the normalized correlation coefficient greater than 0.95. The strain amplitude measured by all four IUs is very consistent and by about 10 per cent larger than the strain measured by the strainmeters. We attribute this minor discrepancy to spatially varying strain–strain coupling caused by the local topography. At frequencies up to 14 Hz we make an intercomparison of IUs, showing no significant variation with frequency. The scatter of strain amplitude in between channels which are spatially near to each other in the same fiber route is about $\pm 10~\mathrm{ per~cent}$ in most cases. The variation of median values in between different IUs and earthquakes is less than $5~\mathrm{ per~cent}$. By subtracting the common mode noise, which is coherent along the fiber route, we lower the background signal level to an rms amplitude of $100\, {\rm pstrain}$ at 0.1 Hz and $5\, {\rm pstrain}$ at 1 Hz in a bandwidth of 1/6 decade for the best cases. This allows the detection of the marine microseisms during times of moderate amplitude level.
15a612cf068a4b11: The application of machine learning to planetary geophysics is frequently bottlenecked by a scarcity of labelled data and the complexity of non-stationary seismo-acoustic signals. While deep learning offers powerful feature extraction, it requires massive data sets that are rarely available for phenomena like Martian quakes or deep-ocean volcanism. Consequently, researchers often rely on unsupervised machine-learning or hand-engineered features that are typically impoverished or hard to interpret. To resolve this, we introduce Spec2VEC, a framework that transforms parameter-dependent time–frequency representations into a robust, interpretable and high-dimensional vector space. Spec2VEC treats spectrograms not merely as energy distributions but as structured, textured images and extracts physics-informed, data-set-agnostic features without requiring massive training loops. The framework systematically extracts a feature vector using two novel pathways: (1) a textural path that utilizes Hilbert space-filling curves to map 2-D spectral patterns into 1-D sequences for advanced information-theoretic analysis (e.g. permutation entropy and fractal dimension); and (2) a spatial path driven by probabilistic distribution fitting for signal identification, a novel probabilistic pre-conditioning engine that quantifies spatial connectivity by dynamically separating coherent signal modes from stochastic noise. We validate this feature space on a comprehensive benchmark of complex synthetic wavefields and two real-world examples: an Exotic Seismic Events Catalog (ESEC) and a distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) data set. Spec2VEC provides objective features for information discrimination and enables highly accurate classification of the diverse geophysical signal classes present in the ESEC catalogue. Furthermore, application on the high data volume DAS data set confirms its computational efficiency and domain-agnostic capability to isolate anomalous seismic arrivals from background noise. Ultimately, Spec2VEC bridges the interpretability of classical signal processing with the discriminative power of modern representation learning, providing a reliable, interpretable foundation for automated discovery across the geosciences.
66e14bfd251f4753: Open, satellite-derived vertical land motion (VLM) products are increasingly used to estimate relative sea-level rise and coastal hazard, often well beyond the studies that produced them. Researchers often infer the reliability of these VLM products from agreement with other products rather than validating them against independent observations. Researchers then sometimes attribute differences between products to processing without testing. Here, we examine three cases: 1) We independently processed Sentinel-1 data for 17 of the 48 coastal cities in a widely cited open dataset provided by Tay et al. (2022) over nearly the same observation window, and compared both products with Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) vertical velocities. After transforming both to IGS14, our rates agree with GNSS at R² = 0.87, whereas the transformed Tay et al. rates agree at R² = 0.3. Tay et al. velocity maps also show patterns consistent with known signatures of coregistration, phase-unwrapping, and pair-selection errors. 2) We show that a recent comparison of InSAR VLM products for coastal California by Govorcin et al. (2025) attributes their differences to Blackwell et al. (2020) to spatial filtering without controlling for observation epoch, using rate values that do not appear in the source, quantifying resolution, or accounting for localized horizontal motion. That untested attribution has since been cited as evidence of inconsistency among InSAR products. 3) Third, a comparison for New York City by Buzzanga et al. (2023) contrasts their products from different epochs with Ohenhen et al. (2023) to conclude that an Ohenhen et al. dataset lacks hot spots, although its time series show those hot spots as transient, and reprocessing with the Ohenhen et al. method over the same epoch as Buzzanga et al. recovers them. In cases 2 and 3, disagreement was attributed to processing. Therefore, we propose a six-step protocol for validating and comparing VLM products, along with a community-maintained open archive to make these checks routine.
d4089e5efc5be5f2: For the 2025 Ocean Hack Week hosted at the University of Washington, we built the framework for an interactive dashboard allowing users to create new musical compositions by remixing marine sounds. Starting from a base library of typical ocean sounds, users can pull audio clips from publicly available acoustic and geophysical datasets. Incorporated datasets include Ocean Networks Canada (ONC), the NSF Seismological Facility for the Advancement of Geoscience (SAGE), OrcaSound, and the National Center for Environmental Information (NCEI). Currently, we pull audio clips from pre-processed libraries managed by these sources. Creators can then drag clips into a visual audio mixer, and change the pitch, speed, and repetition of a clip to form a “song,” which is also rendered as a waveform and spectrogram. A whimsical map diagram is generated when a song is completed, reflecting the varieties of sound sources combined in the piece. This project, representing a fusion of data science, acoustic processing, and fun, invites us to dive into the rich world of ocean soundscapes. Alongside the musical aspect of the project, there are several educational components. First, a thorough description of each dataset is provided, explaining the type of sensors and environment. Secondly, visualization of common waveforms and spectrograms explains general analysis of different signals, allowing the users to understand the scientific context behind the sounds they are hearing. From drag-and-drop music mixing to thorough explanations of seismic waves, there’s something for everyone here.
8764b9c83b84b6ab: The Kharita Formation represents one of the principal Lower Cretaceous clastic reservoirs in the Shushan Basin, Western Desert, Egypt. This study integrates seismic interpretation and petrophysical analysis to evaluate the reservoir characteristics, structural controls, and hydrocarbon potential of the Kharita Formation in the SELKIT and SETHOS fields, South Umbaraka Area. The investigation was based on the interpretation of thirty 2D seismic profiles and conventional well-log data from the SELK-6, SELK-7, and SETHOS-16 wells. Seismic interpretation was conducted to delineate the structural framework, fault architecture, and trapping configurations, while petrophysical analysis was performed to determine lithology, shale volume, porosity, fluid saturation, and net-pay distribution. Neutron-density crossplots were also utilized to identify lithological variations and potential gas-bearing intervals. The seismic interpretation reveals that the study area is structurally controlled by a series of major normal faults and fault-bounded anticlinal closures that significantly influence reservoir distribution and hydrocarbon accumulation. Time- and depth-structure maps of the Kharita Formation indicate that both the SELKIT and SETHOS fields occupy structurally elevated four-way dip closures, providing favorable trapping conditions. Correlation of the Cretaceous succession further demonstrates the influence of fault-controlled compartmentalization and differential subsidence on reservoir geometry and thickness distribution. Petrophysical analysis indicates that the Kharita Formation consists predominantly of sandstone reservoirs with variable shale content and favorable reservoir properties. Seven hydrocarbon-bearing zones were identified, with net-pay thicknesses ranging from 11 to 63 ft. Shale volume values vary between 4 and 20%, total porosity ranges from 8 to 18%, and effective porosity ranges from 6 to 17%. Water saturation values range from 20 to 45%, corresponding to hydrocarbon saturation values of 55% to 80%. The most prospective reservoir intervals occur in Zone D of SELK-6 and Zone F of SETHOS-16, which exhibit favorable combinations of net-pay thickness, porosity, and hydrocarbon saturation. The integrated results demonstrate that hydrocarbon accumulation within the Kharita Formation is controlled by the combined influence of depositional architecture, reservoir quality, and fault-related structural trapping. This study highlights the value of integrating seismic and petrophysical datasets for reducing exploration uncertainty and improving reservoir characterization in the Shushan Basin and analogous Lower Cretaceous reservoirs of the Western Desert.
01f0bbcf589bd0c6: Accurate seismic imaging of deep, low signal-to-noise ratio zones in faulted basins remains a persistent challenge. To address this, we propose a pre-stack depth migration (PSDM) velocity modeling workflow that integrates multiple information constraints. Shallow velocities are derived from micro-logging constrained first-arrival inversion, while intermediate and deep interval velocities are converted from root-mean-square velocities using horizon-constrained constrained velocity inversion in the depth domain. Horizon-guided residual velocity analysis is iteratively applied from top to bottom, generating a low-frequency velocity model that captures the structural trends of the faulted basin. Multi-attribute constrained grid tomography—incorporating logging curves, azimuth, dip, continuity, and other seismic attributes—iteratively updates interval velocities through PSDM. The workflow combines model-based tomography for macroscopic along-horizon velocity trend control with multi-attribute constrained grid tomography for high-resolution interval characterization, enabling robust delineation of the faulted basin's velocity architecture and improved interval velocity accuracy. Application to 3-D data from Block H in an eastern China oilfield demonstrates clear sequence contacts, abundant interval details, a well-defined deep basement boundary, and improved imaging quality.
01a1f1707c05c706: The tectonic evolution and deformation mechanisms of the Pamir remain controversial, partly because the crustal response to deep lithospheric geodynamic processes is insufficiently constrained. Two competing lithospheric tectonic models are under consideration: subduction of the Asian slab and delamination of Pamir lithosphere, each of which predicts distinct crustal anisotropic signatures. Here, we use shear‐wave splitting of Moho P‐to‐S converted‐phases from receiver functions recorded at 198 seismic stations to map crustal anisotropy across the Pamir and the surrounding regions, thereby providing direct constraints on crustal deformation styles. We further determine crustal thicknesses and Vp/Vs ratios using H‐κ‐c stacking. Crustal thickness correlates positively with surface elevation and negatively with Bouguer gravity anomalies, indicating that crustal thickening provides the dominant first‐order support for the high topography. More importantly, Pms splitting measurements reveal strong crustal anisotropy, with a mean delay time of ∼0.66 s, and a systematic rotation of fast‐polarization orientations across the intermediate‐depth seismicity belt. In the southern Pamir, convergence‐parallel fast directions record N‐S‐oriented basal shear imposed by the indented Indian lithospheric mantle, which has likely promoted Quaternary extension of southern Pamir. Conversely, to the north of this belt, orogen‐parallel fast‐directions signify pure‐shear thickening of the Pamir lithosphere. Together with low crustal Vp/Vs ratios of 1.60–1.72 beneath the southern Pamir, which are consistent with a felsic bulk crust and removal of mafic lower crust, these observations favor Indian‐lithosphere‐induced delamination of the Pamir lithosphere rather than a model dominated by uniform southward subduction of Asian lithosphere.
c4df9e5d8272ed70: Slab-derived fluids and melts released during subduction refertilize the mantle wedge, shaping arc magmatism and volatile transfer. Yet the nature and efficiency of the earliest metasomatizing agents active under the warm thermal gradients of nascent subduction zones remain poorly constrained. Here, we report multiphase and polymineralic inclusions from the high-temperature metamorphic sole of the Semail ophiolite (Oman–United Arab Emirates), which record the trapping of COH fluids and hydrous silicate melts derived from both mafic and sedimentary slab components during subduction infancy. Multiphase inclusions act as micro-reactors where fluids react with host minerals during exhumation, driving the abiotic synthesis of solid organic compounds, including nanodiamond-like structures, demonstrating that subduction zones can generate molecules of prebiotic relevance. Combined with the ophiolite record, our results indicate that such COH fluids and melts refertilize the mantle wedge from the onset of subduction, generating proto-arc magmas and promoting deep carbonation and hydration.
44b1637ba51206a5: Crystallisation-driven volatile exsolution (second boiling) is widely invoked to pressurise shallow magma reservoirs, yet its ability to generate eruption-triggering overpressure and detectable ground deformation is poorly quantified. We couple phase equilibria with thermal and viscoelastic models of sill-like intrusions to map pressure evolution and geodetic detectability of second boiling. Thermodynamic calculations for basaltic and rhyolitic magmas from Askja (Iceland) and Puyehue-Cordón Caulle (Chile) are embedded in conductive thermal models for thin (20 m) and thick (200 m) sills at 2-4 km depth, and the resulting volume changes and magma compressibility are propagated into pressurisation histories and volume-change rates. Hydrous magmatic sills can develop overpressures of 20-30 MPa on timescales of months to centuries depending on initial sill size and crustal parameters, whereas relatively dry basalt undergoes cyclic behaviour with contraction followed by modest re-pressurisation. For a given composition and depth, thin and thick sills attain similar overpressures but differ by an order of magnitude in volume-change rate. Only small volatile-rich sills exceed geodetic resolution thresholds. In felsic crust, viscoelastic relaxation further dampens surface deformation, consistent with globally observed reduced deformation at arc volcanoes. Applied to Askja, cooling of a basaltic sill can explain the subsidence from 1983-2021, while second boiling in a small rhyolitic body can plausibly contribute to rapid uplift observed starting in mid-2021. Our results define a regime of “stealth” pressurisation in shallow hydrous reservoirs in mafic-intermediate crust, where eruption-scale overpressure can accumulate with undetectable geodetic unrest and help explain unexpected explosive eruptions with little precursory deformation.
291016f3341622ef: This dataset contains 1,995 focal mechanism solutions obtained in this study for earthquakes beneath northeastern Japan between April 2003 and July 2022, supporting the paper “Mechanical Decoupling Across the Deep Megathrust Boundary.” The file mechanismsSP.csv includes event identifiers, origin times in Japan Standard Time (UTC+09:00), hypocentral coordinates, JMA and moment magnitudes, scalar seismic moments (N m), strike, dip, and rake angles (degrees), the number of stations, variance reduction (%), and theta_max_deg. The column used_as_this_study_solution_in_integrated_catalog indicates whether the solution obtained in this study was adopted in the integrated catalog (1 = adopted; 0 = not adopted). The column integrated_catalog_source identifies the source selected for each event: SP-MT (1,902 events), JMA (87 events), or F-net (6 events). The column theta_max_deg is a solution-stability indicator defined as the maximum Kagan angle between the full-data solution and the retained single-station-deletion solutions, in degrees.
ffe3256828ebccc9: Geophysical data observed in the Earth, planetary and lunar sciences are spatially limited to sampling plans designed to span a feature of interest whose resolution and regularity in discretization are bound by site, observational and instrumental constraints. Common wisdom tells us that the more observations we make, the less variable our estimates of statistical properties of measured physical quantities will be. However, given the limited spatial extent and possibly irregular sampling of any data set, how confident can we be in our estimates of the parameters of statistical processes underlying such fields? We study how sampling geometry contributes to uncertainty in modelling spatial geophysical observations as sampled random fields characterized by stationary, isotropic, parametric covariance functions. We incorporate the signature of discrete spatial sampling patterns into an asymptotically unbiased spectral maximum-likelihood estimation method along with analytical uncertainty calculation. We illustrate the broad applicability of our modelling through synthetic and real data examples with sampling patterns that include irregularly bounded contiguous regions of interest, structured sweeps of instrumental measurements and missing observations dispersed across the domain of a field, which spur behaviours in the estimator. We find through asymptotic studies that allocating samples following a growing-domain strategy rather than a densifying, infill scheme best reduces estimator bias and (co)variance, whether the field has been sampled regularly or not. As our modelling assumptions, too, shape how (well) an observed random field can be characterized, we study the effect of covariance parameters assumed a priori. We demonstrate the desirable behaviour of the general Matérn class and show how to interrogate goodness-of-fit criteria to detect departures from the null hypothesis of Gaussianity, stationarity and isotropy.
eb363b5da7a1d7ff: Constraining the crust beneath Campi Flegrei is critical for understanding its magmatic system, but the resolution of local-earthquake tomography decreases with depth. Here, we adapt receiver-function analysis to intermediate- and deep-focus earthquakes within the Ionian slab beneath the Tyrrhenian Sea, recorded by the dense Campi Flegrei seismic network at regional distances. Deep sources provide steep P-wave incidence, while relatively short source–receiver paths reduce high-frequency attenuation receiver functions are corrected for finite-distance moveout and modelled using ray-theory simulations and global optimization. Synthetic tests assess the resolution of the method. The preferred model identifies a prominent interface at 7.7±0.4 km depth, associated with a low-velocity, high- layer, and a deeper discontinuity at 21.7±0.9 km, interpreted as the Moho. The 7.7 km interface is consistent with the top of the magmatic sill identified by the 2001 active-source experiment. No additional shallow discontinuity is required by the data within the resolution of the method.
7b4ff592ee5fbeb3: Fault stepovers commonly arrest earthquake ruptures, yet shallow sedimentary layers can substantially modify this behavior. We use three-dimensional spontaneous dynamic-rupture simulations to examine how sediment velocity, thickness, background stress, rupture regime, and fault burial affect critical jump distance across extensional and compressional stepovers. In the reference models, sedimentary layers strongly promote transfer across extensional stepovers under high-prestress conditions with supershear rupture. Sediment-guided Mach waves reflect between the free surface and sediment–bedrock interface and sustain favorable dynamic Coulomb stress at large fault-normal distances. The sediment effect is weaker and regime-dependent across compressional stepovers, where transfer is associated primarily with the stopping phase and may be inhibited after supershear transition. At the highest stress level, coexisting and merging Burridge–Andrews and free-surface-induced fronts accompany maximum extensional critical jump distances of 35 km in the low-velocity sediment model and 40 km in the higher-velocity model. These maxima are conditional on the reference stress and friction assumptions. Additional tests show that shallow stress and residual strength substantially change the absolute jump distance. Independent changes in main- and secondary-fault prestress distinguish source-side and receiver-side sensitivity. Fault burial suppresses near-surface supershear development and reduces the enhancement. The results identify a conditional mechanism for sediment-assisted rupture transfer and motivate including shallow structure and fault properties in physics-based assessments of multifault earthquake potential.
5bea97b1ff1828c7: Precambrian supercontinent reconstructions largely rely on robust geological constraints. Among these, the basin affinities recorded by Precambrian sedimentary fragments preserved in orogenic belts provide critical evidence for resolving the paleogeographic configurations of microcontinents and continental blocks. In this study, we integrate detailed field investigations with detrital zircon U–Pb geochronology, zircon Hf isotope analysis, Monte Carlo unmixing modeling, and multidimensional scaling to constrain the depositional age, provenance and paleogeographic significance of the Sayanggou metasedimentary fragment in the southern East Kunlun accretionary belt, southern Qaidam Block. The detrital zircon age spectra of the Sayanggou metasedimentary fragment feature prominent Ediacaran and older Neoproterozoic multimodal age populations. The absence of late‐stage detrital zircons, multiple calculating maximum depositional age approaches and stratigraphic evidence further indicates deposition in a comparatively stable Ediacaran depositional environment, possibly a passive‐margin setting. Corresponding zircon ε Hf ( t ) values are predominantly negative, indicating sediment derivation primarily from recycled ancient crust. Statistical evaluation of these data sets against global detrital zircon archives reveals a diagnostic Gondwanan signature. Monte Carlo unmixing analyses and multidimensional scaling models firmly tether the Sayanggou metasedimentary fragment to the contemporary basins in the South Qiangtang Block and related Ediacaran peri‐Gondwanan margins. Zircon U–Pb ages of crosscutting granitoid and dioritoid intrusions indicate that this metasedimentary fragment was probably accreted to the southern East Kunlun accretionary belt during the early Paleozoic in response to Proto‐Tethyan subduction. Our findings further advance the understanding that the Qaidam and South Qiangtang blocks were located in relatively close paleogeographic positions within the peri‐Gondwanan domain during the Ediacaran.
11d6924f4d428d16: Fault topography exerts a key but poorly constrained control on rupture processes and the nature of seismicity. Through numerical simulations, we directly visualize how fault roughness controls rupture propagation by tracking the evolution of micro‐ruptures and associated stress states. On smoother faults, stress remains concentrated at nearly fixed locations throughout the slip process. In contrast, rougher faults exhibit multiple transient, spatially discrete stripes of stress concentration. Micro‐ruptures initiate at rough contacts and drive rapid localized fault slip, which is subsequently arrested by re‐interlocking at regional rough contacts. Consequently, more extensive ruptures occur on less rough faults with this nucleation potentially extending along the entire fault, favoring the formation of large, destructive earthquakes on relatively smooth fault in nature. Moreover, rougher fault surfaces produce larger b ‐value promoting energy dissipation through multiple small ruptures. These microseismic events cluster in time and indicate the initiation a self‐locking‐rupturing cycle, comparable to small, frequent microseismicity observed in active fault zones. Our findings establish a direct mechanistic link between fault topography, rupture process and microseismicity, advancing the understanding of the nucleation then propagation of earthquakes.
90858893d6cfdc61: Subduction initiation is a fundamental geodynamic process in plate tectonics, yet its mechanisms remain poorly understood due to the scarcity of geological records. Proposed geological records of subduction initiation, including metamorphic soles, fore-arc basalts and fore-arc sediments, are typically associated with spontaneous subduction initiation in hot environments involving mantle upwelling. In contrast, evidence for the more common cold subduction initiation at continental margins is sparse or even absent. Arc volcanic rocks are widely regarded as direct evidence of subduction zones, particularly for identifying ancient subduction zones in orogens. However, the temporal relationship between subduction initiation and the onset of arc volcanism remains poorly constrained. Although arc volcanism is generally considered to develop within ∼10 million years (Myr) of initiation, our analysis of subduction events over the past 15 Myr reveals a highly variable time lag ranging from 2 to 10 Myr. In this study, we investigate the factors controlling this time lag in forced subduction initiation at continental margins, using a newly developed two-phase flow numerical model that incorporates melt transport and melt extraction processes. Our results show that rapid partial melting at shallow depths, primarily driven by high convergence rates, leads to a shorter time lag between subduction initiation and arc volcanism, which is consistent with observations from recent subduction events. These findings suggest that arc volcanic rocks, when considered together with slab age and convergence rate, provide a useful constraint on the timing of subduction initiation in ancient subduction systems.
10705b30a075b742: Subduction zone megathrust faults commonly generate the world’s largest earthquakes and associated tsunami hazards at shallow depths, yet their rupture characteristics remain poorly constrained owing to sparse observations across hundreds to thousands of kilometers from the trench. Here, we integrate inland geodetic data (GNSS and InSAR) with offshore tsunami waveforms to jointly image the coseismic slip distribution and tsunami initial source of the 2025 Mw 8.8 Kamchatka earthquake. Our tsunami-source model reveals that tsunami generation was controlled by three distinct uplifted zones (peaking at ∼5 m), each corresponding to a high-slip asperity (or coupling) on the megathrust. Our slip model shows these asperities slipped more than 6 m, with almost no slip in the deep downdip region and only limited slip at shallow depths. The limited shallow slip may have been largely compensated during the preceding 1952 event. Remarkably, the near-field spatial pattern of tsunami runup is broadly consistent across the 1737, 1952 and 2025 events, with comparable amplitudes for the latter two but more than 3-times higher for the former, a pattern that may reflect repeated rupture of the same along-strike asperities with variable slip amplitudes at similar depths across seismic cycles. This variability implies significant residual strain and future hazard potential, consistent with a supercycle behavior. Our findings underscore the critical role of persistent asperities in governing megathrust rupture variability and long-term tsunami hazard.
0c66f801594cf285: Solutions to geophysical inverse problems are generally non-unique, and greatly benefit from additional geological prior information. Generative Neural Networks (GNNs) are commonly used to parametrise such information, typically restricting solutions to a lower-dimensional latent space. The final inversion result is obtained by mapping the latent space parameters to the original higher-dimensional model space using the GNNs. However, solutions then remain confined to a low-dimensional geological generative manifold; if the true Earth model lies outside of this manifold, standard latent space inversion fails. We propose a Bayesian model space inversion method that uses the generative manifold as a guide to find the solutions that lie outside this manifold. We validate our approach in non-linear travel-time tomography experiments on both simple and more geological structures. By comparing our method with model space inversion using uniform prior probabilities and standard latent-space inversion, we demonstrate that the less informative uniform prior fails to constrain the solution, while the latent space approach fails when the true Earth model lies outside of the generative manifold. Conversely, our new model-space inversion method successfully recovers complex off-manifold geological features while maintaining low solution uncertainty.
b07d271ab89a80b8: We present a large seismological dataset (https://geofon.gfz.de/doi/network/ZK/2021) composed by continuous recordings from 200 temporary stations (seismic network ZK, 10.14470/MX7576871994), which operated continuously for approximately one year in the Southern Apennines (Southern Italy) as part of the DETECT experiment. The dataset is compliant with the seismological standards for the archiving of data and metadata, and with standardized tools for disseminating them, e.g., the International Federation of Digital Seismograph Networks (FDSN) web services. The data set was collected during the DETECT experiment in the Irpinia area (southern Italy), which is one of the regions with the highest seismic hazard in Italy. From August 2021 to August 2022, a constellation of 20 seismic arrays, with a total of 200 seismic stations, was installed above the fault segments responsible for the M 6.9, 1980 Irpinia earthquake, the strongest and most destructive seismic event in Italy in the last fifty years. Each seismic array had a maximum aperture of ~2 km and was composed of one broad-band sensor, one short- period sensor with 1 Hz and eight 4.5 Hz natural frequency geophones. Data and metadata were managed in accordance with the GIPP/GEOFON policy using SeisComP (Helmholtz Centre Potsdam – GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences and GEMPA GmbH, 2008) and the final archive size is approximately 5.2 TB. In this contribution, we provide details on how to download waveform data and station metadata, as well as information on data availability and quality.
b899493df6dcb9c7: Earthquake preparation involves progressive damage accumulation, strain localization, and changes in the organization of seismicity. We investigate preparatory processes preceding seven episodes of major earthquakes in the Kuril - Kamchatka subduction zone during 2014 - 2025, including the 29 July 2025 MW 8.8 Kamchatka megathrust earthquake. We track damage evolution using the seismic regularity coefficient dc and seismic strain dynamics coefficient SSD, defined for seismic series. Before 2022, each episode of strong seismicity was preceded by a pronounced dc minimum, commonly accompanied by an SSD minimum, followed by an increase in dc toward a maximum near the strong event or event group. After 2022, dc minima became shallower and were superimposed on a sustained upward trend. We interpret this transition as evidence that the metrics recorded two superimposed processes. The cycles before 2022 reflect complete strain-localization histories on southern or more distant structures that did not contribute to the segment ruptured in 2025. In contrast, the upward dc trend from 2022, with only shallow minima preceding Episodes 6 and 7, marks coupled behavior within the eventual main rupture segment, also influenced by stress transfer from southern source regions.
81beba12c78aa5d0: Short-term aftershock incompleteness biases Gutenberg-Richter b-value estimates because many small earthquakes remain undetected immediately after large events. Two strategies address this problem. Earthquake replenishment reconstructs missing events to restore a more complete catalog, whereas robust positive-difference estimators infer the b-value directly from incomplete observations. Whether these approaches provide equivalent information on the magnitude distribution remains open. We address this issue using synthetic aftershock sequences generated with the Epidemic-Type Aftershock Sequence (ETAS) model and degraded through a time- and magnitude-dependent incompleteness model. Incomplete catalogs are replenished using AutoBETA, and b is estimated using the standard maximum-likelihood, b-more-positive, and b-more-incomplete estimators. Replenishment reconstructs the overall structure of the missing-event population and substantially improves conventional maximum-likelihood estimates, although small residual biases remain. By contrast, both positive-difference estimators recover the imposed b-value directly from incomplete synthetic catalogs. Applications to the Ridgecrest, Landers, and Hector Mine sequences show that b-more-incomplete is less sensitive to replenishment than b-more-positive. Ten independent replenishment seeds indicate that seedto-seed variability is small relative to differences among estimators. Replenishment and robust b-value estimation therefore address different aspects of catalog incompleteness: replenishment provides a more complete aftershock representation, whereas robust estimators are preferable when accurate b-value estimation is the primary objective.
f5e3e30e2bbd7b33: The physical origin of foreshocks remains one of the major unresolved problems in statistical seismology. In bottom-up (BU) triggering models, foreshocks are interpreted as ordinary earthquakes that stochastically trigger a larger event through cascading interactions, as in the Epidemic-Type Aftershock Sequence (ETAS) model. In contrast, top-down (TD) models interpret foreshocks as manifestations of a preparatory process preceding the mainshock. This ambiguity has important implications not only for earthquake forecasting, but also for declustering itself, since the inferred number of foreshocks may depend on the assumed physical mechanism governing seismicity. Here we investigate the detectability of foreshocks using synthetic catalogues representing two limiting physical scenarios: purely bottom-up triggering and mixed preparatory-triggering dynamics. These cases are implemented through the ETAS and ETAFS models, respectively. We compare the classical nearest-neighbor (NN) declustering metric with a reverse nearest-neighbor metric (rNN) introduced here. While the standard NN metric scales the correlation metric to the magnitude of the earlier event, rNN scales it with the magnitude of the later event. We show that rNN is mathematically equivalent to applying the standard nearest-neighbor metric to the time-reversed catalog, establishing a direct symmetry between the two approaches. Our simulations reveal [...]
9864a29e6fe40cf2: Irregular acquisition geometries in field seismic surveys lead to non‐uniform spatial sampling, which introduces spatial aliasing, reduces spectral utilization and degrades the accuracy of subsequent wavefield reconstruction and imaging. Seismic data regularization aims to resample such irregularly acquired data onto a uniform grid, serving as a critical preprocessing step. In this study, we propose an unsupervised deep learning framework for five‐dimensional (5D) seismic data regularized reconstruction that integrates implicit neural representation with a Transformer backbone and short‐time Fourier transform based time–frequency feature learning. The seismic wavefield is parameterized as a continuous mapping from four‐dimensional (4D) spatial coordinates to amplitudes. A novel 4D positional encoding scheme, extending sinusoidal Transformers to shot and receiver coordinates, is designed to enhance the representation of high‐dimensional spatial structures. The Transformer architecture captures global long‐range dependencies through self‐attention, while the model predicts the real and imaginary components of the time–frequency spectrum, from which waveforms are reconstructed via the inverse short‐time Fourier transform (ISTFT), thereby improving spectral recovery and amplitude‐phase consistency. Experiments on synthetic data demonstrate that the proposed method achieves lower normalized root‐mean‐square errors and superior reconstruction of reflection structures, spectra and detailed waveform features compared with projection onto convex sets, damped rank reduction, robust damped rank reduction, and a baseline implicit neural representation approach. Field 5D data experiments further confirm the method's effectiveness in recovering amplitude, phase and azimuthally anisotropic characteristics on regular grids, with only a small incremental ISTFT cost for the tested workload. The proposed framework enables high‐accuracy, self‐supervised reconstruction of 5D seismic data under irregular sampling conditions without requiring labelled training data.
f3805cd21d48c8ac: We investigate how slab folding impacts the topographic evolution of collisional orogens and the sediment supply to the associated basins, under the effect of different erosion and sedimentation rates. Results show that when slab folding causes the steepening of the subducting slab, it enhances topographic growth in the orogen at rates between 0.008 and 0.310 mm/yr and increases the sediment thickness at rates between 0.05 and 0.3 mm/yr. The topographic growth depends on the erosion rate, which is up to 0.2 mm/yr in our simulations. In the basin, the sedimentation rate not only depends on the erosion rate in the orogen, but also on how efficiently sediments are transported to the basin. Results from a correlation test between the plastic strain and the cumulated sedimentation suggest that the load of sediments affects deformation at two different spatio‐temporal scales. The load caused by sedimentation rates of 0.3 mm/yr or more enhances the regional deformation that causes lithospheric extension in the basin. Conversely, the load of sedimentation rates below 0.3 mm/yr increases the localized deformation that causes tectonic subsidence in normal faults. These results highlight how erosion rates control the topography evolution of the orogen, and how sedimentation rates enhance regional deformation or/and localized tectonic subsidence in the basin.
48e9d7e6f6e9c365: Accurate estimation of seismic magnitudes and focal mechanisms is a key component of seismic monitoring in enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) for evaluating the state of stress in the subsurface, efficiency of geothermal activities, and induced seismicity hazard. We present a reference catalog of point-source, double-couple moment tensors for 123 seismic events in the moment magnitude range ∼0.9 to 3.0 at and in the vicinity of the Cape and Utah Frontier Observatory for Research in Geothermal Energy EGS fields in Milford Valley, southwest Utah, for the time period 1 February 2024 to 9 March 2025. We estimate moment tensors by inverting low-frequency waveforms recorded by local permanent seismic stations at distances ∼1 to 8 km, in passbands ranging from ∼0.6 to 1.5 Hz to ∼0.1 to 0.2 Hz using Green’s functions calculated assuming path-averaged 1D velocity models between event and station locations. We obtain reasonable quality waveform fits between observed waveforms and synthetic waveforms predicted by the best-fitting moment tensors (variance reduction ∼34% to 73%, median ∼53%) at ∼5 to 11 stations (median ∼8). The estimated moment magnitudes differ from the catalog magnitudes by >0.3 magnitude units for ∼29% of the events. We find the primary focal mechanisms in the geothermal field to be strike-slip faulting (∼40% to 50%), followed by oblique faulting with strike-slip faulting being the major component (∼45%) and the minor component comprising roughly similar proportions of normal and reverse faulting. The dominant strike-slip component is consistent among events, with the possible fault planes striking either north-northwest (NNW) (right-lateral) or west-southwest (left-lateral), with ∼10° to 15° of variability (standard deviation) among events. The fault plane striking NNW is consistent with the orientations of linear trends of seismicity and the most dominant set of natural fractures identified in image logs in the reservoir in previous studies.
5e5a7cbcc3fe15f6: Rapid and reliable estimation of epicentral distance and magnitude are pivotal for damage assessment in earthquake early warning (EEW). However, conventional epicentral distance and magnitude estimation approaches for EEW rely primarily on manually defined features to construct empirical prediction equations. Meanwhile, many existing machine learning models focus solely on single tasks (either epicentral distance or magnitude estimation alone), neglecting the correlation and impact between epicentral distance and magnitude. In this study, we design a collaborative attention network (CAN) framework for EEW, named EEWCAN, which combines global and local attention mechanisms. In addition, we explore the feasibility of EEWCAN for estimating epicentral distance and magnitude from single-station data in the Japan region. EEWCAN integrates global and local attention mechanisms to automatically capture more critical features pertinent to epicentral distance and magnitude from seismic waveforms. The EEWCAN framework is composed of two models: the EEWCAN-Dis model for epicentral distance estimation and the EEWCAN-Mag model for magnitude estimation. Meanwhile, the epicentral distance estimated by the EEWCAN-Dis model is incorporated into the EEWCAN-Mag model. We trained and tested EEWCAN using seismic events recorded by the Kyoshin network in Japan, with waveforms serving as the input to EEWCAN. The test results demonstrate that, when data from 3 s after P-wave onset are used, EEWCAN can obtain reliable estimates of epicentral distance and magnitude, outperforming the baseline models. Furthermore, by incorporating the estimated epicentral distance information, EEWCAN enhances the reliability of magnitude estimation. This result demonstrates that our proposed method can provide a certain degree of reliability for epicentral distance and magnitude estimation in EEW.
5ac85a9b8b93f18a: Focal depths provide vital information for seismogenic mechanisms and tectonic structures. Because of sparse seismic stations in the Mariana subduction zone, accurately determining the focal depth of shallow earthquakes is challenging. The amplitude spectra of short-period Rayleigh waves are highly depth sensitive and are applicable at local and regional distances with sparse seismic station coverage. In this study, we collect seismic data at local and regional distances in the Mariana region, and then use the optimal period of short-period Rayleigh-wave amplitude spectra to determine the depths of shallow moderate-sized earthquakes. The difference between our resolved depths and the Incorporated Research Institutions for Seismology (IRIS) results ranges from −12.5 to 17.5 km, whereas the difference between our resolved depths and the Global Centroid Moment Tensor (Global CMT) depths has a range of −7.5 to 12.5 km. To further verify the estimated source depth, we used depth phase modeling to constrain the source depth of the largest Mw 5.9 earthquake. The result of depth phase modeling (27.9 ± 0.3 km) is slightly larger than the depth of 24.4 ± 1.4 km using the optimal period method. In comparison, the estimated depth is quite different from the fixed values of 10 and 12 km in the IRIS and Global CMT catalogs, respectively. The study demonstrates the efficacy of this approach on shallow offshore earthquakes and the need to reassess the depth of earthquakes in the Mariana subduction zone.
3051d04ca4bb0622: On 28 March 2025, the Mw 7.7 Mandalay earthquake ruptured ∼475 km of the Sagaing fault. The surface rupture was mapped using high-resolution satellite optical images guided by displacements from subpixel optical image correlation. The surface rupture was generally continuous where remotely observable (i.e., not tree-covered) and very simple without large steps or bends along strike. We analyze remote surface rupture mapping from pixel tracking and optical images and determine that ∼10% of the surface rupture passed through potentially saturated ground. The ground saturation observed on high-resolution satellite images was compared with Sentinel-2 normalized differential water index and generally agrees spatially. We test for correlations between ground saturation observations and the presence or absence of surface rupture and of strike-slip geomorphology. We infer that transient near-surface conditions, such as ground saturation, may influence the geomorphic and paleoseismic preservation of surface rupture, as well as infrastructure (dam) performance, both in this earthquake and globally.
6d5fcff08af484b5: Subducting lithosphere is a primary driver of plate tectonics. Seismic tomography shows that some slabs are stagnant in the mantle transition zone (MTZ), and it is debated why they do not continue directly across the MTZ base ( d 660). Here we demonstrate by seismic Receiver Function images of the Japan-Kurile subduction system that stagnant slabs may be flat or buckling inside the MTZ, depending on the dip of the incident slab. Shallow dip may result in a flat stagnant slab following a broad, gentle d 660 depression as predicted by thermal effects. Moderate dip (20–35º) causes a buckling stagnant slab and a localized ∼40 km deep d 660 depression, which is deeper than predicted from pure thermal effects. In-phase deformation of a positive converter around 520 km depth (labelled x 520 and unlikely to be caused by exothermic phase transition) and the endothermic d 660 inside the MTZ cannot have a pure thermal origin and indicates that these interfaces correspond to the top and bottom of the buckling stagnant slab. We speculate that the observed dip-dependent in-phase deformation of the d 660 and the x 520 boundaries is affected by both cooling and mechanical impact by the slab, which control their temperature and depth (pressure), respectively. Our findings suggest that slab impact on MTZ may also affect localized d 660 depressions in steeper subduction systems and that thermal effects of slabs on MTZ deformation may often be overestimated.
c033fb70ab8d1d78: This repository contains the source data and analysis materials associated with the study “How Large Are Marsquakes? Revisiting Magnitude Scaling and Implications for Marsquakes and Meteoroid Impacts” by Jung-Hun Song, Doyeon Kim, Gareth S. Collins, Victor C. Tsai, and Philippe Lognonné.The repository is organised by figure and table and includes source parametrisation files, synthetic-source generation scripts, spectral-fitting and waveform-analysis codes, magnitude-scaling results, machine-readable versions of Tables 1 and 2, and supporting data for the main figures. References and links to externally archived InSight waveform data and Martian interior models are also provided where applicable.Please refer to the README.txt file in each directory for details of the included files, analysis workflow, data sources, and software requirements. Large external computational resources, such as Instaseis Green’s-function databases and standard SPECFEM3D_GLOBE files, are not included and must be generated or obtained separately.For questions, clarification, or requests for additional files, please contact Jung-Hun Song ([email]; [email]).
18305c206eddc64b: Fluvial corridors mediate dynamic river-groundwater exchanges and support major transportation infrastructure, yet continuous subsurface monitoring remains limited by sparse point sensors and infrequent time-lapse surveys. Addressing this observational gap is critical during extreme flood events, when transient saturation, pore-pressure buildup, and structural scour drive complex hydro-mechanical changes that threaten both riparian slope stability and bridge foundations. Here, we demonstrate that traffic-excited highway bridges act as persistent, spatially fixed seismic sources; their vibrations, recorded on roadside telecommunication fiber with Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS), enable time-lapse imaging of river corridors. We evaluate this approach using dark fiber recordings along South Korea's Gyeongbu Expressway during a record monsoon flood in July 2025, targeting a 430 m multi-span bridge crossing the Miho River. Vehicle impacts excite flexural resonances of the bridge deck, generating a discrete spectral comb of fundamental-mode Rayleigh waves in the surrounding ground; these 3-6 Hz waves propagate beyond 400 m across both riverbanks to image the alluvial section down to bedrock. Because bridge-structure geometry constrains the source location and dominant modal frequencies, virtual source gathers achieve rapid convergence within 5 min of ballistic wave stacking with high waveform repeatability over the recording period. Relative seismic velocity (dv/v) monitoring resolves velocity drops up to 1.0% during flood passage associated with heavy precipitation and river stage rise, consistent with hydrological softening of the riparian sediments. These results demonstrate that traffic-excited bridges provide persistent, repeatable seismic illumination, turning roadside telecommunication cables into dense arrays for both hydrogeophysical and civil infrastructure applications.
