d55db11511be6c86: The Manda Hararo rift segment in the Afar depression (Ethiopia) represents a key location to study the timing, style, and evolution of volcanic activity within an active continental rift close to the Ocean-Continent Transition (OCT) stage. Despite its importance, the southern part of this segment has remained poorly documented. In this study, we provide a detailed mapping based on a combination of medium-resolution spectral imagery and a unique dataset of very-high-resolution Pléiades images. We combine this map with volcanological observations, major and trace element analyses, and cosmogenic 36Cl surface exposure dating to investigate the very last eruptions and volcanic history of two sub-segments (Gumat Mali and Gablaytu). Our results show that the last volcanic activity occurred at Gablaytu between ~3.20 and 1.50 ka and at Gumat Mali between ~1.90 and 0.61 ka. Petrological data indicate that the Gumat Mali sequence was driven by reservoir recharge with new, less differentiated magma that hybridized with a more evolved mush, enhancing magma mobilization. The Gablaytu sequence records progressive magma differentiation and plagioclase assimilation and/or accumulation. For both sub-segments, these processes control magma evolution prior to eruption and indicate a complex transcrustal plumbing system characterized by magma storage, recharge, and interaction within vertically connected reservoirs. The documentation of these historical and recent volcanologic activities also help to draw potential regional hazards for populations settled nearby these volcanic centres, including parts of Semera district, which should consider both effusive episodes from axial fissures and potentially extremely energetic phreatomagmatic phase, that characterize the initiation of the historical sequence at Gumat mali.Our observations support the recognition of two self-consistent sub-segments within the wide Central Afar magmatic system with their own associated plumbing system: the Gumat Mali sub-segment located in the direct prolongation of the Dabbahu segment corridor and the en-échelon lateral Gablaytu sub-segment along the Manda and Unda Hararo Hararo axis. This illustrates the intimate links between tectonic structures, magma storage and upward migration in controlling the expression of first and second order segmentation in such zones of the Afar depression close to the OCT.
edfe53d9fafe26ae: We investigate fluid flow-deformation interactions in a strongly anisotropic basement during rifting, focusing on the Arize North-Pyrenean Massif. This massif exposes a complete Variscan metamorphic series, from southern migmatites to northern Carboniferous flyschs, tilted northward during the Lower Cretaceous Pyrenean rifting. Structurally, the western and central parts of the massif are characterized by roughly uniform foliation orientations, whereas the eastern section exhibits a heterogeneous foliation pattern within a N140°E-trending transtensional folded and faulted zone. At the core of this transtensional system, a 10 km2 metasomatic zone hosts formerly exploited albitite stocks, formed through a two-stage alteration process. Early-stage metasomatism involves minor plagioclase alteration and biotite destabilization, accompanied by Ca-paragenesis neocrystallization, with whole-rock data indicating significant Ca-enrichment. Advanced metasomatism is characterized by dequartzification and plagioclase albitization, with limited net chemical change. Fluid inclusions in metasomatized apatite reveal H2O–NaCl–CaCl2 brines, trapped at ~300 °C and ~205 MPa.We interpret the Arize system as a transient reservoir of ascending hot fluids, localized above a brittle–ductile transition. Descending fluids accumulate at this transition, where subhorizontal anisotropy planes act as impermeable barriers. Locally, fluids heated to 300–400 °C ascend through vertical anisotropy planes (tilted Variscan foliations) and brittle faults. U–Pb dating of neoformed titanites (~130 Ma) confirms that the Arize upflow system developed during the early Pyrenean rifting. The hydrothermal system is localized within an oblique transtensional zone linking N100°E-oriented rift segments, highlighting the critical role of fluid flow in syn-rift linkage zones.
e9f872aa966c21cd: Diffuse volcanic degassing reflects subsurface magma and fluid transport, but its spatio-temporal relationship to seismicity and eruptions remains poorly constrained. Here, we present ground- and drone-based CO2 flux measurements acquired prior to the August 2024 eruption on the Reykjanes Peninsula, Iceland, together with seismic observations. The study focused on the highly fractured Grindavík and Sundhnúkur areas. A transect through Grindavík reveals a bimodal distribution of CO2 fluxes with values between 0.1 and 28 g·m−2·d−1, reflecting heterogeneous near-surface permeability and local correlations to fractures. Using a new drone-based gas flux detection system, measurements at the inaccessible Sundhnúkur fissure system were possible, identifying elevated CO2 fluxes, with up to 4400 g·m−2·d−1 close to the location where the next eruption initiated. A comparison with seismicity suggests (1) distributed pressurization with localized enhanced gas escape restricted to the Sundhnúkur area prior to the eruption, and (2) strongly focused seismicity in the Sundhnúkur area during the eruption.
671c1d679c763fb8: Forecasting the size of a future volcanic eruption in densely populated areas is a key aspect of volcanic hazard and risk assessment. Estimates of the next eruption's size for both long- and short-term forecasts are typically based on the sizes of past events. Using the erupted volume as a proxy for eruptive size, forecasts are often obtained from the sampling of a power-law distribution. Notwithstanding, the distribution of the measured/inferred erupted volume of past eruptions often appears markedly different from a power-law. Here, we consider how the uncertainty on the volume of past eruptions may affect the shape of a hypothetical power-law distribution. The goal is to understand if the distribution of real data is compatible with an Exponentially Modified Gaussian distribution (EMG) that includes both the power-law and the uncertainty on the observed volumes. We apply this method to two large high-risk calderas, Campi Flegrei, Italy, and Taupo, New Zealand, but it can be potentially applied to any volcano. We find that the EMG distribution provides a good statistical fit to both volcanoes' eruptive records, supporting the use of a power-law distribution for forecasting the volume of the next eruption.
479e80f2fa7dc6c0: Classical elastic dislocation theory (CEDT) has two challenges when applied to faulting problems: 1) fictitious on-fault stresses not defined by ordinary integration and 2) the geometric unreality of infinitely thin fault zones. We show that both can be resolved by a mollified elastic dislocation theory (MEDT) built on Cortez blob (Cortez, 2001) mollified displacement discontinuity Green's functions, which represent deformation across spatially distributed fault zones of finite scale epsilon and produce singularity-free displacements and stresses everywhere. Analytical integration of the mollified source solution over arbitrary planar triangular elements is done with AI, and the resulting closed-form solutions allow for the calculation of non-singular stresses across geometrically complex fault systems. Further, we demonstrate the decoupling of the fault-zone width scale epsilon from the mesh length scale h, the elasticity analog of a result established for regularized viscous flow Stokeslets (Ferranti and Cortez, 2024). We use these mollified kernels to demonstrate numerically stable collocation boundary element models including spatially extended fault zones, material property variations and non-planar topography.
647e2b65d8fc00cb: Finite-fault slip models are widely used to infer earthquake rupture processes, yet they are inherently non-unique and do not guarantee physically consistent rupture evolution. Here, we develop a data-constrained framework that couples Ensemble Kalman Inversion (EKI) with large-scale 3D dynamic rupture simulations to efficiently evaluate the dynamic viability of finite-fault slip models. The framework explores initial shear stress conditions informed by slip models while constraining dynamic rupture scenarios with geodetic observations and the teleseismic moment-rate function. Applying this approach to 32 models of the 2011 Tohoku-Oki earthquake, we identify 26 dynamically viable 3D rupture scenarios using $\sim$285 total forward simulations. Across the ensemble, both smooth and highly heterogeneous finite-fault slip models can be reproduced dynamically. Yet these models converge to three dynamic rupture families, characterized by crack-like, single-reactivation, or multiple-reactivation rupture styles. This convergence suggests that apparent finite-fault diversity may reflect a smaller set of dominant controls on rupture dynamics, including the level of prestress heterogeneity. Multiple-reactivation dynamic rupture models best reproduce the observed depth-dependent rupture behavior and moment-rate complexity. By contrast, large tsunamigenic slip near the trench and comparable partitioning of released strain energy between breakdown and radiated energy persist across dynamically viable models, despite differences in initial shear stress conditions and rupture style. These results show that finite-fault slip model heterogeneity can map onto a smaller set of dynamically viable rupture styles, preserving robust first-order features. Our EKI framework provides an efficient pathway for integrating observations with physics-based simulations and identifying dynamically consistent earthquake source models.
714df137cb2d9f78: The size of a large earthquake depends on how far the rupture runs and how much the fault slips. An early correlation with magnitude can appear while those two contributions are still mixed. Patches at both ends stop every rupture on a 120 km fault, so the length no longer varies and the early order is an order of slip. One background stress is a single value along the fault, and the other also varies along strike. Slip at 20 s is ordered by 2 s for 259 ruptures in the first case, and by 8 s (7-9 s) for 230 ruptures in the second. The extra seconds are not a slower rupture front. Where the stress varies along strike, stations beside the fault and around it show that order when the waves arrive. Stations ahead of the rupture do not lead the waves, and where the stress is one value, stations around the fault are later than the waves. The calculations are an idealized two-dimensional dynamic simulation, with one friction law and no field record.
a9d72416eeb501a9: Code, input files and compacted outputs of the earthquake-cycle simulations of Chapter 6 of the doctoral thesis "How Faults Prepare to Fail" (ETH Zurich, 2026). The simulations follow 2000 years of seismic cycles on a 200-km periodic strike-slip fault with a heterogeneous normal stress (self-affine, ±30 % about 100 MPa). They use a modified version of the quasi-dynamic simulator QDYN in which the gouge layer of every fault element evolves by wear, localization and comminution, and sets the critical slip distance D_c and the evolution parameter b of rate-and-state friction through relations derived from a microphysical model. The deposit contains the 140 simulations of the study (the main set on two stress profiles, four sensitivity sets and a comparison set) and eight simulations that test the pressure-solution constant of the friction table. It also contains the solver, the friction-table generator, the analysis and figure scripts, and the per-cycle catalogues. Every figure and table of Chapter 6 and Appendix D of the thesis can be regenerated from these files. The README describes the contents, the data format and how to reproduce the results.
952814a976da856d: Slow slip events (SSEs) represent an aseismic transient slip mode that repeats quasi‐periodically, near or partially overlapping with the megathrust earthquake zone. However, the process of stress interaction between SSEs and earthquake zones is not clearly understood. Here, we apply an earthquake and SSE sequence model to simulate the interseismic variability of SSE characteristics, and compare to observations pre‐ and post‐2012 M w 7.6 Nicoya earthquake in the Costa Rica subduction zone, including six SSEs from 2003 to 2012 and four from 2014 to 2019. Our model reproduces the slip distribution of shallow and deep SSEs, and predicts higher peak velocity and larger cumulative slip of SSEs late in the earthquake cycle. This variability arises from the reciprocal stress transfer between SSEs and the earthquake zone. Our study suggests that systematically documented variations of SSE characteristics may reflect the long‐term unlocking process on megathrust faults where slow‐to‐fast slip modes coevolve.
60b005add1ad5820: Quantifying earthquake size across scales requires linking physical source parameters to empirical magnitude measures, especially for microearthquakes where attenuation, scattering, and instrumental limitations complicate source characterization. We combine regional results with near‐source observations from the Tony Creek dual Microseismic Experiment, dense nodal data from Ridgecrest, and regional broadband data from San Jacinto to extend potency–magnitude scaling to local‐magnitude . Bayesian spectral inference yields robust potency estimates across seven potency magnitude units and nine units. The combined data sets follow a continuous quadratic relation . Synthetic modeling shows that source scaling, attenuation, and the finite Wood–Anderson passband can produce similar nonlinearity, although rupture‐scaling differences may also contribute. Despite sensitivity to observational and regional factors, the independent data sets are broadly consistent with the established quadratic relation, supporting it as a general empirical scaling over the investigated size range.
d7246ea4e188627a: Large‐offset detachment faults frequently occur at slow‐ and ultraslow‐spreading mid‐ocean ridges, especially where magma supply is limited. Here we use two‐dimensional thermo‐mechanical models to systematically investigate how frictional and cohesive strength contrasts between fault zones and surrounding lithosphere influence faulting styles in nearly amagmatic ultraslow ridge environments. Our models incorporate a self‐evolving thermal structure and Mohr‐Coulomb elasto‐plasticity with friction and cohesion weakening during deformation, along with parameterizations of fluid circulation. We identify three primary deformation regimes: distributed minor faults, sequential flip‐flop detachments, and persistent runaway detachments. Flip‐flop detachments emerge under moderate frictional and cohesive weakening, where faults alternate polarity as antithetic faults periodically replace dominant detachments. Persistent runaway detachments, as produced by models, show excessive cross‐axis migration that is not typically observed in nature. A strong, viscous lower lithosphere promotes distributed deformation and hinders the onset of persistent detachments. Analytical force balance modeling further shows that flip‐flop faulting occurs when fault strength loss balances the defocusing effect of lithospheric flexure, which necessitates moderate frictional weakening (∼0.2–0.3) achievable via serpentinization of the fault zone. In contrast, runaway detachments require further weakening. These findings clarify the mechanical conditions driving flip‐flop detachment formation and highlight how relatively modest rheological contrasts between intact and deformed lithosphere enable large‐offset faulting at ultraslow mid‐ocean ridges.
a4e21a2afab91f69: Great megathrust earthquakes (∼Mw 8–9) that rupture along the Cascadia Subduction Zone pose significant shaking and tsunami hazards to the U.S. Pacific Northwest. Although these large earthquakes are documented in the geologic record, none have been recorded with modern instrumentation, complicating regional seismic hazard assessments. Benchmarking these simulations against the Next Generation Attenuation Subduction (NGA-Sub) ground-motion models shows reasonable fits for non-basin sites, although simulations predict stronger shaking at short (0–2 s) and long (6–10 s) periods. NGA-Sub basin terms improve fits to synthetic shaking within the Seattle Basin but underpredict amplitudes by a factor of 2 at periods of 2–5 s. We also evaluate how rupture characteristics influence regional inland shaking variability and basin response in the Puget Lowlands. Larger magnitude scenarios generally cause stronger inland shaking due to farther inland extents of slip and larger strong-motion-generating fault patches but show little difference in basin amplification within the Puget Lowlands compared to smaller magnitude events. Along-dip hypocenter location strongly influences overall inland shaking, with offshore (updip) hypocenters generating on average ∼45% higher shaking at long periods (>6 s) compared to onshore (downdip) hypocenters due to rupture directivity effects. Offshore splay faults minimally affect inland shaking but alter offshore deformation important for coupled ground-shaking and tsunami scenarios. Finally, we show that rupture directivity increases amplification within the Seattle Basin through the generation and interaction of higher order mode surface waves, an effect of 3D basin geometry that cannot be captured using 1D approximations.
9ef68c64327fb987: Travel times of long period body waves passing through the lower mantle reveal the deep seismic structure and forces shaping our planet . Manual methods measuring P and S wave arrivals produce travel time catalogs with high internal consistency, but have not kept pace with the rapid growth in waveform records. Here we use attention-based machine learning trained on prior manual datasets to develop a catalog spanning 2010-2023 which is consistent with previous catalogs and straightforward to update. The new catalog exceeds millions of measurements for P and S wave travel times and retains features of the previous datasets while improving coverage in the lower mantle, particularly for raypaths turning beneath the southern hemisphere. Comparing our measurements to short period travel times, we find the correlation is different for early versus late arrivals, and that this difference is larger for P waves than S waves. The change in slope we observe is opposite to that proposed for wave propagation effects and warrants further investigation into the origin of this apparent dispersion in Earth's lower mantle.
e9901b7f4e52a0b7: How the convergent strain between the India Plate and the Tarim basin is partitioned by active faults and off‐fault deformation in southwestern Tibet is poorly understood due to limited knowledge of strain localisation and fault kinematics. In this study, we derive high‐resolution velocity fields for the southwestern Tibetan Plateau using both GNSS and InSAR observations. Using these velocity fields, we apply an improved block model to estimate the kinematics of major active faults in the region. Our results suggest significant strain localization along the Altyn Tagh‐Ashikule‐Yulong Kashgar‐Gozha Co fault system and the Karakoram fault, which form the western boundaries of the eastward extrusion of Tibet. We also observe significant oblique thrusting along the Main Frontal Thrust, with convergence rates increasing from ∼16.6 mm/yr at 74°E to ∼25 mm/yr at 86°E. Based on our coupling distribution and slip rate deficit model, we reveal the seismic potential of the major faults.
84aaa85c42019019: Fault slip modeling, based on laboratory-derived friction laws, has significantly enhanced our understanding of fault mechanics. Agreement between model predictions and observations supports the hypothesis that observed slip diversity, including fast earthquakes and slow transient slips (Slow Slip Events; SSEs), originates from frictional heterogeneity. However, quantitative assessments of frictional heterogeneity from geodetic observations while fully incorporating fault mechanics are lacking due to the difficulties of high-dimensional optimization. In this study, we aim to address this gap using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to link frictional heterogeneity with geodetic observations. PINNs employ a neural network to represent the spatially variable frictional properties, making their estimation feasible. Targeting the 2010 Bungo SSE in southwest Japan, our estimation reveals heterogeneous friction coinciding with localized SSE nucleation in southwest Shikoku, and subsequent westward propagation. The calculated fault slip of SSE successfully reproduces the spatio-temporal pattern of observed surface displacements. This PINN-based inversion provides a mechanically consistent fault slip model validated through quantitative comparison with observations. Furthermore, we forecast the future fault slip evolution, demonstrating the importance of assimilating observations spanning multiple SSE cycles. Our results demonstrate the potential of PINN for advancing understanding of fault mechanics and enabling physics-based fault slip forecasting. Spatially variable frictional properties along a fault can be estimated using a physics-informed neural network approach that enables physics-consistent slip modelling, as tested on the 2010 Bungo slow slip event in southwest Japan.
cce8ea5fe672011f: The transpressive plate boundary between the Caribbean and North American plates in Hispaniola is a complex system of strike-slip faults, subduction zones, fold-and-thrust belts, and normal faulting. Tectonic deformation studies in this region have traditionally relied on sparse Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) networks. Here we present a new assessment of deformation in Hispaniola using a dense 3D velocity field generated by integrating existing GNSS observations with new Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) velocities. Our InSAR processing approach utilizes phase linking, statistically-based multi-looking, and wrapped phase time-series estimation to mitigate noise, and a spatial covariance model of the troposphere to reduce its effect on the time-series estimation. We use the resulting high-resolution velocity field to calculate strain rates and model crustal faulting in Hispaniola. Strain rate tensors show a transpressional tectonic regime consistent with expectations from the regional tectonics. Modeling results indicate that the Septentrional-Oriente Fault zone is nearly fully locked with moment accumulation consistent with a Mw 7.9 earthquake every 300 years, while the Enriquillo-Plantain Garden Fault is almost fully creeping at the western end of the fault and has a much lower moment accumulation rate.
4522057c22df1c91: On 24 June 2026, moment magnitude (Mw) 7.2 and 7.5 earthquakes struck northern Venezuela along the right-lateral Boconó and San Sebastián faults, initiating on land west of Morón. Intense shaking and damage, with preliminary subsurface slip estimates, indicate >215 km long, ∼70% offshore eastward rupture propagation, complicating understanding of the shallow rupture process. We investigate surface deformation near five coastal towns intersecting the fault through mapping and subpixel correlation of high-resolution (0.4–10 m) optical imagery. Near Morón, ∼0.78 m of fault-parallel displacement is distributed over >3 km without surface rupture. To the east, displacements increase within narrower zones along towns built on alluvium, from an average of 2.7 m within 69 m at Caraballeda tapering to an average of 0.3 m within 340 m at Camurí Grande. Despite >3 m displacement at Caraballeda, <300 m long discontinuous surface rupture was identified. Airport runway cracking between June 25 and 26 coincides with 0.1–0.2 m of secondary fault afterslip. Shear strains support primarily elastic surface deformation in the west above a fault slip deficit and permanent inelastic deformation consistent with plastic yielding above shallow fault slip in the east. These observations highlight the importance of characterizing distributed near-surface strain and material properties for understanding fault displacement hazard.
78c8e991f6e54a4a: Earthquake‐triggered landslides are a major source of sediment mobilization in steep mountain landscapes, yet the controls that organize regional patterns of coseismic shallow failure remain incompletely understood. We apply the model to two geomorphically distinct subregions affected by the 2015 Gorkha earthquake in Nepal and compare modeled and observed distributions of landslide area, elevation, slope, and aspect. Parameterizations incorporating spatially variable regolith thickness consistently outperform a uniform‐thickness baseline, and model performance is highest for moderate cohesion values (–15 kPa), characteristic of shallow colluvium. The two subregions favor contrasting regolith‐organization hypotheses. In the high‐relief, bedrock‐dominated terrain of Subregion 1, landslide occurrence is reproduced most successfully by parameterizations that impose broad elevation‐dependent thinning of regolith while landslide magnitude frequencies are best represented through a curvature‐informed representation. In the lower‐relief, more extensively regolith‐mantled terrain of Subregion 2, curvature‐informed parameterizations that represent local topographic convergence provide the closest agreement with the mapped inventory. These results indicate that landscape‐scale organization of regolith thickness exerts a strong influence on coseismic shallow‐landslide populations within the tested model framework. More broadly, they demonstrate how landslide inventories can be used to evaluate competing hypotheses of regolith distribution where direct observations remain sparse.
c5a2213737507525: The viscosity of volcanic melts governs magma transport, eruption dynamics, and a broad range of magmatic processes, so predicting it as a function of temperature, composition, and dissolved water content is central to physical volcanology. Yet no freely accessible tool integrates global machine-learning predictions, physically motivated viscosity equations, and composition-specific models calibrated to avoid nanocrystallization and water-loss artefacts — experimental biases that can lead conventional viscometry to overestimate melt viscosity. Nor can existing tools show how different assumptions about the dependence of melt fragility on dissolved water propagate into viscosity predictions at eruptive temperatures — a debated question with direct consequences for conduit-flow modelling and eruption-style assessment.,Here we present MELVIS (MELt VIScosity), an open-source web application built with Python and Streamlit. MELVIS comprises three integrated modules: (1) a viscosity calculator based on the artificial neural network of Langhammer et al. (2022), developed using a database of 3,482 measurements spanning basanite to rhyolite including hydrous compositions, with batch processing and TAS-based compositional classification; (2) a hydrous modelling module that parameterises the glass transition temperature Tg(H2O) and melt fragility m(H2O) under three alternative fragility–water relationships, making explicit how model assumptions propagate into viscosity predictions at eruptive temperatures; and (3) a library of seven composition-specific, artefact-free MYEGA models for key volcanic systems. All modules yield closed-form MYEGA parameterisations suitable for direct implementation in numerical eruption models.
04b623327196c83e: Geological CO 2 storage is transitioning from demonstration to industrial-scale deployment, and faults within and around storage complexes exert a first-order control on its safety and performance. Faults can compartmentalise reservoirs through across-fault sealing, provide pathways for vertical migration of CO 2 and brine across caprocks, and host induced seismicity when reactivated by pore-pressure, thermal and geochemical changes during and after injection. These behaviours are not independent in the sense that the same fault can seal hydraulically while remaining critically stressed, or slip without becoming transmissive, and its state can evolve over engineering to geological timescales. We synthesise structural geology, fault-seal analysis, geomechanics, geochemistry, modelling and the operational record from projects including Sleipner, In Salah, Decatur, Quest, Snøhvit, Aquistore and Gorgon. No measurable fault-related leakage from a storage complex has been documented at any saline-aquifer or depleted-gas-field project. Microseismicity on unmapped sub-seismic and basement structures is recurrent, and in 2026 two events above M L 4.0 near Quest became the first felt events at a storage project, provisionally attributed to injection and without effect on containment. Because the pressure and stress perturbation extends far beyond the CO 2 plume, the faults that host seismicity commonly lie beneath or outside the storage complex and loading there can peak after injection stops. We review across-fault sealing proxies and their CO 2 -specific uncertainty, fault-fracture network controls on leakage, induced-seismicity mechanisms, natural analogues, regulatory frameworks and post-injection behaviour, and identify five priority data classes and the coupled workflows needed to convert them into defensible risk envelopes.
6556f18eba3e8430: Oblique terrane entry can reorganize subduction zones and isolate small oceanic domains, but the conditions controlling whether a second subduction develops remain poorly understood. We use 2D and 3D thermo-mechanical models to investigate the roles of lower-crustal rheology and obliquity. In 2D, both continental-type and arc-type terranes localize a secondary dipping boundary, with contrasting geometries. In 3D, obliquity forces slab bending in two directions and produces structural stiffening. Accretion of weak continental crust and associated topographic loading enhance this effect and abort secondary subduction, whereas stronger arc-type crust permits a short-lived triangular oceanic microplate to form. Continued consumption folds the initial slab at depth, providing an additional mode of accommodation of the classical double-subduction space problem. The Taiwan–South China Sea and Molucca–Mindanao systems illustrate these contrasting outcomes. Our results provide mechanical criteria for reconstructing vanished oceanic domains and their magmatic evolution.
dbe5d72b7920d6de: Slowly deforming continental regions (SDCRs) host large earthquakes with long recurrence intervals that limit direct observations, and therefore, our understanding of how strain accumulates and is released through the seismic cycle in these regions. Mongolia is an SDCR where large earthquake surface ruptures of the 20 th century are exceptionally well preserved. We investigate present-day microseismicity within the fault system responsible for the two Mw>8 Tsetserleg-Bulnay earthquake sequence in 1905, northwestern Mongolia, to constrain fault geometry and ongoing seismogenic processes at depth. Using 16 months of data from a temporary seismic network, we construct a catalog of 8,000 earthquakes with M L ≥-0.6. Seismicity delineates the three-dimensional geometry of the main and secondary faults, but is strongly heterogeneous across the system. Several observations indicate that the ongoing activity represents long-lasting aftershocks of the 1905 sequence. First, earthquakes occur throughout the seismogenic crust, both along faults that ruptured in 1905 and on surrounding secondary structures. Second, the present-day rate is consistent with predictions based on the combined Omori and Gutenberg-Richter relations. Third, in agreement with the rate-and-state predictions, the slowly slipping Tsetserleg fault hosts abundant microseismicity compared to the 10-times-faster-slipping Bulnay fault, which accommodated the largest coseismic slip in 1905. These findings show that aftershock sequences can persist for more than a century in SDCRs and preserve key information about historical ruptures and the long-term behavior of such fault systems.
884fa646df3caacb: The Mexican regulations establish precise criteria for the design of buildings, especially about seismic design. To achieve acceptable levels of safety the seismic design spectra must be adjusted considering variables such as the building scale, ductility, hyperstability, specific irregularities, among others. This research focuses on examining risk increment due to the slenderness irregularity in dual systems with frame-wall systems according to the Mexico City building regulations 2017 (RCCDMX17) and its Complementary Technical Standards (NTC17). A large number of simulated buildings realizations with 11, 15 and 20 levels were extensively analyzed using neural networks (multi-layer feed forward, backpropagation) to investigate reliability trends associated with slenderness effects in dual structural systems designed according to the Mexican building regulations (RCCDMX17). These large-scale parametric evaluations of reliability levels in the multi-degree-of-freedom structural systems were performed under a set of seismic actions that would occur in the most unfavorable soil conditions. Based on selected variables that globally represent the analyzed responses (soil conditions, structural parameters, and earthquake motions), the neural model output corresponds to structural reliability expressed through the Cornell β index. Using the obtained neural-β values, the study identifies reliability trends associated with increasing slenderness in dual-system buildings subjected to seismic demands representative of Mexico City soft-soil conditions. The numerical findings suggest that the interaction between geometry, dynamic properties, and material characteristics plays an important role in the reliability behavior of slender structures under severe seismic conditions. Within the analyzed parameter domain, the analyzed archetypes suggest a tendency toward lower reliability for configurations approaching λ ≈ 3 However, this observation should be interpreted as an exploratory reliability-based trend rather than as a generalized or normative slenderness limit.
6bf62919ddf4387c: Earthquake catalogs underpin studies such as fault structure, earthquake processes and seismic hazard, and their value depends on being both complete and reliable. Machine learning has improved individual tasks of earthquake monitoring, but processing stations independently discards the consistency of arrivals across the network, and running tasks in sequence fragments the information describing each earthquake. We present EQNet2, a geometry-aware multi-station Transformer that jointly predicts phase arrivals, first-motion polarities, source location and magnitude, and the association of arrivals into events. On a Northern California test dataset and on continuous waveforms from Ridgecrest and the San Francisco Bay Area, EQNet2 recovers more weak arrivals, produces fewer false detections, and associates more picks into located events. Its learned attention links information across stations along time--distance patterns consistent with seismic moveout. As seismic networks grow denser, exploiting multi-station coherence and event-centric prediction offers a path to more complete and reliable catalogs.
1314b94b5e1c69f3: To address non-uniqueness in geophysical inversions, Generative Neural Networks (GNNs) are often used to parameterise geological or other prior information in a lower-dimensional space (the so-called latent space), thereby reducing the number of inversion parameters. However, the training samples that represent this information are then always incorrect, because Earth structure is not intrinsically low-dimensional, and all GNNs are subject to training errors. Consequently, even when solutions are mapped back to the original higher-dimensional space, they inherit this imperfection and remain restricted to a low-dimensional manifold. From a mathematical point of view, latent space inversion thus fails fundamentally: generally, it can not even reproduce the best, higher-dimensional approximation to the true Earth. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an `escaping prior' distribution, which provides the necessary freedom to find solutions beyond the manifold of GNN-generated solutions, while still using the GNN as a guide. We use a hierarchical Bayesian approach to adapt the strength of prior information to the observed data and synthetic forward function $\textit{a posteriori}$. We illustrate our method on low-dimensional problems where the escaping prior is defined over a 1D manifold in 2D space. We then compare our approach with standard latent space and model space inversions using a uniform prior distribution in synthetic tomography problems, ranging from simple to more geologically realistic cases. Furthermore, we tested scenarios where the true solution is either far from or close to the manifold. In each case, our escaping prior shows significantly better results than the alternatives. It results in solutions beyond each GNN's generative capabilities, solutions which include the best possible model, and clearly demonstrates the limitations of latent space inversion.
de4b0639ab546dde: Prestack seismic inversion often suffers from inherent ill-posedness and is significantly affected by complex factors such as the wavelets, parameter coupling, heterogeneous media, fault displacements, and stratigraphic variations, making it difficult for the conventional inversion methods to accurately recover subsurface information. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a global inversion method based on multi-dimensional matrix multiplication to optimize the inversion results under structure constraints. This method first represents the inversion model as a four-dimensional tensor representing spatial and parameter dimensions. By performing multi-dimensional matrix multiplication operations in various directions of the model, a multi-dimensional tensor of observed data is effectively constructed. Secondly, multi-dimensional regularization are introduced. By analyzing the impact of different dimensional constraints on the inversion results, targeted parameter selection and adjustment are achieved, significantly enhancing the stability of the inversion process and effectively suppressing noise. Finally, stratigraphic and fault constraints extracted from seismic interpretation are incorporated to improve the geological coherence and reasonableness of the inversion results. Both synthetic and field data experiments demonstrate that the proposed method effectively enhances the robustness of inversion in complex structural areas while maintaining high computational efficiency, validating its effectiveness in practical applications.
c97aa354295386f4: Full-waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful approach for reconstructing subsurface velocity models, but its practical performance is limited by ill-conditioning, sensitivity to the update direction, and the high cost of curvature-based methods. In this project, we investigate whether a neural operator trained on reverse-time-migration (RTM) images can provide a useful learned preconditioner for FWI. We compare projected FWI against neural-preconditioned FWI using either a standard Fourier neural operator (FNO) or a Jacobian-informed FNO (JI-FNO). The neural preconditioner applies the normal operator of the learned RTM map to modify the true Devito FWI gradient. Our experiments show that the JI-FNO preconditioner achieves the lowest model error while maintaining data-residual decay comparable to baseline projected FWI. In contrast, the standard FNO preconditioner is unstable and gives worse model recovery, despite using the same neural-preconditioning framework. We also identify a failure mode of a nonlinear neural Gauss Newton-type inner solve: directly matching the neural RTM output to the FWI gradient creates an objective-space mismatch and does not yield a reliable descent direction. These results suggest that forward RTM-image prediction alone is insufficient for learned preconditioning; accurate learned derivatives and objective-consistent use of the neural operator are critical for producing useful inversion updates.
747bd762dcafecc1: Three-dimensional (3D) velocity model building (VMB) remains computationally challenging with conventional approaches and native 3D neural networks, largely due to the prohibitive memory and training cost of full 3D formulations. Therefore, we introduce a depth-progressive framework that achieves 3D VMB using 2D generative diffusion models through a depth-as-channel formulation, in which the depth dimension of each 3D velocity patch is mapped to the channel dimension of a 2D U-Net. This allows the model to synthesize overlapping depth patches sequentially from shallow to deep while conditioning the prediction of the deeper patch on the shallower one, as well as on any available geophysical constraints, including well logs and structural attributes. During training, paired shallow-deep patch pairs with randomized overlaps are used to teach the network how deeper velocity structures relate to shallower information, and a classifier-free guidance strategy enables the model to handle missing constraints gracefully. At inference, starting from a shallow velocity prior, the model recursively generates deeper patches in a top-down manner, and a depth-attenuated Gaussian blending scheme merges overlapping predictions into spatially coherent 3D volumes while accounting for the progressive accumulation of uncertainty at greater depths. Numerical experiments on both in-distribution benchmark models, including Overthrust, SEAM Arid, and SEG/EAGE, and the out-of-distribution Marmousi model demonstrate that the method effectively propagates shallow velocity priors downward and produces high-quality 3D velocity volumes across a range of geological settings and conditioning scenarios. Compared to a 3D benchmark of equivalent architecture, the proposed method significantly reduces parameter count, training cost, and inference cost, while maintaining superior VMB accuracy.
764b22fcae018935: Characterizing subsurface fracture networks is challenging because geometry and connectivity are sparsely observed and uncertain away from measurements. We develop a latent diffusion framework for unconditional and observation-conditioned generation of two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) fracture networks. Fractures and the surrounding matrix are represented as binary fields and compressed by a variational autoencoder into compact spatial latent representations, where an Elucidated Diffusion Model learns their distribution. The 3D model operates on native volumetric fields, with a reconstruction objective designed to preserve sparse, thin fracture structures. Sparse borehole observations are incorporated through a conditioning encoder, classifier-free guidance, and diffusion posterior sampling. Generated ensembles reproduce key fracture-network statistics, including fracture area/volume fraction, two-point correlation, and chord-length distributions. Reconstructed fracture counts and gas-production responses are comparable to those of the reference networks under the considered multiphase flow scenarios. Conditional generation satisfies 99.6% of prescribed well observations in 2D. In 3D, where vertical boreholes constrain full voxel columns, conditional realizations satisfy 84.2% of observed well voxels while maintaining fracture volume and geometry comparable to the reference ensemble. These results demonstrate the potential of latent diffusion models as compact probabilistic representations for fracture-network characterization, ensemble generation, and sparse-observation conditioning.
76f376edce9aae93: We solve the near-tip coupled hydromechanical problem of a hydraulic fracture propagating in a permeable poroelastic medium, represented locally as a semi-infinite crack moving at constant velocity. In the moving tip frame, all fracture fields are steady. The porous solid obeys linear poroelasticity, fracture propagation follows LEFM, fluid flow within the tensile fracture is governed by lubrication theory, and the fracturing and pore fluids are treated as identical Newtonian liquids. The primary unknowns are the fracture opening and the fluid displacement function along the fracture, determined from the resulting non-linear system of equations. In a viscosity--toughness scaling, the problem depends on four dimensionless parameters: a dimensionless permeability $\varrho$ (associated with the intensity of fluid leak-in), a dimensionless effective confining stress $Σ_0'$ (measuring the relative importance of fluid leak-off and leak-in), the drained--undrained Poisson's ratio contrast $β$, and the poroelastic stress coefficient $η$. The solution evolves from a drained, toughness-dominated near-tip asymptote with uniform net pressure to an undrained, storage-viscosity-dominated far-field asymptote. Numerical solutions are obtained over parameter ranges representative of various rock types. The fully coupled model is compared with simplified models, namely uncoupled and one-way coupled formulations, over distances from the fracture front spanning laboratory-to-field scales. The resulting relative difference maps in the $(\varrho,Σ_0')$ parameter space identify four characteristic regimes: negligible poroelastic effects, dominance of the direct mechanical poroelastic response, importance of the poroelastic backstress, and a fully coupled regime. The latter occurs mainly at large $\varrho$ and small $Σ_0'$, corresponding to strong leak-in relative to leak-off.
6f3f6539477c79e5: Shear wave velocity (Vs) is a key parameter used for seismic data processing and evaluating oil and gas reservoirs. Conventional logging and machine learning methods are hampered by the provision of fixed Vs predictions, which limits their capacity to effectively quantify the uncertainty of predictions. Therefore, we propose a spatiotemporal Bayesian neural network (STBNN), which exploits the advantages of ensemble learning methods in processing logging data and Bayesian methods in modeling uncertainty. STBNN facilitates both accurate Vs predictions and a robust quantification of uncertainty. We initially perform a feature selection on logging data to identify logging-sensitive attributes as input features, and employ Monte Carlo dropout, a Bayesian approximation method, to determine both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties. These uncertainties are integrated into the STBNN framework, which reduces prediction uncertainty and enhances accuracy. Subsequently, we assess the model using a logging dataset derived from actual oil reservoirs, and evaluate its generalizability. The trained STBNN model is applied to an untrained exploration area to predict Vs and its associated uncertainties. Finally, we assess the influence of sample size on network epistemic uncertainty and devise a practical mitigation strategy. The results reveal that compared with spatiotemporal neural network and empirical models, the STBNN model achieves a higher accuracy of prediction. We establish that prediction uncertainty is primarily attributable to epistemic uncertainty, with higher uncertainty observed in areas with limited data. This prediction uncertainty can be effectively reduced by increasing the diversity of sample data. The proposed method delivers excellent Vs prediction results, whilst minimizing the risk of errors in the interpretation of logging.
20a7887da5145149: Time-lapse full-waveform inversion (TL-FWI) is increasingly important in energy-transition applications, particularly for monitoring CO2 geologic storage. Because TL-FWI is highly nonlinear and baseline and monitor surveys commonly differ in acquisition, illumination, and noise conditions, uncertainty quantification is essential for reliable interpretation. Two promising Bayesian approaches are Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) and Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD), which represent the posterior in fundamentally different ways. HMC constructs the posterior through stochastic sampling with gradient-based proposals, whereas SVGD approximates it using a deterministically evolving particle ensemble. Here, the feasibility of 2D vertical-seismic-profile (VSP)-based TL-FWI using these two approaches under a matched computational budget was investigated. Both methods recovered the main injection-related velocity anomaly, but they expressed posterior uncertainty differently. Under this resource-limited comparison, HMC yielded uncertainty fields that remained comparatively diffuse and became increasingly difficult to interpret in deeper and off-well regions where illumination is weak. By contrast, SVGD produced uncertainty patterns that are more strongly organized by acquisition geometry, placing larger uncertainty more explicitly in poorly constrained regions, although this also caused the posterior means and profiles to inherit stronger illumination-shaped artifacts. These results suggested that the practical distinction between HMC and SVGD was not one of better or worse uncertainty quantification, but rather how limited computational effort was converted into posterior information. The preferred method was therefore budget- and objective-dependent. Specifically, HMC remained attractive when more exhaustive posterior exploration was computationally feasible, whereas SVGD provided a more scalable and practically interpretable route for rapid uncertainty assessment in TL-FWI monitoring applications.
325ec87f69c43f6b: Conventional geothermal resources are typically associated with volcanically active plate boundaries, yet collisional orogens can also sustain elevated heat flow through radiogenic enrichment, crustal thickening, and rapid exhumation. Northern Pakistan, encompassing the Himalaya, Kohistan, and Karakoram terranes, hosts numerous hot springs aligned with major fault zones despite the absence of active volcanism. The origin of this anomalous heat remains debated, reflecting the lack of surface heat-flow measurements and limited geophysical constraints on the lithosphere. To address this gap, we apply 1D steady-state, 1D transient, and 2D advective-conductive thermal models with radiogenic heat production and exhumation-driven heat transport to the Nanga Parbat Massif, Kohistan arc, and Karakoram terrane. These models, in the absence of direct heat-flow measurements in the region, remain uncalibrated; however, they bracket a range of plausible thermal states. Steady-state models show a strong dependence of geotherms on crustal radiogenic heat production (RHP): in the NPM, upper-crustal enrichment (4–5 µW m −3 ) yields surface heat flow of 85–120 mW m −2 , whereas Kohistan produces lower values (50–85 mW m −2 ) due to its mafic-dominated crust. Karakoram yields intermediate heat flow (65–103 mW m −2 ), with RHP concentrated in the batholith and metamorphic complexes. These models also reveal that surface-derived RHP values cannot be extrapolated to the mid- and lower crust: doing so yields Moho temperatures inconsistent with petrological and geophysical constraints, implying redistribution of heat-producing elements during partial melting and differentiation. 1D transient models suggest that exhumation of 2–3 mm yr −1 in the NPM can further amplify geotherms, producing surface heat flow up to 220–250 mW m −2 and inverting deep geotherms at 20 km in exploratory end-member scenarios. 2D models capture the combined effects of radiogenic enrichment, exhumation, and rugged topography. Isotherms are compressed beneath valleys and expanded beneath peaks, with the strongest thermal anomalies localized in the NPM and Karakoram. Surface heat-flow patterns reflect these contrasts, ranging from ∼120 mW m −2 (moderate scenarios) to nearly 180 mW m −2 (fast exhumation). Péclet numbers ranging from below unity to greater than unity indicate that exhumation progressively increases the contribution of advective heat transport. Crustal differentiation indices calculated from the model-derived heat-flow estimates are consistent with strong upper-crustal enrichment of heat-producing elements in the NPM and Karakoram, indicating their redistribution during crustal thickening and partial melting. The models suggest that the region can sustain anomalously high heat flow through the interplay of RHP, exhumation, and crustal differentiation. For northern Pakistan, these results provide a physical basis for the widespread hydrothermal activity and indicate elevated subsurface temperatures in the NPM and Karakoram, identifying them as regions that warrant further site-specific investigation of reservoir properties and hydrogeological conditions.
767edf65af2f6973: Low-frequency marine seismic sources are becoming increasingly important for enhancing deep-target illumination and improving the stability of broadband imaging, particularly for Full-Waveform Inversion and quantitative imaging. This study investigates the modeling of a large-volume low-frequency marine source designed to radiate energy down to about 1 Hz. Unlike conventional air guns, this source operates in a distinct physical regime, generating a much larger bubble and a longer oscillation period. In deep water, field observations show that spherical lumped-parameter models already provide a robust first-order description of its acoustic signature. Because the Tuned Pulse Source (TPS) behaves as a single, nearly omnidirectional point source, it produces a simpler and more controlled wavefield than conventional air-gun arrays, creating favorable conditions for precise source characterization and predictive modeling. In shallow-water and transition-zone environments, the larger bubble size, stronger hydrostatic pressure gradients, buoyancy, and free-surface interaction motivate a more refined representation of source dynamics. These effects are expected to influence the low-frequency signature, particularly through stronger coupling between the source pulse and surface ghost reflections. The paper therefore evaluates the range of applicability of conventional spherical source models for such configurations and identifies the conditions under which higher-fidelity approaches can further improve source characterization. It also highlights the potential of Boundary Element Methods (BEM) to capture non-spherical bubble dynamics and more complex boundary interactions, while addressing the associated mathematical and numerical challenges. Overall, the study establishes a physics-based framework for progressively improving TPS modeling in shallow-water settings and supports future experimental validation in transition-zone applications.
d75d49da90383b36: Recent advances in ocean-bottom node acquisition and GPU-enabled computing have established inversion-based methods such as Least-Squares Migration (LSM) and Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) as key tools for high-resolution seismic imaging. However, extending these workflows to higher frequencies and multi-parameter settings introduces persistent challenges, including noise amplification, slow convergence, high computational cost, and severe parameter cross-talk. This study revisits wavelet transform methods as an integral component of the imaging process rather than a pre- or post-processing tool. Exploiting their multiscale, localized, and directional characteristics, we embed wavelet representations directly within inversion workflows to improve scalability, efficiency, and image quality. Applications include wavelet-domain gradient conditioning, adaptive image-domain LSM via Hessian filtering, and practical Hessian-based preconditioning for FWI. We further extend this framework to multi-parameter FWI through a wavelet-domain block Hessian inversion strategy, enabling explicit decoupling of parameter sensitivities without relying on conventional heuristics such as reparameterization or staged inversion. Results from synthetic and field examples, including the Atlantis dataset, demonstrate accelerated convergence, enhanced image fidelity, and substantial reduction of cross-talk. These results position the wavelet transform as a scalable and unifying toolkit for next-generation inversion-driven seismic imaging.
97cc81c1874f4852: On 2 May 2025, an Mw 7.4 earthquake occurred ∼120 km off the southern tip of Tierra del Fuego, at the transition of the Shackleton Fracture Zone and the Chile Trench. This event exhibits reverse‐faulting mechanisms with relatively steeply dipping planes and is the largest recorded along this complex plate boundary. Most aftershocks have similar mechanisms, although some show strike‐slip and normal faulting. To better resolve the activated fault system under limited station coverage, we relocated events and incorporated pP‐sP phases identified using a trained classifier to refine focal depths. A multichannel seismic reflection line provides additional insights into the structure of the subduction complex. We infer that the mainshock nucleated on the subduction interface or within the plate of the southernmost Chilean subduction system, with aftershocks marking activation of steeper structures. This behavior emphasizes how convergent and strike‐slip fault systems interact to complicate earthquake rupture at plate boundary transitions.
b293733499364f19: Accurately forecasting injection‐induced seismicity remains a major challenge that is critically important for energy production and storage as controlling mechanisms are complex and remain opaque. We clarify key processes by following time‐histories of bespoke parameters anticipated to control strength reduction (drawdown) through overpressure during fluid injection. Injection‐driven radial overpressure fields motivate key parameter groups representing magnitudes () and rates () of strength‐drawdown. We emphasize these physics‐informed features as inputs embedded in a two‐stage machine learning (ML) architecture applied to high‐resolution microseismic and injection data from the Utah FORGE and EGS Collab stimulation experiments. Permuted models, selectively including then excluding these physically‐inspired terms, predict temporal seismic evolution and capture trends and peaks with testable and discernible fidelity. Improved predictions result from including these diagnostic parameters—confirming that the derived physical parameters mechanistically mediate seismicity. The magnitude of strength drawdown () dictates the size and localization of seismic events during phases of steep spatial pressurization—particularly early in the injection phase near the well. Conversely, governs the timing and rate of onset of seismic activity during rapid injection transients, accounting for elapsed‐time effects. Our approach demonstrates the broader benefits of embedding physics‐guided features into ML frameworks toward mitigation of seismic hazard.
8c3d40efbe6426b5: Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) allows meter-scale measurements along kilometer-scale fiber-optic cables, offering new opportunities to develop ground-motion models (GMMs) that resolve spatial variations in ground motion. However, developing GMMs from DAS measurements remains challenging because DAS observations are influenced by DAS-specific nonergodic components not present in seismometer-based measurements, including cable coupling and orientation. Moreover, channel correlation in DAS measurements can lead to biased uncertainty estimates of ground-motion variability when DAS channels are treated as independent stations; therefore, configuring correlation is essential for the reliable development of DAS-based GMMs. Here, we present the first regional, partially nonergodic DAS-based GMM using strain-rate data from a 400-channel array in Hualien City, Taiwan. We compile a dataset of peak strain rates and Fourier amplitudes (0.1–10 Hz) from 77 earthquakes (3.2≤Mw≤7.1, 45.75≤Rhypo≤170.80 km). Building upon classical seismometer-based GMMs, we extend the variability framework to consider (1) cable coupling associated with installation and environment types and (2) cable orientation. We further model (3) channel correlation inherent to DAS measurement principles and array geometry using Matérn kernels parameterized by both along-fiber channel and Euclidean distances. The resulting DAS-based GMM achieves magnitude–distance scaling comparable with classical GMMs, while allowing decomposition of ground-motion variability. We observe that the cable-coupling component exerts a broadband effect on ground motions and emerges as a dominant, frequency-dependent source of within-event variability. The orientation component captures frequency-dependent DAS directional sensitivity related to cable orientation and wavefront azimuth, and accounts for only a small portion of the variability. Introducing channel correlation substantially reduces channel-related standard deviations. Overall, our findings demonstrate that DAS-derived ground motions require a fundamentally different framework from classical seismometer-based GMMs, emphasizing the importance of deployment metadata and correlation modeling and providing a foundation for next-generation seismic hazard assessments using dense fiber-optic sensing.
81b48ef9f6cb7984: Accurate seismic source location remains challenging when earthquakes occur outside or near the edges of seismic networks. Standard network methods require favorable azimuthal coverage and suffer from severe distance–depth trade-offs, whereas conventional array approaches assume planar wavefronts and are restricted to distant sources. Here, we introduce NetArray, a methodology that unifies network and array approaches within a single framework. Based on a planar–radial decomposition of interstation delays, NetArray relaxes the plane-wave assumption to explicitly account for wavefront curvature. This yields a semianalytical, velocity-model-independent cost function that jointly constrains back azimuth, epicentral distance, and horizontal slowness. After the slowness vector and epicentral distance are resolved, a velocity model is used to constrain source depth, avoiding the distance–depth trade-off inherent to network methods. Synthetic tests demonstrate that NetArray notably improves back-azimuth accuracy relative to standard array methods at distances up to several times the array aperture while providing reliable estimates of epicentral distance and depth. Compared with conventional network approaches, NetArray yields more stable solutions for out-of-network sources and provides explicit minimum and maximum distance bounds for uncertainty estimation. Application to a virtual array in the Mendocino Triple Junction region highlights NetArray’s potential for earthquake early warning systems: using a limited number of stations, the method successfully mitigates the offshore distance overestimation inherited in network approaches. These results demonstrate that NetArray provides a robust, unified framework for real-time and offline seismic source location.
1cfc30bbf7183eb9: Deep low-frequency earthquakes (LFEs) exhibit unique occurrence patterns distinct from those of regular earthquakes, but the physical conditions governing their occurrence and the spatial variations in their activity remain poorly understood. Among various types of slow earthquakes, LFEs are detected as discrete seismic events by ordinary seismometers, and detailed analysis of their activity has the potential to provide important insights into the underlying mechanisms of slow earthquakes. Therefore, we analyze tectonic LFEs in Shikoku using an epidemic-type aftershock sequence (ETAS) model to investigate spatial variations in seismicity. To account for spatial interactions inherent in spatially distributed seismicity, we modify the classic ETAS approach by incorporating a reference region surrounding the target region. The analysis reveals that the background seismicity rate correlates with the total seismicity rate. Furthermore, we focus on the background fraction, which is defined as the ratio of the background seismicity rate to the total seismicity rate. We find a relatively high background fraction at both shallower and deeper ends of the source region. This result indicates that the depth dependency of the seismicity is not a simple monotonic transition, from shallow periodic to deep continuous, but instead reflects a more complex pattern. At the down-dip end, triggering is likely suppressed because of the dominance of ductile deformation, which not only reduces the elastic stress level but also inhibits efficient stress propagation for triggering. In contrast, at the up-dip end, the proximity to the region of megathrust events, where no dislocation is either allowed or at least observed at interseismic periods, may also inhibit stress propagation, leading to a similar increase in the background fraction. These results suggest that spatial variations in both temperature–pressure conditions and frictional properties influence LFEs in a nonmonotonic manner along the dip direction.
7299b26bfaeb67d7: On 31 August 2025 (UTC), an Mw 6.0 shallow thrust earthquake struck the southern Hindu Kush region of Afghanistan, followed by a largest aftershock (Mw 5.6) on 4 September. This earthquake sequence caused widespread damage and unusually high casualties. To investigate the seismogenic structure, we utilized Sentinel-1 Terrain Observation with Progressive Scans Synthetic Aperture Radar data for Differential Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar processing to derive the coseismic deformation fields of both the mainshock and aftershock. The results show that the maximum cumulative deformation reached 24.2 cm in the ascending track and 17.0 cm in the descending track in line of sight, with consistent trends moving toward the satellites. The optimal earthquake slip model reveals a set of conjugate thrust faults, including the mainshock segment F1 (north-dipping, peak slip ≈ 1.11 m) and the aftershock segment F2 (south-dipping, peak slip ≈ 0.99 m). Integrating the regional fault network with these newly resolved faults, we interpret the earthquake sequence as the reactivation of a positive flower structure, which is likely controlled by flexural bending processes of the Konar fault system, the major tectonic boundary of the local crustal block. A Coulomb failure stress change (ΔCFS) analysis shows that the mainshock had effective triggering effects on the following sequence. Meanwhile, positive ΔCFS has also been loaded in the bend segment of the Konar fault through the earthquake sequence, highlighting this region as a locus of elevated seismic hazard potential for future.
a670fc7a60f9f25f: Dynamic-rupture simulations commonly prescribe rupture initiation, which complicates assessment of where instability would preferentially localize for a given fault geometry and tectonic loading. We present a 3D finite-element workflow that maps relative nucleation tendency on embedded frictional fault systems without preassigning an initiation point. Faults are represented as frictional contact interfaces within an elastic volume. Gravity is retained in both branches to provide the depth-dependent normal-stress background and stable contact closure on embedded frictional interfaces. The workflow employs paired branches on the same undeformed geometry with an identical mesh: a gravity-only quasi-static baseline and a gravity-plus-tectonic branch that differs only by a small displacement boundary condition. Each quasi-static state is transferred to a short implicit transient analysis on the same undeformed mesh under the same gravity and compatible boundary constraints. Slip may occur through the contact-state transition from sticking to sliding in the transient stage. We define the onset slip s(x) as the slip accumulated over the first N dynamic increments (default N = 1) and use the differential onset slip Δs(x) between the paired branches as a single-event indicator of nucleation tendency. Timestep tests over Δt=0.001–0.05 s identify the same peak node, and 1–2 km meshes give consistent localization at 15–16 km depth; coarser 3–4 km meshes shift the peak to 3–5 km depth, whereas the thresholded high-slip footprint remains resolution dependent.
1efa884a9e17dfb5: Slow-slip events (SSEs) have been reported in the Cook Inlet segment of the Alaska–Aleutian subduction zone. Tectonic tremor, a repeating low-frequency signal, has been observed in the subduction zone in the Upper Cook Inlet (UCI) slow-slip zone, but thus far no studies have identified tremor in the Lower Cook Inlet (LCI) region. This study addresses whether or not tremor occurred in the LCI from 2015 to 2017, a time window that includes multiple SSEs. Two methods are used to search for tremor within continuous data from 34 broadband stations. The first approach utilizes envelope cross-correlations across an array of stations to identify clusters of seismic events. The second method tracks relative changes in the frequency content of seismic records over time at a single station. Neither approach provides evidence of events that can conclusively be identified as tectonic tremor. Subsequently, we consider whether tremor in the LCI might be masked by noise and basin effects by simulating seismograms of tremor-like signals. Stations within the basin have high noise levels that may interfere with visual verification of tremor, but methods that leverage cross correlations should identify tremor. The apparent absence of tremor in the LCI during SSEs supports the hypothesis that fundamental differences in subduction zone geometry, thermal state, sediment load, or other properties between the LCI, where the Pacific plate subducts, and the UCI, where the Yakutat slab is found, play a role in allowing or inhibiting tremor. This work underscores emerging evidence that coupled episodic tremor and slip is not globally ubiquitous.
40744d2ee6242725: Rapid spatial characterization of rupture in tsunamigenic earthquakes (Mw≥7.5) is critical for improving tsunami early warning capabilities, particularly for sparsely instrumented regions. We investigate how regional array seismology can be optimized for such settings by enhancing real-time rupture imaging. Using the Multiple Signal Classification (MUSIC) backprojection technique, we evaluate regional array processing performance with the New Zealand broadband seismic network in the Southwest Pacific. Performance is assessed using synthetic earthquakes spanning a range of magnitudes (Mw 8.5–9.1), rupture lengths, directivities (unilateral and bilateral), and source–array geometries (epicentral distances and back azimuths). Results show that the New Zealand seismic network can reliably constrain rupture extent for large regional tsunamigenic earthquakes, with an average rupture length error of less than ∼15%. Earthquake magnitude primarily governs the optimum processing parameters (frequency band and time window length), whereas source–array geometry ultimately limits the rupture imaging quality that can be achieved. Integrating MUSIC-derived rupture extents into tsunami warning workflows generally improves agreement with reference tsunami forecasts compared with magnitude-based scaling alone, demonstrating the value of rapid spatial rupture constraints as a complement to magnitude and ocean observations. These findings provide practical guidance for parameter selection in real-time rupture imaging and highlight the potential of MUSIC-based array processing for rapid characterization of large tsunamigenic earthquakes.
64afbe1a66f0b1fd: Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) provides spatially dense measurements of coseismic deformation, but detection of a deformation signal does not imply that its generating earthquake source is well constrained or that heterogeneous fault slip is spatially recoverable. This study develops an information-theoretic framework that separates three levels of earthquake-source inference: statistical detection, local source-parameter identifiability and finite-fault recoverability. Detection is quantified using a whitened known-template statistic; local identifiability is characterized through the eigenspectrum of a prior-scaled Fisher information matrix, from which an effective identifiable dimension, information gain and invariant weak-subspace diagnostics are derived; and finite-fault recoverability is quantified using a prior-conditioned slip-information operator and an effective recoverable slip dimension. Controlled elastic-dislocation experiments vary earthquake magnitude, centroid depth, fault dip, viewing geometry, spatial covariance, nuisance components, data loss, spatial sampling and complementary observations. To isolate fault geometry, the principal benchmarks use common strike, rake and rupture scaling and vary only dip between ${{30}^ \circ }$, ${{55}^ \circ }$ and ${{85}^ \circ }$. At 10 km centroid depth, the ${{P}_{{\rm{det}}}} = 0.5$ boundary precedes the illustrative ${{d}_{{\rm{eff}}}} = 5$ level by 0.600, 0.533 and 0.436 magnitude units for the three dips, respectively; this ordering persists wherever both transitions lie within the analysed magnitude–depth domain. Complementary line-of-sight geometries and additional geodetic observations increase information when they constrain source directions that remain weak in the existing data, whereas correlated noise, selective removal of informative observations and spatial decimation substantially reduce local identifiability. Finite-fault experiments show that numerical model dimension and information-supported dimensionality can diverge strongly: At 10 km depth, increasing the discretization from 12 to 160 slip patches raises the prior-conditioned effective recoverable dimension only from 5.88 to 6.56, while at 20 km depth it changes from 2.86 to 2.94. The resulting magnitude–depth regime maps demonstrate that InSAR earthquake-source observability is task dependent: Detection, local source identifiability and finite-fault recoverability quantify different properties of the same source-observation system and should therefore be evaluated separately.
02c2b77bd3a9119f: The 2010 M L 6.4 Jiashian earthquake was a significant earthquake in the fold-and-thrust belt region in southwestern Taiwan, rupturing along the Chihshan Transfer Fault zone. In this study, we collected data from a temporary seismic network deployed after the mainshock to construct an aftershock catalog containing 2506 events, surpassing the event counts of previous studies, using deep-learning-based tools. The aftershocks are then relocated using the double-difference method and used as the input for a 3D seismic tomography inversion combined with regional travel time data. The alignment of the relocated earthquake sequence reveals the structure of the seismogenic fault, trending in the northwest direction and gently dipping to the northeast at a depth of 15 km to 25 km, with three clusters: Cluster 1 aligns with the mainshock's northwest propagation, while Clusters 2 and 3 emerge southwest and south, indicating subsidiary faults. The seismic tomography images also reveal the structure of the major Chaozhou Fault in the area as the boundary between contrasting velocity zones and the seismogenic zone characterized by low velocity and a high Vp/Vs ratio structure. We determined 329 new focal mechanism solutions by first-motion P-wave polarity inversion. The P-axes of the aftershocks are predominantly oriented northeast-southwest, with greater variability in the north-south and northwest-southeast directions for earthquakes with magnitudes less than 2. The results of this study reveal the complexity of the Chihshan Transfer Fault zone and southwestern Taiwan's seismotectonics.
59bfd22e7f8f3786: The 24 June 2026 Mw 7.5 Venezuela earthquake caused massive damage in Caraballeda, on the northern coast of Venezuela. No strong-motion records were obtained in the city or anywhere else within 10 km of the rupture. We estimate the time history and intensity of the ground-motion pulse that struck Caraballeda from two closed-circuit television (CCTV) recordings, tracking the frictional sliding of a traffic delineator post and the oscillation of a light pole. In the orientation of strongest horizontal intensity, the inferred motion reaches a peak ground velocity of 202 cm/s and an incremental velocity of 366 cm/s, comparable with the most intense ground motions ever recorded and consistent with the practically simultaneous collapse of eight buildings visible in the footage. The reconstructed displacement spectral ordinate at 1 s in the maximum horizontal orientation exceeds the Next Generation Attenuation-West2 (NGA-West2) median, adjusted for directivity and directionality, by 1.32 standard deviations. NGA-West2 models predict the median intensity from all horizontal orientations, missing the strong polarization of this motion, which for this site is largest close to the strike-normal orientation. Moreover, between 0.5 and 2.5 s, the reconstructed intensities exceed those in Venezuelan seismic design standards by an average factor of approximately 1.88.
eb103e2c7e4268a8: Central Africa marks a major collisional zone of the Pan-African Orogeny, involving convergence of the Congo and Kalahari plates during Gondwana assembly ($\sim$600–500 Ma). This collision formed the Lufilian Belt and one of the world’s most significant metallogenic provinces—the Central African Copperbelt. However, the deep lithospheric architecture underpinning this mineral-rich region remains poorly understood. Fundamental questions persist regarding the role of subduction, convergence polarity and suture-zone geometry. We address this using broad-band seismic data collected across Zambia’s Pan-African orogenic belts to construct a lithospheric shear-wave velocity model via joint inversion of receiver functions and surface waves. Common conversion point stacking of P-to-S receiver functions further enhances imaging of subsurface discontinuities. Our results reveal pronounced crustal deformation below the central Lufilian Belt, where the Moho is deepest ($\sim$48 km) and most gradational, marking the suture zone during continent-continent collision. Elsewhere, Moho architecture is shallower and uniform despite protracted convergence, suggesting lower-crustal flow accompanying orogenesis smoothed crustal thickness contrasts. At mantle depths, thick (160–180 km), homogeneously fast velocity (4.5–4.74 km s−1) lithosphere delineates the unmodified Congo Craton margin. Further south, thinner lithosphere (140–150 km) contains a pervasive mid-lithospheric low-velocity zone (4.3–4.4 km s−1) at 50–80 km depth, interpreted as metasomatically modified Proterozoic lithosphere rich in easily-fusible phases emplaced during Pan-African subduction. This contrast in mantle wave speeds, together with southward-dipping Moho geometry and intracrustal structure, indicates underthrusting of the Congo beneath the Kalahari Plate. The spatial coincidence of mantle metasomes and zones of crustal reworking with critical mineral occurrences across the Copperbelt highlights their role in creating favourable conditions for mineralization in overlying sedimentary basins.
