6c5f3f7f20384d81: The 2025 M 7.8 Mandalay earthquake ruptured ~480 km of the Sagaing Fault, producing one of the longest strike-slip events documented and impacting a vulnerable region. Here we combine remote sensing observations and numerical modeling to show that the subsurface fault geometry and slip distribution could be anticipated from pre-event observations. Along-strike variations in coseismic and interseismic deformation reveal a helix-shaped fault geometry. The average coseismic slip equals or exceeds the interseismic slip deficit, consistent with a minimally slip-predictable model. We generate an ensemble of 3D dynamic rupture models, constrained by the best-fit static slip model, then discriminate among them using independent space-geodetic, seismic, and near-field video observations. The preferred scenario begins bilaterally, then transitions to unilateral southward supershear propagation at depth, while shallow rupture remains subshear. These dynamics are shaped by localized stress heterogeneity and low fracture energy, characteristic of a structurally mature fault zone. Our approach can inform rupture scenarios in understudied regions.
c5606de088f6b74a: Lower Carboniferous Limestone (LCL) is a promising geothermal target in Britain, but uncertainty in subsurface structure and permeability limits resource assessment. Here, we use the Welton area of the East Midlands, where legacy hydrocarbon exploration data provide detailed subsurface coverage, to investigate the controls on LCL geothermal prospectivity. We integrate 3D seismic reflection, well, gravity and aeromagnetic data with gravity forward and inverse modelling to characterise the geometry and structural evolution of the LCL. Seismic interpretation reveals a heterogeneous reservoir partitioned into a western rift-bounding fault corridor, an eastern relay system and a northern fault-intersection zone, together with fault-tip and segment-linkage structures. Seismic-stratigraphic relationships record late Carboniferous reactivation of this inherited extensional architecture, expressed by localised LCL doming and erosion, Namurian absence and onlap, and onlap within the lowermost Westphalian. These relationships indicate variable inversion and possible weathering or palaeo-karst development on uplifted LCL highs. Gravity and magnetic lineaments reproduce and extend seismic-scale structural trends, while source-depth estimates indicate that parts of the fault network were localised above deeper inherited fabrics. Gravity modelling shows that plausible LCL density variations alone cannot explain the observed gravity field, requiring deeper or unmodelled density heterogeneity. The integrated results define three conceptual structural geothermal plays: a fault-damage-zone play, a relay/linkage play and a fault-intersection play. These settings may favour secondary permeability through fracturing, augmented by inversion-related deformation and possible palaeokarst development, although present-day transmissivity remains unconstrained. This study demonstrates how legacy seismic and potential-field datasets can support geothermal targeting in structurally complex carbonate reservoirs.
5b7752836ef9af2f: Over the past billion years, Earth’s large-scale tectonics have been dominated by the assembly and breakup of supercontinents Rodinia and Pangea. It is widely accepted that circum-supercontinent subduction and associated sub-supercontinent upwelling trigger supercontinent breakup. Yet, previous geodynamic simulations predicted that whole mantle convection would stabilize in a fixed, long-wavelength mode, with a common degree-1 pattern resembling a stable supercontinent. In contrast, geological records show that continental arcs rapidly formed along circum-supercontinent passive margins shortly prior to the breakup of Rodinia and Pangea, indicating successful subduction initiation and an evolving supercontinent cycle. Thus, it requires an additional mechanism for subduction initiation along circum-supercontinent passive margins beyond self-organizing mantle flow. Here, we propose a new mechanism for subduction initiation at the passive margin before supercontinent breakup, based on geological records and the recent finding that the cratonic lithospheric mantle comprises a buoyant upper layer, a weak mid-lithospheric discontinuity, and a dense lower layer. We demonstrate that perturbations, such as plume underplating or melt infiltration, could initiate delamination of the dense lower cratonic mantle lithosphere, while the remaining buoyant continent uplifts, weakening the nearby passive margin and decoupling the continental and oceanic lithosphere. Eventually, the enhanced density contrast across the former passive margin leads to the formation of a new ocean-continent subduction zone. We suggest that this new subduction initiation mechanism is a key driver of the periodic operation of supercontinent cycles, modulating Earth’s long-term tectonic evolution.
f2b3c22c7c75fb5c: Data products of the manuscript "Global terrain correction of continental heat flow with a neural-operator surrogate of three-dimensional heat-conduction simulations". See README.md for the data dictionary and usage limitations.
58a745b445616664: Code accompanying "Global terrain correction of continental heat flow with a neural-operator surrogate of three-dimensional heat-conduction simulations".
3a72effa4f1a1b68: Seismic hazard and structural analyses require broadband ground-motion time histories, yet the high-frequency band (above 1~Hz) is the hardest to obtain: physics-based simulations are too costly at these frequencies, and stochastic methods lose the deterministic phase, directivity, and long-period coherence that control structural demand. We present HighFEM-2, a latent denoising-diffusion waveform model trained with rectified flow matching on a multi-modal diffusion transformer. It synthesizes three-component acceleration up to 50~Hz, conditioned on a low-frequency waveform below the source corner frequency and on magnitude, hypocenter and station location, and $V_{S30}$. The low-frequency waveform supplies the deterministic source, path, and directivity, so the network learns only the regional high-frequency scattering. Conditioning each station on its own waveform lets HighFEM-2 generate records for all stations of an earthquake that share its source and low-frequency path terms. Trained on 195{,}138 Italian INSTANCE records ($M_w$ 1.4--6.5, within 200~km), HighFEM-2 produces realistic waveforms: it reproduces observed peak amplitudes with small bias ($0.042 \pm 0.088$ log units for PGA, $0.057 \pm 0.090$ for PGV) and matches observed envelopes, Fourier spectra, and integrated velocity and displacement. The conditioning waveform can come from a simulation or a filtered record, and ensembles of realizations sample the high-frequency variability given that input. HighFEM-2 thus provides fast, regionally calibrated broadband time histories for hazard and risk assessment, including near-fault scenarios where recordings are scarce.
c7fb5f2a99d3a865: Permafrost contains liquid pore water even at subzero temperatures, and the partitioning between pore ice and unfrozen water governs its mechanical and hydrological properties. Resolving this partitioning at depth and across short lateral distances remains challenging because direct subsurface observations are spatially sparse. Here, we apply active-source multichannel analysis of surface waves (MASW) using a long-term distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) cable and conventional geophone arrays at five sites along a ~2 km transect in Utqiagvik, Alaska, that captures a transition from a disturbed roadside environment to the Arctic coast. Shear-wave velocity profiles are converted to seismically inferred unfrozen pore water content (Sw) using a load-bearing effective-medium framework and compared against a depth-dependent reference constructed from local borehole temperatures and laboratory freezing curves measured on permafrost cores. Departures from this reference are spatially organized. The DAS-derived departure metric increases toward the coastal end of the transect, while the geophone-derived profiles show greater variability but also identify the site closest to the coast (Tundra 4) as having the largest departure. At this site, the DAS-derived profile remains higher than the temperature reference through much of the deeper section. These results suggest that temperature and shallow laboratory measurements alone do not fully explain the observed permafrost structure, particularly beneath water-rich coastal tundra surfaces characterized by ponds and lakes. The framework introduced here provides a transferable approach for integrating seismic, thermal, and laboratory data to characterize spatially variable permafrost at depth in locations where the reference estimate process would be expected to deviate most from true subsurface conditions.
afbcf8869a62bf88: Faults accommodate shear motion in the upper crust through brittle deformation like fracturing and cataclastic flow. The width of the embrittlement, the lateral extent of the fault, and the grain size distribution within the fault core seem to scale with shear displacement, though scaling laws have large uncertainties. Inherited structures may drive strain partitioning, restrict damage extension, and either favour or hinder seismic slip propagation. It is difficult to explore these features in natural faults since delicate structures such as crackle breccias and gouges are reworked during exhumation, overprinted during multiple deformation cycles, and altered by surface weathering. The Bedretto Underground Laboratory represents a unique chance to study the structure of immature faults at depth, whose pristine structures are hardly preserved elsewhere in the field. The exceptional exposure allowed for a detailed analysis of a fault zone named Waterfault, which exploited the pre-existing fabrics of a mylonitic shear zone in the Rotondo granite. The limited extension of the damage zone and the scarce presence of cataclastic products indicates that the fault's activity was short-lived, possibly stemming from a single slip event. The presence of pulverised rocks, restricted to the hanging-wall side, suggests that faulting was produced during the propagation of a low magnitude earthquake. The pre-existing mylonitic fabrics provided a strong mechanical anisotropy, which confined the damage zone and favoured the lateral extension of the fault. We argue that the WF structures illustrate the onset of faulting along pre-existing anisotropies, revealing their role in the partitioning of energy and strain.
ecfdcf337a270b1c: Response-spectrum matching is an underdetermined waveform inverse problem in which spectral compatibility must be achieved without uncontrolled changes in other engineering-relevant ground-motion characteristics. This study formulates the problem as differentiable waveform inverse design using a fixed SDOF dynamics engine and configurable optimization modules. An envelope-guided parameterization defines the correction waveform, while a hard projection enforces zero correction-induced terminal velocity and displacement. Differentiable SDOF responses then provide gradients for waveform optimization. Spectral fidelity and Arias-intensity accumulation are treated as adaptive objectives. Spectral feasibility, PGA, total Arias intensity, and displacement-path requirements are incorporated as constraints. The differentiable spectrum operator agrees with an exact solution of the equation of motion to within 0.002%. The complete five-damping configuration achieves a maximum spectral error of 5.00% over 375 ordinates. On a common benchmark, maximum errors of 2.61% and 8.47% are obtained for single- and multi-damping matching, respectively, while retaining the additional waveform constraints. Three-component applications further show that different engineering acceptance requirements can be accommodated through module reconfiguration without changing the forward dynamics.
0129080e768fcd31: Full waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful tool for high-resolution subsurface model reconstruction, but it remains highly nonlinear and ill-posed, especially when the initial model is inaccurate or the acquired data are noisy and incomplete. Annealed Stein variational gradient descent (ASVGD) provides a particle-based Bayesian framework for FWI by approximating the posterior distribution with an ensemble of velocity models, thereby enabling uncertainty quantification beyond a single deterministic solution. However, conventional ASVGD-FWI commonly relies on simple handcrafted priors, such as Gaussian or smoothing assumptions, which are often insufficient to represent complex geological structures. To address this limitation, we introduce a learned diffusion model (DM) as an implicit regularization mechanism within the ASVGD-FWI framework. Instead of explicitly evaluating the diffusion prior density, the trained diffusion model acts as a learned geological projection operator that guides updated particles toward the distribution of plausible velocity models. In this way, the proposed method combines data consistency from FWI, posterior diversity from ASVGD, and structural realism from the diffusion prior. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the diffusion-regularized ASVGD-FWI produces more geologically consistent mean models, suppresses nonphysical artifacts, and yields uncertainty estimates that are more concentrated around structurally complex and poorly constrained regions. These results suggest that learned diffusion priors can effectively enhance Bayesian FWI by improving both inversion stability and the interpretability of posterior uncertainty.
b475b4d9065dacf9: Surface-related multiple elimination (SRME) is an indispensable processing step in marine seismic exploration, comprising two main components: multiple prediction and adaptive subtraction. While the multiple prediction is theoretically data-driven and relies on the data itself, the adaptive subtraction step requires a fairly subjective manual control. Our approach introduces a purely data-driven and physics-based deep learning (PDL) algorithm for improving the adaptive multiple subtraction to significantly enhanced performance. There are two main innovations in the proposed deep-learning (DL) multiple subtraction approaches: first, being data-driven and self-supervised, which removes the dependence on inflexible label preparation and model training processes; secondly, being governed by the adaptive matching filtering (AMF) equation to guide the training process. The DL module serves as a strong regression filter analogous to the traditionally known AMF. We segment a moderately sized seismic profile and an initial multiple model into a large number of patches using a patching scheme for self-contained training. The number of patches is controlled by the patch size and the shift size to enable a sufficient number of training samples required by mainstream DL platforms. The patching-based self-training and regression approach, PDL, is inherently a non-stationary matching approach that aims to obtain a globally optimal matching from the initial multiple models to the input full wavefield data through iterative patching-based training. It is also closely connected with the non-stationary regression approach, which was developed almost two decades ago. However, the PDL approach achieves even stronger regression performance due to the backpropagation-based optimization mechanism in DL, and has shown significantly improved multiple subtraction performance over a number of examples.
3cd8e2f83ba511d9: Recent seismic observations suggest the presence of a basal molten layer above the Martian core that may represent a long-lived basal magma ocean (BMO). However, its influence on the coupled thermal evolution of the Martian mantle and core remains poorly understood. Here, we employ a two-dimensional mantle convection model coupled with parameterized thermal evolution models for the core and BMO to investigate the long-term interior evolution of Mars. Our results show that a long-lived BMO modifies core-mantle thermal coupling by regulating heat exchange between the core and mantle and maintaining elevated temperatures in the lowermost mantle. In particular, enrichment of heat-producing elements (HPEs) within the BMO enhances deep interior heat retention, suppresses secular core cooling, inhibits inner-core growth, and promotes present-day mantle plume activity. We further find that reconciling a long-lived BMO with a present-day solid inner core requires both limited enrichment of HPEs within the BMO and relatively high core liquidus temperatures, which may be difficult to satisfy simultaneously. These results offer constraints on the thermal and magnetic evolution of Mars and highlight the importance of coupled mantle-BMO-core dynamics on Mars.
9e0027e1d72a9dbc: Dynamic topography changes as mantle convection evolves, making its past surface expression difficult to reconstruct. Widespread Neogene‐Quaternary intraplate basaltic magmatism across the Western Mediterranean Region allows us to test whether dated basalts preserve the mantle thermal structure responsible for regional dynamic support. We combine major, trace, and rare earth element (REE) analyses and modeling from six volcanic provinces with calibrated earthquake tomographic models and residual topographic and bathymetric measurements. The geochemical data set includes both newly acquired and published analyses. Rare earth element inverse modeling of samples least affected by lithospheric‐mantle influence indicates that melting occurred beneath lithosphere typically 60–70 km thick and at asthenospheric potential temperatures ranging from approximately ambient to 50°C above ambient mantle. These estimates agree with independent tomographic constraints. Dynamic support calculated from the inferred thermal structure is also consistent with measured residual anomalies. Lithospheric thinning accounts for most of the largest positive anomalies of approximately 0.5 km without requiring large asthenospheric temperature anomalies. The agreement demonstrates that Western Mediterranean intraplate basaltic magmatism records upper‐mantle thermal structure capable of generating regional surface support and provides a basis for reconstructing past mantle conditions and transient dynamic topography from dated basalts.
31d4e74f280a04ee: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) has emerged as a transformative technology for near‐surface site characterization. When a vertical source is activated along the fiber, DAS measures only the in‐line (radial) component of Rayleigh‐wave motion, whereas conventional surface‐wave methods primarily measure the vertical component. Dispersion data extracted from radial‐component waveforms may differ from those obtained from vertical‐component measurements, particularly under complex stratigraphic conditions. Hence, a component‐consistent forward problem is desired when inverting radial‐component DAS dispersion data to retrieve accurate shear wave velocity () profiles. This study presents a radial‐component predominant‐mode (RCPM) inversion framework designed for DAS‐based surface‐wave analysis that explicitly accounts for source–receiver directivity and modal sensitivity of the Rayleigh‐wave radial component. The proposed approach matches measured dominant radial dispersion trends with the theoretical mode exhibiting the maximum modal participation. As a result, the RCPM framework eliminates the need for explicit modal indexing, provides a component‐consistent interpretation of radial‐component dispersion data, and substantially reduces reliance on subjective analyst‐driven modal interpretations. The RCPM approach is systematically evaluated using three synthetic ground models and two field DAS data sets. The synthetic results demonstrate that modal energy distribution differs significantly between vertical and radial components in the presence of strong velocity contrasts and velocity reversals, and that conventional inversion approaches may misinterpret modal behavior, resulting in less accurate profiles. In contrast, the RCPM method consistently captures the correct modal response and yields reliable profiles. Application to two field DAS data sets further demonstrates good agreement between the inverted profiles and independent invasive borehole measurements.
747962d6d8e345b4: Post-earthquake statistics indicate that the existing seismic measures and evaluation methods for subway stations in the Loess Plateau with locally interbedded sand layers are inadequate. During earthquakes, the station roofs are prone to deformation or even failure, posing a serious threat to station safety. Therefore, the primary objective of this paper is to propose a new seismic mitigation method for subway stations in the Loess Plateau with locally interbedded sand layers, thereby addressing the structural seismic issues of such stations. Using a specific subway station in Xi’an’s rail transit system as the engineering context, this method employs the geometric scale of 1/50 to systematically analyze the deformation and failure characteristics, acceleration response, and bending moment patterns of the station equipped with an EPE foam board seismic isolation layer under a 0.35 g horizontal seismic load. It reveals the dynamic response and mechanical evolution characteristics of the station and its surrounding loess, and evaluates the effectiveness of the EPE foam board seismic isolation layer in enhancing the seismic performance of the subway station. The results indicate that the EPE foam board damping layer effectively reduces peak acceleration at all measurement points, with reductions ranging from 13.95 to 14.02%; The extreme values of bending moments at all measurement points were significantly reduced, with the maximum reduction reaching 36.22%. Simultaneously, the stress concentrations of the tensile stress zones in subway station were effectively alleviated, the seismic isolation measures resulted in the optimization of the overall dynamic response of the subway station, and the seismic performance of the station was enhanced. Furthermore, this vibration-damping layer exhibits good damping performance, features a simple construction, is economical, durable, and wear-resistant, and involves convenient construction techniques, making it suitable for widespread application. The research findings hold significant reference value for the design, construction, and safe operation of subway stations in loess region.
e0391cbbd34f8a8d: Dense temporary seismic nodal arrays offer new opportunities for ambient noise interferometry, enabling spatially resolved imaging of subsurface processes at scales inaccessible to permanent networks. Here we demonstrate this potential in a volcanic setting, exploiting the 2024 unrest at Kīlauea volcano, . By inverting velocity changes across 2667 station pairs from both a temporary nodal deployment and the permanent Hawaiian Volcano Observatory network, we reconstruct the full spatio-temporal evolution of the unrest, capturing the pre-, co-, and post-eruptive sequence. The resulting velocity changes are validated against Global Navigation Satellite System and Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar measurements, and conceptual volumetric strain models. Within our study period, we find no significant influence of precipitation and instead we identify three primary mechanisms driving velocity changes: magma reservoir dynamics, including inflation/deflation at the summit reservoirs, dike intrusions indicating down-rift magma transport, and transient changes related to earthquake rupturing. While disentangling effects of overlapping deformation sources remain challenging, our seismic velocity anomalies from distinct processes closely mirror independent geodetic observations. This close alignment indicates that, in the absence of strong environmental influences, high-resolution spatio-temporal velocity changes determined using dense networks can guide interpretations of subsurface strain in regions where geodetic measurements lack sufficient resolution.
de9cd89c2f0831ad: Among the most prevalent features in Earth's deep mantle are the Large Low Velocity Provinces (LLVPs), hypothesized to be hotter and compositionally distinct from the surrounding mantle. LLVPs have previously been viewed as either active superplumes rising through the mantle or passive piles shaped by large scale convection. Recent tomography models suggest LLVPs may exhibit a plume‐shaped morphology. Geodynamic experiments offer insights into the formation, characteristics, and evolution of mantle structures. This study shows LLVPs can form passive piles with a plume‐shaped morphology when the initial condition has a hot isothermal profile and small intrinsic density differences. The background mantle temperature, in addition to the intrinsic density, plays a critical role in determining LLVP morphology. These findings suggest the observed plume‐like shapes of LLVPs in recent tomography models can be explained by either superplumes or passive piles with plume‐shaped morphologies.
b705ef1f0e467960: Studies of postseismic creep often infer a strong reduction in upper‐mantle viscosity after large earthquakes, yet the microphysical mechanism responsible for this behavior remains subject of debate. Here, we present new gas‐medium apparatus experiments at 1100–1200°C on pre‐dried, annealed Åheim dunite (grain size of 400 m) designed to elucidate the microphysical mechanism of transient dislocation creep during postseismic relaxation. We demonstrate that the transient mechanical behavior of dunite matches well with predictions of an intragranular model that involves the evolution of dislocation density and long‐range interactions among dislocations. Extrapolation to upper‐mantle conditions illustrates that this model can also explain the 1–2 orders of magnitude reduction in upper‐mantle viscosity that is inferred from studies of postseismic creep. We highlight opportunities to refine both intra‐ and intergranular models of transient dislocation creep.
e57ec1fe1c1ef5f6: # Repository Overview This repository contains the aerial imagery and digital elevation data used to estimate surface mass removal, together with figure-generation scripts and processed numerical simulation data associated with the manuscript: *Surface mass removal can induce extremely shallow earthquakes despite nominally stable friction: the case of the 2019 Mw 4.9 Le Teil, France, earthquake.* The repository is organized into two compressed archives: 1. `aerial.tar.gz` — aerial imagery and digital terrain data used to estimate surface mass removal.2. `archive_FIGURES.tar.xz` — plotting scripts, processed simulation data, and auxiliary files required to reproduce the figures presented in the manuscript. ## 1. Aerial Imagery and Digital Elevation Data: `aerial.tar.gz` This archive contains two subdirectories: ### 1.1. `etat_major/` This directory contains historical maps from the SCAN État-major® 40K product. The product is generated by georeferencing and tiling scanned État-major maps at a scale of 1:40,000. The original maps were drawn in the nineteenth century, based on surveys conducted between 1825 and 1866. They were subsequently supplemented by partial updates, including the addition of railway lines, through 1889. These historical maps provide information on the landscape before modern surface modifications and are used in the analysis of surface mass removal. ### 1.2. `LIDAR/` This directory contains digital terrain model (DTM) data derived from the classified point clouds acquired through the French national high-definition LiDAR (HD LiDAR) program. The point-cloud acquisition density is at least 10 laser pulses per square meter, decreasing to 5 pulses per square meter at altitudes above 3,200 m. The DTM is derived from points classified as ground, water, and virtual points in the HD LiDAR point cloud. These data provide information on the modern terrain and support the estimation of surface mass removal. ## 2. Figure Scripts and Processed Simulation Data: `archive_FIGURES.tar.xz` This archive contains the scripts and processed data needed to reproduce the figures presented in the manuscript. The numerical simulations were performed using BEM2D, an open-source two-dimensional boundary element method code. The BEM2D source code is maintained separately and is available from its official GitHub repository: https://github.com/esopaci/BEM_2D.git Examples and instructions for running simulations of the type used in this study are available in the `examples/QUARRY_LOADING/` directory of the BEM2D repository. ### 2.1. Repository Structure The archive is organized into one directory for each manuscript figure: - `Figure01/`- `Figure02/`- `Figure03/`- `Figure04/`- `Figure05/`- `Figure06/`- `Figure07/`- `Figure08/`- `Figure09/` Each directory contains the files required to generate the corresponding figure, including, as applicable: - plotting scripts;- processed numerical simulation data or the subsets of simulation outputs needed for plotting; and- auxiliary files required by the scripts. For figures that include maps, the corresponding directories also contain Generic Mapping Tools (GMT) scripts and any required auxiliary files. The archive provides the processed simulation outputs needed to reproduce the published figures without rerunning the complete numerical simulations. ### 2.2. Numerical Simulations The numerical simulations were performed using BEM2D. To reproduce the simulations, users should: 1. Obtain the BEM2D source code from the GitHub repository.2. Compile the code following the instructions in the BEM2D documentation.3. Consult and adapt the examples in `examples/QUARRY_LOADING/` to reproduce the simulation configurations described in the manuscript. The processed simulation data included in `archive_FIGURES.tar.xz` were generated using this workflow. ### 2.3. Figure Generation Each figure directory contains one or more scripts for generating the corresponding manuscript figure from the data stored in that directory. For figures involving maps, the accompanying GMT scripts should also be executed. The scripts are intended to facilitate figure reproduction using the archived data, without requiring the numerical simulations to be rerun. ### 2.4. Software Requirements Depending on the figure and the desired level of reproduction, the following software may be required: - **BEM2D:** to rerun the numerical simulations.- **Generic Mapping Tools (GMT):** to generate maps for figures that use GMT.- **Additional software or libraries:** as specified in the individual plotting scripts. Users should consult the relevant script headers and documentation for specific software dependencies and execution instructions. ### 2.5. Reproducibility Workflow To reproduce the manuscript figures, the recommended workflow is: 1. Extract `archive_FIGURES.tar.xz`.2. Navigate to the directory corresponding to the figure of interest.3. Execute the plotting scripts using the processed data provided in that directory.4. For figures containing maps, execute the accompanying GMT scripts as required. To rerun the numerical simulations, users must additionally obtain and compile BEM2D and configure the simulations according to the manuscript and the examples provided in the BEM2D repository. ## Notes on Reproducibility The figure archive contains processed simulation outputs and the data required for figure generation, rather than the complete set of raw simulation outputs. These archived files are intended to enable reproduction of the published figures without rerunning the full numerical models. The BEM2D implementation is maintained separately in its GitHub repository. The aerial imagery and digital terrain data used to estimate surface mass removal are provided in `aerial.tar.gz`. 10.6084/m9.figshare.34475100
303edc7c90d1097b: This dataset contains the input files and output time series from 55 three-dimensional earthquake-cycle models on planar faults with dip angles ranging from 5° to 90°. The models were performed with HBI (Ozawa et al., 2023). All models use the same friction parameters and initial conditions, so dip angle is the only parameter that varies between runs. Each model covers approximately 10,000 years of fault slip history. The archive contains the following files and directories: input/, which contains the HBI input file (.in) for each model; geometry/, which contains the fault mesh (.stl) for each dip angle; the parameter file; and monitor/, which contains the fault maximum/average output time series, recorded at every time step (refer to the HBI user guide for column info https://github.com/sozawa94/hbi).
c17314a88de6f262: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) and integrated fibre-optic sensing (IFOS) measure an optical phase change that integrates axial strain along a fibre, whose path often bends and loops. We show how planar bending controls the angular and spectral sensitivity of this measurement, an effect we call geometric filtering. Separating the integrated strain into endpoint and curvature terms, we derive the exact plane-wave response of a circular-arc fibre as a Bessel series valid at any wavelength and opening angle. At long wavelengths the response of any fibre path follows from a geometrical tensor, the gauge average of the tangent dyad. It depends on the shape of the path but not on its size. Bending fills the broadside blind spot of a straight fibre to P waves and weakens its sensitivity to SH waves. For smooth, symmetric single-apex bends, the height-to-chord ratio sets the P-wave pattern: dipole-like below about 0.13 and nearly omnidirectional above about 0.46. A closed loop acts as an areal dilatometer: it senses P waves equally from every azimuth and is blind to SH waves at all wavelengths. At finite wavelengths the opening angle filters the Bessel orders. This limits the number of terms required and turns the gauge-length notches of a straight fibre into the Bessel rings of a closed loop. For a point source, the plane-wave response requires the source to be many wavelengths away, far compared with the fibre footprint, and beyond the footprint squared over the wavelength. The last condition defines a Fibre Fresnel Number. We condense these criteria into a Decision Map that selects the response model from fibre geometry, signal frequency, and source distance, and apply it to eight DAS and IFOS deployments. Fibre geometry is thus a design variable for geometric filtering: it can make a fibre segment selectively sensitive to certain azimuths and wavelengths. Preliminary version (v1). Part I of two companion papers; Part II treats helically wound cables. To be submitted to Geophysical Journal International.
0a158d42541ed0df: We analyze deformation fabrics, compositions of melts, metamorphic temperatures, and paleopiezometric data beneath the Tsiknias Thrust, Tinos, Greece, which formed part of the plate boundary that, in Late‐Cretaceous time, absorbed convergence between Africa and Europe associated with final closure of the Vardar Ocean. Sedimentary and mafic rocks of the ocean floor beneath the Thrust experienced metamorphism at pressures of GPa, equivalent to a depth of about 30 km, and at ambient temperatures of °C. Subgrain‐size piezometry indicates that shear stress during this metamorphism was MPa, consistent with estimates of shear stress at comparable depths on present‐day convergent plate boundaries. In the meters immediately beneath the Tsiknias Thrust, apparent metamorphic temperatures vary between 600° and 800°C. In some locations the upper 10 m of the amphibolites are cut by veins, consisting almost entirely of plagioclase, whose compositions cannot be explained by partial melting of the host rock in that temperature range. They are, however, consistent with the products of laboratory experiments on frictional slip at seismic rates. We interpret these veins, and their deformed equivalents, as recording repeated episodes of coseismic melting followed by ductile shearing. Melt‐vein thicknesses of mm imply coseismic energy dissipation of J , which is comparable with seismological measurements of breakdown work in earthquakes on present‐day plate interfaces.
1262c7a38063b25e: We studied the tidal modulation of the rate of seismicity in the Ridgecrest, California area between 2008 and 2024, thus including the 2019 Mw 7.1 earthquake. We combined machine-learning-enhanced earthquake detection and location with a novel methodology to characterize tidal modulation. We identified significant modulation of seismicity in the Ridgecrest fault zone and in the neighboring regions, the Coso volcanic field and the Garlock fault, but tidal modulation in the fault zone exhibits a unique temporal evolution. Modulation in the fault zone shifts, around 2014–2015, from a stress-controlled regime where peak seismicity occurs at peak tidal stress to a stress-rate-controlled regime where peak seismicity occurs at peak tidal stress rate. In contrast, peak seismicity in Coso and along the Garlock fault consistently occurs at peak tidal stress throughout time. Moreover, the strength of tidal modulation in the fault zone increases before the 2019 Mw 7.1 earthquake, unlike in its surroundings. A possible interpretation based on experimental and theoretical work suggests that some characteristic frictional time scale (the nucleation time or the critical period of the fault) becomes shorter than the dominant tidal period after 2015. This change implies that the fault loading rate increases, which may be accompanied by a decrease in effective normal stress. Reduced effective stress, fault zone resonance, or increased mechanical compliance could cause the increase in modulation strength. We propose that these changes manifest a preparation phase before a large earthquake.
06737daf2ada5bc4: Seismic source discriminants comparing earthquakes and explosions have been validated for large-magnitude events (local magnitude, ML>3.5) detected at regional and greater distances (>350 km). However, there is less evidence that existing seismic source discriminants apply to small-magnitude seismic events (ML≤3.5), which are predominantly detected at local distances (≤350 km). In this study, we investigate the performance of a P/S amplitude ratio discriminant for 210 small-magnitude seismic events in the United Kingdom (UK). High-frequency (> 8 Hz) network-averaged P/S ratios can discriminate between earthquakes and explosions, whereas low frequencies (2–4 Hz) can separate offshore explosions and quarry blasts. We derive a path and site amplitude correction model that reduces P/S ratio distribution variability, but using discrimination metrics we show that simple across-network averaging is the most important step to allow effective discrimination. We also applied a machine learning classification model, previously trained to discriminate earthquakes and explosions in France, to our dataset. The model demonstrates high classification accuracy, likely due to similarities between geology and seismic sources in France and the UK. When the predictions from the convolutional neural network are combined with high-frequency P/S ratios, we are able to distinguish other seismic sources, such as longwall mining-induced earthquakes. These results suggest that P/S ratios can be considered a useful seismic source discriminant at local distances across the UK, and network-averaging sufficiently accounts for non-source factors.
bad42abae2a1e916: On 18 December 2023, an Mw 6.0 earthquake struck Jishishan County, Gansu Province, China, rupturing a segment of the Lajishan fault system along the northeastern margin of the Tibetan plateau. To characterize the seismogenic fault geometry and the spatiotemporal evolution of the rupture, we developed a joint inversion framework that integrates Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR), Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) coseismic displacements, and far-field seismic waveforms. The fault geometry was constrained through a nonlinear inversion based on coseismic InSAR deformation. Using the optimal fault geometry, we performed a kinematic finite-fault inversion that jointly incorporates InSAR line-of-sight displacements, static GNSS offsets, and seismic waveforms to resolve the rupture process. Our results show that the rupture was mainly concentrated at depths of 5–12 km, with a maximum slip of ∼30 cm. The estimated seismic moment is 1.0×1018 N·m, corresponding to Mw 5.94. The total rupture duration is ∼20 s. Regional interseismic GNSS velocities and strain-rate fields indicate that the event occurred within a compressional tectonic regime and was dominated by thrust faulting with a minor strike-slip component, providing insights into tectonic loading and seismogenesis within the Lajishan fault system. Coulomb stress calculations further suggest that stress transfer from the mainshock may have contributed to the subsequent aftershock activity. Our results provide constraints on the rupture behavior and tectonic loading of the Lajishan fault system and improve our understanding of seismogenesis along the northeastern margin of the Tibetan plateau, with implications for regional seismic hazard assessment.
bc1128252beaad55: The amplitude source location (ASL) method has been widely applied to volcanic earthquakes that do not show clear wave onsets at active volcanoes. To reduce the effects of shallow velocity structures just beneath seismic stations, observed amplitudes are generally corrected by using seismic coda waves of regional earthquakes. However, even using such amplitude corrections, ASL may not accurately locate the source of volcanic earthquakes occurring in a strongly heterogeneous medium in volcanic regions. To overcome this limitation, we propose a source location-dependent amplitude correction method and introduce seismic velocity structure with a vertical gradient. We analyse 339 volcanotectonic earthquakes (VTs) recorded by eight seismic stations deployed across the Izu Oshima volcano edifice. Reference hypocentres are determined from manually picked P- and S-wave arrival times and used to evaluate the performance of the proposed amplitude-based method. We divide the VT data set into two subsets, which are used as reference and test data sets. The amplification factors, which are the ratio of observed to predicted amplitudes of known VTs, are calculated for the reference data set. The amplification factors are further interpolated onto a 2-D grid using the ordinary kriging method with an exponential variogram model and then replicated at each depth level of the 3-D grid. Using interpolated source location–dependent amplification factors, we correct the observed amplitudes of VTs in the test data set and estimate the source locations by minimizing the amplitude residual in a grid search scheme. We use the 8–16 Hz frequency band, a velocity gradient k of 0.33 s−1 and v0 1.5 km s−1, and a constant attenuation factor (Q) of 50. The obtained source locations show good agreement with the locations determined from P- and S-wave onsets. Median misfits are approximately 1.1 and 1.0 km in the vertical and horizontal directions, respectively. Meanwhile, the median misfits from conventional ASL are approximately 2.2 km vertically and 2.3 km horizontally, with the estimated location concentrated close to the summit. These results demonstrate that our proposed method substantially improves relocation consistency and reduces summit-ward bias.
a7d7ef228ef9a504: This dataset contains seismic velocity change estimates derived from ambient noise interferometry for Kīlauea volcano, Hawaii, during the period of volcanic unrest preceding the September 2024 East Rift Zone eruption near Nāpau Crater. The data were computed using continuous vertical seismic recordings from a dense temporary nodal array and the permanent network of the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory. Relative seismic velocity changes were estimated from ambient noise cross-correlations and subsequently inverted to obtain spatially distributed velocity change fields through time. The dataset includes time series of relative seismic velocity changes, spatial inversion results, and associated metadata describing station pairs, processing parameters, and inversion settings. The velocity change fields resolve spatial and temporal variations associated with magma transport, dike intrusions, and deformation processes at the summit and in the East Rift Zone of Kīlauea. These data support the analysis presented in "Spatiotemporal evolution of shallow seismic velocities associated with the 2024 East Rift Zone eruption at Kīlauea Volcano" (A. Rohnacher, N. Bennington, M. Bagnardi, S. Wiemer, F. Lanza).
e9215b78865e8e95: The Atacama Desert of the Central Andean forearc is the driest non-polar region on Earth, where extremely low erosion rates preserve geomorphic markers over Myr timescales. Between 19°S and 20°S, subtle Quaternary east-vergent reverse faults deform the west-sloping landscape and disrupt drainage development. This setting provides a unique opportunity to investigate fault evolution, uplift thresholds for drainage reorganization, and the seismic significance of slow faulting in hyperarid landscapes. We investigated two faulted interfluves, Pampa de Tiliviche (~19.5°S) and Pampa de Soga (~19.75°S), using geomorphic mapping and cosmogenic ¹⁰Be dating of displaced alluvial surfaces, channels, and terraces. We constrained fault geometry, reconstructed fault-driven incision histories, and quantified uplift and slip rates. Faulting in interfluves started after ~2.6 and ~5 Ma, while warped terraces and riverbeds record accelerated faulting since ~330 and ~35 ka, respectively. Simplified fault geometries yield maximum long- and short-term uplift/slip rates of ~0.011 and ~0.3 mm/yr. Numerical landscape-evolution models incorporating measured rates reproduce observed geomorphic patterns and constrain the uplift rate-catchment area ratio governing drainage reorganization. Observations and modelling indicate that tectonic uplift outpaces fluvial incision in hyperarid landscapes when drainage networks with small catchment areas cannot restore channel-bed slope modified by slow uplift. Regional consistency in fault geometry, distribution, and associated microseismicity suggests these counter-slope faults form an active forearc system capable of generating M6.1–6.8 earthquakes. Our results show that extremely slow faulting can substantially reorganize drainages in hyperarid landscapes and that Quaternary faults commonly considered inactive may represent an underestimated seismic hazard.
90196517421bda3c: The northeastern Tibetan Plateau (TP) and the western North China Craton (NCC) provide a natural laboratory for studying the interaction of tectonic and mantle processes, contrasting the active plateau with the stable craton. In contrast to many prior studies that relied on station‐averaged shear‐wave splitting (SWS) measurements and sparsely distributed stations, this study explores seismic azimuthal anisotropy between the dynamic TP and the stable NCC using 6,409 high‐resolution SWS measurements from 465 broadband seismic stations at intervals of less than 50 km. Some stations in the central study area show splitting parameters with a π/2 periodicity based on azimuthal variations, indicating a complex double‐layer horizontal anisotropy structure. The anisotropy of the upper layer is linked to ductile flow in the middle‐to‐lower crust originating from the TP. This flow encounters the rigid lithosphere of the Alxa Block, leading to a bifurcation into northeastward and southeastward directions. The anisotropy in the lower layer, exhibiting fast orientations in a NW‐SE direction, is consistent with the observed one‐layered anisotropy and aligns with the absolute plate motion of the Eurasian plate. Analysis of the spatial coherence of splitting parameters suggests that asthenospheric flow is the dominant source of anisotropy. This mantle flow is southeastward beneath the Alxa Block and shifts to an approximately eastward direction along the thinner lithospheric passage between the Ordos and Sichuan cratonic keels.
90f86d56741a1ee7: High‐resolution crustal‐scale seismic imaging from long‐offset ocean‐bottom seismometer (OBS) data using full‐waveform inversion (FWI) remains challenging because the large number of propagated wavelengths and waveform complexity make the inversion highly sensitive to time‐shift errors (cycle skipping). To mitigate this nonlinearity, we assess the recently developed time‐domain extended‐source (ES‐) FWI with a well‐documented OBS case study from the eastern‐Nankai subduction zone, Japan. ES‐FWI first reconstructs wavefields that fit the recorded data well using extended sources defined as the sum of the experiment and scattering sources. These scattering sources, which depend on the unknown true wavefields and the sought perturbation model, are estimated at each iteration by fitting in the least‐squares sense the associated data residuals, namely the virtually measured scattered data. The model is subsequently updated by minimizing the scattering sources, keeping the reconstructed wavefields fixed to transfer the perturbation model hidden in these sources toward the current iteration background model. This alternating‐direction optimization for wavefield reconstruction and model updating is iterated until convergence, where both data residuals and scattering sources should vanish. We perform ES‐FWI with a multiscale workflow starting from a model obtained by first‐arrival traveltime tomography. We show that ES‐FWI achieves more accurate results than FWI. Moreover, we refine the final model of the extended‐space approach by classical FWI to further decrease residual data misfit once the linear domain has been reached. Finally, several key structures resolved in the final ES‐FWI model, such as the subduction megathrust overlain by the décollement , provide a first validation of the approach.
38ebcb9bc55e4e95: Imaging magma storage beneath active calderas requires resolving crustal structure at scales comparable to those of individual reservoirs. To identify potential reservoirs beneath Kı̄lauea, Hawai'i, we conducted a hybrid seismic experiment at its summit for 37 days in 2023 that combined more than 1,800 three‐component nodal seismometers with 396 vibroseis source positions, yielding about 15 million ‐ and ‐wave arrivals. Joint inversion of earthquake and active‐source travel times yields three‐dimensional models of , , and within the upper ∼4 km beneath the summit relative to mean sea level, parameterized on a 500 m grid, within which the resolution tests demonstrate recovery of sub‐kilometer to kilometer‐scale structure. The models delineate two principal magma storage regions beneath Halema'uma'u and the south caldera, each on the order of 2 km across. Both reservoirs are expressed as localized zones of reduced and moderately reduced with locally elevated at depths of 1–3 km below sea level. The anomalies are laterally distinct at shallow levels but appear to merge within a broader zone of reduced velocities at depth. Surrounding higher‐velocity domains likely represent mechanically stronger intrusive complexes that confine magma storage. Spatial correspondence between seismic velocity anomalies and independently modeled geodetic deformation sources supports the interpretation that the imaged structures represent magma storage regions. These results demonstrate that dense nodal arrays combined with hybrid passive‐active tomography can resolve reservoir‐scale structure at active volcanoes and provide an improved framework for interpreting magma storage and transport beneath Kı̄lauea.
8645db6caa32468a: More than 20 years after their discovery, the physical mechanisms of slow earthquakes remain enigmatic. Here, we develop a simple quasi‐static elastic model that reproduces both the migration patterns of elastic/frictional models, and the statistical properties of Brownian models. Fault elements are either slipping or locked, with locked elements having either a fully healed static strength , or a reduced static strength if they slipped recently. By adjusting , the fixed slip speed , and the grid spacing , the model can generate characteristic events with recurrence intervals of about 1 year and propagation speeds of about 10 km/day, consistent with observations and with analytical estimates derived from fracture mechanics. The simulated events also exhibit a proportionality between squared moment acceleration and moment rate, and an amplitude spectrum decaying as at high frequencies, consistent with both observations and Brownian walk models. We approximate the simulated moment rate functions using a linear birth‐death process, with birth and death rates estimated from properly weighted elastic interaction kernels and the reduced static strength, and obtain analytical estimates of the equilibrium moment rate, the ratio , and the lower corner frequency of the amplitude spectrum, all in good agreement with the simulations. This approximate model thus links the elastic/frictional and Brownian attributes of the simulated events. The ratio is orders of magnitude lower than inferred from subduction zones, suggesting that our fixed of order 1 μm/s is averaging over a wider range of slip speeds.
51ecfebcab40c928: Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) can provide high-density spatial measurements, enabling precise estimates of the source parameters of earthquakes. We analyzed nine small earthquakes in central Shikoku, Japan, using DAS observations obtained from two nearby fiber-optic cables with different orientations. Differential travel times measured by waveform cross-correlation enabled high-precision hypocenter relocation. The relocated hypocenters were substantially shallower than those reported in the catalog of the Japan Meteorological Agency. Eight of the nine relocated earthquakes formed a compact cluster; seven of these were aligned along a northwest-dipping structure consistent with a major geological boundary. We also applied the empirical Green’s function method to P-wave DAS data and estimated corner frequencies after evaluating their spatial variation across the focal sphere. The resulting stress-drop estimates ranged from 0.6 to 2 MPa. Compared with conventional seismic stations, the dense DAS observations yielded smoother spectral ratios and better-constrained source parameters. These results demonstrate the potential of DAS for high-precision characterization of microearthquake locations and source properties.
b78f7939b5a03ff0: Strong earthquakes can have a dual impact on the slow‐moving landslide budget of a landscape by either triggering new actively deforming hillslopes or stabilizing existing ones. However, their regional‐scale influence on hillslope processes remains poorly understood because of limited observational coverage and the masking effects of long‐wavelength post‐seismic signals. This knowledge gap constrains post‐seismic landslide hazard assessment, particularly since actively deforming hillslopes may evolve into rapid failures, especially under the influence of meteorological factors following a major earthquake. This study addresses this gap by analyzing slope instability across approximately 66,800 km 2 of southeastern Türkiye following the 6 February 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake sequence using Sentinel‐1 InSAR time series. We cross‐validated these locations using high‐resolution optical imagery, manually delineated and validated the polygons, and assigned confidence levels based on observable surface features indicative of slow‐moving landslides. Our results show that the total area affected by slow‐moving landslides increased from 12.36 km 2 before the earthquakes to 159.39 km 2 afterward, a 12.9‐fold increase. We identified that newly activated slopes were primarily associated with steeper terrain across a broad range of ground shaking, whereas stabilized slopes were preferentially linked to very high shaking levels on intermediate slopes. Slopes that were already moving were largely influenced by intermediate shaking intensities and gentler topographic gradients. These results demonstrate that earthquake‐induced changes in slow‐moving landslides depend on both the pre‐event activity state and the combination of seismic, topographic, and geological conditions.
30ad4127a6b52d5d: Subduction zones govern Earth’s deep volatile cycle. The slab-mantle interface is a key locus of volatile exchange between the subducting crust and the overlying mantle wedge, yet whether and how chemical reactions at this interface affect arc magmatism remains poorly constrained. Arc magmas typically lack a geochemical hallmark of garnet fractionation, leading to the prevailing interpretation that they derive predominantly from the shallower, garnet-free mantle wedge. Here, we challenge this view using Mg isotopic data from Nicaragua, the South Sandwich Islands, and the central-eastern Aleutian arc, integrated with a global arc magma compilation. We show that heavy Mg isotopic signatures in mafic arc magmas vary with indicators of volatile enrichment, pointing to a volatile-rich source, most likely the heavily metasomatized base of the mantle wedge. The heaviest Mg isotopic compositions occur in arcs underlain by the most steeply dipping subducting slab, suggesting a focusing effect by the geometry of the downgoing slab. Monte Carlo isotope mixing models indicate that up to 50% of the Mg budget in some arc magma sources derives from deep, water-saturated melting near the slab-mantle interface. These findings highlight the base of the mantle wedge as a volumetrically and geochemically significant contributor to arc magmatism and the water cycle.
e0b1f840fc3e3665: We present P- and S-wave seismic tomographic models for southern mainland Portugal, specifically for the region south of the 39° N parallel. These models were obtained using local seismicity and wide-angle refracted and reflected seismic profiles, considering a spatial resolution of approximately 10 km in latitude and longitude, and 3 km in depth, the highest spatial resolution so far compared to previous models of similar or broader regional scope. The aim is to improve the understanding of continental seismicity and to correlate seismic heterogeneities with crustal tectonic structures. For this purpose, the fast marching method was employed to solve the forward problem, while subspace inversion was used for the inverse problem, both implemented within the Fast Marching Tomography package (FMTOMO). The resulting tomographic model shows a segmented crust between upper, middle and lower. Some of the seismic structures show orientations consistent with Variscan tectonic features, generally following a northwest–southeast direction within the Ossa-Morena and South Portuguese Zone. Contacts between major geological units are discernible and well delineated in the model. Within the Ossa-Morena Zone, a negative velocity anomaly was identified which may be related to a possible fractured zone between the Boa Fé Shear Zone and Ciborro–Aldeia da Serra Fault. In the South Portuguese Zone, the most pronounced velocity contrast is associated with the syenite intrusion of the Monchique Massif in the southwest, characterized by a positive velocity anomaly, extending down to 20 km depth. To the southeast, seismic activity may be related to the Alcoutim and Ribeira do Vascão Faults. These structures impose a velocity anomaly suggesting that they are near-vertical faults extending to the top of the lower crust. A good correlation is observed between seismicity, seismic anomalies and regional geology.
fff024e234f6b866: Tectonic deformation on stagnant-lid planets reflects the interaction between long-lived lithospheric structures and evolving stress fields. Whether the ancient tectonic fabrics can localise present-day seismic failure under contemporary stress fields remains poorly tested by direct geophysical observations. Here we show that the farside seismic event, S0976a, detected by InSight in the western hemisphere is a marsquake that occurred in Valles Marineris and involved strike-slip faulting in the deep crust. The stress orientation inferred from the focal mechanism is consistent with reactivation of pre-existing fault systems under a present-day stress field shaped primarily by long-term planetary cooling, regional Tharsis-related loading, and surface erosion-related local unloading. These observations provide direct seismic evidence that inherited fault systems on Mars can remain mechanically favourable for reactivation over billion-year timescales, suggesting that slip on deeply rooted faults remains a key mechanism of long-term strain release in a cooling single-lid planet.
c142ed36b38874d1: Globally, numerous modern and ancient examples of active spreading-ridge subduction ‘slab windows’ are documented, whereas definitive examples of extinct spreading-ridge subduction are lacking or controversial. Published high-resolution P-wave tomography of southwest Alaska and the eastern Aleutians reveals an unmistakable >1000 km-long slab gap, expressed as a low-velocity anomaly within the subducted Pacific slab at depths of ~200–500 km between ~158.5°W and 168°W. We unfold the Pacific slab and integrate it into a quantitative plate-reconstruction model, demonstrating that the slab gap aligns with the extinct Kula-Pacific mid-ocean ridge that became inactive at ~40 Ma. Initial subduction of the extinct Kula-Pacific ridge after ~8 Ma was concurrent with documented Aleutian Trench arc and Kodiak Island forearc exhumation at ~7–5 Ma. The nascent extinct Kula-Pacific ridge slab gap may explain uplift of the Bristol Bay and St. George basins, slab-edge magmatism at the Quaternary Hayes volcano, and intraplate mafic volcanism at the Pribilof volcanoes. The modern slab gap may partially control the limit of deep Benioff seismicity along the Alaska-Aleutian margin, including the westward-shallowing Benioff zone beneath the Aleutians. We infer that the slab gap continues another >1000 km westward into tomographically less-resolved regions beneath the central-western Aleutians and likely terminates near the remnant Kula-Pacific spreading ridge around the Near Islands, explaining the origin of a previously recognized slab “portal” in this region. Our reconstruction arguably provides the archetypal example of extinct spreading ridge subduction – a separate class of ridge-trench intersection that is distinct from active ridge subduction.
350b64c376ce26a3: For large-scale wind turbines subjected to sudden seismic excitation during operation, a self-adaptive fuzzy pitch (SFP) control method is proposed to mitigate the structural seismic response. The displacement and velocity of tower-top fore-aft (TTFA) are used as input variables for the fuzzy controller, and a self-adaptive proportional factor is established through an exponential function. The pitch angle adjustment is taken as the output variable, which is then superimposed on the pitch angle given by the baseline pitch controller to realize SFP control. Through co-simulation of OpenFAST and Simulink, the results demonstrate that compared with the traditional proportional–integral (PI) control, the proposed SFP strategy reduces the peak TTFA displacement and acceleration by approximately 25% and 31% on average, respectively, under various earthquake records. Seismic fragility analysis further shows that at a peak ground acceleration (PGA) of 1.0 g, SFP control reduces the failure probabilities corresponding to yield displacement and elastic limit displacement by 43.05% and 20.82%, respectively. These quantitative findings confirm that the proposed method significantly enhances the structural safety of wind turbines under combined wind-seismic loading, providing a practical and robust intelligent control solution for wind farms located in seismically active regions.
5a195a5a5f9b6ef9: Tectonic tremor and repeating/regular earthquakes off Iwate in the shallow Japan Trench occur episodically and in spatially overlapping areas, implying a common aseismic driver. We investigate how small aseismic slip triggers events across multiple slip‐rate regimes using fully dynamic earthquake‐cycle simulations governed by rate‐and‐state friction. Along‐fault heterogeneity is imposed by alternating velocity‐weakening (VW) and velocity‐strengthening (VS) patches, and events are classified based on peak slip velocity . A single VW patch produces only aseismic events, whereas a multi‐patch heterogeneous model generates sub‐seismic slip and earthquakes, often nearly synchronous across VW patches. Inter‐event transient slip in VS patches raises stress during subsequent VW nucleation. Transitions in and rupture properties are controlled by subtle stress differences between nucleating VW patches and surrounding VS patches. This mechanism provides a simple physical explanation for why slow and fast earthquakes can emerge from interacting fault patches with spatial overlap and close temporal proximity.
3b8a3825523ea7cb: Details about this repository can be found in the README.md file within the repository.
333c16cb78c73369: The surface nitrogen (N) cycle is dominated by biological activity, yet its impact on the deep N cycle is poorly constrained. Although recycled sedimentary N is observed in modern magmatic systems, it remains unknown when it first became identifiable in mantle-derived magmas and to what extent it affects the deep mantle N budget. Kimberlites provide a unique opportunity to study mantle N reservoirs because they may sample the subcontinental lithospheric mantle (SCLM), deeper plume-influenced sources, or both. Here, we present N isotope measurements of olivine-hosted fluid inclusions from 13 kimberlite pipes spanning eight cratons and emplaced from 14 ka to 558 Ma. Kimberlites with near-zero δ 15 N (+0.8 ± 1.1 ‰) are observed throughout the Phanerozoic, whereas isotopically heavier N (+5.3 ± 0.5 ‰) is only observed in kimberlites younger than 180 Ma. Elevated δ 15 N values correlate with K 2 O enrichment, indicating interaction with phlogopite-bearing, sediment-modified lithospheric mantle. K-poor kimberlites with plume-like Ne isotopes have δ 15 N and N 2 / 36 Ar consistent with a primordial deep mantle N reservoir. The emergence of 15 N-enriched signatures in Earth’s surface reservoirs is attributed to increased primary productivity and biomass burial following the Cambrian Explosion, which produced N-rich, isotopically heavy sediments that were subsequently subducted. We hypothesise that 15 N-enriched subduction signatures impacted metasomatic fluids that overprinted the SCLM during the Phanerozoic. These observations provide additional temporal resolution into the link between biosphere evolution and the deep N cycle.
3a3ea02714e5dde6: A swarm sequence initiated in November 2018 in the Palghar region near the western coast of India, and continued with high intensity for two years. About 8300 earthquakes were found with horizontal and depth uncertainties of ≤1.5 km after relocation. The earthquakes were distributed along two narrow N-S oriented clusters, separated by ~5 km. We performed time-domain regional waveform full moment tensor inversion to compute focal mechanisms of the 33 M L ≥ 3.5 earthquakes, followed by stress inversion. Source parameters for 28 of these events were estimated from frequency spectra analysis. The focal mechanisms indicate dominant normal faulting along steeply dipping, N-S-oriented nodal planes, with high non-DC components (~42%). Stress inversion also reveals a normal-faulting regime, in contrast to the regional India-Eurasia compressive stress regime. The Palghar swarm has been previously linked to rainfall, and our results also show contrasting earthquake source properties during the post-monsoon period, when cumulative rainfall is highest, compared to summer. During the post-monsoon period, the strikes are strictly N-S, slips are ~−100°, and a pure normal-faulting regime is observed, accompanied by increased non-DC components and reduced static stress drops. In contrast, during the summer season, oblique-normal faulting occurs along NNE-SSW-oriented planes, with slip angles reduced to about −65°. We infer that pure normal faulting induced by vertical rainwater load during the post-monsoon transitions to a combination of regional convergent stress regime and vertical loading due to remnant water during summer, resulting in oblique normal faulting. This interplay possibly sustains the rain-induced swarm.
550a9121444e5b37: Mid‐mantle (660–2,000 km) seismic observations are commonly attributed to thermo‐chemical heterogeneities or phase transitions, yet many observed features remain difficult to reconcile with these mechanisms alone. It has been shown that the depth‐dependent behavior of bridgmanite deformation generates a strain‐induced seismic discontinuity around slabs at depths broadly consistent with these observations. Its signal in the data, however, remains largely unknown. Here, we investigate the detectability of anisotropic discontinuities produced by the (100)[001]/(010)[100] slip transition in bridgmanite beneath a subduction zone by combining geodynamic and mantle fabric modeling. We then employ full waveform simulations, and then process synthetics using array seismological methods. Our results show that the anisotropic discontinuity is detectable and can be clearly distinguished from reflections at the slab‐mantle interface. For horizontally flattened slab morphologies, the reflector associated with the anisotropic discontinuity consistently exhibits positive polarity for all propagation azimuths, implying that the anisotropic layer formed beneath the slab acts as a seismically slow region. We further assess the implications of this mechanism in real data using two examples of double reflections beneath Alaska‐Aleutian and Middle America. In both cases, the S phase corresponding to the deeper reflector exhibits positive polarity that is difficult to explain either in terms of a thermo‐chemical layer or mineral phase transitions, but is consistent with the anisotropic discontinuity interpretation. These results suggest that mantle deformation plays an important role in the formation of mid‐mantle structures that may not exhibit velocity and density contrasts across their boundaries, but can nonetheless generate observable reflections.
d0fc6d9d441aa844: Effective monitoring of active volcanoes relies on the integrated analysis of multidisciplinary datasets to constrain magma migration and its temporal evolution. Here, we present a multidisciplinary study, which combines plume geochemical data, volcano-seismic signals and thermal satellite data, to gain insights into the magmatic processes in Mt. Etna's shallow plumbing system. The multiparametric study enables assessing magma ponding, convection and degassing dynamics, with particular emphasis on halogen gas emissions. Halogen and sulphur emission rates provide constraints on magma residence efficiency and the steadiness of the magma supply in the shallow system. From January to May 2023, persistent thermal anomalies, low infrasound activity, stable volcanic tremor, and sustained halogen and sulphur degassing indicate a steady-state degassing regime and efficient magma rejuvenation at shallow levels. From late May 2023, an increase in SO₂ emissions without a corresponding increase in HCl emissions, alongside enhanced infrasound activity, increased tremor amplitude, and sporadic thermal anomalies, point to a decoupling between deep gas ascent and magma ascent within the main conduit. These observations suggest that halogen flux monitoring, owing to the high solubility of halogens in silicate melts, provides a sensitive indicator of changes in the magma supply rate and near-surface magma residence time in basaltic volcanic systems.
11362e291e1122ef: Reliable estimates of seismic source size on Mars are critical for interpreting tectonic activity and impact processes, constraining the planet's interior evolution, and informing the design of future Martian seismic experiments. However, because InSight observations are limited to a single station, magnitude estimates cannot rely on empirical averaging of site and path effects as on Earth, and instead depend on comparisons between observed and modeled waveform amplitudes. Consequently, inferred magnitudes are sensitive to assumptions about interior structure, attenuation, and source parametrization. Existing Marsquake Service (MQS) magnitude‐scaling relations were calibrated using pre‐InSight interior models and tectonic source assumptions, potentially biasing magnitude estimates. Here, we reanalyze spectral amplitudes using InSight seismic data and investigate how post‐InSight interior models and source‐dependent parametrization influence inferred moment magnitudes. Using waveform simulations for a suite of 1‐D interior models, we quantify the effects of velocity structure, attenuation, three‐dimensional heterogeneity, and source physics on long‐period magnitude scaling. We introduce separate source representations and scaling relations for marsquakes and impacts. Across the tested post‐InSight models, the shallow crustal structure beneath InSight primarily controls scaling. Recalibrated marsquake magnitudes are lower by approximately 0.5 on average relative to MQS magnitudes, with the reduction varying across plausible shallow structures. Applying impact‐specific scaling brings seismic and crater‐derived estimates into closer agreement, although differences remain for large distant impacts, and the recalibrated magnitudes enable tentative matching of seismic detections to cataloged Martian impact craters. These relations provide site‐specific calibration for InSight observations and tighter constraints on Martian seismicity and impact processes.
890e8ef9275cd237: Earthquakes are among the most destructive natural hazards. As populations in seismically active regions grow, the need for effective risk mitigation strategies is more urgent than ever. In that regard, earthquake early warning systems are a key component to reduce the impact of seismic shaking.
002cff41ff711fe0: Numerous seismic studies have reported the absence of a resolvable subducted slab beneath parts of northern Kamchatka, though the mechanism for this anomaly remains debated. We utilize 1,696 P‐to‐S receiver functions to image the mantle transition zone (MTZ) beneath the Kamchatka Peninsula and surrounding areas. Beneath southwestern Kamchatka, the thickened MTZ and the pronounced 520‐km discontinuity support cold Cretaceous Pacific slab‐related material with possible hydration within the MTZ. In contrast, significant MTZ thinning is observed beneath northern Kamchatka, where previous tomography studies also show slab absence in the shallow upper mantle. This argues against the presence of a large cold detached slab remnant in the sampled MTZ. Combined with previous seismic anisotropy, tomography, and geodynamic constraints, our results support a model that thermally buoyant mantle material flows around the slab edge and ascends into the upper mantle, forming a semi‐toroidal mantle flow. The inferred slab‐edge mantle flow may extend to at least MTZ depths and provide a plausible setting for progressive modification and weakening of the slab margin beneath northern Kamchatka, while allowing slab penetration farther southwest. These observations highlight the first‐order role of slab–mantle interaction in controlling slab fate at convergent margins.
132d46114d30a819: The North Anatolian Fault Zone beneath the Sea of Marmara in NW Türkiye displays a 50% probability of an earthquake within the next decades. The proximity of the fault to the Istanbul megalopolis highlights the need for high‐resolution microseismicity monitoring to identify seismicity transients including pre‐mainshock clustering. We analyze six 4.0 M L 5.8 earthquake sequences in the eastern and central Marmara region from 2016 to 2023 and focus on the occurrence of seismicity immediately prior to the mainshocks. We combine borehole and surface seismic waveform data with deep‐learning phase picking, automated phase association, and non‐linear relocation to compile a comprehensive seismicity catalog. Compared with conventional processing, our workflow allows us to detect about eight times more events in time windows around the mainshocks in the area instrumented with borehole sensors. We then apply waveform cross‐correlation, refined location techniques, and template matching to quantify waveform similarity and characterize seismic activity preceding moderate events. We observe a strong increase in waveform similarity and decrease in inter‐event distance prior to a 2016 M L 4.5 event in the Çınarcık Basin, consistent with earlier results from manual processing, and identify additional highly similar events preceding the mainshock. The 2019 M L 5.8 Silivri sequence shows increased waveform similarity but more heterogeneous spatial clustering. We demonstrate that borehole seismic arrays are critical for resolving these subtle signals due to higher signal‐to‐noise ratios. Our workflow provides a robust basis towards near‐real‐time microseismic monitoring in the Istanbul‐Marmara region and systematically identifying seismicity transients and localization processes.
f9e91f456d698576: Velocity‐model building is a fundamental component of seismic imaging workflows, yet they remain challenging inverse problems due to limited data coverage, strong nonlinearity, and the need to incorporate heterogeneous sources of information. Such information, like wells, can have a localized influence on the velocity model. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for velocity model editing and velocity model building that combines learned diffusion priors with structurally preconditioned inverse problem formulations. A diffusion model is trained on high‐resolution synthetic velocity models to learn a data‐driven prior, which is then exploited through Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models inversion and guided sampling. For localized velocity model editing, we integrate the diffusion prior with a structurally preconditioned Tikhonov inversion, enabling controlled modification of target regions while preserving the global characteristics of the background model. For full velocity model building, we formulate a well‐matching inverse problem augmented with imaging‐based regularization and solve it using a conventional least‐squares approach, the proposed Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model guided method, and Diffusion Posterior Sampling. Numerical experiments on synthetic benchmarks demonstrate that diffusion‐based approaches consistently recover sharper interfaces and higher‐resolution structures than classical least‐squares inversion. Field data applications on the Viking Graben data set further validate the robustness of the proposed framework for both editing and model building under realistic acquisition conditions.
