abcd369338d89073: We characterize seismic site response across a densely instrumented region of the Los Angeles basin by combining data from the community seismic network (CSN) and regional networks in the Advanced National Seismic System (ANSS). Mixed-effects regression is used to partition ground-motion model residuals and compute pseudospectral acceleration (PSA) site residuals (ηs) from the Next Generation Attenuation-West2 Project ground-motion database and a CSN dataset. For short periods (T < 0.3 s), CSN and ANSS site residuals agree closely, whereas observed differences at longer periods are likely related to signal-to-noise limitations of the CSN sensors rather than sensor accuracy. Correlations between CSN and ANSS site residuals are high, and the dense CSN network reveals localized amplification not resolved by the ANSS network. Along the northeastern basin margin, PSA at 1 s reaches amplitudes up to approximately twice those predicted for reference rock conditions, consistent with basin-edge amplification effects. Systematic variations in site response are observed across major fault zones, particularly in areas north of the Lower Elysian Park fault (LEPF) and between the LEPF and Puente Hills faults. These findings demonstrate the value of dense seismic networks, such as the CSN, for resolving localized amplification and improving seismic hazard assessment in urban sedimentary basins.
fce66dbb12c64727: On 24 June 2026, northern Venezuela was struck by a large and destructive earthquake with a scalar seismic moment equivalent to Mw 7.6. A preliminary source inversion yields a finite-fault model with two distinct plane solutions, providing evidence that the rupture propagated across two fault segments: an initial rupture along the right-lateral Boconó fault system, followed by propagation onto the offshore San Sebastián fault (SSF). The duration of ∼70 s is approximately twice the value predicted by global scaling laws, consistent with an unusually extended or multisegment source process confirmed by a multiple point source W-phase analysis. Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar surface deformation models support the two-fault rupture geometry. Critically, strong-motion recordings and backprojection analysis from Alaska, European, and western United States networks indicate that the rupture along the SSF reached supershear velocities of up to ∼ 5.5 km/s at distances of ∼50 km from the hypocenter. The event released strain consistent with the slip deficit inferred from regional Global Navigation Satellite System deformation data, which had accumulated to a potential Mw 7.6 equivalent along these faults. Only a few aftershocks are observed in the inferred supershear velocity zones of the fault plane.
d1b80a5ea74170f1: Full waveform inversion (FWI) aims to recover high‐resolution subsurface velocity models but remains highly ill‐posed due to strong nonlinearity, cycle‐skipping, and solution non‐uniqueness. Implicit neural representations (INRs) with multiresolution hash encoding provide an efficient continuous parameterization for implicit FWI (IFWI). However, IFWI can still produce geologically unrealistic structures and spurious high‐frequency artifacts. We propose a learned regularization framework that integrates a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) into multiresolution hash encoding‐based IFWI, as a Gradient‐Coupled Diffusion Prior for IFWI (IFWI). The inversion is guided by the joint optimization of the physics‐based IFWI gradient and the score gradient derived from the diffusion prior. If available, well‐log measurements are further imposed through guidance to anchor the inversion locally. Experiments on both synthetic examples and a challenging short‐offset field data set demonstrate that the proposed framework improves inversion stability, suppresses artificial high‐frequency features, and enhances reconstruction accuracy.
80c45562621fd50e: The continental lithosphere preserves the record of tectonic evolution while hosting resources and structures of major scientific and societal importance. In Finland, lithosphere has been investi-gated through numerous geological and geophysical surveys, but differences in spatial coverage, acquisition and resolution limit their integration into a consistent national-scale representation. Global initiatives have shown that the modern way to image the lithosphere is systematic, at national or even continental scale, with uniform coverage and standardised acquisition, an approach that is more effective, more economical and more environmentally sustainable. Syvä-Suomi is Finland’s contribution to this movement, at unprecedented resolution, and the foundation of a digital twin of the Finnish lithosphere into which decades of legacy geophysical data and complementary geoscientific data and models can be integrated. The initiative is intended to be multiphysics, opening with a nationwide long-period magnetotelluric survey and designed to grow through further geophysical methods. Past, present and future observations can then be assimilated into a single representation of the subsurface, maintained and updated continually. A national model can support applications in resources, energy, infrastructure, geological waste disposal and geohazards, while advancing understanding of Fennoscandian tectonic evolution. The multidisciplinary scope of the initiative also makes it a training ground for the next generation of geoscientists, data scientists and AI researchers in Finland and beyond.
01795c0f16974530: The Southern Apennines in Italy represent a geologically complex and seismically active region shaped by the ongoing convergence between the African and Eurasian plates. In this study, we present a high-resolution 3D crustal model of the Southern Apennines, parameterized on a 5 × 5 × 1 km³ grid and constructed through the systematic integration of geological, geophysical, and petrophysical data. The considered dataset includes laboratory velocity measurements (vp) under different pressure and temperature conditions, stratigraphic well logs, seismic tomography (vp), and geophysical models from inversion of gravimetric and magnetic data. Pressure- and temperature-dependent corrections were applied to P-wave velocities derived from regional seismic tomography, enabling us to delineate key intra-crustal boundaries, including the top of the Mesozoic limestones, the base of the Mesozoic sedimentary succession, the onset of the felsic crystalline basement, and the deeper transition to mafic, gabbroic lower-crustal units, within a 3D volume extending down to the Moho discontinuity. This modelling strategy ensures full internal consistency across spatial scales and tectonic domains, and is validated using independent borehole data, receiver functions, and other geophysical interpretations. The resulting 3D volume offers a robust framework for investigating crustal architecture and supports applications in geophysical modeling and seismic hazard assessments. All datasets are openly accessible under FAIR principles, promoting transparency, reproducibility, and interdisciplinary reuse of the results.
6fea99ac3535c124: The long range propagation of acoustic waves in Earth's atmosphere is sensitive to winds and temperature variations in the upper atmosphere. Thus, infrasound observations have a strong potential to improve numerical weather models by data assimilation methods. However, because acoustic waves propagate slowly, the atmospheric parameters can change during the propagation of the acoustic waves. This change of atmosphere properties is usually not taken into account by infrasound simulation tools which generally assume stationary atmosphere models. In order to close this modeling gap, we present here a method to compute the linear sensitivities of infrasound observables to atmospheric parameters varying both in space and time. We show that adjoint based methods can easily handle this computation of 4D sensitivity kernels, also called time variable observation operators in the data assimilation community. Then, we discuss the capabilities of various data assimilation methods to handle such observation operators. We demonstrate that only variational methods with data assimilation windows longer than the propagation duration of the long range infrasound can accommodate these observations, as well as their ensemble counterparts. Finally, we demonstrate the benefit of assimilating such long range infrasound observations, and we quantify the relative impact of linear approximation of observation operators and stationary approximation of the atmosphere model by assimilating propagation time observations of circumnavigating Lamb waves in Lorenz'96 low-order model. The results of this data assimilation experiment demonstrate that the time variability of atmospheric parameters should be taken into account even for infrasound propagation times limited to 2 or 3 time steps of the atmosphere model.
0a87951d4196ea1c: We have discovered an inverse relationship between the earthquake source deactivation coefficient and the magnitude of the main shock. Recently, this pattern was confirmed through an analysis of earthquakes in the Central Himalayas (Poudel et al., 2026). On the one hand, independent confirmation of a previously unknown pattern strengthens our confidence in the relevance of the phenomenological theory of aftershocks, upon which we have based our method for processing and analyzing aftershocks. On the other hand, Poudel et al. (2026) presented our method in a distorted manner. Poudel et al. mistakenly believe that our method is based on a modified Omori law. Both circumstances provide an occasion and a basis for a simple and clear explanation of the essence of our approach to the study of aftershocks. First and foremost, our approach to the problem is diametrically opposed to Omori approach. Omori law and its modification, proposed by Hirano and Utsu, describe the decay of aftershocks. In contrast, we formulated and solved the inverse problem. The essence of the inverse problem lies in the need to calculate the source deactivation coefficient based on aftershock observation data, without making any prior assumptions regarding the law governing the decay of aftershocks. A crucial concept in our theory is the rather complex notion of the proper time of a source. Proper time differs radically from astronomical time. The paper describes the continuous and discrete representations of proper time. This paper is methodological in nature and may prove useful to researchers studying the dynamics of an earthquake source following the formation of a main rupture within the rock mass. Keywords: earthquake source, main shock, relaxation, deactivation coefficient, proper time, inverse problem.
5ec111abd03c3a2a: Scientific drilling has produced large archives of physical, chemical and magnetic measurements linked to descriptions of the rock recovered. These archives are mostly incomplete: instruments sample at different intervals, recovery is partial, and destructive analyses preclude later measurement of the same material. We train an self-supervised embedding model on the LILY ocean drilling database using six routinely logged properties (bulk density, magnetic susceptibility, natural gamma radiation, and red, green and blue reflectance) across 236,963 observations from 296 boreholes, with a masked variational autoencoder that has a heteroscedastic Gaussian decoder and learnable mask tokens. The embeddings separate geologist-assigned lithologies as well as a variant trained with those labels, and increasing the weight on the labels degrades reconstruction while leaving classification unchanged. The labels are recoverable from the measurements geologists use to assign them, so training on them adds nothing. Lithological categories compress continuous measurements into classes, and compressing them discards what the measurements record about the processes that produced the rock. The embeddings also predict physical properties that were absent from training, on boreholes the model has never seen. While depth should account for this since sediments compact with burial, it does not. On held-out boreholes depth alone reaches a median $R^2$ of -0.02, against 0.20 for the embedding.
8b96e7b10fb1c374: Magnetic vector inversion (MVI) is widely used because it can account for both induced and remanent magnetization by inverting for a magnetization vector model. This flexibility comes at the cost of nonuniqueness, since the number of unknowns is three times that of scalar inversion, and prior information can be required to make the result geologically useful. Recent work has applied sparse norms to the vector model, but many of the other tools for incorporating prior information within scalar inversions remain either unavailable for a vector model or unavailable without introducing artifacts or significant nonlinearity. We introduce a vector regularization, formulated in Cartesian coordinates, that generalizes existing sparse Cartesian formulations. We formulate the smallness term to admit a Cartesian reference model, from susceptibility and oriented remanence, and a magnitude reference model, from unoriented remanence or total magnetization. Because a nonzero magnitude reference model makes the Hessian of the smallness term indefinite, we derive its eigendecomposition analytically and modify the eigenvalues so that standard conjugate-gradient solvers can be applied. We formulate the smoothness term to penalize changes in both the direction and magnitude of magnetization. It is independent of the choice of Cartesian basis, so sparse norms can be applied without coordinate-aligned artifacts, and it admits arbitrary preferred smoothing directions through a rotated gradient operator. We demonstrate the method on synthetic data from a folded body with spatially variable magnetization direction, where each form of prior information improves the recovered model. We then apply it to airborne magnetic data over the DO-27 kimberlite, where incorporating petrophysical measurements yields a model more consistent with the measured properties and the geologic model inferred from drilling.
0291acdb0a6c2328: Single-station ambient noise measurements, analyzed through the horizontal-to-vertical (H/V) spectral ratio, are widely applied in seismic hazard assessment and in stratigraphic reconstructions of the subsurface. In mining exploration and other applied geophysics contexts, large-scale surveys often involve hundreds of measurements to support preliminary bedrock mapping. Under these conditions, there is a strong need for tools that can rapidly evaluate the quality of collected data and guide users—expert or not—in their interpretation. To address this need, we developed and trained a supervised feed-forward neural network to classify different sections of microtremor spectra into seven categories: normal, 1D resonance, 2D or 3D resonance, artifact, velocity inversion, data requiring cleaning, and malfunctioning sensor. The training dataset comprised 3000 examples from over 20 yr of field measurements in diverse geological and environmental settings, processed with consistent windowing, smoothing, and spectral normalization procedures. By analyzing both the individual spectral components and the H/V curve within selected frequency intervals, the neural net produces a probability-based classification for each interval, which can be aggregated into a synthetic quality assessment—accept, reject, or reanalyze—based on predefined criteria. Testing on unseen data yielded an accuracy of about 80%–82%, with the main classification challenge being the distinction between 2D/3D resonances and artifacts due to their spectral similarities. The neural net proved robust to changes in instrument type, analysis window length, and smoothing parameters. This approach offers an alternative to fixed-threshold guidelines such as the SESAME (2004) criteria.
350994a83fb2c124: Physics-based dynamic rupture and ground-motion simulations provide critical constraints for seismic hazard and risk assessment. However, their reliability is limited by the poorly constrained initial stress conditions on faults. To address this issue, we constrain the initial stress distribution in our simulations using geodetic estimates of interseismic locking distribution and slip deficit rate (from Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar and Global Positioning System). We apply this geodetically constrained stress framework to the Jinqianghe–Maomaoshan (JQH–MMS) fault system located within the Tianzhu seismic gap. Scenario dynamic rupture simulations indicate that the fault can generate an earthquake, which would produce peak ground motions exceeding intensity XI on the Chinese Seismic Intensity Scale, highlighting the high seismic risk in the region. To evaluate the impact of our approach, we compared simulated dynamic rupture processes and kinematic ground motions from models with and without geodetically constrained initial stress. The results demonstrate that the locking-derived stress model significantly affects rupture propagation and extent. It also provides a physically grounded framework for seismic risk assessment and mitigation.
f461ac5d41a364f9: Geospatial liquefaction models are scalable predictive tools with global applications, but they can exhibit regional bias due to differing local characteristics or varying input data quality. This study proposes a regionalized geospatial liquefaction model framework based on Bayesian logistic regression (BLR), which leverages globally trained models as informative priors and incorporates regional data to update model parameters within a principled Bayesian framework. Two regional case studies—Türkiye and Alaska—are used to evaluate the proposed method. Results show that BLR models significantly improve upon global models in predictive accuracy, reducing bias and uncertainty while maintaining generalizability and mitigating overfitting risks associated with purely local models. A covariance-scaling strategy controls the trade-off between global priors and regional likelihoods, enabling flexible model tuning. Using data from the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake for validation and the BLR model updated with data from Europe and Türkiye, accuracy improves from 0.77 to 0.84 and the F1 score from 0.74 to 0.85, with model coefficients remaining broadly consistent with the global model in terms of contributing variables (peak ground velocity [PGV], VS30, precipitation, water table depth, and distance to water). The resulting model reduces model bias for the region. Using data from the 2018 Anchorage earthquake for validation and the BLR model updated with data from that earthquake, accuracy increases from 0.62 to 0.71 and the F1 score from 0.46 to 0.73. The updated model reduces contributions from water table depth and precipitation to near zero while increasing those from PGV and distance to water. The proposed BLR framework offers a robust and adaptable solution for developing region-specific geospatial liquefaction models, particularly in regions where global model predictions exhibit significant bias.
f18884cba25e9043: Reliable measures of phase-pick confidence are essential for using neural-network phase pickers in automated seismic monitoring and catalog construction. Using the Pacific Northwest Seismic Network data set, we show that the spread of predicted probability mass functions (PMFs) tracks relative picking difficulty even when models are trained only with one-hot arrival-time labels, which assign probability one to the catalog pick time and zero to all other times, and without explicit quality information. Controlled label-perturbation experiments indicate that the predictive distributions inherit both systematic bias and label variability from the training targets, allowing probabilistic structure to emerge under deterministic supervision. We also find that disagreement across separately trained models increases for more difficult samples but can be substantially reduced by training on ensemble-averaged soft labels. PMF interquartile range follows the expected ordering of analyst-assigned quality tiers more consistently than either signal-to-noise ratio or a simple magnitude–distance metric, whereas its modest correlations with these measures indicate that it provides complementary information about picking difficulty. Together, these results show that PMF-derived measures such as interquartile range provide data-driven, reproducible indicators of picking difficulty, with practical value for both seismic monitoring and retrospective catalog construction.
faa16b9c1fc44f0e: Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) provides unprecedentedly dense wavefield observations for high-resolution near-surface structural imaging, yet its application often relies on specific active sources or ideal noise conditions. To address this limitation, this study proposes a workflow that leverages localized seismic signals, with human footsteps used as a representative source type. Our approach integrates an object detection algorithm to automatically identify and extract footstep signals from continuous DAS recordings. We then construct datasets from numerous events, extract and stack the dispersion spectra of subarrays using multichannel analysis of surface waves, and obtain fundamental-mode surface-wave dispersion curves. Finally, the near-surface velocity structure underneath the study area is obtained. The imaging results reveal distinct velocity variations along different cable segments that are broadly consistent with outcropped geological conditions, supporting the feasibility of the workflow. This approach provides a cost-effective and environmentally adaptive imaging solution that operates without relying on conventional sources. Although demonstrated using footstep signals, the workflow may be adapted to other suitable localized anthropogenic or controlled sources, potentially expanding DAS applicability in complex settings.
d727fbd07a49838f: Microseismic monitoring is often used at subsurface industrial sites, such as hydraulic fracturing for shale gas, stimulation of engineered geothermal systems, mature hydrocarbon reservoirs, and carbon capture and storage. Microseismic observations can be used to map growing fractures in the subsurface, to understand the geomechanical response of subsurface reservoirs to industrial operations, and to identify and characterize nascent induced seismicity. Downhole microseismic datasets are acquired using multistation geophone strings placed in deep boreholes at reservoir depths, with sampling rates at 1 kHz or higher. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools have driven a step-change in the processing of surface-based seismological data. However, similar improvements are yet to be realized for downhole microseismic processing tasks. To date, a major barrier in the development of AI tools for downhole microseismic monitoring has been the lack of publicly available data with which to train models. We seek to eliminate this barrier by curating an AI-ready downhole microseismic benchmark database (AMBER) consisting of waveforms and labels (arrival time picks) drawn from 10 downhole microseismic datasets. AMBER contains over 4,000 events with over 150,000 individual P and S wave picks. All picks have been manually verified. The database also contains over 10,000 examples of signal-free noise, which have also been manually verified. The database is provided in an AI-ready format, with Python functions for data ingestion and data augmentation. It is hoped that AMBER will stimulate and support the development of AI tools for downhole microseismic processing.
7f30c0fdcde9dd4f: Pretrained deep-learning phase pickers are now widely used in earthquake monitoring, but their transferability to deep-focus earthquakes recorded by regional seismic networks remains poorly constrained. We evaluate three SeisBench pretrained pickers, PhaseNet, EQTransformer, and generalized phase detection (GPD), using manually picked Northeast China deep-focus earthquake records. The fine-tuning set contains 1638 manually picked arrivals (875 P and 763 S arrivals) from 29 events during 2008–2022, 400 noise windows, and data augmentation applied to S-phase waveforms. The blind test uses 660 analyst-reviewed arrivals from four 2023–2025 events recorded by 135 stations, including 86 stations not used during fine-tuning. At validation-selected thresholds and a ± 1.0 s matching tolerance, fine-tuned PhaseNet, EQTransformer, and GPD yield P-phase F1 scores of 0.893, 0.673, and 0.350, respectively, and S-phase F1 scores of 0.315, 0.377, and 0.252. At a stricter ±0.5 s tolerance, the corresponding P-phase F1 scores are 0.758, 0.601, and 0.195, and the S-phase F1 scores are 0.243, 0.283, and 0.154. Post hoc blind-test F1-optimal thresholds are retained only as upper-bound estimates. Record-level bootstrap intervals, matching-tolerance tests, and leave-one-event-out analyses show that PhaseNet P-phase picking improves most clearly. In contrast, S-phase picking remains the primary empirical limitation. One event located near the edge of the source–station geometry strongly affects the pooled performance metrics for S-phase picking. We therefore interpret this result as an illustrative case suggesting possible sensitivity to source–station geometry, rather than as evidence for a general event-level pattern.
a0dc09ce7c09aea1: Accurate, readily available shaking estimates can improve situational awareness and rapid response efforts following a major earthquake. The spatial distribution of shaking relative to population and infrastructure has major implications for expected fatalities, damage, and disruptions. For large earthquakes, the location, size, and orientation of the causal fault plane (i.e., fault finiteness) play primary roles in determining the distribution of shaking. However, such a description of the causal fault is difficult to establish in the immediate aftermath of a major event, when observations are typically sparse and uncertain. However, during the time window between an event’s detection and the completion of quantitative constraints on the source, tectonic context can provide evidence for the rupture’s likely spatial orientation, thereby improving shaking estimates prior to formal finite-fault inversion results. Here, we propose a new method using tectonic context to describe a constrained, but still uncertain, source to improve early shaking estimates for large earthquakes. We demonstrate its implementation in the U.S. Geological Survey ShakeMap software by applying the proposed method to a catalog of 40 large (Mw>7), impactful global events from 2018 to 2026 and present an analysis of the results. We find that for 18 of the catalog events, the ShakeMap could be automatically constrained based on the seismotectonic context, whereas 14 events would require expert user input to determine whether a constrained approach is appropriate, and 8 events would not benefit from a constrained approach (but could be automatically identified). The results show that using seismotectonic context to constrain the source can substantially improve shaking estimates in the immediate minutes to hours following a major earthquake. We show a detailed comparison of the proposed (constrained) approach to the existing (unconstrained) approach for four earthquakes, each occurring in a distinct tectonic environment, to highlight the advantages and limitations of the method’s application.
d6d6dbde86e7d80b: Summary Earthquakes are preceded by a transition from diffuse to localized deformation, yet quantifying the mechanical conditions that define this onset and connecting them to routine seismic catalogue observables remains an open challenge. We derive, from the continuum damage constitutive law, a characteristic trajectory in the spatial mean and variance of the inelastic strain-rate field during progressive fault preparation: the mean $\langle \overset{.}{\gamma} ^{in}\rangle $ increases monotonically as damage-reduced viscosity declines, while the spatial variance $var( \overset{.}{\gamma} ^{in} )$ passes through a minimum as the production of new stress heterogeneity declines during the coalescence of damage into the forming shear band. This trajectory is a direct mechanical consequence of the damage law: under progressive localization, the variance minimum is expected to precede the mean inelastic strain-rate maximum, distinguishing coherent localization from distributed acceleration, and explaining why rate-only seismic precursors may fail to identify rupture nucleation. We show that two seismicity-derived metrics — seismic strain dynamics (SSD) and the seismic regularity coefficient (dc) — provide observational proxies for $\langle \overset{.}{\gamma} ^{in}\rangle $ and $\sqrt {var( \overset{.}{\gamma} ^{in} )} $, connecting routine catalog observables directly to the governing equations. Cross-scale validation across laboratory stick-slip experiments, physics-based dynamic rupture simulations, induced seismicity, and tectonic earthquakes spanning eight orders of magnitude in spatial scale confirms the predicted SSD–dc trajectory. These results provide a quantitative basis for assessing fault-zone evolution and for improving the physical interpretation of earthquake preparation processes.
972831006f737442: On 1956 July 9, the southeastern Cyclades were struck by an earthquake doublet, consisting of an ∼Ms 7.4 main shock, the largest recorded in Greece during the instrumental era, followed shortly afterward by a twin earthquake of magnitude greater than 6.0. The sequence caused severe damage on Santorini, leading Greek authorities to declare the island a disaster area and triggered a major tsunami that affected much of the Aegean basin. Despite the historical significance of this catastrophe, ground-motion observations in the near-source region remain sparse and sometimes contradictory 70 years later, limiting our understanding of the rupture process and hindering reliable seismic hazard assessment. This is particularly true for Amorgos, located less than 30 km from the rupture zone, where available macroseismic evidence suggests unexpectedly low earthquake impacts. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted the first comprehensive geophysical investigation of Amorgos, combining passive and active seismic methods, including ambient vibration arrays and multichannel analysis of surface waves. Taking advantage of the remarkable seismic sequence that occurred between Santorini and Amorgos in early 2025, we further compared the seismic responses of both islands to a set of local crustal earthquakes with magnitudes greater than 3.2. Our results provide a geophysical characterization of the island’s main inhabited areas and reveal moderate to high near-surface shear- and compressional-wave velocities, consistent with the local geology and indicative of stiff soil conditions with limited amplification potential. Combined with the analysis of seismicity, these observations confirm the absence of site effects in Amorgos, in sharp contrast with the strong amplification and directivity observed in Santorini. Conversely, the permanent seismological station on Amorgos exhibits remarkably short-duration ground motions and a pronounced attenuation of high-frequency energy (> 6 Hz), corresponding to the frequency range of traditional Cycladic buildings. These findings offer a new perspective on the ground-motion pattern of the 1956 earthquake and suggest that the geological setting of Amorgos played a major role in mitigating earthquake impacts. However, the geophysical evidence does not account for the large spatial variability in the reported macroseismic intensities, raising questions about the reliability of the intensity assessments. More broadly, this study highlights the complexity of near-fault ground motions and demonstrates the relevance of integrated geophysical approaches for overcoming the limitations of macroseismic data sets and improving seismic hazard assessment.
9573233b3d085de1: Probabilistic seismic hazard analysis is commonly used to estimate the likelihood of ground motion exceeding a certain threshold, over a given time horizon, at a single location. This is different than knowing the probability that any location within a region will experience ground motion exceeding that threshold, information that would be useful for assessing short-term hazards from aftershocks or induced seismicity, guiding emergency managers’ response planning, identifying which areas an earthquake early warning system should alert, or even validating existing probabilistic seismic hazard models. In this paper, we develop a methodology for estimating ground motion hazard across a region, specifically determining the probability of ground shaking anywhere in that region exceeding a prescribed threshold. We benchmark the efficiency of several stochastic sampling algorithms; compare various spatial covariance models including a new spatial covariance model based on dense observations of shaking from aftershocks of the 2019 Ridgecrest, California earthquake sequence; determine the minimum required spatial discretization for estimating shaking hazard across a region and explore assorted computational efficiencies. With this new methodology, we then present a case study of seismic hazard across California’s San Francisco Bay Area, computing probabilities that somewhere in the Bay Area will experience peak ground acceleration exceeding 0.1g, 0.2g, 0.4g or 0.8g at least once over timescales of one to 30 yr. Finally, we use these results to explore the impacts on the estimated seismic hazard of short-term versus long-term earthquake rates, ground motion variability and source selection,.
9b8b3f25d933bd23: Dynamic topography above subduction zones is widely inferred, but its magnitude and controls remain poorly constrained at the global scale. Here, we estimate residual topography across a range of back‐arc basins by correcting bathymetry for sediment loading, crustal structure, and lithospheric age, and compare the anomalies with slab geometry and subduction parameters. Most basins show negative residual topography, and the anomalies become more negative with increasing slab dip. Continental–oceanic back‐arc basins tend to show more negative residual topography than ocean–ocean systems. Residual topography further covaries with cumulative subducted water content, consistent with a possible influence of hydration‐modified mantle rheology on slab‐driven flow. Although the number of basins with complete slab constraints remains limited, these results suggest that slab geometry is associated with negative residual topography in back‐arc regions and provide observational constraints for geodynamic models of mantle flow around subduction zones.
48cf0c0117c96c8b: The 2010 Yushu (eastern Tibetan Plateau) Ms 7.1 strike‐slip earthquake ruptured unilaterally toward the southeast but left a hypocentral segment without mapped surface rupture, followed by a two‐stage reorganization of aftershocks. We present a 3‐D electrical resistivity model from 70 quality‐controlled magnetotelluric sites acquired shortly after the event. Alternative data‐component inversions, 2‐D/3‐D comparisons, and anomaly‐focused forward tests identify the best‐resolved features. A conductive mid–lower crust beneath the Qiangtang block abuts more resistive Bayan Har crust. The mainshock and early aftershocks lie near upper‐crustal resistivity transitions, while a broad shallow conductor extends beneath and beyond the hypocentral surface‐rupture gap. The late conjugate swarm extends into a sparsely sampled sector. The underlying electrical structure is therefore not well resolved. The results indicate that crustal heterogeneity may have influenced rupture segmentation and early aftershock redistribution, whereas the relation to the late swarm requires denser observations.
4c4a1bd943fb6725: Relative and calibrated stress drops for the Ridgecrest earthquake sequence from the spectral-ratio-asymptote graph inversion of Knudson, Shaw, Ellsworth & Beroza. Preferred configuration: k_nn = 8, 1.5 km edge cap, adaptive LF band, P+S combined, relay threshold M2.3, slope weight W = 0.25 (Table 1 of the paper). One row per event in the inversion graph. Columns: event_id SCSN event identifier origin_time_utc origin time (ISO 8601, UTC) from the SCEDC relocated catalog latitude, longitude degrees; depth_km in km (GrowClust location where available) catalog_magnitude SCSN catalog magnitude; magnitude_type: l = ML, lr = Mlr, w = Mw, blank = no type recorded (1-D/3-D located events) location_method gc = GrowClust (Trugman & Shearer 2017), 1d = Hypoinverse, 3d = SIMULPS growclust_relocated True if GrowClust relocated the event (nbranch > 1) role dual-band (M2.5-4.0, both LFL and HFL solved; the reported population), relay (M2.3-2.5, in the LFL block and additionally admitted to the HFL block to connect it; excluded from reported statistics), LFL-only (M 4.0) hf_group main = connected to the main high-frequency group (1961 dual-band events); disconnected = one of the 24 groups whose level relative to the main population is undetermined (their relative values are internal to the group) n_pairs number of spectral-ratio pairs involving the event (graph degree) mean_pair_separation_m mean 3-D separation of the event's pairs, metres LFL_rel, HFL_rel relative low- and high-frequency levels, log10 units (Eqs. 23-25; each block is zero-mean over the dual-band population) SD_rel_log10 relative log10 stress drop, 1.5*HFL_rel - 0.5*LFL_rel (Eq. 26); dual-band only SD_log10_MPa, SD_MPa calibrated stress drop (Brune model, k = 0.37, beta = 3.5 km/s; Section 6.3); calibration constant C = 6.75 for stress drop in Pa sigma_jackknife per-event uncertainty from the delete-20% pair jackknife, log10 units sigma_bootstrap per-event uncertainty from the station bootstrap, log10 units Catalog and waveforms: Hauksson et al. (2012) relocated catalog, 1981-2024 GrowClust extension distributed by the SCEDC; waveforms and parametric data from the Caltech/USGS Southern California Seismic Network (doi:10.7914/SN/CI) stored at the SCEDC (doi:10.7909/C3WD3xH1).
1fb7b75de54c0809: We present a large seismological dataset (https://geofon.gfz.de/doi/network/ZK/2021) composed by continuous recordings from 200 temporary stations (seismic network ZK, 10.14470/MX7576871994), which operated continuously for approximately one year in the Southern Apennines (Southern Italy) as part of the DETECT experiment. The dataset is compliant with the seismological standards for the archiving of data and metadata, and with standardized tools for disseminating them, e.g., the International Federation of Digital Seismograph Networks (FDSN) web services. The data set was collected during the DETECT experiment in the Irpinia area (southern Italy), which is one of the regions with the highest seismic hazard in Italy. From August 2021 to August 2022, a constellation of 20 seismic arrays, with a total of 200 seismic stations, was installed above the fault segments responsible for the M 6.9, 1980 Irpinia earthquake, the strongest and most destructive seismic event in Italy in the last fifty years. Each seismic array had a maximum aperture of ~2 km and was composed of one broad-band sensor, one short- period sensor with 1 Hz and eight 4.5 Hz natural frequency geophones. Data and metadata were managed in accordance with the GIPP/GEOFON policy using SeisComP (Helmholtz Centre Potsdam – GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences and GEMPA GmbH, 2008) and the final archive size is approximately 5.2 TB. In this contribution, we provide details on how to download waveform data and station metadata, as well as information on data availability and quality.
a1c9830afa4f2c5b: Scientific drilling has produced large archives of physical, chemical and magnetic measurements linked to descriptions of the rock recovered. These archives are mostly incomplete: instruments sample at different intervals, recovery is partial, and destructive analyses preclude later measurement of the same material. We train an self-supervised embedding model on the LILY ocean drilling database using six routinely logged properties (bulk density, magnetic susceptibility, natural gamma radiation, and red, green and blue reflectance) across 236,963 observations from 296 boreholes, with a masked variational autoencoder that has a heteroscedastic Gaussian decoder and learnable mask tokens. The embeddings separate geologist-assigned lithologies as well as a variant trained with those labels, and increasing the weight on the labels degrades reconstruction while leaving classification unchanged. The labels are recoverable from the measurements geologists use to assign them, so training on them adds nothing. Lithological categories compress continuous measurements into classes, and compressing them discards what the measurements record about the processes that produced the rock. The embeddings also predict physical properties that were absent from training, on boreholes the model has never seen. While depth should account for this since sediments compact with burial, it does not. On held-out boreholes depth alone reaches a median $R^2$ of -0.02, against 0.20 for the embedding.
868f812779203a4f: Seismic methods for estimating sea ice thickness traditionally rely on surface-sited instrumentation and, consequentially, are limited in duration and spatial extent by the inherent logistical challenges of polar field deployments. We present a novel method for measuring sea ice thickness from the seafloor, utilizing distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) on a trenched seafloor telecommunications cable in the Beaufort Sea, Alaska. We apply a frequency–slowness transformation to DAS observations of flexural-gravity (FG) waves to extract phase velocity dispersion curves, which we then invert to estimate sea ice thickness using a simple grid search across ice thickness and rigidity space. We show that this method yields equivalent results for broadband FG waves generated by windstorms, hovercraft traffic, and thermal fracturing. DAS-derived estimates obtained throughout January to March 2023 are consistent with sea ice thicknesses measured at collocated ice boreholes, and with estimates from an air temperature cumulative freezing-day model. This novel method enables continuous, high resolution, multiyear seismic monitoring of sea ice thickness without the risk or burden of annual surface deployments.
3175c94bf2fa57c1: Summary Enhancing frequency resolution as much as possible from finite-length and noisy observations to identify a larger number of harmonic and quasi-harmonic signals has long been a central objective in data analysis; owing to the intrinsic complexity of the Earth system, this demand is particularly acute in the geosciences. For finite records, the effective resolution of classical Fourier-based spectra is governed by the spectral-window width, commonly characterized by the Rayleigh scale. Although non-Fourier approaches, such as autoregressive (AR) methods and Hankel total least squares (HTLS), are in principle capable of achieving higher frequency resolution, they typically rely on accurate prior information, including the locations of narrow frequency bands and the number of embedded harmonics K, and operate through direct parametric estimation rather than forming an explicit spectrum for visual inspection, thereby limiting their applicability as general blind identification techniques. To address these limitations, we propose a Super-Resolution Spectral Analysis (SRSA) method. This approach constructs a two-dimensional (2D) super-resolution (SR) spectrum ${{\bf I}}( {L,{{{\bf f}}}_c} )$ by exploiting the orthogonality between the multi-scale noise subspaces derived from the singular value decomposition of Hankel matrices (Hankel-SVDs) formed with different window lengths L, and the Vandermonde matrix. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed method is robust to moderate perturbations in K and supports reliable signal identification without requiring exact prior knowledge of individual spectral peak locations or the true model order. In addition, SRSA can improve effective frequency discrimination relative to a Fourier benchmark. For a fixed record length T, its resolving capability depends jointly on the sampling frequency ${f}_s$, the intrinsic model order, and the noise level. Under the noise-free simulation setup adopted in this study, numerical experiments show roughly an order-of-magnitude improvement in effective resolution relative to the Fourier benchmark, while the noisy experiments still demonstrate a clear gain in frequency resolution across the tested SNR levels. Using superconducting gravimeter observations following the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman and the 2011 Tohoku earthquakes, we apply the SRSA method to detect the splitting of Earth’s free oscillation eigenmodes. The method improves spectral resolution and weak-signal detectability, successfully resolving multiple low-frequency spheroidal and core-sensitive modes. These results both corroborate previous findings and provide independent constraints on mode splitting, highlighting the broad potential of SRSA as an effective tool for harmonic analysis in geophysical observations.
3f9d79c7f271d22a: Continental rifting reflects the balance between tectonic forces and lithospheric strength, yet the mechanisms of breakup remain debated. Rapid rifting of the Gulf of California oblique rift (GOCOR) ~6 million to 8 million years ago is a key example; it may have resulted from the lithosphere responding to external kinematics or acceleration of long-lived extension. The dynamics of either scenario remain incompletely understood. In this study, we highlight that the rapid rifting of the GOCOR coincides with the initiation of Western Pacific double subduction. Using three-dimensional geodynamic models, we show that such subduction reorganization can transmit extensional stresses of ~5 to 15 megapascals across the Pacific plate, loading the GOCOR and the southern San Andreas fault. Subduction reorganization may represent the missing driver for the initiation of rapid GOCOR rifting within a preconditioned lithosphere and may be an overlooked tectonic force behind other rifting events.
8c790c7c0c7555b6: Dykes are a key mechanism for material transport within volcanic arcs and typically propagate over days to months. We document an unusually slow dyking episode in the arc of southern Peru that lasted for 1.5 years. The dyke opened up to 0.5 m from 2-8 km depth and was coupled with inflation of an underlying arc-parallel magma reservoir. To reconcile the slow opening of such a thin dyke with physical models of magma flow and heat transfer, magma with viscosity $\sim$10$^{6}$ Pa s was likely injected into wall rock within $\lesssim$100 $^\circ$C of the magma's solidus. Pre-heating of the shallow crust by previous plutonic intrusions may have enabled the viscous magma to have propagated as a dyke to within 2 km of the surface. Our findings suggest that significant pre-heating will be preferential for the transport of evolved, silicic magmas in dykes to depths where magmatic-hydrothermal mineral deposits form.
8fee5744e43444d3: The 24 June 2026 Venezuela earthquake was cataloged as a doublet (Mw 7.2 and 7.5, separated by 30–40 s). Studying its source process is challenging due to the uncertain location of the second event. We invert full displacement waveforms for multiple-point moment-release models constrained only by the fault trace, without imposing the cataloged location or timing as prior constraints. We estimate positions, times, and moments of N subevents at discrete fault points, assuming a constant source depth and a broad time range, and combining the sequential and joint parameter searches. At 0.005–0.010 Hz, the earthquake is a doublet (N = 2) formed by Mw 7.3 and 7.4 subevents spaced by 25 s. At 0.010–0.025 Hz, N = 5, the subevents exhibit a relatively compact, ∼200-km-long rupture lasting ∼60 s, with eastward directivity. Temporal separation of the early western subevent and the late eastern subevents is 20–42 s. The patch model, obtained by assuming constant stress-drop scaling, matches the 46 cm Global Navigation Satellite System vector. Large aftershocks are notably absent, whereas smaller ones are irregularly distributed. A possible supershear rupture on an aftershock-free fault segment is indicated. The earthquake highlights the complexity of ruptures in the region, which is crucial for ground-motion hazard scenarios.
b1d6709e709b69b5: Seismic and geodetic monitoring prior to destructive earthquakes may reveal transient signals that are essential for earthquake forecasting and seismic hazard management. Extensive research indicates that these transient deformations, which can exhibit non-linear variations as fault instability approaches, may be linked to the preparatory processes within fault zones. These preparation signals suggest the approach towards a critical point, which marks a phase transition in the physical state of the fault. However, detecting the earthquake preparation process in situ remains challenging due to the spatial density and resolution of monitoring networks, and the complexity of fault zones. The exact role of these transient deformations in driving the system towards a mainshock remains elusive; therefore, it is essential to understand the physical mechanisms behind preparatory processes for the development of next-generation earthquake forecasting models. In this thesis, we integrate acoustic emission (AE) monitoring and distributed fiber optic strain sensing (DFOS) within a laboratory setting to measure broadband deformation during fault preparation in intact rock samples. First, we investigated the spatio-temporal evolution of the DFOS strain field during triaxial tests performed on an intact sample of Berea sandstone in wet and dry conditions. The results show that in dry samples, the deformation progressively localizes in response to the power-law acceleration of the largest strain increments. As failure approaches, the distribution of the strain increments gradually evolves to a power-law regime, suggesting a critical (predictable) phase transition. However, this criticality is suppressed by elevated fluid pressure, with the largest strain increment exhibiting exponential growth within highly diffuse deformation. Integrated measurements of AEs and DFOS were then performed during rock failure tests on two lithologies with different microstructural compositions: a relatively homogeneous sandstone and a more heterogeneous granite. The aim was to examine how microstructural heterogeneity affects non-linear preparation signals in both seismicity and surface deformation. The initial preparatory process in both samples is characterized by progressive strain localization, with the largest increment exhibiting a power-law acceleration. Differences in grain-scale heterogeneity control the coupling between strain localization and seismic clustering in late-stage preparatory physics. In the sandstone sample, the seismicity gradually shifts from background levels to a clustered pattern adjacent to the localized strain just before failure. However, in more heterogeneous granite, seismicity clusters within isolated patches that are more localized than the strain field. This results in enhanced seismic interactions, attributed to structural energy barriers. The breakdown of these energy barriers drives the system into a state of intermittent criticality, triggering a cascading failure process. Building on these results, we revisited integrated measurements on samples of sandstone and granite to investigate the relationship between local stress fields, as inverted from AE focal mechanisms, and damage evolution during fault preparation. To this end, the spatial variation of seismic moment release and Gutenberg-Richter $b$-values was compared with the strain field to analyze the source process of damage networks. The results for the sandstone sample show that seismic activity progressively clusters within the damage zone and exhibits short-range correlations. The associated stress field gradually rotated towards the angle of localized strain, interpreted as the development of a shear band within a homogeneous microstructure. However, structural energy barriers in the more heterogeneous granite sample distorted this stress alignment by dissipating seismic energy into isolated patches. The breakdown of these energy barriers redistributes the stress field to establish long-range correlations, coalescing an incipient fault plane for a system-spanning failure. This work highlights the complex seismo-mechanical coupling expressed as progressive strain localization and seismic clustering during the preparatory processes leading to dynamic failure. This coupling process can be modulated by both external loading conditions and internal heterogeneities, serving as an indicator of the system’s state and its proximity to a critical point. This provides a new perspective on preparatory processes, bridging earthquake-genesis paradigms such as progressive localization, pre-slip, and cascade-up.
8ba2c4a4d0bf1647: The Carajás-Bacajá boundary preserves complementary archives of continental rifting, passive-margin development, subduction, collision and post-collisional exhumation across the Archean-Paleoproterozoic transition. We present whole-rock lithogeochemistry, Sm-Nd isotopes, U-Pb zircon geochronology and thermobarometry from the Vila Santa Fé-Rio Preto association, a mafic-felsic granulitic assemblage tectonically above the Buritirama succession. Rio Preto-type mafic granulites define a comparatively juvenile pole, whereas arc-modified felsic orthogneisses have negative εNd at ca. 2.10 Ga, TDM ages of ca. 2.44-2.46 Ga and Archean inherited zircon. U-Pb zircon records lower-crustal melt growth at 2097 ± 19 and 2093 ± 25 Ma, followed by granulite-facies recrystallization, migmatization and charnockitic to enderbitic melt generation between 2073 ± 3 and 2067 ± 7 Ma. Thermobarometry constrains a 9-10 kbar, 760-800 °C granulitic root, followed by hydrated decompression at 7-8 kbar and 690-710 °C; Carajás-side amphibolite records ca. 700-720 °C. Structural, geophysical and 40Ar/39Ar constraints define southwest-verging stacking of Bacajá lower crust over Buritirama and northern Carajás between ca. 2.10 and 2.05 Ga. Published data extend the reconstruction backward. A 2549 ± 5.9 Ma A2-type granite and proximal ca. 2.55 Ga detritus date rift initiation; upward provenance broadening, seawater-like carbonate chemistry, positive pre-ore δ13C and later manganese accumulation record margin maturation and sediment starvation. Apparent Paleoproterozoic detrital ages in Buritirama are reproducible by low-discordance Pb loss from Archean zircon. The same correction applies to the Novolândia granulite belt, whose sedimentary protoliths carry a 3.32–3.18 Ga Paleoarchean provenance peak, 2.75 and 2.55 Ga magmatic populations and a rift-type granite crystallized at 2567 ± 22 Ma with 2744 ± 21 Ma inheritance, identifying the far side of the closed ocean as a detached fragment of the Carajás margin. Bacajá arc magmatism at ca. 2.21-2.13 Ga and coeval fluid-assisted re-equilibration in Carajás define upper- and lower-plate responses consistent with slab-pull extension. Decompression, rapid cooling and the unconformable Águas Claras basin, whose basal marine interval is exposed at Azul and Serra Pelada, record collapse and renewed marine transgression. The direct result is the Rhyacian collisional stack; the full Wilson cycle is the integrated model that explains the ordered regional evidence.
877e8d98de3d2288: Post-stack acoustic impedance inversion is ill-posed because seismic data are band-limited and contaminated by noise. Regularization improves the stability of the inversion, but Tikhonov regularization tends to blur formation interfaces, whereas total variation (TV) regularization may introduce staircase artifacts. To simultaneously characterize abrupt interlayer discontinuities and gradual intralayer variations, we propose an inversion method based on anisotropic Tikhonov-TV regularization and automatic parameter selection. The method decomposes the logarithmic impedance model into piecewise-constant and smooth components. TV and Tikhonov constraints are imposed on these components, respectively, in both the vertical and horizontal directions. The performance of the inversion depends critically, among other factors, on the relative weight of the total regularization term with respect to the data misfit, the relative weight of the two regularization components (the balancing parameter), and the efficiency of computing a candidate solution for a given set of parameters. In this paper, we propose a new adaptive algorithm based on alternating directions, in which (i) a fast candidate-solution computation scheme is developed in the spectral domain by exploiting the Sylvester structure and fast Fourier transforms, thereby reducing the computational cost of parameter searching; (ii) the regularization parameter is selected adaptively using the residual whiteness principle; and (iii) the balancing parameter is adaptively updated according to robust statistical characteristics of the impedance-model gradients. Synthetic and field-data tests demonstrate that, compared with conventional Tikhonov and TV methods, the proposed method better preserves impedance interfaces while reducing staircase artifacts and inter-trace discontinuities, thereby improving the reconstruction of impedance structures.
dbc38fc04c66c1ed: Long-term forecasts say how likely a fault segment is to rupture, not where the rupture will begin. The b-value, the slope of the earthquake size distribution, falls as stress rises. After the 2016 Kumamoto sequence in Japan, b-values rose along the ruptured faults but fell in the unruptured central part of the Hinagu fault zone, which we identified in 2019 as where the next rupture was most likely to begin. The 2026 M7.1 Kumamoto earthquake began at the edge of this area, inside the low-b-value volume at 16 km depth. To our knowledge, this is the first starting point of a large earthquake named in print beforehand. The rupture stopped at a fault bend where b-values have stayed low since 2000 and raised Coulomb stress on faults beyond it; the low-b-value zone at this bend is where the next rupture is most likely to begin.
5d70974613f4103c: To understand the mantle evolution that has caused the observed histories of mare volcanism and radius change of the Moon, we developed a 3-D regional spherical shell mantle convection model with magmatism. Magma generated by decompression melting segregates from the convecting matrix and percolates upward through it. In our model, internal heating forms a basal partially molten layer during the first several hundred million years. Finger-like magma ascents then grow from the top of this layer and evolve into buoyant, partially molten plumes. The plumes ascend by the buoyancy of magma, while decompression melting in the ascending plumes generates more magma that further drives the ascent. Magma supply to the top of the mantle peaks between 4 and 3.5 Gyr ago, coincident with a maximum in radial expansion driven by volume change of the mantle associated with melting, and both decline as the mantle cools and solidifies. Magma supply, however, persists for billions of years because earlier plumes leave thermally softened conduits, through which later plumes repeatedly rise at fixed locations. These stable conduits are a consequence of the 3-D geometry. Recycling of magmatic products formed in the uppermost mantle also triggers renewed magma ascent through the conduits. Our results provide a mechanism for the observed long-lasting localized volcanism that peaked at 4-3.5 Gyr ago and quantitatively account for early expansion followed by contraction. The conditions required for consistency with the observed history imply an initially hot but mostly solid mantle with a dense basal layer.
3f9f628d69c0ae4b: Models of injection-induced aseismic slip commonly assume uniform in-situ stresses along the fault, and thus predict rupture growth symmetric about the injection point. We relax this assumption and account for linear variations with depth of the resolved shear and effective normal tractions. We consider a planar fault with constant friction under plane-strain conditions, subjected to fluid injection at constant overpressure. Vanishing stress intensity factors at both rupture tips yield two coupled equations for the up-dip and down-dip tip positions. We solve them semi-analytically and compare the results with numerical simulations. The stress gradient notably breaks the self-similarity of the uniform-stress solution. Growth is then governed by two parameters. The first is the fault-stress injection parameter $\mathcal{T}$, ratio between the initial distance to failure at the injection point and the effect of the fluid overpressure. The second is the ratio of the diffusion length $\sqrt{4αt}$ to a stress-gradient length scale $L_c$, namely the initial distance to failure at the injection point divided by its gradient along the fault. Growth is symmetric at early times. In the marginally pressurized regime, rupture lags behind the pressure front and the relative asymmetry grows as $1.1\,(4αt/L_c^2)^{1/2}$. The up-dip tip then accelerates markedly compared to the down-dip tip. In the critically stressed regime, rupture outpaces diffusion by a factor of order $1/\mathcal{T}$, and the relative asymmetry grows as $\sim 0.34\,(4αt/\mathcal{T}^2L_c^2)^{1/2}$. The up-dip tip reaches $\sim L_c$ earlier, and the ratio of up-dip to down-dip rupture lengths remains below two.
14c60adfd4174696: Unexploded ordnance (UXO) clearance relies on electromagnetic induction (EMI) methods to detect and classify buried and submerged metallic objects, but the standard classification workflow requires physics-based inversion and manual expert review. We present a fully convolutional neural network (CNN) that classifies UXO directly from multicomponent time-domain EMI data, bypassing the inversion step entirely. The CNN uses a segmentation-like architecture that preserves the spatial dimensions of the input and outputs a high-resolution classification map suitable for generating a diglist. Two CNNs are used in sequence: the first detects anomalies due to metallic objects and characterizes the spatially correlated noise present in the preprocessed field data; the second performs multi-class classification using synthetic training data augmented with that noise. A physics-based parameterization of the clutter class is used to train the network to discriminate clutter from UXO across a broad range of object types. We validate this approach on two field datasets acquired with the UltraTEMA-4 system at the Sequim Bay marine test site. On a calibration grid with 21 seeded objects, the CNN detects all UXOs and discriminates two out of four clutter objects. On an independent blind grid with 35 seeded objects (17 UXOs, 18 clutter), the CNN detects and classifies all UXOs and achieves a false-positive count comparable to that of the physics-based inversion approach. We see the two methods as complementary: once trained, the CNN classifies rapidly and with minimal supervision, making it well suited as a fast first-pass tool or as an independent check on physics-based results.
8affb938788df009: Airborne magnetic anomaly navigation provides a passive, unjammable alternative to Global Navigation Satellite Systems positioning by matching magnetometer measurements against a lithospheric magnetic anomaly map. Existing map-matching algorithms either assume a Gaussian posterior (extended Kalman filter), require Monte Carlo sampling (particle filter), or discard posterior uncertainty in favour of a single optimal path (Viterbi algorithm). Here we formulate map matching as inference on a chain-structured factor graph and solve it segment by segment using the forward-backward algorithm, which yields a discrete posterior over candidate positions and its Shannon entropy $H_t$ at time $t$. Over the \texttt{Renfrew\_395} map, $10^3$ synthetic trials yield a median position error of $32.7$ m, $91\%$ below the median inertial drift of $362$ m. On these trials and $10^3$ flight paths, the median error is $43\%$ below the extended Kalman filter and particle filter. Across these paths, a threshold on segment-level entropy detects $47\%$ of segments with errors above two map cells and $94\%$ of those above three, at a $10\%$ false-alarm rate. The foregoing results indicate that $H_t$ provides a truth-free diagnostic of map-conditioned navigation ambiguity.
4e5378c3bb6fa551: We develop a unified joint inversion framework that integrates traveltimes from teleseismic body wave, local body wave, and surface wave data to construct 3‐D Vp and Vs models. The method builds upon a joint inversion framework based on the direct surface wave tomography (DSurfTomo) and local body wave double difference tomography (tomoDD), and is extended by incorporating the teleseismic station‐pair double difference differential times within a regional teleseismic inversion framework. This enables full exploitation of the complementary sensitivities of different data types, allowing the construction of a unified regional model spanning a broader depth range from the upper crust to the upper mantle. We validate the proposed method by applying it to both synthetic tests and real data inversions using realistic array configurations. We first apply it to the southern California plate boundary region, where extensive seismic observations are available, and the resulting 3‐D lithospheric‐scale Vp and Vs model is consistent with previous studies, thereby validating the feasibility of the proposed approach. The method is subsequently applied to the Weifang array in the Tanlu Fault Zone (TLFZ), demonstrating its effectiveness for small‐scale temporary dense arrays. By using teleseismic body wave data, the method enables the construction of a unified model with an extended depth range, revealing flexibility across different array scales and highlighting its potential to enhance the utilization of small‐scale temporary dense array data sets. The construction of a unified model provides important constraints for linking tectonic processes with the underlying geodynamic mechanisms.
ba682d784b688b44: InSAR‐constrained finite fault slip models are often used to characterize fault geometries and slip distributions of large continental earthquakes. A common feature of these models is a decrease in slip near the surface, commonly expressed as a percentage shallow slip deficit (SSD). This often does not seem to be accommodated interseismically and its causes are still debated, with some studies attributing large deficits to off‐fault deformation along structurally immature faults. We explore this hypothesis through a survey of ten, well‐documented strike‐slip earthquakes from the Tibetan Plateau which occurred on faults that sample a wide spectrum of structural maturity. We collate published SSD values and also compute our own, modified “effective shallow slip deficit” based on the total (on‐ and off‐fault) surface offsets from optical imagery, where available. For the 2021 7.4 Maduo and 2022 6.6 Menyuan earthquakes, we assess the consistency of 10–13 independently modeled slip distributions by comparing them with each other. Slip models vary the most in the uppermost 1 km and around fault bends and other geometrical complexities, leading to large ranges in SSD of 0%–88% (for Maduo) and 0%–51% (for Menyuan). This highlights the need to scrutinize slip models carefully before considering shallow slip deficits. The influence from modeling choices, together with factors such as fault roughness and near‐surface geology, obscures any simple relationship between shallow slip deficits and fault structural maturity for large strike‐slip earthquakes on the Tibetan plateau.
ec2f3ce1394e9fa4: We utilized geodetic data from the 16 May to 4 August 2018 caldera collapse sequence to refine the geometries and pressure evolution of two summit reservoirs at Kīlauea volcano: the shallower Halema‘uma‘u (HMM) and deeper South Caldera (SC) reservoirs. We modeled magma reservoirs as pressurized spheroidal cavities and constrained reservoir geometries with Global Positioning System (GPS) and Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar displacements. Inverting high‐rate GPS and borehole tilt time series recovered time‐dependent reservoir pressure changes and caldera ring fault shear stress. During the collapse sequence, the HMM reservoir accommodated episodic, co‐collapse pressure increases of 1.9 MPa (median) and a net 5.8 MPa (median) decrease. Simultaneously, the SC reservoir underwent monotonic depressurization of 6.7 MPa (median). Negligible co‐collapse pressure changes in the SC reservoir imply it was not exclusively supplying magma to the eruption vent. These results provide a coherent view of magma reservoir pressure evolution during the 2018 eruption.
3095ceae0e027cf7: Foreshocks in laboratory experiments are directly linked to fault stress states and the relative position within the seismic cycle. However, foreshock sequences in nature are generally difficult to identify and characterize due to overall lower seismicity rates and sparse instrumentation. Here, we analyze foreshock activity in one of the seismically most active parts of the world, that is, Taiwan, where frequent large-magnitude earthquakes lead to pronounced space-time clustering of seismicity. We examine foreshock activity associated with ML≥5 mainshocks from 2012 to 2022 and explore the effect of depth, background seismicity rates, and mainshock focal mechanisms. We apply a high-resolution statistical method, that is the nearest-neighbor clustering method, to identify foreshock–mainshock sequences. The percentage of mainshocks with foreshocks in Taiwan varies systematically with focal depth and mainshock mechanisms so that lower differential stress at shallower depth and on normal faults leads to a higher percentage of mainshocks with foreshocks. The spatial extent of the foreshock area correlates with mainshock magnitude; however, this areal extent also correlates with the largest event within the foreshock sequence. Overall, only ∼25% of mainshocks in Taiwan are preceded by at least one foreshock, which is significantly lower than in many other regions, including California and Italy. Our observations support a global trend of lower background rates correlating with higher foreshock percentages. Taken together, these results suggest that there are significant regional variations in the percentage of mainshocks with foreshocks both at the scale of Taiwanese faults and at the larger scale of different tectonic areas. Differential stress and background seismicity rates are primary drivers of foreshock activity, with foreshocks being most likely to occur on shallow normal faults in areas of low background seismicity.
7be37293ff2688bd: The 28 March 2025 Mw 7.7 Myanmar earthquake showed that a large regional earthquake can produce extensive ground shaking throughout Thailand even though it occurred 1000 km away. This earthquake caused prolonged shaking of high-rise buildings and disruption of activities in major cities, emphasizing the need for rapid earthquake information to support community response. Although Thailand maintains national seismic monitoring networks, there has been no operational earthquake early warning (EEW) available to the public. This article presents RUGON (Real-time Ubiquitous Ground-shaking Observation Network), a community-based earthquake observation and rapid response platform designed to deliver timely ground-motion information by integrating distributed microelectromechanical systems accelerometers, edge computing, cloud processing, and web-based decision-support tools. The platform supports community notification, structural vibration monitoring, and real-time situational awareness during earthquake emergencies. Analysis of strong-motion records from the 28 March 2025 Myanmar earthquake shows that, if rapid detection and communication are implemented, a regional earthquake may provide more than one minute of available lead time for major Thai cities. Sensor performance was verified through laboratory calibration against laser Doppler vibrometer measurements. Field deployment during the 18 May 2026 ML 5.3 Myanmar earthquake successfully demonstrated the complete RUGON workflow, from sensing and communication to notification and visualization, under real earthquake conditions. RUGON is a rapid earthquake information and situational-awareness platform that reports observed ground motion in near-real time for rapid alert and response. It is not a substitute for a national EEW system. Nevertheless, because regional earthquakes affecting Thailand originate from distant sources, even peak-ground-acceleration-based observations without P-wave prediction still provide a usable interval for alert and response. Community-scale observations of strong shaking upstream can provide actionable information before it reaches distant communities.
6544c4ba1120f700: Summary The Emilia-Romagna portion of the Po Plain (Italy) hosts part of the outermost sector of the Northern Apennines orogenic front. The low strain-rate and the shortening gradient acting in these areas are well documented by means of recent studies, although it is still unclear which fault segment plays the dominant role in accommodating the deformation during the interseismic period. A fraction of this strain was released during the seismic sequence in Emilia-Romagna with mainshocks the May 20 and 29, 2012 (Mw 6.0 and ∼5.8, respectively), which several authors primarily attributed to two major segments of the Ferrara Arc fault system. In this work, we propose a comprehensive kinematic block modeling approach that integrates available information on fault geometry and GNSS data to identify the fault segments that most effectively accommodate the ongoing contractional geodetic velocity gradient through long-term uniform slip-rates. Our solution shows that the modeled front reproduces the observed velocity gradient by predominant dip-slip rates (∼1.0 mm/yr) and subordinate strike-slip rates (∼0.5 mm/yr). We therefore discretize the proposed fault model using a 3D triangular dislocation element (TDE) mesh to estimate the spatial distribution of slip-deficit rate. This modeling allowed us to identify possible locked asperities, characterized by high interseismic coupling coefficient values, and to distinguish them from areas likely affected by aseismic behaviour and low coupling. A resolution estimate is provided on the obtained coupling model, highlighting areas that are better resolved than others due to the uneven distribution of GNSS data. Finally, we propose a set of end-members rupture scenarios based on different coupling thresholds. This type of study shows the importance of having as many high-precision geodetic measurements as possible to accurately estimate seismic hazard in areas with slow tectonic deformation rates.
8119043280876ffd: Geodetic inversion converts surface and remote sensing data into estimates of concealed Earth system parameters, including fault slip, magma-source geometry, subsurface mass changes, crustal strain, and time-dependent geohazard activities. This review explores geodetic inversion as a computational challenge that involves combining diverse data, optimizing and quantifying uncertainty, and providing explainable decision support. A narrative technical review was compiled using literature records from Scopus and Dimensions on topics such as geodetic inversion, Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) measurements, Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR), gravity and seismic source modeling, Bayesian inversion, sparse regularization, and physics-informed learning. The literature was sorted based on the data types, inverse-problem structures, algorithmic groups, uncertainty management, and reporting standards. This review highlights five common computational layers in contemporary geodetic inversion: data harmonization, forward-model encoding, inversion and optimization, uncertainty propagation, and explainable decision support. These layers are synthesized into an explainable artificial intelligence-uncertainty quantification-computational geodetic inversion (XAI-UQ-CGI) framework for multi-source Earth observation. To show that the framework is computationally executable rather than only conceptual, it is demonstrated on a controlled synthetic same-model experiment in which a Mogi volcanic point-pressure source is inverted from synthetic InSAR and GNSS data, yielding empirically assessed least-squares uncertainty intervals and a quantifiable reduction of depth non-uniqueness under sensor fusion. Future geodetic inversion studies should move beyond single best-fit solutions toward reproducible, physics-constrained, uncertainty-preserving, and human-interpretable computational workflows suitable for geohazard monitoring and Digital Earth applications.
0a85569002210909: A new unified joint inversion framework integrates surface wave dispersion data with local and teleseismic body wave traveltimes The method is validated through application to the southern California plate boundary region from the upper crust to the upper mantle Application to the Weifang array demonstrates its potential for imaging both shallow and deep structures using temporary dense arrays
68b9ceb545f996d0: Horizontal compressive stress in subduction zones is accommodated by both brittle and ductile deformation, from the deep megathrust to the seafloor. Compaction of sediments is an important, but poorly understood, component of the overall strain budget. Combining seismic depth imaging, P-wave velocities, sediment physical properties, and age constraints, we characterize horizontal shortening in the southern Hikurangi trench (New Zealand) and assess its contribution to the accommodation of plate motion. A distinct change in the lateral seismic velocity gradient of trench sediments, ∼20 km seaward of the main frontal thrust, marks the onset of lateral compaction and is accompanied by an onset of tectonically driven stratigraphic thickening. Compaction of the trench wedge has accommodated ∼3 km of shortening, far exceeding the 20% of the time-averaged, long-term convergent strain rate, thereby significantly reducing the amount of strain that would otherwise be accommodated by slip on the shallow megathrust and overlying upper plate faults. Detailed analyses of trench and outer wedge compaction are critically important for understanding shallow megathrust strain partitioning, which has implications for the megathrust’s slip behavior and tsunamigenic potential.
55c1147a5fea9a43: We thank the opportunity to respond to the Comment by Aires et al. (2026) on the tectonic interpretation of Braga et al. (2026) for the northwestern Borborema Province. The Comment argues that recent studies by the authors were not considered in our discussion and questions evidence for ultrahigh-pressure metamorphism, exhumation mechanisms, and the interpretation of the C1 conductive anomaly.
