We clarify that the studies cited in the Comment present an alternative interpretation of regional metamorphic evolution and that the article used as the main basis for questioning coesite was published after submission of our manuscript. We emphasize that much of the Comment focuses on reevaluating petrological, spectroscopic, and geobarometric interpretations from previous studies. These data were neither generated nor reanalyzed by Braga et al. (2026), but were incorporated into the discussion because they derive from peer-reviewed studies established in the regional literature. We demonstrate that the reinterpretation of coesite is based on samples and analytical domains different from those originally analyzed and therefore does not constitute a direct reanalysis of the identified inclusions. Petrological and geobarometric constraints do not justify a regional exclusion of the HP–UHP record. Regarding exhumation, alternative mechanisms, including crustal channel flow, may represent late stages in the evolution of the collisional orogen rather than mutually exclusive solutions. More importantly, these interpretative differences do not affect magnetotelluric result of Braga et al. (2026): C1 is a robust west-dipping crustal conductive anomaly, consistently recovered in 3D inversions. Its geometry is compatible with a paleosubduction-related structure along the eastern margin of the Santa Quitéria Continental Magmatic Arc. The origin of the anomaly and its electrical response do not depend solely on the volumetric abundance of graphite, but mainly on connectivity and continuity along grain boundaries and foliation. These characteristics were discussed and substantiated in our manuscript.
8955e036dedbd03f: Summary Automatic first-arrival picking is crucial for microseismic monitoring as it directly influences event location and focal mechanism calculation. Current deep-learning based methods typically predict first-arrival time using only temporal features from individual traces, while overlooking coherent features across traces. For industrial microseismic monitoring, dense and regular receiver arrays produce spatially distinctive first-arrival patterns. To capture these multidimensional spatial features, current studies tend to use more complex model architectures, which result in higher training costs but do not necessarily improve picking accuracy. To address this issue, we propose a coordinate-driven framework based on explicit coordinate encoding. Specifically, the seismogram of microseismic event is reorganized into 2-D image, and the X and Y coordinates of each pixel are extracted and concatenated to the waveform image as two additional channels. Then, the combined data tensor is fed into a U-Net-based model to predict first arrivals. This gives the network direct awareness of absolute spatial positions, breaking the translational invariance of standard CNNs. Thus, the network can capture both temporal characteristics and spatial continuity of first arrivals with negligible additional model complexity and computational cost. Tests on a real dataset show that the coordinate-driven models significantly outperform non-coordinate-driven counterparts in training performance and picking accuracy. The average minimum loss is reduced by ~54%, while the model parameters increase only ~0.015%. The average excellent rate of P-arrivals rises from 73.06% to 92.24%, and the average error drops from 9.51 to 3.36 ms. Ablation experiments show that coordinate convolution accounts for most improvement, whereas attention gates and residual connections provide only marginal refinements. Compared to a single-trace-based model (PhaseNet) retrained on the same dataset, our model achieves ~10% higher excellent rate and half the average error. These results demonstrate that explicit coordinate encoding substantially improves the extraction of complex spatial features with negligible additional model complexity and computational cost.
6cfc7c29bde3b47c: Meteoroid impacts are frequent on the Moon and provide valuable natural seismic sources for probing the lunar interior. However, accurately locating lunar impacts remains challenging because intense scattering within the highly fractured lunar crust obscures direct P- and S-wave arrivals. Coda-based localization methods exploit scattered energy, but their accuracy has so far been limited by the parameterization of the method. In this study, we reformulated a coda-based localization approach within the framework of seismic quanta scattering theory by introducing four distance proxies: peak amplitude, rise time, differential arrival time, and the overall coda shape. By jointly combining these proxies, we obtain locations that agree well with independent travel-time-based solutions. We then apply the method to locate forty-nine high-amplitude local impact events recorded by the Apollo seismic network, while also estimating their localization uncertainties and impact momenta. Our results demonstrates that coda waves contain robust distance information even in a strongly scattering lunar crust, enabling reliable impact localization and providing new constraints on the connection between seismic source properties and impact crater formation.
1758d32ee7754520: Rollback-style lithospheric recycling has been proposed for a subset of Venusian coronae and other tectonic features based on the presence of trench-outer-rise systems, but the mechanism and conditions required to initiate recycling remain poorly understood. Peel-back delamination (PBD) is a proposed mechanism in which dense lithospheric mantle decouples and peels away from a thin layer of overlying crust, resulting in slab rollback. PBD has only been modeled in 2D, and therefore its 3D surface expression is unknown. Here, we present the first three-dimensional models of peel-back delamination on Venus and compare their predicted trench geometry and flexural topography with observations from Artemis Corona, Atahensik Corona, and Derceto Plateau. PBD initiation is facilitated by increasing lithosphere thickness which enhances the negative buoyancy of the lithospheric mantle and drives decoupling from the weak, buoyant crust. Once initiated, rift geometry, lithosphere structure around the rift, and maximum yield strength control the evolution of trench geometry throughout PBD. Elastic thickness (Te) provides an independent constraint on lithospheric thickness, increasing with thermal lithospheric thickness. Comparisons with observations indicate that models of Artemis and Atahensik Corona best satisfy both trench geometry and flexural topography constraints, whereas the Derceto Plateau model reproduces trench geometry but not flexural topography. At Artemis Corona, along-trench variation in Te may reflect differences in subsurface slab morphology and plate bending. Te estimates from the southeastern trench at Artemis Corona favor a thermal lithospheric thickness of approximately 200-250 km for a 1700 K mantle.
a39dbb065dd11ce9: Prior studies have cataloged thousands of icequakes at Ross Ice Shelf (RIS) Western Rift 4 (WR4) and linked them to tidal cycles, thermal stress, and temperature fluctuations. Building on this foundation, we apply a full moment tensor inversion using Green's functions for a layered firn, ice, water and sediment model. A prominent extensional Lamb wave propagating at 2.7–3.2 km/s is identified in both observed and synthetic waveforms. Moment tensor solutions reveal crack‐opening, crack‐closing, and double‐couple mechanisms oriented subparallel or oblique to the rift. Crack‐opening and shear motions are more common than crack‐closing events. Low corner frequencies imply long, narrow rupture geometry with stress drops of ∼1 MPa for the largest events, consistent with shallow firn fracturing. These results provide the first quantitative constraints on brittle deformation at the WR4 rift and reveal diverse source mechanisms not clearly controlled by tidal or thermal forcing alone.
9d98a9ce2d06690c: Although cratons are stabilized by their thick and highly viscous lithosphere, their long-term thermal evolution remains poorly understood. Here, kimberlite-hosted mantle xenoliths can provide constraints on past craton thickness, as they erupt almost exclusively beneath thick cratons that protrude into a ‘kimberlite window’ of 160–250 km. Global compilations indicate that kimberlite eruptions become more frequent and continuous after 1500 Ma. Therefore, we link two fundamental questions: how craton thickness evolved through time, and whether this evolution influenced kimberlite magmatism. We present 27 two-dimensional numerical models of craton evolution within a convecting mantle, and explore the effects of initial craton thickness, compositional buoyancy, radiogenic heating, and mantle cooling. Although cratons originated as hot and thick layers in the Archean, gravitational flattening likely thinned them above kimberlite-generating depths. With progressive cooling, craton viscosity and density increased, allowing cratons to undergo gradual thickening after ~ 2000 Ma. We conclude that thickening processes, such as tectonic compression and cooling, operate faster than thinning processes, such as sub-lithospheric dripping, to slowly thicken cratons into the ‘kimberlite window’. Such thickening is a possible explanation for the increasing frequency of kimberlite eruptions after ~ 1500 Ma.
64aff98c3ccc68d4: We examine stress and strength across the deep subduction plate boundary at ∼60 km depth offshore northeastern Japan, near the downdip seismic limit of the megathrust. High‐frequency (2–5 Hz) moment tensor inversion of ∼2,000 M 2–3.5 earthquakes, integrated with existing catalogs, increases the number of focal mechanisms by more than a factor of six, enabling detailed mapping of the stress field near the interface. The results reveal an abrupt, kilometer‐scale stress contrast across the interface: downdip‐compressional stress in the upper slab persists to within ∼2 km of the megathrust, whereas the immediately overlying plate is under nearly strike‐parallel compression, producing a ∼90° rotation of maximum compression over only a few kilometers. Because the principal stress axes remain nearly parallel or normal to the interface, this geometry implies very low shear traction on the deep megathrust: only ∼11% of the maximum shear stress in the underlying slab. In absolute terms, the estimated megathrust shear stress is only ∼108 MPa even assuming hydrostatic pore pressure within the slab (slab maximum shear stress, ∼0.98 GPa; μ ′ = 0.07), and decreases to ∼11 MPa for a weaker slab sustaining a maximum shear stress of 100 MPa (pore‐pressure‐to‐lithostatic‐pressure ratio, 0.93; μ ′ = 0.006). These results indicate that the deep megathrust is a weak, aseismically shearing fault zone that mechanically decouples the slab and overriding plate, allowing large unbending‐related stresses in the slab to coexist with strike‐parallel compression in the overriding plate.
a3e0923d8443ead5: Earthquake sequences are stochastic on two separated timescales: the seismic waves of any individual earthquake propagate over seconds to minutes, while the earthquakes themselves arrive as a sparse, self-exciting occurrence process, with inter-event intervals from seconds to months. Respecting both scales in one training objective is the open challenge. Foundation models (FMs) for seismic waveforms instead import their learning targets from audio and vision, where every target is computed from a single fixed-length window. Such a window holds one realization of the wave propagation (an earthquake trace), never the occurrence process that decides when earthquakes happen. We develop nine model designs sharing one Mamba encoder-decoder, trained on a fixed corpus of 3M windows, varying the self-supervised objective, quantization bottleneck and mixer; the two key comparisons are architecture-matched, varying the objective alone. Each checkpoint is evaluated frozen on three downstream tasks. Varying the target redistributes downstream skill rather than raising it, and no checkpoint wins everywhere. Adding masking pressure to our strongest classifier re-specializes it rather than making it a generalist: it gains 6.9 points of few-shot P-wave picking precision and loses 9.6 points of few-shot classification accuracy. By the standard imported from language and vision, these models are feature extractors rather than FMs. Controls on capacity, architecture, and domain proximity do not explain why skill moves rather than rises. Against task-specific baselines the advantage is regime-dependent: our checkpoints beat them few-shot on classification and ground-motion prediction, and trail them on full data. We argue the binding constraint is the target, and that settling the question requires a learning target defined across events, the timescale that makes seismicity stochastic in the first place.
2a6974bf05272284: Structural validation of a prospect is invariably applied after the interpretation is finished, by restoring one or two key lines in 2D or, rarely, by a full 3D restoration that needs finished horizons and a specialist. The authors propose that a simple 3D kinematic forward model, built in minutes using a few explicit structural rules, fully restorable and scaled onto the mapped horizons, is a highly effective way of building structural validation into the early stages of interpretation. The rules are taken from the published literature and built into a software module, referred to herein as the rules module. The rules module is made available together with the crestal collapse graben solution used in this paper. The structural rules are those of the published literature: (1) fault-parallel flow, (2) slip decaying towards the fault tips and (3) syn-rift deposition to a datum. The fourth rule is that any accommodation problem arising when using them in a restorable forward model is flagged to the user. The resolution of the accommodation problem is a decision made by the user as part of the model build. Where the hangingwall of a listric fault cannot be carried over a bend in the fault without strain, that resolution is a crestal collapse graben. How the graben scales with slip is part of scaling the model onto the data, and it may differ between geological provinces. The method is tested here on the Katnook Graben of the Penola Trough, the main gas province of the onshore Otway Basin, which the authors interpreted twenty years ago as bounded by a basement-rooted, thick-skinned fault and its antithetic. The dip of the listric Hungerford Fault and its top basement cutoff are taken from 2D regional sections and the geometry of the graben from 3D interpretation. With these inputs the authors' model fits the mapped thickness of the base Laira to top Crayfish growth interval along dip to within about 120 m, roughly 10% of the 1.2 km by which the interval thickens along dip. It also reproduces the proportions of the syn-tectonic thickening into the graben. The detachment depth is projected and two parameters are fitted, namely the proportion of the slip pre-dating the base Laira horizon and the keystone throw. No basement fault beneath the graben is needed to account for the mapped geometry. Thus the authors now interpret the Katnook Graben as a crestal collapse graben, detached within the sedimentary fill and formed as a consequence of the large displacement on the listric Hungerford Fault. This has important implications for fault seal integrity risk in the area. The model also implies that the mapped basement, poorly imaged and broken by faults carried down from the reservoir level, can reasonably be re-interpreted as a simpler and less faulted surface. The value of the approach lies in structural validation carried out while the horizons are still being picked. Several structural ideas can be tested against the fault geometry, the growth pattern and the isopachs within hours, and the scenario that survives carries a structural history into trap definition, charge timing and volumetric uncertainty. The method is at an early stage of development. The purpose of this paper is to outline a new method and demonstrate its usefulness at prospect scale for reducing structural risk and the associated risk to fault seal.
d13498b4e8289214: Near-field tsunamis can leave coastal communities with only minutes to reach safe areas, so how quickly people begin moving after the earthquake shaking is critical to evacuation success. Static evacuation maps do not represent this time dependence, whereas more complex evacuation models can be data-intensive, costly, or difficult to scale. We introduce a simple, low-cost tool that combines Global Positioning System (GPS) tracks recorded with mobile applications during evacuation drills with tsunami inundation modeling. As a proof of concept, we apply the tool in Viña del Mar (central Chile), where a large tsunami is expected and evacuation is particularly challenging because of the long distances required to reach safe areas. We analyzed 119 GPS trajectories collected during drills between 2022 and 2026 and compared them with simulated inundation for a plausible subduction earthquake scenario. For illustration, each trajectory was evaluated under three departure times measured from the earthquake origin time: 0 min (T0), 8 min (T8), and 12 min (T12). T0 represents immediate evacuation, T8 departure when a warning is issued, and T12 departure when the tsunami is already reaching the coast. A trajectory was considered feasible if the participant completed the evacuation before being reached by the simulated inundation. Of the 119 trajectories, 100 were feasible under T0, 49 under T8, and only 3 under T12, showing how strongly evacuation success depends on when people begin moving. Most trajectories followed 13 main evacuation corridors. Feasibility varied sharply among corridors, even between neighboring routes within the same departure scenario. By overlaying the trajectories on the advancing inundation, the approach produces intuitive videos that make the consequences of delayed departure visible to residents, authorities, and decision-makers. Inexpensive and easily replicable, the method complements detailed evacuation modeling and may be particularly useful in tsunami-prone communities with limited resources, supporting evacuation awareness, preparedness, and risk communication.
6f267333b5487b59: Stratovolcano morphology reflects the influence of magma supply, composition, eruptive style, tectonic setting, and erosion. Morphometric parameters such as height, volume, slope, and ellipticity capture the influence of these processes during volcanic growth. Here, we present a statistical-physics-based analysis of 392 stratovolcanoes from seven volcanic zones, examining frequency-size distributions of these four morphometric parameters to assess whether scale-invariant patterns describe stratovolcano growth. All parameters exhibit heavy-tailed behaviour characteristic of power-law distributions. However, the data are better described by dual scaling relationships. Log-log plots reveal distinct linear segments separating abundant, morphologically variable small-to-intermediate volcanoes (sub-population 1) from rarer and more similar, large volcanoes (sub-population 2). Shallow slopes in the log-log plots reflect high dispersion, whereas steeper slopes associated with larger volcanoes indicate reduced dispersion. Using thermodynamic entropy and its information-theoretic extension (Shannon entropy), we quantify dispersal and variability within volcanic zones, providing a measure of morphometric and size spreading, complementing scaling exponents, and revealing a systematic transition between sub-populations. Sub-population 1, represented by a high-entropy regime, transitions to a low-entropy phase found in sub-population 2. This transition may reflect the evolution of volcanoes toward more morphometrically constrained systems. Together, dual power-law and entropy-scaling relationships indicate non-uniform volcanic growth across scales. These results provide a comparative framework for quantifying morphometrical variability among volcanic zones and indicate that stratovolcano growth is governed by scale-dependent transitions between variable and mechanically constrained growth regimes.
ca20c4f38b433e3f: We carried out 3D inverse modeling of full tensor gravity gradiometry data, its derived products (Tz and Tz residual), and magnetic data to recover the density and magnetic susceptibility distributions of the Yaouré Greenstone Belt in Ivory Coast, West Africa. The study area presents significant challenges: it lacks well-defined stratigraphy and structural measurements, and it lies close to the magnetic equator, where the magnetic inclination is low. Inverted models were analyzed using isosurfaces and histogram curves to characterize physical properties distribution and highlight geophysical sources. We extracted vertical slices through the 3D inverted models across significant mapped structures and lithotypes, and measured magnetic anomaly dips within these sections to create an artificial structural map. We identified positive and negative density contrasts as well as magnetic susceptibility sources in the region that correlated with mapped surface geology. Our results revealed that sedimentary and volcano-sedimentary rocks in the region present higher susceptibility than some intrusions, contrasting with their comparatively lower density. The 3D inverted models provided insights of some mapped structures, such as major faults, that may act as physical property boundaries. Ranking magnetic susceptibility and density contrast of geological units alongside the structural map offers a systematic first approach to maximizing the value of geophysical inversions. This integration may serve as a petrophysical or geological constraint when prior information is limited for subsequent inversions, acting as useful information for starting or reference models.
d70f9d696bcdad82: In field seismic acquisition, consecutively missing traces, local acquisition gaps and large‐scale sampling incompleteness commonly arise from complex near‐surface conditions, acquisition‐geometry constraints, receiver failures and field obstacles, which can degrade detailed imaging. Compared with scattered dead traces, consecutively missing traces interrupt the lateral coherence of reflection events over a wider spatial range, making event continuation, fault‐boundary continuity and thin‐bed response recovery more difficult. Conventional prediction filtering, transform‐domain interpolation and low‐rank completion methods usually rely on local linearity, sparsity or low‐rank assumptions. Under strongly nonstationary structures and wide missing‐trace bands, these assumptions can lead to oversmoothing, boundary mismatch and high‐frequency loss. Deep‐learning methods have improved the non‐linear representation capacity of reconstruction models, but slice‐wise 2D modelling does not fully exploit 3D spatial correlation, whereas existing 3D methods often suffer from high training cost, long sampling chains and insufficient stable structural constraints. To address these issues, we propose a low‐frequency structure‐guided 3D conditional diffusion method for seismic data reconstruction. The method first extracts stable low‐frequency components from an incomplete 3D seismic volume and completes the long‐wavelength structure within the missing‐trace band by combining 3D structure‐tensor dip estimation, event‐oriented low‐frequency interpolation and reliability‐weighted fusion. The completed low‐frequency volume preserves the dominant reflection geometry, long‐wavelength phase trend and 3D horizon distribution and is used as a structural condition for subsequent full‐band recovery. The reconstruction problem is then formulated as a 3D conditional diffusion process constrained by the low‐frequency structure, in which a 3D U‐Net denoiser progressively restores mid‐ and high‐frequency reflection details during reverse sampling. To adapt the model to the spatial organization of 3D seismic wavefields, the volumetric convolutional feature extractor supports an optional lightweight 3D attention module to strengthen local waveform information and structural associations across the missing‐trace band along the time, inline and crossline directions. The experiments include tests with consecutively missing traces using the SEG C3 synthetic data and a controlled test with artificially removed traces in a prepared field‐data volume. Ablation tests and comparisons with 3D tensor completion, slice‐wise 2D diffusion and 3D U‐Net show that the completed low‐frequency structural condition reduces the structural ambiguity inside missing‐trace bands and enables the diffusion model to recover high‐frequency details while preserving event continuity, phase consistency and amplitude compatibility. By combining low‐frequency structural modelling, 3D wavefield continuity and conditional posterior generation, the framework provides a feasible route for high‐fidelity reconstruction of seismic data with wide missing‐trace bands.
b1e46d9467dd23fc: Seismic imaging of the Earth’s interior has steadily improved in the past 40 yr. Full-waveform inversion (FWI) has been the most recent driver of global and local tomography. Although mineral physics experiments link seismic properties to temperature, pressure and composition of the mantle, direct integration of seismic observations and thermodynamic calculations has not yet been achieved. This work illustrates a framework that integrates FWI techniques with mineral physics to directly invert seismic waveforms for mantle temperature and chemical composition. The forward model is based on interpolation of pre-calculated tables of mantle properties, namely density and P- and S-wave speeds. The inverse problem is formulated as an optimization problem. The gradient of the objective function with respect to temperature and composition is computed using the chain rule which allows us to split it into independent seismic and thermodynamic parts. For the seismic part, the gradient is computed with the adjoint method. For the thermodynamic part, gradients of the pre-calculated tables are obtained by analytically deriving the interpolation function, while accounting for the pressure–density coupling, under the assumption of hydrostatic loading. As a proof of concept, we applied this approach on 2-D synthetic models containing thermal and compositional anomalies where P–SV elastic wave propagation is simulated. The optimization problem is solved using the L-BFGS algorithm. We mitigate the trade-off between the effect of temperature and composition by applying a linear transformation to the model parameters before carrying out the minimization and then transforming back once a solution is found. The proposed framework enables the integration of diverse geophysical data sets as well as the incorporation of additional information on the potential origin of certain mantle anomalies based on petrological constraints, which are crucial to tackle the non-uniqueness of the inverse problem.
4534b78ef120e530: Seismic data offer a unique window into planetary interiors. Here, following a note from Russell et al. (2026), we provide further analysis to solidify our identification of a seismic phase detected by the InSight mission as one which interacts with a basal mantle layer (BML) on Mars (Samuel et al., 2023a). We show that other mantle discontinuities or other seismic structures invoked in the aforementioned note are unlikely to produce this seismic signal. We further illustrate how our proposed layered structure is compatible with other available geophysical observations and geodynamical constraints, and can be used to make inferences about Martian evolution.
c39fb97877c73f0d: Knowledge gaps remain regarding strain localization mechanisms that may initiate the transition to late-phase rifting and break-up along active rifts hosted in thick continental lithosphere. Here, we conduct a multiscale study of the East African Rift System (EARS) using one of the highest-resolution seismic tomography models of Africa, along with a comprehensive compilation of lithospheric structure models from active- and passive-source seismic studies. We estimate mantle temperatures and the lithosphere-asthenosphere boundary using this model. Combined with estimated crustal thicknesses, we estimate the thinning factors of the crust and lithospheric mantle, as well as the deformation decoupling parameter, defined as the ratio of the lithospheric mantle to the crustal thinning factors. Our results reveal intriguing magnitudes of lithospheric mantle necking beneath both the eastern (magma-rich) and western (magma-poor) branches. However, the eastern branch ubiquitously exhibits commensurate crustal and lithospheric mantle thinning, whereas the western branch exhibits a complex mix of segments with coupled-thinning and those with significantly decoupled thinning. We note the key influence of inheritance, lithospheric foundering and delamination, and melt-induced ductile strain on decoupling of lithospheric thinning. The dearth of necked crust and the common occurrence of necked lithospheric mantle along the EARS suggest that necking of the lithospheric mantle probably precedes crustal necking along evolving rifts, which, where observed, manifest a weakened lithosphere primed to progressively transition to the later phases of continental extension.
575031967a94b1dd: We employed an unconventional teleseismic tomographic inversion method, referred to as source‐side teleseismic tomography (SSTT), to enhance the resolution of 3‐D P‐wave velocity (Vp) structure beneath the active Taiwan orogenic belt down to a depth of ∼400 km. Unlike traditional teleseismic tomography, which uses travel‐time residuals from teleseismic events to local stations, we utilize travel‐time residuals from local earthquakes to distant stations. This method significantly increases the spatial sampling of ray paths at mantle depths due to the substantially larger number of local events distributed at depths and along subduction zones compared to the limited number of broadband stations confined to the surface. Our findings reveal detailed 3‐D geometry and interaction of the subducting Eurasian Plate (EP) and Philippine Sea Plate (PSP) beneath Taiwan. In the south, the high‐Vp anomaly, interpreted as the subducting EP, descends eastwardly down to a depth of 400 km at approximately 123°E longitude. Moving from central to northern Taiwan, the EP steepens and becomes detached at depths of 200–300 km. This slab detachment progressively widens northward, and extends beneath the northward‐dipping PSP. The detached EP segment beneath the PSP indicates its prior subduction location beneath the southern Ryukyu and supports the slab breakoff model rather than the lithospheric tear model. This newly derived model resolves the intricate 3‐D plate interaction between the EP and PSP that drives complex spatiotemporal tectonic processes of the Taiwan orogen, and demonstrates the efficacy of SSTT in enhancing mantle imaging in Taiwan and other seismically active regions.
747001786efe38db: Dynamic rupture models have been widely used to enhance our understanding of earthquake processes and associated hazards. A commonly held insight among modelers is that if the initial stress, rheological parameters, and space and time coordinates are scaled by certain factors in a specific manner, the solution will scale accordingly and remain similar. While this principle has been applied in numerical simulations, particularly to optimize parameter studies and interpret results through non‐dimensionalization, its general applicability to more complex modeling scenarios has not been rigorously established. In this study, we provide a proof of the generality of solution scaling in linear elastic dynamic rupture problems using a boundary integral equation formulation. We demonstrate how dynamic rupture solutions, including slip and traction evolution, scale with initial stress, fault rheology parameters, space and time coordinates, and elastic medium properties. The proof holds under arbitrary complexity in fault geometry and medium velocity structure, as well as with heterogeneous on‐fault rheology parameters, provided that solution uniqueness is satisfied. We consider four types of fault rheology: linear slip‐weakening, rate‐and‐state friction, linear time‐weakening, and general composite rheology with different slip rate dependencies at different slip rates. Our results have practical implications for the design of large‐scale simulation campaigns and for interpreting laboratory dynamic rupture experiments. More broadly, our work provides theoretical support for widely used scaling practices in the dynamic rupture modeling community by establishing a mathematical foundation.
e3a4871dfd7e7122: Seismic body waves provide valuable insights into the interiors of the Earth, the Moon, and Mars. By analyzing their waveform characteristics, we can effectively reveal deep seismic velocity structures and associated dynamic processes. For the Earth, incorporating various body waves helps improve the ray path coverage and therefore the resolution of seismic imaging. For other planets with limited data, identifying seismic phases beyond the main P and S arrivals can provide critical insights into the picture of the deep interior. PKPPcP and PcPPKP phases propagate along the major arc of the great circle path, and are theoretically degenerate—arriving simultaneously—in a 1‐D spherical Earth model. Their splitting offers a unique opportunity to resolve 3‐D mantle heterogeneity, yet this potential remains under‐explored. Here we compile a global data set of high‐quality PKPPcP waves from 94 large events. Using PKKP ab as a reference phase, we quantify the observed PKPPcP–PcPPKP splitting and evaluate it against predictions from 3‐D mantle tomography models. Mantle tomography models generally underestimate the observed splitting, but the spatial correlation suggests that the observed splitting is linked to large‐scale structures in the deep mantle. We further analyze the features of PKPPcP travel time sensitivity kernels and conduct numerical simulations with various heterogeneous models. The simulations indicate that large‐scale velocity anomalies, such as large low‐velocity provinces and high‐velocity subducted slabs, are the primary contributors to PKPPcP–PcPPKP splitting. Our results highlight both the potential and the limitations of the PKPPcP phase in imaging 3‐D mantle heterogeneities.
1369797bad36040b: The Nelson Thrust Belt (NTB) is a contractional structure within the Australian crust, northwest of the Pacific-Australian plate boundary in the northern South Island of New Zealand. Its structure and evolution record the influence of faults inherited from Paleozoic–Early Mesozoic terrane assembly and Late Cretaceous to Eocene rifting. We integrate revised regional mapping, LiDAR imagery, trench and borehole observations, and reinterpreted vintage seismic reflection lines to reconstruct how inherited fabric controlled fault localization and reactivation. The NTB comprises three principal fault groups, F1–F3, in decreasing order of structural elevation, and a local frontal splay, F4. Geometry, reverse ​reactivation, and association with syn- to late-rift deposits indicate that F2 and F3 are inverted normal faults. Fault inversion began in the Late Miocene and continued through the Pliocene–Pleistocene, but activity on F3 ceased earlier than on F2. F1 is a low- to moderate-angle thrust fault that truncates the underlying structures out of sequence. Together, these relationships suggest a long-term break-back transfer of deformation, while Late Pleistocene–Holocene seismic rupture of the major faults indicates that multiple structures were reactivated within overlapping earthquake cycles. The NTB provides a test case for recognizing how inherited crustal heterogeneity controlled long-term fault evolution and distributed active deformation in a contractional belt where modern subsurface imaging is limited.
9c92ed19177ad0a3: SeisBench has become the premier open-source library for accessing pretrained deep-learning seismic phase pickers through a unified Python interface. Because SeisBench distributes models exclusively in PyTorch, phase pickers originally developed in TensorFlow must be converted to PyTorch before integration into the library. Although retraining is possible, doing so produces new learned weights that can alter the numerical behavior and picking characteristics of the original model while demanding substantial time and compute. We present a four-step workflow for converting static TensorFlow/Keras phase pickers to PyTorch that preserves original model weights without retraining: (1) architectural alignment, (2) weight extraction and layout transformation, (3) explicit parameter mapping, and (4) staged validation from intermediate activations through waveform traces and phase picks. We demonstrate the workflow by converting the Earthquake Compact Convolutional Transformer (EQCCT), a production phase picker used by the Texas Seismological Network, from TensorFlow to PyTorch. Across 100,000 STEAD and TXED waveform windows, CPU and GPU mean absolute errors remained between 1.46 × 10^(-9) and 1.82 × 10^(-9) with TF32 disabled. Detection decisions at thresholds of 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5 were identical on both devices, while argmax locations agreed for all but one CPU P-wave window, which differed by one sample. The converted EQCCT models are now available in the main SeisBench repository as EQCCTP and EQCCTS. This workflow serves as a reference for integrating TensorFlow-based seismic phase pickers into SeisBench by converting their original weights into a PyTorch-compatible format while preserving their operational behavior. Validation in this study is limited to EQCCT.
55aaef9111dd6dac: Coseismic ionospheric disturbances (CIDs), observed in the total electron content (TEC) measured by Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers, are often interpreted with a point source at the epicenter. We present a three-dimensional forward model that propagates the acoustic pulse from an extended rupture to the ionosphere and returns synthetic slant TEC along each observed line of sight. The source is a moment-weighted distribution of sub-sources along the fault, each radiating at its own rupture time. Rays are traced through a moving, stratified atmosphere into the far field, with absorption and ray-tube spreading; the neutral motion is projected onto the geomagnetic field, and the electron-density perturbation follows from the three-dimensional continuity equation. We apply the model to the 28 March 2025 Mw 7.7 Myanmar earthquake, which ruptured more than 400 km south of the epicenter along an almost straight fault, ideal for isolating the effect of rupture geometry. We compare finite-fault and point-source predictions with CID arrivals identified on 249 satellite-receiver arcs. The model reproduces the shape of the disturbance and its broadening with distance. The finite fault almost halves the median timing error of the point source (202 s against 383 s) and moves the strongest response toward the southern arcs, where observed amplitudes peak. Arrival times and amplitudes are ordered by distance from the fault rather than from the epicenter, which biases epicentral travel-time analyses. Misfits that grow with distance, common to both sources, point to the modeled propagation and to Rayleigh-wave-induced arrivals in the far field.
f4b3a8883f9edc8a: This paper proposes that the peridotite solidus (about 1300°C, dry conditions) is the thermodynamic anchor and negative-feedback target of plate tectonics. To distinguish different physical quantities, we define a thermally equivalent thickness to be heated, km; a kinematic return-channel thickness, km; and a dynamic effective return thickness, . Using and a mantle heat flux of about 0.07 W/m² as inputs, the thermodynamic path yields 282.5 Myr (baseline km; about 263–282.5 Myr for 80–100 km, all on the order of 2.6–2.8 × 10⁸ yr); the kinematic path yields about 278 Myr (thickness ratio about 1:2.5; if the more conservative 1:2 is used, 222 Myr, a lower-bound estimate biased short). The standard dynamic estimate is 233.6 Myr (global mean trench–ridge distance km; trench–ridge horizontal temperature difference K). The 600 K corresponds to about 700°C at the trench and about 1300°C at the mid-ocean ridge; it is the maximum temperature difference when the trench temperature is at its lower limit, so 233.6 Myr is a lower-bound estimate biased short. After confining-pressure correction by the overlying lithosphere, the dynamic estimate is about 283 Myr (confining-pressure factor , Pa·s; rounding to 1.77 gives about Pa·s, which does not affect the conclusion). If a high-end member within the literature range is adopted, the confining-corrected estimate is about 259 Myr, close to 282.5 Myr (about 8% lower) and near the lower edge of the 260–285 Myr convergence range. The three paths converge on about 260–285 Myr, centered at about 280 Myr; the standard dynamic value of 233.6 Myr and the kinematic 1:2 value of 222 Myr are lower bounds biased short. Using actual trench–ridge distances, the Pacific is about 318 Myr, Nazca about 179 Myr, Africa about 337 Myr, and South America about 300 Myr (standard viscosity); with confining-pressure correction, each plate time is multiplied by about 1.21. Asthenospheric viscosity is exponentially sensitive to temperature; the model implies that only about 20–50 K of temperature adjustment beneath each plate is needed for the circulation time to trend toward the statistical center of about 280 Myr. This adjustment is a theoretical mechanism hypothesis and is subject to dispersion from three-dimensional flow and other disturbances: about ±20–30 Myr within a single plate and about ±70–90 Myr as systematic differences between plates. The deviation output of the three-equation framework diagnoses four situations: shortened effective heating path (with lateral outflow), overdue retention, non-initiation of circulation, and three-dimensional flow. In reality, new trenches can be triggered incidentally on transform faults/fracture zones and truncate the original circulation; however, because the asthenosphere between the mid-ocean ridge and the trench has already been preheated, the ridge does not die immediately but enters a decay phase. Therefore, most systems do not complete even one full cycle, and a few complete at most two or three. Temperature (about 1300°C) is the invariant anchor; time (centered at about 280 Myr) is its response—the thermodynamic metronome of plate tectonics.
f4ba5ba9b7fe6416: Reconstructing paleo-earthquake ruptures from sparse geological observations is inherently non-unique because evidence of past surface ruptures is commonly preserved only at isolated sites. We develop a stochastic sampling-filtering framework that represents this ambiguity as an ensemble of rupture scenarios consistent with geological, chronological, and mapped fault constraints. Candidate ruptures are sampled in timing, center position, and length and retained only when they satisfy these constraints. Applied to the Yanzhi Shan Fault, the framework identifies eight rupture-age density modes and a persistent southeastward trend in the spatial density of admissible ruptures. Criteria-based enumeration yields broadly similar first-order temporal concentrations, while prior-sensitivity tests show that filtering reduces differences among ensembles generated from contrasting priors. These results indicate constraint-induced convergence rather than prior-distribution independence. The framework therefore extracts observation-supported statistical rupture patterns while preserving uncertainty associated with non-unique rupture timing and geometry.
599b9f531f8e7994: The July 28, 2026, M7.1 Kumamoto earthquake occurred on the Hinagu Fault zone in southwest Japan, near the southern termination of the 2016 Kumamoto earthquake sequence. We investigated coseismic deformation from Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data and inferred a two-segment fault source model to examine the spatial relationship among coseismic slip, structural heterogeneity, and the 2016 rupture extent. The 2026 main slip was located south of the southern termination of the 2016 rupture, with a peak of right-lateral slip at shallow depth near the hypocenter, while a normal-slip component was concentrated at greater depth near a fault bend. Slip decreases toward the southwest, where weak slip remains at shallow depth on the southwestern segment; cross-validation tests and a strong-motion waveform inversion supported its robustness. Changes in slip characteristics occur near the fault bend and independently identified contrasts in seismic velocity and geological structure.
1088968ba7fdb664: Stress-drop heterogeneity is widely recognized as an important control on rupture dynamics of multi-fault earthquakes, yet the influence of its scale dependence remains poorly understood. This study derives analytical expressions for the stress intensity factor and static energy release rate for ruptures propagating through heterogeneous stress-drop distributions in Mode II and III. This solution can approximate the effects of the non-planar fault geometry in Mode III. For a single-wavelength heterogeneity, the effect on rupture energetics is described by a dimensionless response function, involving the Fresnel integrals, that reaches its maximum when the heterogeneity wavelength is comparable to the current rupture length. The influence of both shorter- and longer-wavelength heterogeneities decays away from this characteristic scale. Extending the analysis to self-similar multi-wavelength heterogeneity demonstrates that the dominant contribution to rupture energetics always arises from wavelength components comparable to the rupture length, while shorter-wavelength effects are progressively averaged out due to the integral nature of the energetics. This scale-specific property is inherited by rupture arrest conditions, rupture velocity, and fault slip rate through the energy balance and stress intensity factor. The slip-pulse solution in the current model implies that the characteristic wavelength controlling rupture behavior is correlated with the seismogenic-layer thickness. These results imply that unresolved short-wavelength heterogeneity contributes only weakly to the dynamics of large earthquakes, providing a physical explanation for the reproducibility of large-scale rupture processes in dynamic rupture simulations. The theory suggests that uncertainty in earthquake rupture dynamics is intrinsically scale-dependent and that observational constraints on mechanical structures at scales comparable to the rupture dimension are most important for improving the forecastability of large-earthquake rupture scenarios.
8b427989d0c0e6d4: Seismic radiation and dynamic faulting have rarely been observed concurrently, limiting observational constraints on earthquake rupture processes and seismic hazards. Here we report the first directly validated observation of both surface rupture and strong-motion generation captured by a security camera and independently corroborated by nearby seismic records and field measurements during and after the 2026 Kumamoto, Japan, earthquake. Image-retrieved displacement time series matched nearby seismic records. We further find that the very-near-fault ground motion comprised two velocity pulses generated by subsurface and surface fault rupture, respectively, with comparable amplitudes (~1 m s -1 ) and durations (~1 s). The pulse characteristics may reflect the depth-dependent variations in seismic velocities and stress conditions across a sedimentary cover overlying the basement rock. These observations provide rare constraints on the coupling between dynamic faulting and seismic radiation, offering new insights into earthquake source physics and seismic hazard assessments near faults.
36011bc74596a972: The 2025 M w 6.6 Sanriku-Oki earthquake occurred in a region where slow fault-slip phenomena coexist with ordinary earthquakes. We estimated its source process and investigated relationships of the slip model with seismic and aseismic activity. Joint inversion of S-net seismic and pressure-gauge records revealed a main slip region northeast of the epicenter, with a maximum slip of 1.2 m. Within this region, the rate of increase in cumulative tremor counts gradually decreased, while intervals between tremor bursts increased, possibly reflecting the long-term evolution of postseismic deformation following the 2011 Tohoku earthquake. The average stress drop within the main slip region was 1.4 MPa, which may reflect low effective normal stress associated with low confining pressure and elevated pore-fluid pressure. The spatial coexistence of slow and fast fault-slip phenomena may reflect heterogeneous frictional properties under such a low effective normal stress.
5754bec476ba878f: Magmatism can substantially modify continental crust during rifting, yet the distribution of melt and intrusive additions to the crust is often difficult to resolve, particularly in rift sectors where volcanism is spatially localised. Unlike the Ethiopian and Eastern rift sectors of East Africa, volcanism in the Western Rift is concentrated in a few spatially isolated volcanic provinces, raising questions about where magma is stored and how it interacts with fault-controlled extension during the early stages of rifting. We use teleseismic Ps receiver functions (RFs) from the Kivu Rift sector (networks 7G, YA, and KV) to constrain crustal thickness, bulk P-to-S wave velocity ratio (κ), and the character of intracrustal and Moho impedance contrasts across the Kivu Rift that includes the Virunga and South Kivu volcanic provinces. We combine H–κ stacking, 1-D receiver function waveform inversion, and forward modelling to map lateral variations in crustal structure. Crustal thickness varies systematically with tectonic setting: the thinnest crust occurs at stations within the rift (∼28–34 km), whereas thicker crust (mid-30s to low-40s km) characterises the flanks and the broader province. Elevated κ values and increased waveform complexity are concentrated around the Virunga Volcanic Province, consistent with mid- to lower-crustal modification by mafic intrusions and/or melt–fluid effects. We also assess whether topographic variations are isostatically compensated after accounting for the dynamically-supported broad plateau uplift. The thinner crust within the fault-bounded basin confirms extension by a mean stretching factor of ~1.23, locally reaching ~1.32 where crust thins to ~28 km, but the basin–flank elevation contrast is smaller than expected from crustal thinning alone, suggesting that lower crust and/or sub-crustal density variations are important. Together, these observations indicate that the crust beneath the Kivu Rift sector is felsic in composition, has magmatic modification localised to the Virunga Volcanic Province, and crustal stretching is comparable to other Western Rift sectors with deeper basins.
e8be7482cc1df065: Seismic velocity is widely used to estimate water stored in subducting upper mantle, but the same velocity reduction can result from very different combinations of serpentinization and fluid-filled porosity. We develop a rock-physics framework that treats serpentinization as modification of the solid matrix and crack porosity as a separate fluid reservoir, while explicitly accounting for uncertainty in crack geometry. For single Vp or Vs observations, absolute water contents remain strongly nonunique, whereas relative velocity differences provide more robust hydration contrasts. When Vp and Vs are available together, their combined behavior restricts the crack geometries that can explain the observations, providing stronger constraints on water partitioning. Applications to Cascadia, Alaska, and Nankai reveal substantial differences in how water is stored in the incoming mantle: propagator wakes in Cascadia are more hydrated than surrounding mantle; Semidi permits appreciable serpentinization, whereas Shumagin’s very low velocities require little serpentinization and only trace water in very thin cracks; and Nankai data are consistent with appreciable free water in thicker fractures with only moderate serpentinization. These results show that low mantle velocity does not uniquely imply high water content and that distinguishing structurally bound from crack-hosted water is important for assessing water transport into subduction zones.
2ea85a439e97bca2: Debris flows usually generate large basal impact forces because of their gravity-driven nature and moving mass, posing catastrophic threats to mountain communities. This basal impact force is a key parameter for understanding debris-flow dynamics and offers insights for hazard mitigation. However, developing cost-effective and easy-to-maintain approaches to measure or estimate this force remains challenging. While theoretical models have been developed to invert basal impact force from seismic signals, data-driven deep learning approaches offer greater flexibility and scalability, yet their performance for this task remains underexplored. Here, we train a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model and an eXtended LSTM (xLSTM) model to invert basal impact force from debris-flow seismic signals. Formulating the inversion as a regression task, we used 2019 seismic and impact-force data from seven debris-flow events at Illgraben (Switzerland) for training and validation. The 2020-2023 dataset, comprising 21 events, was used to evaluate the trained models and empirical relationships between basal impact force and physical properties. The xLSTM performs similarly to the baseline LSTM across metrics, including root mean squared error and peak inverted basal impact force. Peak-force estimates achieve a mean absolute percentage error of ≤ 5%, equivalent to ≤10 kN. Using xLSTM, we further find a strong correlation (Pearson's r = 0.867) between observed debris-flow volume and cumulative inverted impact force, supporting volume estimation without direct flow measurements. This work provides insights into using seismic signals to estimate debris-flow physical properties, supporting seismic-based early-warning systems that extend beyond event detection to characterize event magnitude and impacts.
