0f0970053ef93027: Summary This study investigates a particular instantiation of the distributional finite-difference method (DFDM) based on B-splines in the context of solving the 1D scalar wave equation, focusing on two key numerical properties: stability and numerical dispersion. By comparing DFDM against finite-difference and spectral-element methods, we assess the trade-offs between time step restrictions and accuracy. We introduce a cost metric to quantify the computational effort required to achieve a target dispersion error threshold. The results show that, while DFDM has more restrictive stability bounds, it offers superior dispersion performance at lower points per wavelength, making it particularly attractive for applications with tight memory requirements.
e1e3c3017c705bc4: The rate and efficiency of stress transmission across continental interiors during collision remain poorly constrained. The >1600-km-long Altyn Tagh Fault, bounding the northern Tibetan Plateau, offers a key test of stress propagation models. Here, we integrate multiscale structural analysis with K–Ar dating of synkinematic illite to date its faulting history. The data document episodic faulting spanning >110 million years, including an ~115 Ma event marking a lithospheric weakness zone predating Cenozoic collision, and an Early Eocene faulting age (~56 Ma), which is nearly synchronous with India–Asia collision onset, implying rapid far-field stress transmission across distances exceeding 1500 km within 10 million years of collision initiation. Reactivation at ~26 Ma, ~2.7 Ma and ~0.6 Ma reflects localization during plateau growth. These results show that inherited lithospheric structures enable efficient, long-distance stress transmission and remain persistent deformation loci, indicating that continental interiors respond to plate-boundary forcing faster than slow, progressive propagation models predict. K–Ar dating reveals >110 Myr of episodic Altyn Tagh Fault activity, beginning at ~115 Ma along a Cretaceous lithospheric weakness. Reactivation at ~56 Ma records rapid India–Asia collisional stress transmission >1500 km into the continental interior.
49f6618c367db134: We present a spectral decomposition applied to nearly 10,000 earthquakes (ML 2.0–5.5) recorded along the East Anatolian Fault Zone (EAFZ) between January 2019 and February 2024, focusing on spatial and temporal variations in source parameters surrounding the 6 February 2023 seismic doublet. Results indicate that M0–fc scaling is consistent with approximate self-similarity, with nearly constant stress drop Δσ across the analyzed magnitude range. The observed linear relationship between M0 and radiated energy Er demonstrates the internal consistency of the estimated source parameters, although this relationship alone should not be interpreted as evidence of stable energy partitioning. Despite the structural segmentation of the EAFZ, Δσ remains statistically similar across the Nurdağı and Sürgü segments, indicating no clear segment-scale difference in Δσ within the analyzed dataset. To investigate spatial variations across fault segments, we examined normalized stress-drop and scaled-energy anomalies (Δσ* and E˜r*, respectively) as proxies for mechanical heterogeneity and scaled radiated energy. Δσ* exhibits relatively smooth spatial variations, whereas E˜r* shows more localized variability. These distinct spatial patterns may reflect differences in the sensitivity of the two parameters to stress conditions and local structural or mechanical heterogeneities. Our results indicate that small-magnitude earthquakes encode meaningful insights into fault segmentation and stress evolution, providing a multiscale perspective on rupture mechanics. These observations can enable detailed segment-level analyses and offer a transferable framework applicable to other tectonically complex fault systems, improving our understanding of earthquake physics and mechanical heterogeneity in strike-slip environments.
2f060139fe2904fa: Here, we develop a supervised framework for identifying probabilistic earthquake-risk states in the central and southern Tan-Lu fault zone and adjacent areas of eastern China using multiple catalog-derived seismicity features and a deep learning approach. Using the China Earthquake Networks Center catalog from 1979 to 2025, seven seismological parameters (b, M, η, D, Mf, N, and Rm) were calculated for ML≥2.0 earthquakes. These parameters were transformed into probability-based time-series features and used as inputs to an enhanced long short-term memory model with dual-task learning and dropout regularization. The model was trained using data from 1979 to 2020 and evaluated on an independent testing period from 2021 to 2025. Training was repeated using five predefined random seeds, and same-date predicted probabilities were averaged with equal weights. In the broad study area, the seven-parameter probability-transformed ensemble achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.650 and average precision (AP) = 0.297, compared with 0.535 and 0.258 for the raw-parameter ensemble; the no-skill AP baseline was 0.209. Input-feature ablation showed that the full seven-parameter model outperformed models using N alone or N together with b. Comparison with an epidemic-type aftershock sequence model indicated that the relative performance of statistical and data-driven models depends strongly on the forecasting task. Although elevated scores were not restricted to labeled pre-earthquake windows and the separation between positive and negative score distributions weakened in the independent test period, the continuous scores retained some ranking information. Accordingly, the model output is interpreted as a continuous risk-ranking score rather than as a deterministic forecast of earthquake occurrence on any specific date. Probability-based representations of multiple catalog-derived seismicity parameters, combined with deep temporal modeling, may provide a useful complementary approach to regional identification of pre-earthquake risk windows.
35117295372e4c79: Remarkably strong anomalies in seismic properties of the mantle beneath the East African rift are plausibly explained by elevated mantle potential temperatures and/or the presence of partial melt. Previous studies have attributed strong attenuation to elevated temperatures that possibly extend as deep as the mantle transition zone. Although petrologic work clearly infers elevated temperatures, the ∼140°C anomaly is less than at many other hotspots. The anomalies in seismic velocity are stronger than can be explained by this modest excess in temperature, and hence additional mechanisms such as melt are often invoked. We measure the attenuation of a large dataset of teleseismic P phases stretching from the Arabian Platform to the Kaapvaal craton to constrain the nature of seismic anomalies beneath this plate boundary. Anomalies in attenuation are modest along our nearly 6000 km long profile, with the strong exception of the Main Ethiopian Rift (MER). We show that the anomalies in seismic velocity and attenuation beneath the Afar Depression and MER are jointly explained best by a relatively thin layer of high attenuation, akin to other regions of rifting, which we attribute to either “pre-melting” relaxation or an effect of an in situ melt phase. Because our data are path-integrated, thickness and QP trade off directly, and a thicker, more weakly attenuating region spread over hundreds of kilometers is an admissible end member. The opposite occurs further south—rifting occurs along the edges of the Tanzania craton and beneath Lake Malawi without strong attenuation, including beneath the Turkana Depression where the asthenosphere conditions must differ from the MER.
6c6093465a98b59d: The Ryukyu subduction zone offshore eastern Taiwan possesses significant seismogenic potential, exemplified by the 1920 earthquake. However, the scarcity of near-field observations leaves the ground-motion characteristics of such mega-earthquakes poorly constrained, limiting the reliability of seismic hazard assessments. This study investigates long-period ground-motion characteristics of a potential M 8 Ryukyu earthquake using large-scale 3D ground-motion simulations. We simulated an M 8 scenario earthquake using characterized source models based on the “Recipe” procedure and conducted 3D finite-difference simulations for 192 source–velocity-model combinations, incorporating variations in hypocenter location, rupture velocity, asperity distribution, two tomographic velocity models, and topography. Varying the Gaussian source time function (STF) duration in postprocessing expands the dataset to 1728 scenarios. Synthetic waveforms were generated at 4950 virtual stations, producing more than 8.5 million synthetic ground-motion records, and analyzed using RotD50 spectral accelerations (SAs) at periods of 1.0, 3.0, and 5.0 s. Results indicate that rupture directivity and rupture velocity dominate the spatial variability of long-period ground motions, with parameter sensitivity exhibiting strong spatial nonuniformity across the study region. Calibration against the empirical CH20 ground-motion model (GMM) suggests Gaussian STFs of 2, 6, and 8 s provide the most consistent spectral representation for SA at 1.0, 3.0, and 5.0 s, respectively. The nonergodic path terms (δP2P) derived from two alternative velocity models, which capture the path effects of the deep 3D structure (VS≥2.4 km/s), reveal spatially consistent features, including a persistent amplification zone near Hualien linked to the Longitudinal Valley low-velocity structure, a deamplification belt along the Coastal Range and Central Range high-velocity material, and a frequency-dependent amplification in the Ilan Plain attributable to deeper crustal focusing or trapping rather than near-surface site effects. The workflow established here provides a transferable framework for refining GMMs and advancing nonergodic seismic hazard assessments in data-sparse subduction environments.
a3c09c008d6a56dc: Earthquake monitoring balances competing demands. Organizations must track small-scale seismicity visible on perhaps just a handful of sensors while assessing large earthquakes recorded globally. They must deliver authoritative information within seconds, while curating a research-grade catalog over decades. They need to remain operational precisely when communications, power, or cloud infrastructure may be degraded. These challenges are in tension and are particularly acute in Alaska. The region comprises 5%–10% of global seismicity. Station spacing varies by two orders of magnitude. Earthquake depths range from above sea level to below 200 km. A substantial fraction of seismicity occurs offshore and is essentially out of network. In late 2025, the Alaska Earthquake Center completed a ground-up rebuild of our acquisition, analysis, and product dissemination systems. We address the challenges above with a series of major design choices. Parallel on-premises and cloud-based deployments provide mostly independent paths for producing information. Detection algorithms are tuned to capture the full range of phase arrivals, whether they originate in our mission region or elsewhere in the world. Multiple association pipelines accommodate the wide range of station densities and tolerances for latent data. Together, they handle teleseismic earthquakes that spread arrivals across the region, routine in-state events, and in-state earthquakes large enough to benefit from using data from far outside our area of responsibility. Finally, we balance response time and event quality with a catalog workflow that allows the highest-quality real-time solutions to be published automatically, while lesser-quality events are held for review by the on-call seismologist, or for postprocessing during the final steps of catalog curation. Though our implementation is tailored to Alaska and remains a work in progress, our hope is that these strategies can help inform networks facing similar competing demands.
de338d7f76b06672: Deep learning models can help mitigate the need for analyst intervention in seismic classification of local earthquake and explosion signals, but optimizing model performance across multiple localities is challenging. Here, we seek to advance multilocality classification through hyperparameter optimization, evaluation of training data selection, and incorporation of phase pick probabilities from a pre-existing deep learning model into the new source type classification models. One-branch and two-branch convolutional neural network model designs are tested with 16 local data sets, each containing earthquakes and shallow borehole explosions observed by the same receivers. The one-branch model uses a conventional input of time–frequency scalograms and the two-branch model adds vector inputs of P-wave and S-wave probabilities output from a pre-existing phase picking model, which are increasingly available in modern event detection workflows. Hyperparameters for the one- and two-branch models were optimized by a guided search algorithm. For in-distribution data tests spanning all 16 data sets, the two-branch model’s single-station balanced accuracy (95.7%) slightly outperforms the one-branch model (94.7%). In addition, the optimized two-branch model is simpler, with about half as many model parameters and faster convergence in training. Relative performance of the two-branch model increases for out-of-distribution tests (using a locality held out from training), with an average increase in single-station balanced accuracy from 84.4% to 87.6% across 16 held out localities. The two-branch model also substantially outperforms P/S amplitude ratio discrimination accuracy by 14% on average for out-of-distribution tests. The results suggest that the added context from phase detection probabilities, which are a common by-product of event catalog building, can provide an efficient means to improve generalization of event-type classification models when applied to new regions.
aef86dbc64561201: Understanding fault geometry and mechanics is key to interpreting the seismotectonic setting of a region. We analyze data from a 1‐year dense seismic array deployment in Southern Italy to infer focal mechanisms and stress field from low‐magnitude earthquakes using machine‐learning techniques. We derive 289 focal mechanisms, including nearly all events with , yielding a data set comparable to that obtained from 6 years of conventional monitoring. The retrieved mechanisms are consistent with the orientation of the main tectonic structures, and the stress field, inverted from the principal fault planes, indicates a dominant normal faulting regime. We illustrate that dense monitoring enables investigation of spatio‐temporal characteristics of the stress field, showing homogeneity at ∼20 km spatial scale and temporal stability of principal stress orientations. Furthermore, seasonal variations in the stress ratio are observed, that could be modulated by hydrological loading.
b11384505486cb75: Validating the controversial hypothesis that precursory gravity changes arise from sudden acceleration of subducting plates potentially triggering great earthquakes is of paramount importance. To rigorously evaluate proposed precursors for the 2011 Mw 9.0 Tohoku and 2010 Mw 8.8 Maule earthquakes, we develop a statistical framework that enables (a) robust assessment of their statistical significance, (b) characterization of temporal evolution, and (c) integrative analysis across multiple GRACE gravity solutions with differing error characteristics. Additionally, we test the precursor hypothesis using independent GNSS‐measured surface displacements within a physically consistent framework. Our results show no evidence supporting the proposed precursor in either alternative GRACE solutions or high‐precision GNSS observations. The anomalous gravity changes previously interpreted as earthquake precursors are indistinguishable from solution‐specific data errors or other non‐tectonic signals, lacking evidence for tectonic origin.
9d270f173cd84500: Few fragments of Earth's earliest crust have survived, and so this formative period of our planet's history is shrouded in mystery. To leverage the limited data available, it is important to understand all the processes that could have shaped our young planet. Here, I explore a previously neglected aspect of early‐Earth dynamics: rotation. Earth after the Moon‐forming impact was rapidly rotating with its rotation rate slowing significantly during the first tens of millions of years after the impact as the Moon tidally receded. Using planetary structure and tidal evolution calculations, I show that the initially distorted structure of Earth would likely have led to significant latitudinal variations in primary crustal thickness. Further, the subsequent changes in Earth's shape in response to its slowing rotation rate could have driven extensive tectonic activity and modulated the response of the crust to other forces. There was extension of the crust in polar regions and convergence in the equatorial regions at rates potentially comparable to those forming the Himalayas today in high‐angular momentum scenarios. Depending on the rheology of the earliest crust, such motions could have led to burial of hydrated and weathered surface material, extensive volcanism, and degassing of Earth's interior. Phase changes due to increases in internal pressure could have led to delamination of parts of the crust, producing early mantle heterogeneities. Hydrated secondary melting of the crust and the production of evolved magmas could explain the emergence of a diversity of rock types within tens of millions of years of Earth's formation.
cc2a73b84e5b7d5e: Whether and how the subduction processes result in water enrichment at the base of the mantle transition zone (MTZ) remain elusive. The major orogenic belts of the Asian continent, including the Central Asian, Tethyan, and Alpine–Himalayan belts, which record extensive subduction processes, offer an ideal target to address the hydration of the MTZ and its relationship with subduction. Here, we map water content at the MTZ base by combining mineral physics constraints on hydrous pyrolite and global seismic observations of velocity structure and 660-km discontinuity topography. Our results indicate an average global water content of approximately 0.14 wt%, with pronounced hydration anomalies in parts of Asia. Linking these anomalies with reconstructions of past subduction events since 410 Ma reveals extensive water delivery to the MTZ, particularly beneath parts of the Mongol–Okhotsk suture zone, the Central Asian Orogenic Belt, and the Tethyan orogenic domain, where water content exceeds 0.5 wt%. These results connect ancient subduction history to present-day mantle hydration, offering insights into Earth’s deep water cycle.
3f6d93c33808aae9: We investigate the three-dimensional seismogenic architecture and along-strike evolution of the Longitudinal Valley (LV) suture zone in eastern Taiwan, where arc–continent collision between the Philippine Sea Plate (PSP) and Eurasian Plate progressively evolves into northward subduction of the PSP. Using seismic waveforms recorded by CWASN, BATS, and TSMIP between 1991 and 2024, we apply a machine-learning phase picker to obtain internally consistent P- and S-wave arrivals and relocate all events with a nonlinear probabilistic location algorithm and a 3-D velocity model of Taiwan. This procedure yields a more complete and structurally coherent earthquake catalog, allowing us to image the geometry of major fault systems and their relation to tomographic velocity and Vp/Vs anomalies. The relocated seismicity and tomography show that the west-dipping Central Range Fault (CRF) and east-dipping Longitudinal Valley Fault (LVF) and interaction change systematically from south to north. In the southern collision segment, the CRF is steep and bounds a strong, uplifted Central Range block, whereas the LVF is a moderately to steeply east-dipping fault localized beneath the Coastal Range. Northward, the CRF dip shallows and truncates the shallow LVF, producing a structurally complex interaction zone. In the northern transition to subduction, LVF-related seismicity deepens into a near-vertical, high-Vp/Vs structure accompanied by a west-dipping back-thrust, together defining the western boundary of the descending Philippine Sea Plate. We further document a high-angle left-lateral strikeslip fault within the suture zone that is active mainly in the southern LV but remains confined to the Central Range. Finally, a high-velocity, low-Vp/Vs block beneath the Southern Longitudinal Trough is interpreted as remnant forearc crust. Together, these results provide a unified seismological framework for the structural evolution of Taiwan’s suture zone from collision to incipient subduction.
5e387bbf840e0930: Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) is a fundamental inverse problem in geophysics to estimate subsurface properties, such as velocity, from seismic measurements. Recently, self-supervised learning methods remove the need for ground-truth velocity maps during training by leveraging a forward operator to simulate seismic data from predictions and backpropagate the gradients of reconstruction loss through it. In this work, we consider a more challenging setting without accessing such gradients. To this end, we incorporate reinforcement learning into self-supervised FWI and propose a framework named DeepWaveRL. Specifically, we reformulate FWI as a policy learning problem, where the policy network predicts velocity maps as actions, and a forward operator is used solely for simulation. A global scalar reward is computed based on data misfit for each prediction and used to weight policy gradients. Thus, learning proceeds without accessing the gradients from the forward operator. Given the indirect and coarse supervision signals, we further identify key strategies to stabilize learning and mitigate the spatial credit assignment bottleneck. Experimental results show that, despite relying entirely on a single scalar reward, DeepWaveRL achieves competitive performance compared to supervised and self-supervised baselines. These findings suggest that our framework offers a flexible and complementary learning paradigm for the FWI research community.
79a4e5ffd08177c4: This study presents an integrated approach combining seismic refraction tomography and electrical resistivity tomography to evaluate the structural integrity of supporting pillars in an underground cave in Burgundy, France. A three-phase petrophysical joint inversion (P-JIv) was performed using a finite-element model on an unstructured triangular mesh. Compared with independent inversions, the joint inversion improved spatial resolution and enhanced the consistency between the two geophysical methods. The results revealed distinct zones of electrical resistivity and P-wave velocity, reflecting variations in rock fracturing and weathering. The geophysical interpretations showed strong agreement with visual inspections and borehole logs. Furthermore, rock porosity and water content were estimated from the P-JIv results. Finally, an automated clustering procedure was used to establish a proxy indicator of pillar integrity, enabling the prioritization of cave reinforcement measures.
0f8c0bb51ea1a59f: Environmental seismology investigates mechanical vibrations generated by external processes or influenced by phenomena originating outside the solid Earth. It encompasses interactions between the solid Earth and other environmental systems, including the cryosphere, hydrosphere, and anthroposphere, as well as the specific sources of seismic vibrations associated with these systems. This field also examines how environmental factors, such as temperature fluctuations and hydrological variations, affect seismic wave propagation. Recent advances in data-processing techniques, combined with increased computational capabilities and the growing density of seismic sensor networks, have enabled novel observations and contributed to the emergence of environmental seismology as a distinct research field. This article reviews how subtle changes in the Earth's subsurface can be detected and interpreted through variations in seismic wave propagation induced by external environmental processes, with applications to geomechanics, hydrology, and natural hazard assessment. In particular, we demonstrate how ambient seismic noise can be used to monitor: (1) thermal variations in the subsurface, within buildings, and in rock columns; (2) the temporal and spatial evolution of groundwater levels; and (3) changes in the rigidity of the material forming a landslide, with particular emphasis on the reduction in rigidity that may precede slope failure.
88a06b52ff5144fe: This study aims to protect an exceptional population of soda straw stalactites from vibrations generated by nearby rock blasting activities. The Choranche Cave, located in the Vercors region of France, hosts thousands of remarkably slender soda straws, reaching several meters in length while measuring approximately 0.5 cm in diameter. These speleothems are particularly susceptible to vibrations because of their structural fragility and potential for dynamic amplification. Our analyses revealed that their fundamental natural frequencies fall within the frequency range of nearby blasting-induced vibrations, typically spanning tens to hundreds of hertz. To assess the effects of blasting, we combined in situ vibration measurements, laboratory-based material characterization, and dynamic two-dimensional finite element simulations to estimate the loads experienced by the soda straw population. The results indicate that resonance can amplify the induced loads by a factor of five. Consequently, shorter soda straws (0.1--1 m) were found to be more vulnerable to blasting-induced vibrations than longer speleothems (>1 m), despite the greater weight and inertial forces associated with the latter. Based on simulations of several blasting tests, we established an allowable peak particle velocity (PPV) threshold of 2.4 mm/s within the cave. Subsequent blasting operations were conducted in compliance with this limit, successfully protecting the soda straw population from damage. We also investigated the dynamic response of soda straws to regional earthquakes. In contrast to blasting-induced vibrations, the lower-frequency content of earthquake ground motions preferentially excites resonance in longer speleothe
7b3f4adbc22dc38d: Repeated passive seismic surveys were conducted over more than a decade on the unstable La Praz rock slope in Savoie, France, which involved an estimated rock volume of approximately 13,000--15,000 m${}^3$. The final survey took place two months before the complete collapse of the slope in August 2023. The amplitude of the Horizontal-to-Vertical Spectral Ratio at the peak frequency (*aHVSR(fp)*) was used to distinguish stable and unstable areas and identify fractures associated with significant mechanical decoupling. Rock compartments were also classified according to their rockfall hazard. The compartments most susceptible to failure exhibited the highest *aHVSR(fp)* values, ranging from 26 to 157, compared with values of 7.5--19 in intermediate-hazard areas and 2.7 in the adjacent stable rock mass. The main HVSR peak frequency (*fp*) exhibited distinct decreases of 15%, 14%, and 11% in three unstable rock compartments before the collapse. These reductions substantially exceeded the range of environmentally induced resonance-frequency fluctuations observed at the site and commonly reported in the literature as a limitation of this method. The frequency decreases were interpreted as indicators of progressive damage extending into the rock slope. Notably, these changes were detected exclusively in the three compartments identified as the most susceptible to failure, which also exhibited the highest *aHVSR(fp)* values. This study demonstrates, for the first time, the potential of passive seismic monitoring to reveal progressive in-depth damage within a complex, heterogeneous, and highly fractured rock slope. The findings highlight the value of combining HVSR amplitude and peak-frequency variations to characterize unstable rock compartments and identify potential precursors to catastrophic slope failure.
21c29dc2c7f4fbe0: Electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) is widely used to investigate landslide morphology and dynamics. Landslide behavior is strongly influenced by clay content, pore pressure, and the spatial distribution of permeability. However, conventional direct current (DC) resistivity methods have limited capacity to characterize permeability, as materials with low electrical resistivity may exhibit either high or low permeability depending on their clay content and the relative contributions of surface and electrolytic conduction. Induced polarization (IP) offers a valuable complementary approach for investigating the petrophysical properties of geological materials. Despite its potential, IP has been rarely applied to landslide studies and has not yet been widely used for landslide monitoring. This study investigates the added value of IP measurements alongside conventional DC resistivity for landslide characterization and monitoring. Three time-domain induced polarization (TDIP) surveys were conducted at different time steps on an active landslide in the French Alps. Time-lapse inversions of resistivity and chargeability were performed, and spectral IP parameters were derived using Debye decomposition. The results were then compared with surface displacement estimates obtained from optical image processing. The findings demonstrate that TDIP is particularly valuable for delineating unstable volumes within the landslide. The geophysical results show strong agreement with independent measurements from piezometers and inclinometers. Furthermore, applying an empirical relationship between IP parameters and permeability enables the spatial distribution of permeability within the landslide to be estimated, as well as its seasonal variations. Overall, this study highlights the potential of combining IP and DC resistivity measurements to improve the characterization of landslide properties and support the monitoring of their temporal evolution.
6f496f91f6c48ff8: We conducted passive seismic monitoring of the unstable La Praz rock slope (approximately 14,000 m${}^3$) in the French Alps over a period of more than 10 years. During the six months preceding collapse, we observed a pronounced 24% decrease in the slope's fundamental resonance frequency ((f\_0)), indicating a reduction in the overall stiffness of the rock mass. Joint analysis of (f\_0) variations and slope deformation revealed alternating phases dominated by sudden brittle damage and more ductile behavior, potentially involving sliding. Seismic monitoring identified damage processes that were either ambiguous or undetectable through surface deformation measurements alone, while also highlighting critical periods of intensified damage. Although some of these periods coincided with identifiable external triggers, such as intense rainfall events, others could not be clearly linked to external forcing. These findings demonstrate the potential of passive seismic monitoring to provide insights into the internal structural condition of unstable rock slopes at depth. Combining surface deformation measurements with seismic tracking of rock mass stiffness could therefore improve the identification and characterization of active slopes undergoing progressive damage, contributing to the development of more effective slope monitoring systems.
15087cae5bb040c6: The velocity and attenuation structures of near-surface soils play an important role in controlling earthquake ground motions. While numerous passive techniques have been developed for estimating velocity structure, practical methods for estimating attenuation from microtremor array measurements remain limited. We developed a spatial autocorrelation (SPAC) method for estimating Rayleigh-wave attenuation coefficients using an attenuation-aware formulation of the SPAC coefficient. A theoretical analysis of directional aliasing showed that attenuation estimation requires denser azimuthal sampling than conventional phase-velocity estimation, motivating the use of a regular heptagonal array. The method uses a two-stage procedure in which initial estimates of phase velocity and the attenuation coefficient are obtained using a first-order approximation and then refined by fitting the complex SPAC coefficient. Synthetic data analyses demonstrated that the proposed method can recover attenuation coefficients under ideal conditions and clarified how directional aliasing, record length and sensitivity to attenuation affect the estimates. Comparison with a beamforming-based method showed that the proposed method is less sensitive to wavefield directionality and can be applied at longer wavelengths relative to the array size. The method was further validated using microtremor-like waveforms generated by independent P--SV wave-propagation simulations. Finally, a preliminary application to field microtremor records yielded attenuation coefficients that were broadly consistent across array sizes and with values expected from existing empirical attenuation relationships. These results demonstrate the applicability of the proposed method to passive estimation of Rayleigh-wave attenuation.
27ebdbf67a759023: Quantum circuit simulators are essential for quantum algorithm development, yet systematic runtime benchmarks comparing major frameworks across CPU and GPU backends are limited. We benchmark three open-source frameworks - Cirq (qsim), CUDA-Q, and Qiskit (Aer) - on statevector simulation of the 2D quantum acoustic wave equation, evolved via Trotterized Hamiltonian dynamics, for problem sizes from 7 to 29 qubits on a single Azure virtual machine. The evaluation spans four categories: CPU runtime versus qubit count, strong scalability on multi-core CPUs at 27 qubits, GPU runtime versus qubit count, and GPU-over-CPU speedup. Relative rankings shift from one category to the next. On CPU, Cirq is fastest up to 23 qubits (2.4x faster than Qiskit at 21 qubits), but Qiskit overtakes it at larger sizes and higher thread counts, sustaining 80% parallel efficiency at 16 threads. On GPU, CUDA-Q leads between 13 and 21 qubits, while Cirq becomes the fastest GPU backend at large problem sizes, achieving 1.5x and 2.3x speedups over CUDA-Q and Qiskit at 29 qubits. GPU-over-CPU speedup ratios should be interpreted alongside absolute GPU runtimes; CUDA-Q's 1500x at 21 qubits is largely driven by the limited scaling of its CPU backend (qpp), and the absolute GPU runtimes show that the three frameworks' GPU backends differ by less than these ratios alone suggest. These results indicate that no single framework dominates across configurations, and that backend selection for statevector simulation should be guided by both target hardware and problem size.
dce6baab206b17b2: Scalar representations of geodetic strain rate tensors are widely used to characterize crustal deformation and, in seismic hazard assessment, to convert strain rate to expected seismic moment rate. Existing scalar definitions of shear strain rate, total strain rate and deformation style are not defined consistently and, because they depend on eigenvalues that carry both dilatation and shear, cannot be read as a partition of mixed-strain deformation. We propose definitions motivated by fault kinematics. The strike-slip strain rate (e_s), derived from the shear on zero-length-change orientations, is twice the geometric mean of the principal strain rate magnitudes and zero when both share a sign. The total strain rate (e_t) is the explicit sum of and the absolute dilatation (); except for uniaxial strain it exceeds the Frobenius norm (e_f), by up to a factor sqrt(3). The style parameter equals the fractional dilatational contribution in mixed-strain deformation and is extended to classify deformation in which both principal strain rates share a sign. We also propose a moment rate (M_split) that releases the strike-slip and dilatational contributions on separate strike-slip and dip-slip faults; for Andersonian dips it exceeds the minimum moment (M_min) by up to 37% for mixed-faulting settings. An application to southwestern U.S. geodetic strain rates shows that the 37% maximum difference is not a corner case: in the 53% of the area where each of the strike-slip and dilatational contributions is at least a quarter of the total strain rate, M_split exceeds M_min by 34%. The southwestern U.S. example demonstrates that these differences can be regionally significant, with moment-rate estimates differing by tens of percent in mixed-style deformation zones.
a4898ec8590b8897: Population models treat a static arrest as the end of the rupture, although some of those arrests span the fault in a fully dynamic calculation. This paper tests whether the static crack itself shows which ones. A static stress-intensity criterion and a fully dynamic rupture were compared on 180 new random stress fields on one 120 km antiplane fault with linear slip weakening. The predictor is the subcritical width, the extra distance one crack tip must be extended, with the other tip held fixed, before the static stress intensity factor returns to its critical value. Two logistic models were fitted on 52 earlier antiplane ruptures, 10 of which span the fault. One uses the static arrest length alone and the other adds the width. Both were applied unchanged to the 158 new ruptures that the static criterion stops. Of the 158, 24 span the fault dynamically. Adding the width raises the probability that a spanning rupture ranks above an arrested one from 0.880 to 0.956, a gain of 0.076 with a 95% interval from 0.037 to 0.126. The test and the required gain were fixed before the new fields were drawn. Halving the grid spacing along strike left the outcome of all 158 ruptures unchanged. On 120 earlier ruptures on the same fault, the static criterion and the dynamic rupture disagreed 22 times, and all 22 were static arrests that spanned the fault. Population models and induced earthquake estimates that use the static balance make that error in one direction. The width read from the static crack can rank which of those static arrests should be run dynamically first, at the correlation length tested here. At a correlation length 1.78 times longer, a width threshold flags 19 of 38 spanning ruptures and a length threshold flags 34, so that ranking is not shown to carry over. The test covers antiplane rupture, one correlation length, three stress amplitudes, and linear slip weakening.
de2af80b5b8c4b6e: The Bangladesh is comprising up to 20 km of sedimentary deposits over the lithosphere and surrounded by India-Asia collision zone. Thus, deciphering the crustal architecture is essential for understanding the tectonic evolution. The sparse broadband seismic stations have provided estimates of Moho depth, however, the regional-scale variation in Moho topography remains poorly constrained. In this study, we performed a 3D gravity inversion constrained by seismically-derived Moho depth, to better delineate the crustal structure and thinning factor of the region. The inverted Moho depth beneath the Bangladesh varying from 22 – 32 km and exceed 32 km in the adjacent regions, while crustal thickness is less than 22 km in the Bengal Basin. The west-east lithospheric structure shows that the lithospheric thinning preceded crustal thinning in the northern Bangladesh, whereas in southern Bangladesh they occurred synchronously. Gravity modelling and stretching factors derived from tectonic subsidence support the presence of 5–8 km of magmatic underplating beneath the volcanic rifted margin in Bangladesh. 3D flexural backstripping analysis reveals that onshore Bengal Basin thermally subsided 5 – 7 km and adjacent region experienced a tectonic uplift < 2 km. The plume-related magmatism combined with prolonged sediment loading produced ~ 1 km of uplift of Shillong Plateau and remaining topography is generated by slip on the major thrust faults during the late Cenozoic shortening. Our findings highlight the key factors shaping the present-day crustal structure and topography of northeastern India.
fed6a7ede34ea395: Tsunami source models commonly convert seafloor deformation into an initial sea-surface displacement with the classical Kajiura filter, which is exact for an ocean of uniform depth. Seafloor motion enters through the bottom-normal forcing $q=U_z+ abla h\cdot\Uh$, and the exact rapid-source response is $\eta=\opC q$ with $\opC=\opB^{-1}$, a nonlocal operator determined by the actual bathymetry. This is not obtained by simply replacing $H$ with $h(\xh)$ in $\sech(KH)$: slope enters the exact bottom boundary condition, and spatially varying bathymetry couples the response globally. Exact wedge and three-dimensional seamount tests reveal a clear hierarchy. Local water depth controls the dominant attenuation and broadening, gentle slopes add a mainly phase-like correction, and surrounding geometry produces a smaller but genuinely nonlocal redistribution that local formulas cannot always improve. A 2011 Tohoku-Oki application shows the same hierarchy for realistic bathymetry and demonstrates that the full solution restores global volume consistency. The operator also appears in $\eta_{tt}+g\opG\eta=\opC q_{tt}$, making generalized Kajiura transfer the rapid-source limit of a single time-dependent generation framework rather than an independent initialization rule.
25df6bdbc26118f2: Learning reliable surrogates for geodynamic models requires benchmarks that resolve coupled fields and temporal stability. We present GeoSim, a benchmark of high-resolution two-dimensional mantle-plume simulations generated with I2VIS, comprising 237 trajectories across two parameter regimes, with six coupled fields, physical timestamps, and trajectory-level splits. GeoSim defines short-window prediction and autonomous rollout, and evaluates representative neural operators field by field. Across models, we observe a pronounced scalar--velocity gap: scalar fields are reconstructed accurately while velocity errors remain large, and short-window accuracy does not imply stable rollout. We also evaluate MFGNO (Multi-Field Graph Neural Operator), a joint multi-field graph baseline designed for this benchmark; on GeoSim-Plume1, under a fixed per-field objective, it reduces horizontal and vertical velocity errors by 58.4% and 38.5% relative to an independent-field graph baseline, while an explicit field-difference input shows no measurable benefit at this scale. GeoSim provides a reproducible benchmark for field-wise diagnosis and long-horizon evaluation of geodynamic surrogates.
0c6fd068093036c0: Mechanical disturbances such as seismic shaking can set a granular slope in motion. Understanding the resulting transport before arrest is important for predicting topographic change, assessing landslide hazards and controlling powder flows in industrial processes. Experiments show that smaller disturbances can trigger avalanches and larger areas are mobilized as slopes approach their stability limit. Yet how much transport varies between events under the same macroscopic conditions and forcing remains unclear. Here we use numerical simulations to show that transport variability is amplified near the critical angle. We apply identical basal pulses to static granular layers with the same macroscopic conditions but different initial particle configurations. Although the mean transport increases approximately in inverse proportion to the angular distance from the critical angle, the standard deviation increases even faster and can exceed the mean. Thus, identical forcing can produce widely different transport amounts. Deterministic constitutive laws that assign a unique response to given macroscopic conditions cannot capture this variability. We introduce fluctuations into the energy balance to develop a stochastic model that captures the main features of the broadening transport distribution. These results show that assessing transport near the critical angle requires considering its distribution, not just its mean, and motivate constitutive descriptions that incorporate fluctuations.
f1a8233c415521d4: Lunar seismic records are characterized by long-lasting spindle-shaped coda, which has long been considered to be caused by strong velocity contrasts in a continuous-medium lunar crust; however, simulated waveforms could not well match the observation even with unrealistically strong velocity contrasts, demonstrating its mechanism still unsolved. Here we propose a novel model of coda wave generation with random fractures in the lunar crust, where vacuum fractures prevent seismic wave propagation as insulating boundaries, causing strong persistent reverberation in terms of total reflection among fractures. Our model can easily reproduce the typical characteristics of observed Apollo data even using a limited number of simplified fractures in homogeneous matrix, with envelope correlations over 0.9, much higher than previous studies. Numerical simulations suggest that fractures in the uppermost ~1 km of the crust may dominate lunar seismic scattering. This model enables us to investigate the shallow lunar fracture system using seismic data and to suppress seismic coda for detecting critical phases reflected from deep interiors.
1f987c524eba1f83: Accurately characterizing near-fault ground motions, particularly permanent tectonic displacements and velocity pulses associated with rupture directivity, is essential for seismic hazard assessment and infrastructure design. However, conventional ground-motion processing can distort or remove these characteristics. This study extends existing baseline correction methods by synchronously processing all three components of strong-motion recordings to preserve near-fault effects. Comparison with nearby Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) observations demonstrates that the method reliably captures the amplitude and orientation of permanent tectonic displacements. Analysis of the processed recordings reveals pronounced velocity pulses and permanent displacements, with the largest peak-to-peak velocities concentrated along the direction of rupture propagation. A classification framework is also introduced to distinguish fling-step pulses from dynamic velocity pulses. The results indicate that fling-step pulses typically occur early in the ground shaking, whereas dynamic pulses span a broader temporal range. Furthermore, the spatial distribution and orientation of near-fault effects are consistent with bridge damage documented during post-earthquake reconnaissance. The resulting dataset provides ground-motion time histories that preserve near-fault characteristics for seismic hazard assessment and engineering applications.
79af5b7f9cb6c6ec: We present SeidarT , an open-source, community-driven software package for full-waveform finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) modeling of elastic and electromagnetic wave propagation in heterogeneous, anisotropic, and attenuating media. SeidarT natively incorporates full-tensor anisotropy (all 21 stiffness coefficients), frequency-independent attenuation through a generalized Q formulation, and unified treatment of both seismic and electromagnetic wave physics on a simple Cartesian grid. The software prioritizes accessibility and extensibility by combining the computational efficiency of Fortran with the user-friendly scripting capabilities of Python. Model construction leverages an intuitive image-based geometry workflow and JSON project files, eliminating the need for complex mesh generation while allowing flexible specification of arbitrary stiffness or permittivity tensors, material distributions, and boundary conditions. We implement the Convolutional Perfectly Matched Layer (CPML) with explicit tuning strategies adapted for anisotropic media, and provide automatic stability checking via the Courant-Friedrichs-Lévy and wavenumber-bandlimit criteria. The software is validated against analytical solutions for elastic wave propagation and empirically constrained through comparison with ground-penetrating radar and seismic field observations in snow and ice. We document the physical property parameterizations for ice and snow as functions of temperature, pressure, and liquid water content, and provide multiple material homogenization schemes (Hill average, Gassmann substitution, Self-Consistent Approximation) to accommodate variable porosity and fluid saturation regimes. SeidarT is designed to lower economic and technical barriers for scientists, engineers, and students integrating sophisticated wave-physics simulations into workflows spanning cryospheric research, environmental monitoring, subsurface characterization, and civil infrastructure assessment. The open-source development model on GitHub and PyPI encourages community contributions and iterative improvements, positioning SeidarT as a versatile platform for advancing both fundamental understanding and applied geophysical imaging.
bca9dc504bd282d6: High-speed trains generate highly repeatable seismic vibrations, whose changes are expected to reveal how railway infrastructure changes over time. From a dense array and 28 days of trains, we use seismic interferometry to extract a fast guided wave along the viaduct hour by hour. Fitting attributes the diurnal cycle to the resonance frequency and the coupling parameter, both tracking air temperature.The multi-day change can come from the waveguide velocity and coincides with an irrigation-driven groundwater fall. Together, these observations indicate that the viaduct system is locally resonant, and the frequency pattern identifies which internal parameter of the system has changed. This offers a new seismological means for monitoring railway bridge health.
257cd6d6638649e0: Human activities generate seismic ground motions that dominate the high-frequency (>1 Hz) seismic spectra in urban environments. Here, I analyze seismic recordings from dense urban networks in Japan and combine them with observations from outdoor gatherings in the United States and Israel to characterize crowd-generated seismic signals. Through clustering analysis of ground motions recorded by the dense Metropolitan Seismic Observation Network in the Tokyo metropolitan area, I identify distinct temporal and spatial patterns associated with vehicular traffic. Crowd-generated seismic energy is strongest in the 1–2 Hz band, consistent with human walking frequencies. Distance-corrected seismic amplification factors scale approximately linearly with the logarithm of crowd size across five orders of magnitude but form two distinct populations: energetic outdoor protests produce larger distance-corrected amplification factors and stronger scaling than routine student activity in Tokyo schools, suggesting that crowd-generated seismic excitation depends on collective crowd behavior. This relationship provides a framework for using seismic observations to detect and characterize large human gatherings in urban environments.
aaea8a93647dca75: Summary Earthquake focal mechanisms provide important constraints on the crustal stress field. In stress inversion based on focal mechanism data, each mechanism contains two nodal planes, whereas the actual seismogenic fault plane is often difficult to identify. Consequently, Bootstrap resampling with random nodal plane selection is widely used to estimate uncertainties in stress inversion results. However, the reliability of these uncertainty bounds remains poorly understood. In this study, we evaluate the reliability of this approach using synthetic experiments and real fault-slip datasets. The results show that the reliability of Bootstrap-derived uncertainty bounds is jointly controlled by fault geometry and the true stress shape ratio (R). When seismogenic faults are distributed on both sides of the maximum compressive stress axis, the uncertainty bounds of principal stress orientations generally encompass the true solutions, whereas the uncertainty bounds of R may exhibit systematic biases depending on the true R value. By contrast, when faults occupy only one side of the fault space, the uncertainty bounds of both stress orientations and R may deviate from the true values. Further analysis indicates that this behavior reflects variations in the kinematic consistency between auxiliary-plane slip and the stress field under different R conditions, causing the influence of misselected nodal planes on inversion results to vary systematically. These findings highlight the importance of correctly identifying seismogenic fault planes and provide important implications for the interpretation of stress inversion uncertainties in practical applications.
5680002f59b3c24c: Summary Seismic coda-correlation methods have revealed numerous body-wave-like features in globally stacked correlograms, offering new opportunities to constrain the structure of Earth’s deep interior. Unlike the common assumptions about the diffuse ambient noise field that enable reconstruction of surface waves, earthquake coda-correlation features arise from cross-terms in reverberating body waves of common slowness that share a subset of propagation legs. However, quantitative interpretation of these features for tomographic imaging has been hindered by the lack of distributed sensitivity kernels relating observed correlation signals to Earth heterogeneities. Here, we develop a forward modeling framework for the earthquake coda-correlation wavefield that bypasses conventional cross-correlation of late-coda waveforms. Our approach simulates correlation features directly by treating the time-reversed generating wavefield as a distributed source throughout Earth’s interior. The forward-modeled correlograms reproduce features obtained through conventional stacking with a significantly improved signal-to-noise ratio. Building on this framework, we derive finite-frequency traveltime banana-doughnut sensitivity kernels using adjoint methods, which quantify how correlation time measurements of correlation features depend on perturbations in P-wave velocity, S-wave velocity, and density. We compute sensitivity kernels for prominent correlation features (P*, ScS*, K*, and others) at station separations ranging from 30° to 180°. The kernels reveal extensive sampling of Earth’s mantle, outer core, and inner core, with spatial-sensitivity patterns fundamentally different from those of classical body-wave tomography. For antipodal station pairs, correlation features exhibit strong sensitivity throughout the deep interior, including regions poorly sampled by traditional seismic phases. Our results confirm that correlation features form through constructive interference of body-wave pairs with similar slowness, rather than representing Green’s functions between station pairs. This work establishes the theoretical foundation for coda-correlation tomography, enabling future three-dimensional imaging of Earth’s internal structure with unprecedented sampling of the deep interior. The sensitivity kernels provide a pathway to exploit the wealth of information contained in earthquake coda for high-resolution mantle and core tomography.
de6cb91533d68188: There is a growing appetite for parametric Japanese earthquake insurance products that use Japanese Meteorological Agency seismic intensity, IJMA, triggers. However, most earthquake risk models used to price these contracts do not compute IJMA directly, instead relying on conversions that introduce additional basis risk. Here, we present empirical parameterisations of IJMA as a function of all combinations of moment magnitude, hypocentral distance, peak ground acceleration (PGA), and spectral acceleration (Sa(T)) at 0.2, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 2.0, and 3.0 s, derived from earthquake risk model outputs. Parameterisations are fitted using ridge regression applied to 21,354 ground motion recordings from 112 Japanese earthquakes spanning January 1997 to December 2025. When applied to a synthetic parametric insurance portfolio exposed to 25 years of Japanese seismicity, this parameterisation yields a measurable reduction in basis risk. These results support more reliable and transparent pricing of parametric earthquake insurance products.
6861b26f430179a9: Tunnel Boring Machines (TBMs), characterized by superior advancement rates and integrated operational sequences, have emerged as the predominant construction methodology for urban subsurface tunnel development. However, TBMs are less capable of coping with faults, isolated rocks, and other adverse geological conditions common to shallow urban subsurface. This has led to serious challenges in the safe construction and disaster prevention of urban subsurface tunnels. Due to the strong energy and large amplitude of surface waves, analyzing them provides an effective way to characterize the subsurface and ensure the safety of urban shallow tunnel construction. Inspired by the seismic-while-drilling method, surface-wave detection using tunnel-drilling noise has been widely applied due to its advantages of real-time detection and non-invasiveness. However, it is difficult to remove the body-wave interference signals brought about by factors such as the excitation mode of the seismic source, which in turn affects the subsequent extraction of the dispersion curves. Thus, we analyze the three main types of interference signals present in tunnel drilling noise-based surface-wave data, and a synthetic dataset incorporating realistic field interference signal characteristics is constructed. Then, we achieve the suppression of interference signals by constructing a special convolutional self-encoder that pays attention to the morphological features of the signal. Besides, a transfer learning method is proposed to suppress the inter-trace interference due to irregular acquisition and to make the method directly applicable to field data. The results of synthetic and field data processing show that the proposed method has good denoising capability and exhibits higher accuracy in subsequent dispersion-curve extraction.
62a104cdd1956593: High-resolution seismic data is crucial for accurately characterizing thin reservoirs and small-scale faults, providing the foundation for lithology and fluid identification. To address this problem, we develop a dual-attention transformer termed Seis-DAT. The core of Seis-DAT is a dual-attention transformer block that integrates window-based self-attention to capture local textures with channel attention to provide a global receptive field. This design enables the model to learn local details and global geological trends, ensuring both fidelity and structural consistency in the reconstructed results. To mitigate the scarcity of high-quality labeled data, we construct a large-scale synthetic dataset incorporating complex faults and folds. Furthermore, a composite loss function combining the ?1 loss and multiscale structural similarity loss is employed to dynamically balance pixel-level accuracy and structural integrity through a linear weight scheduling strategy. Synthetic tests demonstrate that the proposed method achieves higher peak signal-to-noise ratio and structural similarity index measure values than conventional comparative methods. Applications to real seismic data show that Seis-DAT generates clearer seismic events with enhanced lateral continuity, thereby improving seismic data resolution.
65ef5a8b16625ad8: The Laxmi Basin (LB), a marginal depression, is a prominent geomorphic feature in the northern Arabian Sea. Understanding how the basin formed has important implications for the India–Seychelles breakup and the evolution of the western Indian Ocean. In this study, we reexamine existing geodynamic models using new geochemical and Sr–Nd–Pb isotopic data obtained from the igneous basement recovered during the International Ocean Discovery Program Expedition 355. The new data from the basaltic crust show that it formed from mid‐oceanic ridge basalt‐like magmas derived primarily from the depleted asthenospheric mantle, with a minor contribution from the subcontinental lithospheric mantle (
4c4102a90e011a30: Giant Antarctic tabular icebergs travel northward until they disintegrate and melt.Tracking their movement and state is challenging because remote sensing is sporadic. Combining a close-by seismic station and evidence from the SWOT KaRIn SSHA and MODIS True Color imagery, we achieved daily reconstruction of the A-76a iceberg's late-stage evolution (March-July 2023). Seismic spectrograms revealed bursts, harmonic tremors, and a micro-tsunami signal, with locations validated by satellite images. Bursts were associated with iceberg fracturing, tremors with seafloor scraping and collisions, and a micro-tsunami with capsizing. This study demonstrates the value of integrating remote sensing and seismic data to monitor iceberg dynamics. It is the first to observe a micro-tsunami with SWOT that generates a seiche-like signal on the 37-km-distant II.HOPE station. This approach astutely combines the strengths of continuous seismic monitoring and large-area satellite imaging to monitor this massive tabular iceberg.
347094a7e17fc081: Landslides are common geological hazards worldwide, often associated with by heavy rainfall. Jixi City, located in southeastern Heilongjiang Province, experiences frequent rainstorms from July to September. Long‑term unregulated quarrying has destroyed vegetation and reduced slope toe stability in the area. In early August 2023, Typhoon Doksuri increased rainfall. The Jixi landslide occurred on August 10 following this heavy rainfall. This study integrates aeromagnetic data, electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), multi‑temporal satellite and UAV remote sensing, borehole data, and surface displacement monitoring. Aeromagnetic anomalies support a magnetically quiet basement without deep magmatic activity. ERT 2D and quasi‑3D inversions, calibrated by six boreholes, reveal a three‑part electrical structure: a shallow discontinuous high‑resistivity landslide deposit, a continuous low‑resistivity slip zone interpreted as mudstone with elevated moisture content and fault fracture zones, and a deeper blocky high‑resistivity slip bed. Steeply dipping low‑resistivity belts are interpreted as possible water‑bearing faults. Multi‑temporal images show progressive quarry expansion. Post‑landslide UAV orthophotos indicate that the main landslide body showed approximately 20 m of cumulative displacement toward the southwest between 2020 and 2023, with a fan‑shaped morphology exhibiting apparent retrogressive geomorphic characteristics. Surface monitoring from August 17 recorded horizontal displacements of 0.2–35.2 cm, with the dominant direction toward the southwest and elevation changes showing rear subsidence and frontal uplift. Boreholes support the transition from intact slip bed to fractured landslide mass. Based on these results, a possible evolutionary chain is proposed as an evidence‑supported interpretation: quarrying disturbance, typhoon‑induced rainfall infiltration, fault‑controlled water conduction, slip zone softening, and retrogressive sliding. The multi‑method approach provides cross‑scale constraints from regional background to shallow detailed structures, offering a scientific basis for post‑disaster identification, investigation, and mitigation of similar landslides.
c5a751456c371a4c: Landslide volumetric erosion is fundamental to regional sediment budgets and downstream hazard assessment, yet accurately constraining material mobilization remains a primary bottleneck in Earth-system research. Here, we examine whether the erosional and accumulation (i.e., runout) domains provide information beyond source area alone for volumetric erosion. Using neural-guided symbolic regression, we identify an expression that preserves source area as the first-order control on erosional volume while introducing a dimensionless descriptor of the accumulation counterpart, as a geometric correction. For the 2016 Kaikōura earthquake inventory, the framework estimates a cumulative eroded volume of 54.9 Mm3, compared with the measured 56.5 Mm3. The formulation was additionally applied without recalibration to the independent 2018 Hokkaidō inventory and subsequently used for blind inference on 32 landslides from the 2013 Lushan earthquake, yielding a cumulative estimate of 1.95 Mm3 of volumetric erosion. Because independent volume observations are unavailable for Lushan, this application is treated as inference rather than external validation. Polygon-generalization experiments further indicate that our new formulation remains stable across different mapping resolutions. These results show that scale-normalized planform geometry can provide complementary information to source area when constraining landslide erosion. The proposed framework is therefore intended as an empirical extension to, rather than a replacement for, established area–volume scaling.
bd5702700731a801: We believe that macroseismic scales are not static, but they should instead be updated based on new experimental observations."-Tosi et al. (2015) Macroseismology plays a crucial role in earthquake hazard and risk analyses, linking past earthquake occurrences and impacts with those of the present and future.The popularity of internet-based community contributions and the use of intensities for communicating seismic hazards, early warning, and impacts to the public have all bolstered the use of macroseismology beyond its traditional utility in characterizing sources and shaking from historical and modern earthquakes (Wald et al., 2023).Nevertheless, many modern approaches for collecting building damage data and assigning macroseismic intensities suffer limitations.Many countries do not or no longer routinely collect such data, and even after significant and catastrophic earthquakes, building damage data are often not collected or shared systematically, nor are field-based macroseismic intensities professionally assigned.Here, we describe how the International Macroseismic Scale of 2025 (IMS-25, Grünthal et al., 2026) could be used to replace other macroseismic intensity scales.For example, the United States, Canada, and other nations still use variations of the modified Mercalli intensity (MMI) scale (Wood and Neumann, 1931) for assigning macroseismic intensities.At nearly 100 yr old, the MMI scale predates most modern building types.It says nothing about single-or multiunit wood-frame buildings, the predominant type of residential structure in the United States and Canada, whose damage is a particularly important indicator of shaking intensity.Reliance on the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) "Did You Feel It?"
