4cc91bb4cd693882: First-arrival traveltimes underpin near-surface velocity modeling and static corrections, but in low signal-to-noise mountainous land data the first arrival is often weak, intermittent, and masked by strong direct waves and noise. Energy-based pickers then pick later arrivals or noise, and deep-learning pickers usually require retraining for a new survey. Because erroneous picks bias first-arrival tomography, many difficult zones are still inspected and corrected manually. We present FA-Agent, an agent framework for first-arrival picking built on a multimodal large language model. It combines a model that performs visual recognition and makes decisions, tools that process the data, and skills that carry experience of processing mountainous data. The framework is open and extensible: new pickers, denoising methods, and quality-control tools can be added, and new experience can be written into the skills. It is restricted neither to mountainous data nor to a particular model. Emulating a seismic data processor, the agent first surveys the whole gather to find zones needing attention, then examines them in enlarged views, and finally keeps, corrects, or removes the initial picks. On semi-synthetic gathers with known first arrivals and real mountainous noise, the agent picked the first arrival with high accuracy where it was clearly visible and removed the picks where it was invisible and could not be judged. Applied to randomly sampled gathers from a mountainous survey, it corrected picks onto weak first-arrival branches and removed picks where no first arrival could be confirmed, and it performed well on the most difficult data. Cases reviewed by experts are added to the skills automatically, so the agent improves with use, and a locally deployed model keeps confidential data on site. FA-Agent can thus become an essential component of future automated seismic data processing workflows.
c308f3fac3567048: Array‐based surface wave tomography has significantly enhanced the resolution of crustal imaging; however, rigorous quantification of posterior uncertainty in these regularized inversions remains a critical challenge. Conventional statistical methods, such as raw bootstrap resampling, often underestimate uncertainties in data‐sparse regions due to the dominance of regularization terms. This underestimation creates an artificial precision that risks misinterpreting inversion artifacts as robust structural features. To address this, we propose a hybrid uncertainty quantification strategy tailored for regional‐scale dense arrays, integrating data‐driven bootstrap resampling with model‐based resolution matrix correction. By utilizing the resolution matrix to explicitly debias the bootstrap variance, our approach provides a first‐order uncertainty metric for identifying and down‐weighting poorly constrained model estimates in the inversion's null‐space while retaining sensitivity to data inconsistencies in well‐resolved regions. We applied this workflow to ambient noise data from the ChinArray‐Himalaya project, extracting multimodal dispersion curves via the frequency‐Bessel (F‐J) transform. The derived hybrid uncertainty metric serves as a quantitative validity mask, successfully delineating reliable imaging regions for both fundamental and higher‐order modes, thereby facilitating objective, automated quality control for large‐scale data sets. Semi‐synthetic robustness tests further demonstrate that, unlike analytical or raw bootstrap methods, the hybrid strategy reliably distinguishes among data gaps (null‐spaces) and data conflicts. Ultimately, incorporating this resolution‐corrected uncertainty to weight subsequent 1D shear wave velocity inversions significantly suppresses regularization artifacts, laying a robust statistical foundation for constructing physically reliable 3D structural models.
686f2893cadd771b: Constraining magma storage and transport through the entire crust at a variety of arc volcanoes is essential to understand how subduction parameters may influence these processes. However, constraints throughout the crust are often limited to volcanoes that either fortuitously have properties that illuminate the entire crustal system, or volcanoes where high‐resolution geophysical imaging has been performed. Seismic receiver functions (RFs) offer sensitivity to the whole crust independent of local seismicity distribution using a few instruments. However, near volcanoes, they are often complex, requiring detailed analysis and potentially non‐unique velocity model solutions. Here, we introduce a novel, data‐driven method to identify and map RF variability using spectral clustering and kernel logistic regression. We apply it to 16 volcanoes in the Aleutian arc, enabling systematic comparisons of RF patterns without need for detailed velocity modeling. We observe that a subset of these volcanoes has RF variability that is spatially well‐separated in the crust, while others appear to have minimal spatial organization. Based on comparisons with previous results, we find that the former tends to occur at volcanoes with relatively simple magma storage systems, and the latter at volcanoes with complex, multi‐layer storage. This suggests that our technique reveals first‐order variability in crustal magmatic architecture. Furthermore, the ability to recover spatially coherent RF patterns shows no clear correlation with along‐arc subduction parameters but instead appears associated with edifice morphology. This work establishes a systematic framework for comparing arc volcanic structure and a foundation for future RF velocity modeling, extendable to other heterogeneous settings.
2158f4cdc279a805: Cerro Machín Volcano (CMV) ranks third among the 21 preliminary geothermal areas identified in Colombia, with an estimated electrical power of 129.94 MWe (Alfaro et al., 2021), yet its shallow structure had not been resolved at high resolution. We conducted terrestrial gravity and magnetic surveys within and around the volcanic edifice: 137 gravity stations and 38,789 magnetic records in walk mode. Gravimetric reductions used a Nettleton-derived reference density of 2.65 g/cm 3 , magnetic processing included diurnal correction, IGRF subtraction, and reduction to the pole. Residual anomalies were isolated through upward continuation to 500 m, and two joint 2D geological–geophysical models were built along NW–SE (~5.1 km) and SW–NE (~5.2 km) profiles with GMSys-2D. The dome is 720–840 m thick, its base resting directly on the Cajamarca Metamorphic Complex, shallower than previous seismic estimates of up to 2 km. Lateral variations in density (2.4–2.55 g/cm 3 ) and susceptibility (0.002–0.12 SI) record weathering and hydrothermal alteration restricted to discrete fault zones, so that no continuous clay cap is developed. Beneath the dome, a fractured metamorphic conduit (ρ = 2.6 g/cm 3 , k = 0.008 SI) is interpreted as the upflow reservoir (~0.6 km 2 , at least 800 m thick, truncated at the base of the models), while an outflow zone of about 2 km 2 extends at least 2 km toward the Santa Marta ravine. The dome base, resolved between 1920 and 1850 m a.s.l., coincides with the reservoir top independently imaged by the seismic and magnetotelluric models of Herrera and Calò (2025), to within less than the vertical resolution of either dataset. Two methods with unrelated physical sensitivities therefore converge on the same boundary, which we interpret as the top of the upflow zone, sealed above by the unaltered dome core.
54b85efafc9d6a66: A depletion of earthquake slip in the shallow crust (shallow coseismic slip deficit, or coseismic SSD) has been observed on <30, Mw ≥ 6 continental earthquakes, and attributed to the immaturity of the ruptured faults. We question the factors that contribute to the coseismic SSD. We built the largest earthquake source model database available to date, with 1078 models providing coseismic SSD estimates on 163 Mw ≥ 6, various slip mode, continental earthquakes worldwide since 1990. We also built a database providing their fault maturity parameters (initiation age, net displacement, length, slip rate). Our combined earthquake‐fault analysis reveals that coseismic SSD of continental earthquakes, whatever their slip mode, is primarily controlled by the relation between their magnitude and peak slip depth, and, to a much lesser extent, by the fault maturity. A model where earthquake slip produces zero stress drop on the shallow velocity strengthening fault section reproduces the data well.
d3e8b2005827856c: Although active‐source seismic methods can image the oceanic Mohorovičić discontinuity (Moho) at high resolution, their high cost motivates passive approaches using OBS, for which receiver functions (RF) are often complicated by instrument tilt, azimuthal misalignment, sedimentary layers, and water‐column reverberations. Here we apply teleseismic P‐wave coda autocorrelation to hydrophone data from OBS to image the oceanic Moho. Compared with vertical‐component data, hydrophone data provide a simpler interpretation because they avoid P‐to‐S conversions and are dominated by reflected and transmitted P‐wave energy. By analyzing autocorrelation results from 22 long‐period and 24 short‐period stations in the NoMelt experiment, we identify a Moho reflection with a TwTT of ∼2.56 s and resolve lateral variations in crustal TwTT that are smoothed out in the radially averaged representations of global velocity models. Combined with previous studies and model tests, this longer‐than‐expected crustal TwTT suggests that a crust‐mantle transition zone may exist beneath the NoMelt region.
5f02a76848e13b1d: Code for Lindsay and Bürgmann, Periodic slow slip events on the Hayward Fault (in preparation). This release is the state of the code for the paper's run. The executed notebooks (01–15) hold every output, and every number in the paper is registered with the notebook and section that computes it. Data and results: Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23850500. It contains the rebased OPERA DISP-S1 stacks, the external inputs, the PyLith model files, the sensitivity tables, and all products and figures. Forecast: notebook 13 issues the forecast of the next Tule Pond slow slip event (forecast_statement.txt). It was issued and archived on 4 November 2026 and is conditioned on no event through 24 October 2026. To reproduce: see README.md for the environment (environment.yml), setting the data root (TULEPOND_DATA_DIR), and running ./run_all.sh. Licence: MIT (code). The data in the Zenodo record are CC BY 4.0.
55311328b950346d: How and when the subduction megathrust recovers its locking state after a great earthquake is important to understanding earthquake-cycle physics and future hazards. Here we report the delineation of the relocking process after the 2011 magnitude 9 Tohoku earthquake with 14 years of postseismic seafloor geodetic observations. These data, combined with onshore geodetic observations, analyses of repeating earthquakes, and numerical modeling, reveal how the recovery of locking is interrupted by afterslip on the megathrust and accompanied by stress relaxation in the viscoelastic upper mantle. The results indicate that the megathrust has already arrived at a locking state today similar to that before the earthquake despite the ongoing stress relaxation. The acquired knowledge aids understanding of megathrust earthquake cycles at other subduction zones.
245b3bb1cb548906: Long-term monitoring reveals how a fault relocks for a future earthquake after a massive rupture
dfdef13f1288b509: Acoustic logging while drilling (LWD) provides formation shear-wave velocity in real time during drilling, supporting geosteering and geomechanical evaluation. Shear-wave velocity is currently extracted by slowness–time coherence (STC) processing, which relies on a grid search for the global extremum; its hard decision is prone to dense outlier spikes in multi-event wavefields, and its computational burden is unfavorable for downhole real-time evaluation. We propose a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) that regresses the inter-receiver moveout directly from array waveforms; five-fold cross-validation on a synthetic dataset yields a median relative velocity error of 2.51% ± 0.16%. The numeric and image-inversion domains, with either a threshold mask or an Attention U-Net segmentation mask, give consistent velocities, with differences between mask methods of ≤0.6%, and 2.5–4.5 kHz band-pass filtering brings the two domains into convergence. As a control, supervised regression labeled by a measured STC log attains per-gather r = 0.72 over the full well interval under random splitting, but r drops to 0.20 under depth-blocked cross-validation that removes near-neighbor leakage, delimiting the applicability boundary of this proxy route. Inference is a single deterministic forward pass, the model occupies only 266 KB, and it runs approximately 25× faster than vectorized STC, making it suitable for edge deployment.
6c3cb9808edfad11: Overview. Data products and model files for Lindsay and Bürgmann, Periodic slow slip events on the Hayward Fault. The code is archived separately (below). The deposit holds the three rebased OPERA DISP-S1 Sentinel-1 displacement stacks over the Hayward Fault (2016 to 2026), the inputs the analysis reads, the PyLith slip-model files, and every product and figure of the analysis. Other published datasets the notebooks read are cited. gnss_velocity.zip: GNSS station tables, the GNSS-InSAR tie, the tied velocity mosaics. aperture_sweep.zip: the cross-fault aperture sweep. models_inputs.zip, models_3d_sfsvm.zip.part*, models_homogeneous.zip: PyLith meshes, spatial databases and output points; for each run used, the points, fault and elastic_info outputs, parameters and G matrix; homogeneous (CSI) Green's functions. sensitivity.zip: sensitivity tables and L-curves. outputs.zip, figures.zip: all notebook products and the number registry, all figures (paper figures under paper/). The executed notebooks, with all their outputs, are in the code release. extension_check_2026-10-30.zip: the bridging check behind the forecast: Sentinel-1 from December 2025 to 30 October 2026 processed from OPERA CSLC-S1 with Dolphin 0.42.5 and the DISP-S1 settings (scripts, environment, configurations, Dolphin time series, the step check and its result). OPERA DISP-S1 (doi:10.5067/SNWG/OPL3DISPS1-V1) and TROPO-ZENITH (doi:10.5067/SNWG/OPL4TROZEN-V1) products are public from NASA ASF DAAC. The USGS San Francisco Bay region 3D seismic velocity model v26.0 is doi:10.5066/P13AEJFI. Processing uses opera-utils 0.25.4, MintPy 1.6.3, PyLith 5.0.2 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.21909051) and CSI (doi:10.5281/zenodo.14170821). Code: github.com/Dani-Lindsay/TulePond_DISP, archived at release v1.0.0 (the paper's run), doi:10.5281/zenodo.23934127. Acknowledgements. We thank the data providers: NASA JPL OPERA, ASF DAAC, USGS, NOAA NCEI and the Nevada Geodetic Laboratory. The forecast in this deposit was issued and archived on 4 November 2026, conditioned on data through 24 October 2026.
3c58580e65e3c465: Slip instabilities leading to earthquakes, landslides, and glacier surges may be triggered by high fluid pressures at the slipping interface. High fluid pressures may, however, also suppress instability because of large nucleation length-scales in overpressured systems. We review geological, glaciological, and rock mechanical observations and highlight two key scales that control fluid pressure-enabled frictional instabilities: (1) the length scale over which fluid overpressure is maintained, and (2) a time scale defined by relative rates of deformation propagation and fluid transport. These scales are also dependent on rheological regime, and we suggest three end-member regimes: (1) brittle-localising (BL) regimes where deformation and fluid flow localise to discrete interconnected structures; (2) brittle-delocalising (BD) regimes where deformation and fluid flow are distributed over a broad region, and instability typically stabilised by fluid diffusion; and (3) transiently brittle (TB) regimes where in dominantly viscous rock or ice, fluid pressure may induce a transient frictional rheology that is typically delocalised and stabilised by dilatant hardening. In the BL regime, fluid overpressure can be sustained over a sufficient length scale to enable the nucleation and propagation of frictional instabilities. In the BD and TB regimes, however, fluid-driven instabilities tend to be suppressed, confined to local areas of overpressure, or rate-limited by fluid diffusion, because deformation delocalises in the bulk and/or dilatant hardening limits slip propagation. The three regimes can also be applied to glaciers, where viscous flow of ice competes with frictional sliding on the glacier base—here, sustained and interconnected high water pressure at the glacier base is commonly invoked as promoting frictional instability. In both rock and ice, these concepts imply that fluid-driven frictional instabilities are limited to areas where fluid overpressured patches can be interconnected, and therefore highlight the key role of fluid pressure heterogeneity in development of slip instabilities.
2d35d0edcee3cc6f: The thermodynamic acceleration induced by atmospheric thermal tides has a major impact on the rotation of temperate rocky planets, where gravitational and radiative tidal forcings are of comparable strength. This acceleration drives planets away from synchronous rotation, thereby affecting their climate, large-scale circulation, and surface conditions. These implications underline the need to better constrain the dependence of the thermotidal torque on the tidal frequency and on the physical parameters characterising the star-planet system, as this relationship remains insufficiently understood. In particular, the role of resonantly excited Lamb waves requires clarification due to its potential impact on Earth's length of day (LOD) during the Precambrian. Building on a previous work, which provided a fully analytical formulation of the atmospheric tidal response of rocky planets, we apply this framework to isentropic and isothermal atmospheres. We perform a comprehensive functional analysis of the resulting torque and compare the analytical predictions with numerical solutions from earlier general circulation model (GCM) studies. The analytical model agrees well with GCM results, accurately capturing the frequency dependence of tidal torque both for paleo-Earth and present-day Earth. More generally, the solutions capture the torque peak near synchronous rotation and the amplification associated with Lamb-wave resonance. Near resonance, the GCM results exhibit a stronger braking torque than accelerating torque. This asymmetry is reproduced by allowing tidal heating to lag behind insolation. The agreement with GCM spectra suggests that thermal tides in the benchmark simulations are driven predominantly by an indirect thermal forcing characterised by a substantial time delay, in contrast to the direct absorption of sunlight that dominates semidiurnal tides on present-day Earth.
7d202fe14d345e49: Seismic noise, particularly the microseism generated by the oceans, is a fundamental limitation on using short period (1–10 s) teleseismic data to study the deep Earth. Deep learning auto‐encoders have proven effective at denoising seismic data in other applications. Here, we provide a demonstration of their potential for improving the quality of deep Earth seismic data, using S diff post‐cursors generated by ultra‐low velocity zones (ULVZs) as a case study. We present a computationally efficient and accessible workflow, utilizing a supervised learning process with 1D synthetics and real, global seismic noise. This workflow does not require real teleseismic signals, which are limited in number and quality, and is computationally efficient, not requiring expensive 3D spectral‐element simulations. We present a series of example applications, finding the denoiser to be effective at removing noise and extracting S diff signal despite having not been trained with real teleseismic signals. Furthermore, we provide recommendations on how performance could be improved, including demonstrating transfer learning as an efficient and effective way to improve extraction of specific signals. Lastly we apply denoising to seismic data sampling known ULVZs, identifying previously unreported short‐period signals from several different ULVZs and obtaining observations of the Hawaiian ULVZ along a novel source‐receiver geometry from the East Pacific Rise to Japan, which is perpendicular to previous ray paths. These observations reveal previously undocumented frequency‐ and azimuth‐dependent S diff waveforms associated with ULVZs, demonstrating that denoising can expand observational constraints on deep Earth structure.
6e0ad2b1f6258711: Physics‐based models of the earthquake cycle could be used for time‐dependent hazard assessment. For such an application, their parameters must be calibrated so that simulated earthquake sequences reproduce the statistics of past earthquakes, including recurrence statistics and magnitudes. This is challenging because the dynamics are described by nonlinear partial differential equations, initial conditions are unknown, and records of past earthquakes are sparse, incomplete, and noisy. To address this challenge, we present a Bayesian inverse‐problem framework to infer heterogeneous parameters in an earthquake‐cycle model from observations of past large earthquakes. Rather than matching a time‐series of individual events, we exploit ergodicity (long‐term statistics independent of initial conditions) and invert for stationary, spatially distributed summary statistics of event timing and slip, including mean interevent times, coefficients of variation, burstiness, and average coseismic slip, which are quantities that can in principle be estimated from paleoseismic and historical records. Observational noise and event‐detection thresholds are explicitly accounted for in the construction of these statistics. The inverse problem is solved using a derivative‐free ensemble Kalman inversion method, and uncertainty quantification is enhanced by an emulate–sample strategy that leverages machine‐learning for surrogate modeling, in which a Gaussian‐process surrogate of the parameter‐to‐statistics map enables efficient MCMC sampling without further expensive forward simulations. Synthetic experiments with realistic data noise suggest that the model parameters can be inverted from statistical quantities observable from paleoseismology at a limited number of observation points. The framework provides a principled and computationally tractable method to calibrate earthquake‐cycle models, providing a foundation for forecasting.
36e6299dacb7abcd: Safe CO 2 storage requires injection designs that manage both when faults yield and how yielding spreads, yet temporal schedules and well layouts are often evaluated separately. We developed a two-dimensional quasi-static hydromechanical model of immiscible CO 2 –brine flow around an offset normal fault and compared constant and variable-rate histories, well-placement configurations, and well–fault distances over 30 d. Coulomb failure function (CFF) threshold attainment with frictional weakening defined modeled onset; failure-area ratio and maximum shear plastic strain served as within-mesh comparative indicators of domain-scale localization. The simulations reveal a hierarchy of controls: injection rate primarily governs pressure buildup and onset timing; rate history reorganizes transient stress paths and localization; and well placement and distance redistribute pressure and yielding across the fault. Higher rates increased the within-mesh failure-area ratio, whereas variable histories produced distinct responses that cannot be attributed to cycling alone because peak rate and shut-in transitions were confounded. Local threshold indicators and domain-scale metrics were complementary rather than interchangeable: temporal onset, spatial extent and deformation intensity were distinct response dimensions. These findings motivate joint optimization of injection schedules and well layouts against both temporal onset and spatial localization, while providing model-scale guidance for early quasi-static risk screening rather than predictions of seismicity, dynamic rupture or long-term stability.
16bb2a18b16c2ade: This study comprehensively and in detail analyzed the spatial and temporal distributions of earthquakes, tidal responses, focal mechanisms, rupture directions, coseismic stress transfer, and stress field characteristics associated with the Mw 6.0 Yangbi earthquake that occurred in May 2021. This earthquake constitutes a typical foreshock–mainshock–aftershock sequence, monitored by permanent and dense temporary seismic networks. Detailed and precise hypocenter determinations revealed complex and previously unknown seismogenic fault structures located several kilometers away from the well-documented active faults in the region. The foreshocks were found to be closely associated with both the main fault and the conjugate faults surrounding a fault stepover. Notably, the onset timing of three foreshock episodes and the occurrence time of the mainshock were clearly coincident with the peak of dilational volumetric tidal strain, indicating a potential tidal triggering effect. By synthesizing findings from other research teams, this study proposes that the Yangbi earthquake foreshock swarms were the result of the combined effects of deep overpressured fluids, transitional slow-slip events, and cascade triggering. Among these factors, deep fluids are inferred to have served as the initial driver and the most critical controlling factor. Similar to the Haicheng earthquake, for which a successful short-term and imminent prediction was issued, the Yangbi earthquake likewise demonstrates that tectonic complexity (primarily stepovers in this case) and the action of deep overpressured fluids facilitate the occurrence of short-term and imminent foreshocks, thereby potentially enhancing earthquake predictability.
ca45845baee1af1b: Debris flows are a seasonal hazard in Tahoma Creek in Mount Rainier National Park, Washington, United States. We present seismic recordings spaced every 100–200 m along the path of a debris flow triggered by a glacial outburst on 15 August 2023. These recordings capture changes as the debris flow deposits ∼24,000 cubic meters of material along an ∼800 m stretch of channel, approximately 2.5 km from the glacial source. As the flow deposits material, the seismic signal onset shape associated with the debris flow snout recedes, resulting in an elongation of the delay between the signal onset and the peak amplitude from 100 to 300 s. In parallel, the peak frequency increases by more than 20 Hz, and energy below 20 Hz fades, indicating deposition of larger particles and changes in sediment concentration within the flow. We interpret these changes to correspond to the transition from debris flow to hyperconcentrated flow, a distinction based on sediment concentration by volume and on rheological criteria such as yield strength. We find that the frequency content of the seismic signal depends on grain size and sediment concentrations within the flow, among other factors, complicating the starting assumptions of many physical models of debris flows.
a57ed6a41f1ba9ad: Identification of potential source regions, pinpointing where large earthquakes are most likely to occur, is fundamental to seismic risk assessment. Previous results often suffer from significant uncertainties due to the limitations of individual observations. To address this issue, here we apply the self-organizing map method to the Nankai trough, which has been considered to have high-seismic potential. By integrating multisource observations (b value, slip-deficit rate [SDR], and cumulative slip deficit [CSD]), we cluster regions of low b value, high SDR, and large CSD to delineate potential source regions. We identify four potential earthquake sources along the Nankai trough. Among them, the Tokai segment shows the highest potential for generating earthquakes in the near future. Using pre-2011 observations, the identified source regions agree well with the rupture zone of the 2011 Mw 9.0 Tohoku-Oki earthquake, validating the reliability of this approach.
d7fb61d0d6c7025e: Earthquake‐triggered decreases in relative seismic velocity ( dv / v ) of the crust have been reported for many events, but regional variations in dv / v susceptibility to shaking are not well understood. Here, 14 Alaskan earthquakes with Mw 6.8–8.2 are consistently analyzed with single‐station coda‐wave interferometry. For peak ground velocities (PGV) >1 cm/s, significant dv/v drops are found for ∼40% of seismometers, with a moderate linear correlation coefficient of −0.3 between dv / v and PGV. Sites in the highest susceptibility decile, indicated by the largest dv / v drops per unit PGV, are all located near active volcanoes: Akutan, Makushin, Shishaldin, Pavlof, Katmai, and Augustine. Some Cook Inlet basin sites are among the largest decile of dv / v drops but have lower susceptibility due to amplified PGV. Frequency‐dependence of dv / v indicates concentration of velocity changes at <500 m depth, consistent with hydrothermal systems and weakly consolidated volcanic rocks influencing heterogeneous and high susceptibility near volcanoes.
444d06f41f8ae79f: North–south‐trending rifts in southern Tibet accommodate active east–west extension, but how normal‐faulting rupture varies with rift development remains unclear. Here we use Synthetic Aperture Radar observations to investigate the 2025 Mw 7.0 Dingri earthquake in the southern Xainza–Dinggye rift. Our rupture model shows that the 2025 earthquake ruptured multiple segments and likely triggered three meter‐scale slope failures within surface‐rupture gaps at the rift margin. Together with preceding Dingri events, our results reveal contrasting along‐rift coseismic rupture behavior: larger, shallower, and more complex slip in the higher‐elevation, narrower northern Dengmo Co rift, but smaller, deeper slip in the lower, wider southern half‐graben. Combined with other geodetically constrained normal‐faulting sequences across southern Tibet, these observations show an apparent northward ordering along certain rift segments. Our study provides new insight into the relationship between long‐term rift development and earthquake rupture behavior in the southern Tibetan rift system.
bcfbda695f1717e4: Multiphase hydro-mechanical modeling was used to assess the pilot CO2 test injection at Trüllikon, northern Switzerland (project CITru), a pioneering project which aims to inject 10,000 tonnes into the Muschelkalk aquifer at ∼ 1100 m depth over two years. A site-specific geological model (4 × 4 × 2.3 km3) was constructed around the Trüllikon well (TRU1-1) using local and regional 3D seismic data and implemented in one-way coupled TOUGH3-FLAC3D simulations for three different reservoir permeability scenarios. In all scenarios, the supercritical CO2 plume migrates up-dip and predominantly northward along the inclined reservoir-caprock interface, where it becomes trapped in a small anticline before dissolving into the pore water in the longer term (thousands of years). The CO2 approaches the nearby Neuhausen Fault but never reaches it. For the lowest permeability scenario (most probable case), maximum pressure changes of 0.7 MPa and 0.25 MPa are simulated at the Neuhausen and Trüllikon faults, respectively, which is below estimated fault reactivation thresholds. Coulomb failure stress changes incorporating mechanically-induced elastic stresses remain below 0.05 MPa on both faults, indicating that injection-induced compression stabilizes them. Moreover, displacements and strains simulated in the overlying sealing formations are minimal (∼ 1 mm). In a hypothetical industrial-scale scenario (250,000 tonnes)—unlike CITru—the CO2 plume crosses the nearest branch of the Neuhausen Fault during the injection period and reaches the Trüllikon Fault within decades. Our results will directly support future planning and risk assessment within the CITru project and are likely to be useful for future onshore pilot, demonstration, and industrial-scale CO2 storage projects.
a9c75528e4f702c3: We invert horizontal S-wave Fourier acceleration spectra between 0.5 and 25 Hz from 7,637 earthquakes in the 2010 Mw 8.8 Maule aftershock sequence to estimate source, path, and site terms in south-central Chile using a nonparametric generalized inversion technique. The dataset contains 95,515 event-station records from 117 stations during the first 10 months after the mainshock. To account for propagation heterogeneity, we divide crustal and slab-related earthquakes separately into spatially coherent clusters and invert each one independently. We use 100 randomized clustering iterations to evaluate the variance of the recovered terms. Relative site responses remain stable across these iterations, with site amplification above a factor of 10 at 2–4 Hz at some stations. Effective attenuation varies markedly across the rupture area, with Q0 values of 36–159 and frequency exponents of 0.35–1.4. Crustal clusters generally have lower Q0 and stronger frequency dependence than slab-related ones. We fit the recovered source spectra with an ω² model and obtain well-resolved source parameters for 6,279 events. Stress-drop distributions overlap between crustal and slab-related earthquakes, with median values of 2.93 and 2.76 MPa, respectively. For Mw ≥ 3, corner frequency scales approximately as M0^(−1/3), broadly consistent with self-similarity. Stress drops are systematically higher in a slab-related seismicity band between 42.5 and 52.5 km depth, with a median of 6.3 MPa. These results show that accounting for spatially variable propagation is important for interpreting source variability. The empirical model provides a basis for regional ground-motion characterization and for tracking postseismic fault evolution across the Maule rupture zone.
e142291ed11fad5f: Arctic landfast sea ice is subject to mechanical forcing from winds, waves, currents, and interactions with drifting ice. However, the resulting wavefields and their effects on the mechanical properties of the ice remain difficult to characterize using existing in situ and remote-sensing observations due to limited spatial and temporal coverage. Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) of fiber optic cable offers dense spatial sampling and continuous temporal coverage that can complement these approaches. We present the first DAS observations on Arctic landfast sea ice, using a 2-km-long armored fiber-optic cable installed at the snow-ice interface on ice near Utqiaġvik, Alaska for two weeks in spring 2025. The DAS recorded various signal types, including controlled hammer-generated signals and ambient flexural-gravity (FG) waves. We apply Bayesian dispersion-based inversions of the observed guided-wave modes to estimate ice properties. Hammer-generated waves yield estimates of Young's modulus and ice thickness of 5.4 GPa and 0.98 m, respectively; the inferred thickness agrees with independent field measurements. Directional beamforming of the L-shaped cable segment indicates a dominant FG-wave arrival direction from offshore with an effective Young's modulus of 0.6 GPa and compressive stress of 0.6 MPa. The lower effective modulus is consistent with previous reports of reduced effective moduli inferred from FG waves. The compressive stress shows a positive correlation with squared wind speed (r=0.37), indicating sensitivity to wind-related changes in the ambient wavefield. These results demonstrate that DAS can complement existing observations of sea-ice wavefields and mechanics, while highlighting the need to characterize its coupling and directional response.
3c05ac1be23c31dd: Summary Classical full waveform inversion (FWI) is sensitive to kinematic inaccuracies in the initial velocity model, converging to local minima due to cycle skipping when low-frequency data are absent. The recently developed deep-learning-matching FWI (DLM-FWI) framework mitigates this by dynamically bridging the phase gap between synthetic and observed data, utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN) within the inversion loop as a robust kinematic preconditioner. However, because standard deep learning (DL) automatic differentiation (AD) engines scale poorly to large-scale wave equations, deploying DLM-FWI on practical field-scale data has been computationally prohibitive. To overcome this, we introduce a memory-efficient, hybrid computational workflow that interfaces the Flux machine-learning ecosystem with the Julia Devito Inversion framework (JUDI) finite-difference library. By decoupling the network’s AD graph from the physical solver and evaluating the chain rule strictly in the data domain, we avoid storing massive spatiotemporal wavefield histories. After verifying that this decoupled architecture maintains resilience to source-wavelet mismatch and ambient noise on the Marmousi2 synthetic model, we apply the workflow to the Mobil AVO Viking Graben Line 12 marine dataset to evaluate its practical scalability. Compared to classical L-BFGS FWI, the field-scale DLM-FWI results exhibit robust convergence, mitigation of shallow cycle-skipped artifacts, and geologically coherent structural continuity. This study addresses the gap between small-scale synthetic DL studies and field-scale 2D implementations, demonstrating that physics-guided matching strategies can be deployed in practice to improve FWI robustness on complex field datasets.
b281064f1a3ce545: Investigating the geologic record of near‐trench coseismic strain release is critical for estimating the slip distribution and tsunamigenic potential of future large subduction zone earthquakes. However, the style and extent of upper plate coseismic deformation offshore in subduction zones is poorly constrained. To address this knowledge gap, we integrate shipborne multichannel seismic and multibeam data with targeted autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) bathymetry and chirp data to resolve the updip limit and mode of coseismic slip along the frontal thrust fault zone in central and southern Cascadia. Detailed fault mapping and characterization reveals four distinct styles of Holocene deformation along the frontal thrust fault zone, including fault propagation folding, imbricate thrusting, breakthrough thrusting, and frontal erosion through widespread mass wasting. Joint interpretation with crustal‐scale seismic data shows that these variations in near‐surface deformation style are clearly linked to changes in megathrust geometry and accretionary mode at depth. Additionally, AUV data provide abundant on‐fault geologic evidence for discrete and episodic near‐surface deformation, including primary fault and fold scarps, bending moment fault scarps, punctuated growth strata, and discrete single event fault offset, that we consider to be predominantly coseismic. The widespread distribution of Holocene active, likely coseismic, frontal thrust deformation presented in this study highlights the potential for variable mode coseismic slip to the trench in Cascadia. These results provide an unprecedented view into the shallow megathrust structure and heterogeneity in Cascadia that is critical for estimating earthquake and tsunami hazard impacts locally and for understanding shallow megathrust slip behavior globally.
4fdd853d6b3e093f: In subduction zones, shallow crustal faults accommodate part of the tectonic deformation and modulate the distribution of marine sediments. The interplay between active faults and sedimentary basins influences seismic hazards and submarine landslides, making imaging these structures essential to constrain their geometry, physical properties, and contributions to regional geodynamic processes. Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) offers an opportunity to passively image offshore sediments at high spatial resolution by converting submarine telecom cables into dense seismic arrays. DAS enables ambient seismic noise tomography with a hundred‐meter resolution, revealing detailed velocity structures with strong impedance contrasts and localizing diffracting structures, such as faults and basin edges. In this study, we combine different imaging techniques that rely on both ambient noise and earthquake records from over 2 years of continuous DAS data to investigate marine sediment structures offshore central Chile. We first analyze the scattered wavefields in earthquake recordings to locate structures of strong impedance contrast along the cable at sub‐kilometer scales. We then apply autocorrelation and cross‐correlation of ambient noise to associate those features with faults and basin edges that both produce scattering patterns. Finally, we analyze high‐resolution power spectral density to investigate the relationship between high‐frequency resonances, shallow sedimentary deposits, local attenuation, and basin‐edge effects, and we validate our interpretations using numerical simulations. Together, these methods reveal sedimentary accumulations within basins and fault‐related structures, consistent with regional geological constraints, demonstrating the ability of DAS to resolve fine‐scale structures and its potential for studying offshore faults, sediment dynamics, and site effects.
f9ffa48cc6c0b442: Aftershock sequences record how fault zones recover and weaken after earthquakes, but the roles of fluid migration and stress heterogeneity remain difficult to isolate. Earth tides impose predictable stress perturbations and thus provide a natural probe of faults near failure, although their signals are often obscured by aftershock clustering. Here we apply bootstrap‐based spatial spectral analysis to the 2022 M6.8 Luding earthquake sequence to resolve tidal sensitivity. We identify a systematic shift from a fluid‐rich region before the mainshock to the margins of the high‐slip zone, bypassing the rupture core. This pattern suggests coupled interaction between coseismic stress heterogeneity and postseismic fluid redistribution. Elevated pore pressure enhances sensitivity to weak tidal stress in high stress‐gradient regions, whereas permeability contrasts promote localized fluid accumulation and triggering. Our results show that tidal forcing can reveal where postseismic faults are closest to failure, offering an indirect window into fluid migration and fault‐zone weakening.
f75a125359426193: Transformational faulting in olivine has been widely invoked as a possible triggering mechanism for deep‐focus earthquakes, yet its dynamics remain debated. It is unclear whether it requires the combined effects of heat release, volume change and mechanical strength contrast, or whether it can be triggered by any one of these alone. Here, we tested if transformational faulting can be caused solely by a large volume change, through deformation experiments on novaculite during the quartz‐coesite transition. Under sluggish reaction kinetics, acoustic emissions and microstructural observations indicate strain localization and fault plane formation. Under fast kinetics, deformation was distributed and associated with fewer, lower‐magnitude events. b ‐values of ∼1 and ∼3 reflect these two regimes. Our results provide the first evidence of transformational faulting during the quartz‐coesite transition, suggesting that volume change is the primary driver of brittle failure at high pressure, broadening the range of mineral transitions generating deep and intermediate‐depth earthquakes.
15a8b66ef4538427: Southern Italy preserves a well-studied record of deformation and uplift related to migrating oblique collision, trench retreat, and tearing of subducted ocean slabs. However, the surface expression of these processes is incompletely understood due to a lack of reliable ages for marine terraces >200 m above sea level (masl). Here we use luminescence methods to date shallow marine sands from terraces ~ 100 to 1,000 masl in southern Calabria and interpolate the results with regional surface mapping. Burial ages overlap across the full range of sampled elevations with a weighted mean of 118.8 ± 8.7 thousand years before present (ka). These ages, combined with map data and fault-zone morphology, indicate that the terraces are erosional remnants of a single, once-continuous deformed surface. Calculated uplift rates vary from 12 mm yr-1 and throw rates on active normal faults are 0.8–4.2 mm yr-1. We infer that rapid post-120 ka uplift is an ongoing isostatic response to an active tear in the Ionian slab, consistent with recent geophysical observations and predictions of geodynamic models. These results have important implications for assessment of geohazards in southern Calabria and northeast Sicily, one of the highest seismic risk areas in the Mediterranean region.
94c5a0a2bfad62bd: In multichannel analysis of surface waves (MASW), the suitability of an active source is evaluated by its ability to generate coherent and continuous surface-wave dispersion over a usable frequency and wavelength range, as these characteristics influence the reliability of mode identification and the attainable depth of investigation. We present a hierarchical paired comparison of hammer and gun acquisition protocols using 13 matched source positions and identical 12-receiver geometry (5m spacing, 55m aperture and 30m nearest offset). All 26 SEG-2 gathers were processed individually using the same phase-shift imaging and automated ridge-extraction criteria, followed by independent manual fundamental-mode picking to verify the automatic interpretation before acceptance and inversion. The verified individual gathers were then combined through normalized common-offset trace stacking and normalized dispersion-image stacking for each source. Every gather yielded an accepted fundamental-mode path. At the individual-gather level, mean maximum usable wavelength was 30.14m for the hammer and 29.45m for the gun (gun minus hammer = −0.69m; 95% paired bootstrap interval −3.81 to 1.50m). The hammer contained a greater proportional 4.5–10Hz spectral fraction (0.967% versus 0.672%), but this exploratory contrast did not remain significant after Holm correction [14]. Source-composite curves spanned 21.0–46.0Hz for the hammer and 20.5–43.5Hz for the gun, with maximum wavelengths of 32.14 and 33.41m, respectively. The stacked gun-minus-hammer wavelength difference was 1.27m (paired spatial-bootstrap 95% interval −1.39 to 2.50m), equivalent to upper screening depths of 16.07 and 16.71m under a 0.5 wavelength convention. Fixed-layer conditional inversions produced overlapping shear-wave velocity intervals in all four model layers; gun-minus-hammer differences ranged from −17.6 to +14.1m/s and all 95% intervals included zero. Agreement between independently extracted trace-stack and image-stack curves was 7.16m/s for the hammer and 4.15m/s for the gun. These results show that source ranking is endpoint- and threshold-dependent: the hammer supplied more relative low-frequency energy, whereas the gun stack gave a slightly longer wavelength, but neither a reliable depth advantage nor a distinct velocity structure was resolved. The proposed individual-to-stack consistency framework, strengthened by manual verification of automated modal picks, provides a reproducible way to prevent source-energy observations from becoming unsupported claims of deeper MASW investigation
375ccf9848e89bf0: The 2020 Mw 7.0 Samos normal-faulting earthquake produced damaging ground shaking and a destructive local tsunami. We construct a three-dimensional kinematic rupture model from a finite-fault inversion and use its shear stress changes to inform two dynamic rupture models. We initialize a non-linear shallow-water tsunami simulation with instantaneous Okada displacement and source one-way linked simulations with evolving seafloor deformation from the kinematic and dynamic rupture models. Fully coupled three-dimensional earthquake-tsunami simulations resolve rupture and elastic, acoustic, and gravity waves together. The coupled sea surface wavefield contains the developing tsunami, dispersive oceanic Rayleigh waves, first-mode ocean acoustic waves, and signals consistent with dispersive Scholte waves. We track crests and troughs over time as the respective means of the most extreme 0.1 percent of positive and negative sea surface height anomalies. For each time-dependent source, following transient seismo-acoustic waves, the one-way linked and fully coupled models agree within 0.10 m on both metrics from 50 to 360 s in water deeper than 100 m. At 6 min, all models share a leading drawdown with trough metrics near -0.5 m, whereas the instantaneous Okada source yields a crest metric of 0.35 m, compared with 0.5–0.6 m for time-dependent sources. Instantaneous sourcing, common in hazard assessment, may therefore underestimate tsunami crests from moderate normal-faulting earthquakes. The preferred dynamic rupture source captures the main tsunami periods at Syros, with larger tide gauge mismatches elsewhere. At Samos, full coupling resolves the early near-source seismo-acoustic wavefield, whereas time-dependent one-way linking provides an efficient estimate of the large-scale tsunami.
34b01f88af53f238: The upper mantle sampled by mid-ocean ridges carries the volatile imprint of past subduction, but the global distribution of hydration through time and how long that imprint survives mixing and melt extraction are poorly known. We investigate the history of mantle hydration by calculating where and when hydration occurred using a plate reconstruction model of subducted water over the past 410 Myr. We compare model results to present-day mantle hydration based on H₂O/Ce in ~1,340 mid-ocean ridge basalt (MORB) glasses from ~1,050 sites. Estimated hydration ages vary by region: ~120 Ma for the Arctic, ~320 Ma for the northern Mid-Atlantic Ridge (NMAR), ~220 Ma for the mid-latitude Mid-Atlantic, and ~380 Ma for the southern Mid-Atlantic (SMAR). Most Pacific ridges show no evidence of hydration. Globally, MORB derived from mantle with a modeled hydration age has a higher median H₂O/Ce than MORB from mantle with no modeled water delivery (249 versus 200). Neither hydration age nor duration affects H2O/Ce in present-day MORB. Agreement between model and data is particularly strong in the North Atlantic and Arctic. Here, hydrated mantle remained largely undisturbed until the post-130 Ma westward migration of North America. Subduction signatures may remain detectable as long as 400 Myr after hydration, well beyond the lifetime of the plate configuration that produced them.
3dc4e5fa383ca25f: Groundwater is the largest accessible store of freshwater on Earth, yet its depletion has been difficult to quantify globally, because satellite gravimetry senses total water storage rather than groundwater alone, the record is coarse and interrupted, and the models used to isolate groundwater underestimate the largest trends. Here, a continuous and physically bounded record of global groundwater storage change was reconstructed for April 2002 to December 2022 at half-degree resolution. Total water storage from the GRACE and GRACE-FO missions was separated from its land-surface components, and a physics-constrained decomposition network learned the groundwater signal as the sum of a trend, a seasonal cycle, and a residual. The trend of every cell was held within the net moisture that the atmosphere can supply, and the mass balance of each river basin was enforced during training, so the learned field could not violate water availability. The reconstruction reproduced withheld observations with a root mean squared error of 6.97 centimeters and a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.69, and against an independent network of monitoring wells it achieved a lower trend error than an independent hydrological model and a data-assimilation product at every aggregation scale tested. Gross groundwater depletion over significantly declining cells was estimated at 358 +/- 12 cubic kilometers per year, while net storage change across all land cells was -36 +/- 18 cubic kilometers per year, equivalent to 0.10 +/- 0.05 millimeters per year of sea-level rise. The associated mass redistribution implies a drift of the Earth's rotational pole of 6.9 centimeters per year toward 68.6 degrees East, within 4.5 degrees of the direction inferred in an earlier study.
b6373af4def2a653: The role of subducted seamounts on slip behavior is debated: they have been proposed to act as seismic asperities, or to favor aseismic slip and rupture arrest. We use numerical simulations and fracture mechanics to investigate how seamounts affect the seismic cycle. Motivated by long‐term subduction models, we assume that seamounts cause a down‐dip region of enhanced compression, and an up‐dip region of reduced compression (“weak patch”). We first consider a shallow section of the megathrust and we identify three seismic cycle regimes: (a) the seamount has no effect on earthquake nucleation or arrest; (b) the seamount's weak patch promotes nucleation of runaway earthquakes; (c) the seamount produces aseismic slip and alternating runaway and confined ruptures. The transition between regimes is controlled by a competition between low normal stresses at the seamount, and high stressing rates down‐dip. Partial ruptures at the seamount are caused by an increase in fracture energy as ruptures propagate out of the weak patch, and they require the normal stress contrast to exceed a critical scale‐dependent threshold. Finally, we consider the entire megathrust and find that partial ruptures at depth can trigger seamount earthquakes and slow transients; however, spontaneous nucleation at the seamounts is rare due to the increased frictional stability with low normal stresses in the weak patch. Our simulations reproduce the variety of slip behavior documented in nature, suggesting that contrasting observations may be due to either variable levels of heterogeneity (i.e., distinct regimes), or to the time‐dependent, supercycle behavior arising from high heterogeneity.
e9e0fe5ede6b2a4e: Geological slip rates on faults are crucial inputs to modern seismic hazard models. This use often involves large compilations of slip rates spanning different data types, qualities, and methods, which may lead to incomplete handling of uncertainties and biases in slip rates. First, seismic hazard models need a slip rate for every potentially hazardous fault, but typically only a fraction of faults will have had offsets directly measured, and slip rates on the remaining faults are inferred qualitatively. Second, when a slip rate is measured from a cumulative fault offset over a small number of earthquakes, natural variability in the earthquake process creates biases and uncertainties in the estimates. Finally, the inclusion of open intervals on either end of the paleoseismic record can bias slip rates lower. These effects are not typically captured in the large slip rate compilations and workflows used by seismic hazard models. Here, we explore how handling these factors more fully impacts the slip rates and uncertainties used in the Aotearoa New Zealand National Seismic Hazard Model. We find that correcting for limited observational timespan has the largest effect on slip rate uncertainties, which on average increase by up to 2.9 times. This effect is largest on faults that have slip rates calculated over short timeframes and low activity rates. Faults with inferred (rather than measured) slip rates also experience a large change in uncertainty, becoming on average 2.7 times wider. For most faults, correcting for open intervals does not change slip rate substantially. However, open intervals remain important to consider on faults with long recurrence intervals and short slip rate timeframes. The work presented here is an initial exploration into the uniform treatment of slip rate in large fault datasets and illustrates the impact these additional sources of uncertainty have on slip rate variability.
7d6a4534bbec98b5: The Slumgullion landslide in Colorado, USA, is a well‐known natural laboratory for studying mass‐wasting processes, owing to its ∼4 km length and sustained movement averaging a couple of centimeters per day over the past ∼300 years. However, key questions remain about how its margins and internal boundaries evolve, whether the headscarp still supplies material, and whether motion is accelerating or slowing over decadal timescales. Here we conducted offset tracking on light detection and ranging (LiDAR)‐derived shaded relief images to resolve three‐dimensional landslide displacements, revealing previously unrecognized secondary mini‐slides close to Slumgullion's margins. Comparing our results to those from previous displacement studies revealed the landslide's long‐term deceleration of motion since 1939. The secondary failures near the landslide margins and at the headscarp confirm continued material supply to the active slide. The Slumgullion landslide remains structurally dynamic with the maximum shear strain rates at ~1 yr −1 . Despite this activity, toe advance has decelerated by ∼36% since the 1990s. The approach provides a transferable framework for mapping three‐dimensional deformation using high‐resolution shaded relief images for landslides and other geohazards.
e54de2196d4fc1d4: Seismic velocity provides key insights into the structure and thermodynamic state of the Earth's mantle. Leveraging the dense broadband coverage of the Transportable Array (TA) in Alaska, we compiled a data set of 67,671 ‐wave differential travel times and 114,205 multi‐frequency differential travel‐time measurements for ‐waves, including arrivals. We independently inverted these data using finite‐frequency sensitivity kernels to produce co‐located three‐dimensional tomographic models of and . By analyzing spatial variations in the ratio, we identify regions where departures from purely thermal behavior may indicate the presence of partial melt. Our models reveal along‐strike variations in the geometry of the Pacific slab and its interaction with the mantle transition zone. We identify an elusive Wrangell slab fragment down to km, which appears to be surrounded by melt that may feed the Wrangell Volcanic Field. Low velocities characterize the Alaskan back‐arc, the Queen Charlotte Fault Zone, and the Seward Peninsula, where intraplate volcanism appears to be connected to transition‐zone structure. Together, these results provide new constraints on subduction dynamics and the potential distribution of mantle melt beneath Alaska.
0f6439c5099fca03: Seismicity exhibits complex spatiotemporal patterns that are critical for hazard assessment. Using the Chinese mainland earthquake catalog (1970–2025), we analyze seismicity parameters across 20 seismic belts. After estimating the completeness magnitude ( M c ) for each belt, we apply nearest-neighbor distance declustering and calculate b -value and spatial fractal dimension ( D c ) before and after declustering using the maximum likelihood and correlation integral methods. We examine their spatial distributions and relationships with heat flow and maximum shear strain rate. Declustering increases D c -value (from 1.30 to 1.65) while decreasing a - and b -values, confirming that aftershock removal diffuses spatial patterns and reduces the proportion of small events. The relationship between b -value and D c -value varies regionally: negative in the Tibetan seismic region, positive in the South China seismic region and Xinjiang seismic region, and weakly negative in the North China seismic region. Heat flow modulates seismicity parameters in a consistent manner. The b -value is positively correlated with heat flow both before and after declustering, whereas the D c -value is negatively correlated with heat flow before declustering but not after. These results suggest that thermal weakening promotes microcracking, raising the b -value, and facilitates strain localization along major faults, lowering the D c -value. The D c -value and maximum shear strain rate relationship is positive in eastern extensional regions and negative in western compressional regions, reflecting contrasting strain energy partitioning mechanisms. These findings provide quantitative constraints on deep controls of seismicity complexity and offer new criteria for seismic hazard assessment.
9e6060eec29d907e: Inter-sensor coherence loss carries information about the wavefield that conventional array processing discards. The array-covariance matrix is modelled using a mixture of energy distributions over slowness with analytical characteristic functions, e.g., skew-normal and angular-harmonic distributions, and inverted using variational Bayesian inference. The posterior supports uncertainty quantification, experimental design, model comparison and hypothesis testing. For a synthetic hydroacoustic T-phase, information is increased by an additional sensor and decreased by noise; the data favour a distributed source over a point source. For an observed thermospheric infrasound return, energy is skewed back towards the source. The method is implemented in the software Topophone2.
b2f9fa6409551795: Multiparameter elastic full-waveform inversion (EFWI) provides a powerful means of reconstructing subsurface elastic properties, but its practical application remains challenging because of strong nonlinearity, parameter crosstalk, and the different sensitivities of seismic data to individual elastic parameters. We develop a robust implicit neural representation (INR) framework for multiparameter EFWI, using continuous neural representations to parameterize the subsurface model and provide an effective model-space constraint during inversion. Within this framework, we systematically investigate different elastic parameterizations and demonstrate that parameterization plays a critical role in controlling parameter coupling and inversion stability. Among the tested formulations, combining P-wave velocity (Vp), P-wave impedance (Ip), and the Vs/Vp ratio provides the most robust overall performance, yielding improved parameter separation and more reliable reconstruction of elastic properties. We evaluate the proposed approach on the Marmousi and Overthrust models under increasingly challenging inversion conditions and further apply it to the field Volve ocean-bottom-node dataset. Both synthetic and field-data results demonstrate that the INR-based formulation, together with the Vp-Ip-Vs/Vp parameterization, improves inversion stability, suppresses parameter cross-talk and inversion artifacts, and produces geologically coherent multiparameter models. These results highlight the importance of jointly considering model representation and physical parameterization in multiparameter EFWI and demonstrate the potential of robust INR-based inversion for complex synthetic and field seismic applications.
499c0c10d5ec9bf6: When heat and solute both destabilise a rapidly rotating fluid, do their buoyancies add? Codensity models assume so, giving a straight onset diagonal; spherical shells show curved and kinked thresholds. We study the Busse--Simitev rotating annulus, whose normal modes obey an exact complex cubic dispersion relation. Combining the Bilharz criterion with the neutral-curve envelope yields, in the rapid-rotation limit, an explicit swallowtail wave front, in Arnold's sense, that bends the codensity diagonal into smooth and then kinked thresholds as the diffusivity ratio decreases. Its cusp edges lie inside the unstable domain and its exposed kink ends at the swallowtail singularity; these are singularities of wave-number selection, without coalescence of temporal eigenvalues, and the swallowtail diffusivity ratio has analytical small- and large-Prandtl-number limits. At a kink, broad, fast thermal and narrow, slow compositional Rossby waves become neutral together; hidden arcs mark the birth and merger of unstable wave-number bands. The same geometry enters nonlinear selection: mean-scalar feedback factors through neutral-arc normals and scalar responses, so the mean-profile coexistence margin vanishes with the kink angle as the waves merge. Complete cubic coefficients predict robust coexistence at a reference corner and a narrow bistable interval near merger. Exact finite-rotation corners and periodic-cell simulations confirm the coexisting waves and their invasion thresholds.
dc6a5dcd38b87b1c: Subsurface flow systems often involve hierarchical geological uncertainty, meaning both higher-level metaparameters and cell-by-cell properties are uncertain. This leads to challenges for data assimilation because both sets of parameters must be estimated. In this work we develop an adaptive-tempered sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) procedure for joint Bayesian estimation of these quantities. The method uses noncentered geological parameterizations, with geomodel realizations represented by metaparameters and Gaussian latent variables that are independent under the prior. Adaptive likelihood tempering, importance weighting, resampling, and blockwise Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) mutation are applied at each iteration. Flow surrogates are used for all function evaluations. The hierarchical SMC procedure is further extended to treat successive data assimilation. In this case, existing posterior particles are updated in a manner that accounts for correlations in surrogate model errors across observation batches. We consider two distinct 3D systems with hierarchical uncertainty. The first is a faulted carbon storage system containing three stacked aquifers and two extensive faults. Principal component analysis is used to represent target-aquifer heterogeneity, while geological metaparameters characterize uncertain aquifer and fault properties. The second is a channelized oil-water system containing three facies with uncertain properties. A latent diffusion model represents variability in channel geometry and facies realizations. For the four synthetic true models considered, SMC posterior metaparameter distributions and flow predictions agree closely with reference MCMC results. SMC, however, requires fewer function evaluations and provides speedups of 2.5--7.0 for single-stage data assimilation. Even greater speedups are achieved with multiple GPUs.
53e404053a5fd48c: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) logging provides a nondestructive method for characterizing pore structure and fluid distribution in reservoir rocks. Conventional permeability models, such as the Schlumberger-Doll Research (SDR) and Timur-Coates (TC) equations, have been widely used to estimate permeability from NMR T2 relaxation time distributions. However, these empirical models require calibration against core-measured permeability, and their fitted coefficients often vary substantially across lithologies and pore systems. In this study, we formulate and evaluate an NMR-informed implementation of a physics-based permeability relationship derived from critical path analysis (CPA) by linking the characteristic pore length scale to the dominant NMR relaxation time. We estimate permeability (k) using NMR T2 distributions and electrical formation factor (F) for 14 carbonate rock samples collected from the Morro do Chaves Formation in the Sergipe-Alagoas Basin, Brazil. We compare the predictive performance of this formulation with that of calibrated SDR and TC models. The proposed CPA-NMR formulation achieves a root mean squared logarithmic error (RMSLE) of 0.56 without calibration against measured permeability from the investigated formation. These findings indicate the potential of combining NMR relaxation measurements with electrical formation factor for physics-based permeability estimation. Further evaluation using independent datasets is needed to assess applicability across formations and lithologies.
977e31ec9a858d55: Estimating intrinsic permeability from nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) logs is difficult in heterogeneous carbonates because a single calibration may not represent distinct pore systems. We evaluated whether flow-zone-indicator (FZI)-based rock typing improves empirical calibration of the modified Schlumberger-Doll Research (SDR) model in the Arbuckle Group, Kansas. The analysis used 470 depth-matched core-permeability and NMR measurements from the Wellington and Cutter wells. FZI calculated from measured permeability and NMR-derived porosity was grouped using K-means clustering. Six clusters were identified, but one singleton cluster was excluded, leaving five rock types for SDR calibration. Relative to the global model (without clustering), rock-type-specific calibration reduced testing root mean square log-transformed error (RMSLE) from 1.215 to 0.240-0.427 and increased coefficient of determination (CD) from -0.106 to 0.578-0.924. The fitted porosity exponents ranged from 0.053 to 0.521, indicating that porosity provided limited additional information in some rock types and that the SDR parameters should be treated as empirical calibration quantities. Because measured permeability was used to calculate the FZI before the within-cluster splits, these results represent conditional performance for samples with known FZI membership, not blind permeability prediction. Field implementation will require a permeability-independent method for assigning rock types.
2f300bb63f31cb64: The Rongxian shale gas field in the southern Sichuan basin has experienced increasing induced seismicity, with frequent earthquakes adversely impacting local communities and even causing casualties. In this study, we investigate the short-distance attenuation characteristics of strong ground motions from induced earthquakes with local magnitudes (ML) ranging from 2.0 to 3.9, using 7249 high-quality recordings selected from a total of 11,161 accelerograms captured by a dense network of 52 microelectromechanical systems accelerometers. To ensure data reliability, we evaluate a deep-learning denoising technique for the acceleration records and apply a magnitude-dependent usable-period cutoff. Our analysis reveals that the induced earthquakes in Rongxian exhibit regional attenuation and source-scaling features distinct from those of the selected reference ground-motion models (GMMs). Specifically, the BSSA14 model (Boore, Stewart, et al., 2014), developed within the Next Generation Attenuation-West2 project, shows distance-dependent residual trends for peak ground acceleration (PGA) and selected short-period intensity measures, whereas the induced-seismicity NAA18 model (Novakovic et al., 2018) provides a more compatible reference but retains period- and magnitude-dependent residuals. To address these discrepancies, we developed a region-specific GMM using nonlinear mixed-effects regression. Within the observed moment magnitude range (Mw 1.8–3.7), the model successfully reproduces the main attenuation and source-scaling behavior of horizontal RotD50 PGA, peak ground velocity, and spectral accelerations with residuals generally centered near zero. For larger-magnitude scenarios, the GMM smoothly transitions from the empirically calibrated model to relative magnitude–distance scaling derived from regional stochastic simulations, with extrapolated predictions explicitly distinguished from the empirical calibration range. These findings highlight the ground-motion characteristics of induced seismicity in the Rongxian shale-gas region and provide a regional ground-motion basis for rapidly estimating short-distance shaking and the spatial extent of felt or affected areas, including the consideration of selected source-model epistemic uncertainty beyond the observed magnitude range.
36b54996cdad47e2: Accurately characterizing fault geometry is fundamental to understanding earthquake processes, including stress transfer and rupture dynamics, as well as for assessing seismic hazard. Recent advances in earthquake detection, phase picking, and relocation have produced high-resolution hypocenter catalogs that can be viewed as three-dimensional point clouds recording the geometry of active fault systems. Extracting individual fault structures from these catalogs remains challenging due to complex fault geometries and heterogeneous seismicity distributions. Here, we present FaultNet, a deep learning framework that formulates fault extraction from earthquake hypocenters as a three-dimensional semantic segmentation problem. Built upon PointNet++, the denoising and feature-learning models in FaultNet hierarchically process point coordinates to learn feature embeddings and are trained on synthetic earthquake catalogs. These feature embeddings are used to identify individual fault clusters and reconstruct continuous three-dimensional fault surfaces. We apply FaultNet to three catalogs representing induced seismicity, mainshock-aftershock sequences, and volcanic seismicity. Across these diverse settings, the method successfully resolves coherent fault structures, including intersecting and segmented faults. The reconstructs fault geometries perform well across our evaluation metrics and are consistent with independent geological and seismological observations. Our results demonstrate that deep learning provides an effective and generalizable approach for reconstructing complex fault systems directly from earthquake hypocenter distributions.
322a8d54ba2acd1f: In‐dip double subduction systems (IDDS) represent the most common variety of complex subduction configurations in the modern plate tectonic settings. Previous studies have described the IDDS evolution, but mostly from kinematic models; their spontaneous growth (dynamic) behavior, particularly in asymmetric modes remained virtually unexplored. Using scaled laboratory experiments and thermomechanical model simulations, we investigate the primary mechanisms in the dynamic evolution of IDDS systems and demonstrate how amplification of their incipient initial geometrical inequality results in asymmetric configurations depending on the inter‐trench separation ( λ ). Quantitative analyses of slab and trench motion rates, mantle flow patterns, and slab penetration depths are also presented to illustrate the impact of λ on the IDDS slab dynamics. This study provides a full spectrum of IDDS configurations with varying asymmetry as a function of λ . λ ≥ 2,500 km gives rise to nearly non‐interacting, symmetric slab dynamics, which become strongly asymmetric due to intense inter‐slab interactions as λ λ results in a systematic transformation of the mantle flow patterns beneath the overriding plate. Finally, the article presents three currently active IDDS systems of varying λ : the Manila‐Philippine, the Vanuatu and Vitiaz‐Tonga, and the Central America‐Antilles systems, to assess the applicability of our model findings.
74199deed55ef32f: This study investigates how elastic wave propagation effects influence on apparent seismic attenuation. Our goal is to improve the reliability and credibility of teleseismic body-wave attenuation measurements by separating components that are extrinsic (due to focusing) from intrinsic (due to anelasticity). We first use simple idealized models of low velocity, high attenuating anomalies to assess the effects of aspect ratio and size on apparent attenuation. Using SPECFEM2D to calculate synthetic waveforms, we predict seismically observable parameters with methods identical to observational data. Since anelasticity can be turned on or off within our simulations, we can isolate and observe purely elastic wave propagation effects. We find that elastic focusing effects can contribute >50% to apparent differential attenuation (Δt*) signals. With increasing diameter and aspect ratio, the fraction of total attenuation that is extrinsic decreases overall. We validate a quantitative metric for the amount of elastic focusing to serve as a potential quality control step for real-world data. This metric relies on divergence between amplitude and phase spectra for stations manifesting strong extrinsic attenuation effects. As a synthetic case study, we consider mid-ocean ridges (MORs), since seismic waves may be particularly prone to focusing effects (owing to their geometry and velocity contrasts) and where isolating intrinsic attenuation could provide powerful constraints on Earth processes and structure. To do this we utilize outputs from sophisticated geodynamic models of MORs. We find that elastic focusing from low velocity structures can contribute up to 0.2 seconds of Δt* near the ridge axis and elsewhere. Comparing MOR models from simulations with varying volatile content and spreading rate, we find that differences in simulated Δt* and differential travel time (ΔT) are small, and likely below observational noise. This suggests caution in using these data to identify MORs’ thermodynamic state, and calls for simultaneous interpretation of multiple geophysical datasets. We discuss implications for body-wave attenuation measurements as well as the potential impacts of approximations in the SPECFEM forward modeling.
1aab5c503cfedcf2: Summary Identifying and characterizing seismic arrivals in seismic waveforms is fundamental to imaging Earth and planetary interiors. For example, robust estimates of arrival time and slowness enable identification of seismic phases and their origins, while polarization characteristics provide additional constraints on wave type and can reveal the effects of anisotropy, scattering, and local heterogeneity. In this study, we present a transdimensional Bayesian framework that jointly infers the number of seismic arrivals and their attributes, including arrival time, slowness, amplitude, and polarization, from three-component seismograms recorded at one or more seismic stations. By representing the waveform as a superposition of an unknown number of parameterized arrivals and their phase attributes, our approach samples posterior distributions that provide a probabilistic description of seismic signals and their uncertainties. Applications to synthetic and real data demonstrate that the framework successfully identifies multiple phases, including direct, reflected, and core-sensitive arrivals, and recovers their properties in agreement with theoretical predictions. When projected into the time-slowness domain, the posterior distributions provide a probabilistic analog to conventional vespagrams, offering improved interpretability and explicit uncertainty quantification without requiring thresholding for phase detection. Tests on synthetic SKS waveforms further show that the method recovers expected polarization behavior associated with shear-wave splitting. The framework is well suited for analyzing complex and noisy datasets, including settings with limited observational constraints. Its flexibility enables application to both array and single-station configurations, making it particularly useful for planetary seismology.
b0a1b61f5ced83f2: Summary Full Dispersion Spectrum Inversion (FDSI) reconstructs near-surface velocity structures by directly minimizing the misfit of energy spectra in the dispersion domain. By avoiding the error-prone process of dispersion-curve picking, it enables the joint use of multi-mode information for high-resolution imaging. Different objective functions offer complementary advantages in initial-model robustness and reconstruction resolution, often motivating staged inversion strategies.
